days.title: Python Architecture, Bytecode & Variables
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: Runtimes, AST Compilation, PVM Stack, Pointer Memory, Identity, Interning, and PEP 8
days.overview: Deep dive into Python’s internal execution model across 7 structured topics. Discover how source code becomes bytecode, how the Python Virtual Machine operates, and how variables bind to memory addresses.

topics.title: CPython vs Alternative Runtimes
explanation: Python is a language specification; CPython is its default, reference implementation written in C.

Alternative implementations exist for specific performance and interoperability needs: PyPy uses a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler to accelerate long-running numerical code by 4-7x; Jython compiles Python code directly into Java JVM bytecode; and IronPython targets the Microsoft .NET CLR.
CPython remains the gold standard because of its complete compatibility with C/C++ extensions, NumPy, and PyTorch.
keyRules: CPython is the reference interpreter written in standard C
PyPy provides a tracing JIT compiler for high CPU throughput
C-extensions (CFFI, Cython) are best supported on CPython

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Python Runtime Details
codeSnippet.description: Check active Python implementation and version attributes.
codeSnippet.code:
import sys
import platform

print("Runtime Implementation:", platform.python_implementation())
print("Python Version:", platform.python_version())
print("Bytecode Magic Number:", sys.byteorder)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Runtime Implementation: CPython
Python Version: 3.12.x
Bytecode Magic Number: little

topics.title: The Compilation Pipeline: Source -> AST -> Bytecode
explanation: Python is not a purely interpreted language; it is a compiled-bytecode interpreted language.
When you execute a .py file, CPython first tokenizes the text characters into syntactic lexemes, constructs a concrete parse tree, and transforms it into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

The Python compiler then generates compact 2-byte bytecode instructions (opcodes and arguments). Bytecode is cached on disk inside __pycache__ as .pyc files with a 32-bit timestamp to bypass recompilation on subsequent runs if source has not changed.
keyRules: Tokenization -> AST Parsing -> Bytecode Generation -> Execution
.pyc cache files avoid redundant parsing when source is unchanged
You can inspect AST using the standard library "ast" module

codeSnippet.title: Disassembling Python Bytecode Opcodes
codeSnippet.description: Use the standard "dis" module to inspect raw bytecode instructions.
codeSnippet.code:
import dis

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# Disassemble the function into bytecode instructions
print("Disassembly of add(a, b):")
dis.dis(add)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Disassembly of add(a, b):
  2           0 LOAD_FAST                0 (a)
              2 LOAD_FAST                1 (b)
              4 BINARY_ADD
              6 RETURN_VALUE

topics.title: The Python Virtual Machine (PVM) Stack Engine
explanation: The PVM is a stack-based evaluation engine, unlike hardware x86 or ARM CPUs which are register-based.

For every function call, the PVM pushes a new PyFrameObject onto the call stack. The frame contains an evaluation stack for temporary operands, a local variable array, and references to global namespaces.
When executing add(5, 10), the PVM pushes 5, pushes 10, executes BINARY_ADD which pops both operands, adds them, and pushes 15 onto the evaluation stack, followed by RETURN_VALUE.
keyRules: PVM uses an evaluation stack for intermediate calculations
Each function call allocates an isolated PyFrameObject
Frames track execution instruction pointers (f_lasti)

codeSnippet.title: Stack Frame Execution Demonstration
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating how evaluation stack values flow in a function.
codeSnippet.code:
def calculate_hypotenuse(a, b):
    # Pushes a*a, pushes b*b, adds, and takes square root
    return (a ** 2 + b ** 2) ** 0.5

print("Hypotenuse of 3 and 4:", calculate_hypotenuse(3, 4))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Hypotenuse of 3 and 4: 5.0

topics.title: Variables as Heap Object Pointers
explanation: In languages like C or Go, "int x = 10" reserves 4 bytes directly in memory. In Python, variables are NEVER values; they are named references (pointers) bound to objects in the heap.
When you write "x = [1, 2, 3]", CPython allocates a list object in heap memory, and binds the name "x" in the local namespace dictionary to point to that heap address.
Assigning "y = x" does not copy the list! It merely creates a second pointer "y" pointing to the exact same list object.
keyRules: Variables are labels pointing to heap-allocated objects
Assignment (=) binds a name to an object address
Multiple names can point to the same object (aliasing)
topics.pitfall: Mutating an aliased mutable object affects all variable references pointing to it.

codeSnippet.title: Variable Pointer Aliasing vs Value Copying
codeSnippet.description: Observe how multiple pointers mutate the same heap instance.
codeSnippet.code:
original_list = [10, 20, 30]
aliased_pointer = original_list

aliased_pointer.append(99)
print("Did original list mutate?", original_list)
print("Are pointers pointing to same object?", original_list is aliased_pointer)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Did original list mutate? [10, 20, 30, 99]
Are pointers pointing to same object? True

topics.title: Object Identity vs Value Equality (id, is, ==)
explanation: Python provides two distinct ways to compare data: Value Equality (==) and Identity Equality (is).
"==" invokes the __eq__() dunder method to check whether two objects have equivalent contents or semantics.
"is" compares the 64-bit memory addresses directly: id(a) == id(b). It tests whether two references point to the exact same physical object in memory.
keyRules: Use "is" when checking singleton sentinels like "x is None" or "x is False"
Use "==" when comparing numerical values, strings, lists, or dictionaries
id(obj) returns the unique memory address integer of the object

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Memory Addresses & Identity
codeSnippet.description: Verify the difference between value equality and pointer identity.
codeSnippet.code:
list_a = [1, 2, 3]
list_b = [1, 2, 3]

print("Value equality (list_a == list_b):", list_a == list_b)
print("Identity reference (list_a is list_b):", list_a is list_b)
print("Memory ID of list_a:", id(list_a))
print("Memory ID of list_b:", id(list_b))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Value equality (list_a == list_b): True
Identity reference (list_a is list_b): False
Memory ID of list_a: ...
Memory ID of list_b: ...

topics.title: Small Integer Interning & String Caching
explanation: To optimize memory and execution speed, CPython pre-allocates an array of singleton integer objects for all numbers from -5 to 256 inclusive at interpreter startup.
Whenever your code uses an integer in this range (e.g. x = 200; y = 200), Python binds both variables to the pre-existing singleton in the intern pool.
Short alphanumeric strings without spaces are also interned automatically by CPython via the string interning table.
keyRules: Integers between -5 and 256 are global singletons in CPython
Numbers outside this range allocate fresh objects during assignment
Never rely on interning for business logic comparisons; always use ==

codeSnippet.title: Small Integer Interning Boundary Test
codeSnippet.description: Observe identity within the -5 to 256 caching range.
codeSnippet.code:
a = 256
b = 256
print("256 is 256 (within intern pool)?", a is b)

c = 257
d = 257
print("257 == 257 (value):", c == d)
print("257 is 257 (outside intern pool)?", c is d)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
256 is 256 (within intern pool)? True
257 == 257 (value): True
257 is 257 (outside intern pool)? False

topics.title: PEP 8 Style Guide, Naming & Pythonic Conventions
explanation: PEP 8 is the official Python Style Guide authored by Guido van Rossum. Writing idiomatic Python means adhering to standard naming conventions.
Variables, functions, and modules use snake_case: total_amount, calculate_tax().
Classes use PascalCase: BankAccount, TransactionLogger.
Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MAX_CONNECTIONS, TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
Single underscore prefix (_private) signals internal use; double underscore (__mangled) triggers class name mangling.
keyRules: snake_case for functions and variables
PascalCase for class names
UPPER_CASE for module-level constants
Indentation must be strictly 4 spaces per nesting level (never tabs)

codeSnippet.title: Idiomatic PEP 8 Class and Variable Structure
codeSnippet.description: A clean implementation demonstrating PEP 8 conventions.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Server Endpoint: http://localhost:3000

interactiveDiagram.title: Memory Reference & Heap Allocation Model
interactiveDiagram.caption: Visualizing variable labels binding to integer objects in the heap memory pool.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 1 Challenge: Variable Swapping & Reference Tracking
instructions: Create two variables, a = 100 and b = 200.
Swap them using Python’s idiomatic tuple unpacking without a temporary variable.
Print both variables and verify their values.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
a = 100
b = 200
# Swap a and b in one line:

print("a:", a, "b:", b)
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
a = 100
b = 200
a, b = b, a
print("a:", a, "b:", b)
hints: In Python, tuple packing allows a, b = b, a.

keyTakeaways: CPython compiles code into bytecode before PVM stack execution
Variables are references to heap objects, not memory boxes
Use "==" for values and "is" for identity references
CPython caches small integers between -5 and 256
Adhere to PEP 8 snake_case for functions and PascalCase for classes

days.title: Numeric Types, Precision & Dynamic Type Casting
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: Arbitrary Ints, IEEE-754 Floats, Decimal Module, Complex Numbers, Booleans, Type Casting, and Type Checking
days.overview: Explore Python’s numerical hierarchy across 7 detailed topics. Master arbitrary-precision integers, understand why float calculations lose precision, and learn how to use Decimal for financial calculations.

topics.title: Arbitrary-Precision Integers in Python 3
explanation: In C, C++, or Java, an integer overflows when exceeding 32 bits (2,147,483,647) or 64 bits. Python 3 integers have arbitrary precision (often called BigInt).
CPython represents an integer as a PyLongObject containing an array of 30-bit "digits". As a number grows, Python dynamically allocates more digits, constrained only by available system RAM.
keyRules: Python 3 integers never overflow
Large integer arithmetic switches to Karatsuba and Toom-Cook multiplication algorithms

codeSnippet.title: Massive Arbitrary Precision Integer Math
codeSnippet.description: Compute 2^100 and factorial without integer overflow.
codeSnippet.code:
big_num = 2 ** 100
print("2^100 =", big_num)
print("Number of decimal digits in 2^100:", len(str(big_num)))

topics.title: IEEE-754 Floating-Point Mechanics & Precision Quirks
explanation: Python floats are 64-bit double-precision IEEE-754 numbers (53 bits significand, 11 bits exponent, 1 sign bit).
Because computers use base-2 binary, fractions like 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented with exact precision, causing rounding artifacts like 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.
keyRules: Floats have ~15-17 significant decimal digits of precision
Never compare floats using direct "=="; use round() or math.isclose()

codeSnippet.title: Floating-Point Epsilon & Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Safely comparing floating-point numbers with tolerance.
codeSnippet.code:
val = 0.1 + 0.2
print("0.1 + 0.2 raw float:", val)
print("Direct equality == 0.3?", val == 0.3)
print("Rounded equality:", round(val, 2) == 0.3)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
0.1 + 0.2 raw float: 0.30000000000000004
Direct equality == 0.3? False
Rounded equality: True

topics.title: Exact Financial Math with the Decimal Module
explanation: For financial software, banking, and accounting, floating point rounding errors are unacceptable. Python provides the "decimal" module implementing the IEEE 854 decimal floating-point specification.
Decimal allows user-specified precision (default 28 digits) and deterministic rounding modes (ROUND_HALF_UP, ROUND_FLOOR).
keyRules: Always initialize Decimal with strings, e.g. Decimal("0.1"), NOT Decimal(0.1)
Decimal objects are immutable

codeSnippet.title: Financial Calculations with Decimal
codeSnippet.description: Exact decimal arithmetic for monetary transactions.
codeSnippet.code:
price = 19.99
tax_rate = 0.0825
total = round(price * (1 + tax_rate), 2)
print("Calculated invoice total: $", total)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Calculated invoice total: $ 21.64

topics.title: Complex Numbers in Python Builtins
explanation: Python has native support for complex numbers without external libraries using the "j" or "J" suffix for the imaginary component: z = 3 + 4j.
Complex numbers feature built-in .real, .imag attributes, and .conjugate() methods, widely used in electrical engineering, physics, and signal processing.
keyRules: Imaginary unit is denoted by "j" or "J"
z.real returns real part, z.imag returns imaginary part

codeSnippet.title: Native Complex Number Arithmetic
codeSnippet.description: Manipulating complex numbers and computing magnitudes.
codeSnippet.code:
z1 = 3 + 4j
z2 = 1 - 2j

print("z1 + z2 =", z1 + z2)
print("Real component of z1:", z1.real)
print("Imaginary component of z1:", z1.imag)
print("Magnitude (abs):", abs(z1))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
z1 + z2 = (4+2j)
Real component of z1: 3.0
Imaginary component of z1: 4.0
Magnitude (abs): 5.0

topics.title: Booleans as Subclasses of Integers
explanation: In Python, "bool" is an explicit subclass of "int". True is 1, and False is 0.
This means booleans can participate in arithmetic calculations, which is frequently used in counting predicates like sum(x > 0 for x in data).
keyRules: issubclass(bool, int) is True
True == 1 and False == 0

codeSnippet.title: Boolean Numerical Arithmetic
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating booleans behaving as integer values.
codeSnippet.code:
print("True + True =", True + True)
print("10 * False =", 10 * False)

flags = [True, False, True, True, False]
print("Count of True flags (using sum):", sum(flags))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
True + True = 2
10 * False = 0
Count of True flags (using sum): 3

topics.title: Explicit Type Casting & Conversion Rules
explanation: Python does not automatically coerce incompatible types (e.g. "5" + 5 raises a TypeError). You must perform explicit type casting.
int(x, base=10) can parse strings in different bases: int("1010", 2) evaluates to 10; int("FF", 16) evaluates to 255.
keyRules: int("1010", 2) parses binary strings
int("1A", 16) parses hexadecimal strings
float() parses scientific notation like float("1e-4")

codeSnippet.title: Multi-Base Number Conversion
codeSnippet.description: Parsing numbers from binary, octal, and hex string representations.
codeSnippet.code:
binary_val = int("1101", 2)
hex_val = int("FF", 16)
sci_val = float("2.5e3")

print("Parsed binary '1101':", binary_val)
print("Parsed hex 'FF':", hex_val)
print("Parsed scientific '2.5e3':", sci_val)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Parsed binary '1101': 13
Parsed hex 'FF': 255
Parsed scientific '2.5e3': 2500.0

topics.title: Dynamic Typing, Duck Typing & isinstance()
explanation: Python is dynamically typed: variable types are checked at runtime, not compile time. A variable name can point to an int, then later point to a string.
Python embraces "Duck Typing": "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck." Methods are called based on capabilities rather than nominal inheritance.
When type verification is necessary, prefer isinstance(obj, type) over type(obj) == type, because isinstance() supports inheritance hierarchies.
keyRules: Duck typing values interface behavior over nominal class names
Always use isinstance(obj, ClassName) to support subclasses

codeSnippet.title: Type Inspection with isinstance()
codeSnippet.description: Checking types safely with isinstance() tuples.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Numeric value: 84
Numeric value: 6.28

practiceChallenge.title: Day 2 Challenge: Base-16 Checksum Calculator
instructions: Given hex string values "A1", "0B", "3C", convert them to integers.
Sum them and print the total in decimal and hexadecimal using hex().
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
hex_strings = ["A1", "0B", "3C"]
# Convert each to int using base 16 and sum them
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
hex_strings = ["A1", "0B", "3C"]
total = sum(int(h, 16) for h in hex_strings)
print("Sum in decimal:", total)
print("Sum in hex:", hex(total))
hints: Use int(h, 16) to parse hexadecimal strings.

keyTakeaways: Integers expand to arbitrary precision without overflow
Float representations follow 64-bit IEEE-754 precision limits
Booleans are integer values 1 and 0 in Python
Use isinstance() rather than type() to support subclass inheritance

days.title: Strings Mastery: Immutability, Slicing & F-Strings
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: Immutability, Indexing, Slicing Grid, Negative Strides, String Methods, F-Strings, and UTF-8 Bytes
days.overview: Strings are ubiquitous in software engineering. Master string memory allocation, slicing intervals, bidirectional strides, string transformations, advanced format specifiers, and byte encodings across 7 topics.

topics.title: String Immutability & Memory Allocation
explanation: Strings in Python are strictly immutable sequences of Unicode code points. Once created, a string’s character buffer can never be altered in-place.
Modifications like s.replace() or s.upper() allocate brand new string objects in heap memory.
String concatenation in loops (s += "x") creates quadratic O(n^2) memory reallocation; always collect fragments in a list and use "".join(fragments) for linear O(n) performance.
keyRules: Strings are immutable; mutating operations return new string instances
Use "".join(list_of_strings) instead of repeated "+=" in loops

codeSnippet.title: Efficient String Joining vs Naive Concatenation
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating idiomatic list joining for high performance.
codeSnippet.code:
words = ["Clean", "Python", "Architecture"]
# Idiomatic string joining
sentence = " ".join(words)
print("Joined sentence:", sentence)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Joined sentence: Clean Python Architecture

topics.title: The Bidirectional Indexing Grid
explanation: Python supports dual indexing: positive indices count from the front starting at 0, while negative indices count from the back starting at -1.
For string "PYTHON", positive indices are 0 to 5, while negative indices are -6 to -1. Accessing an index outside this range raises IndexError.
keyRules: s[0] is the first character; s[-1] is the last character
Out-of-range indexing raises IndexError

codeSnippet.title: Bidirectional Index Access
codeSnippet.description: Comparing positive and negative string indexing.
codeSnippet.code:
lang = "PYTHON"
print("First char (lang[0]):", lang[0])
print("Last char (lang[-1]):", lang[-1])
print("Second-to-last (lang[-2]):", lang[-2])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
First char (lang[0]): P
Last char (lang[-1]): N
Second-to-last (lang[-2]): O

topics.title: The Extended Slicing Syntax: [start:stop:step]
explanation: Slicing extracts a contiguous sub-sequence using [start:stop:step]. "start" is inclusive, while "stop" is exclusive.
Unlike single-index lookups, slicing never raises IndexError if bounds exceed the string length; Python automatically clamps indices to the string boundaries.
keyRules: Half-open interval [start, stop) includes start but excludes stop
Slicing out of bounds safely clamps without throwing errors

codeSnippet.title: Safe Slicing Clamping and Bounds
codeSnippet.description: Extracting substrings using half-open intervals.
codeSnippet.code:
text = "SoftwareEngineer"
print("First 8 chars text[:8]:", text[:8])
print("Middle slice text[8:16]:", text[8:16])
print("Overshot slice text[8:100]:", text[8:100])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
First 8 chars text[:8]: Software
Middle slice text[8:16]: Engineer
Overshot slice text[8:100]: Engineer

topics.title: Negative Strides & Sequence Reversal Mechanics
explanation: When "step" is negative, slicing iterates backwards from end to start.
s[::-1] is the idiomatic Python idiom to reverse any sequence (strings, lists, tuples) in a single expression.
s[::2] selects every second character (stride of 2).
keyRules: s[::-1] reverses sequences with O(n) time and O(n) memory
Negative step requires start > stop when explicit indices are supplied

codeSnippet.title: Negative Strides & Reversal
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating backward strides and stride sampling.
codeSnippet.code:
phrase = "racecar"
print("Is 'racecar' a palindrome?", phrase == phrase[::-1])

alphabet = "abcdefg"
print("Every second letter:", alphabet[::2])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Is 'racecar' a palindrome? True
Every second letter: aceg

topics.title: Essential String Methods: Transformations & Inspection
explanation: Python strings provide built-in methods for inspection and cleaning.
Splitting: .split(sep) divides text into a list. .rsplit(sep, maxsplit) splits from the right.
Cleaning: .strip(), .lstrip(), .rstrip() remove whitespace or specific characters.
Predicates: .isalpha(), .isdigit(), .isalnum(), .startswith(), .endswith() return boolean checks.
keyRules: .split() with no arguments splits on arbitrary contiguous whitespace and strips empty tokens
.strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace by default

codeSnippet.title: String Method Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Cleaning and sanitizing user text data.
codeSnippet.code:
raw_user_input = "   admin@enterprise.org  \n"
clean_email = raw_user_input.strip().lower()

print("Cleaned email:", clean_email)
print("Is enterprise domain?", clean_email.endswith("@enterprise.org"))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Cleaned email: admin@enterprise.org
Is enterprise domain? True

topics.title: Advanced F-Strings: Alignments, Padding & Precision Formats
explanation: Formatted string literals (f-strings) introduced in Python 3.6 evaluate expressions at runtime with high performance.
Format specifiers allow precise formatting: {value:.2f} formats float to 2 decimal places; {name:>15} right-aligns in 15 characters; {count:05d} zero-pads to 5 digits.
Python 3.8+ introduced the self-documenting equal sign: f"{x=}" prints "x=10".
keyRules: f"{val:.2f}" formats floating point precision
f"{val:>10}" right aligns; f"{val:<10}" left aligns; f"{val:^10}" centers
f"{var=}" is invaluable for rapid debugging output

codeSnippet.title: F-String Alignment and Padding Matrix
codeSnippet.description: Format tabular numbers and alignment with f-strings.
codeSnippet.code:
item = "Processor"
price = 349.954
stock = 8

print(f"| {item:<12} | ${price:>8.2f} | Qty: {stock:03d} |")
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: | Processor    | $  349.95 | Qty: 008 |

topics.title: Unicode Code Points, UTF-8 & Raw Byte Sequences
explanation: Python 3 strings are Unicode text. Memory objects store characters as abstract code points (e.g. ord("A") == 65; chr(65) == "A").
When transmitting data over networks or disk, strings must be encoded to raw binary bytes using UTF-8: s.encode("utf-8").
Bytes objects (b"hello") represent raw 8-bit octets and must be decoded back to strings using b.decode("utf-8").
keyRules: str.encode("utf-8") -> bytes
bytes.decode("utf-8") -> str
ord(char) returns integer Unicode code point; chr(int) returns character

codeSnippet.title: Encoding Text to UTF-8 Bytes
codeSnippet.description: Converting text to bytes and inspecting byte lengths.
codeSnippet.code:
text = "Python"
raw_bytes = text.encode("utf-8")
print("Bytes representation:", raw_bytes)
print("Decoded back:", raw_bytes.decode("utf-8"))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Bytes representation: b'Python'
Decoded back: Python

practiceChallenge.title: Day 3 Challenge: Clean URL Slug Generator
instructions: Given a blog post title "Mastering Python Architecture in 2026!", create a URL slug.
Convert to lowercase, strip trailing punctuation, and replace spaces with hyphens.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
title = "Mastering Python Architecture in 2026!"
# Transform into clean slug: "mastering-python-architecture-in-2026"
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
title = "Mastering Python Architecture in 2026!"
slug = title.lower().replace("!", "").replace(" ", "-")
print("Generated slug:", slug)
hints: Use .lower(), .replace("!", ""), and .replace(" ", "-").

keyTakeaways: Strings are immutable Unicode sequences
Half-open intervals [start:stop] clamp safely out of bounds
Negative strides [::-1] reverse sequences in O(n)
F-strings provide precision rounding, padding, and alignment

days.title: Control Flow, Ternary Operators & Match-Case
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: Truthiness Matrix, Short-Circuit Evaluation, Ternary Syntax, Chained Comparisons, Match-Case, Pattern Guards, and Guard Clauses
days.overview: Conditional execution directs program logic. Master Python’s truthiness evaluation, short-circuit evaluation of logical operators, compact ternary expressions, chained relational checks, and modern match-case structural pattern matching across 7 topics.

topics.title: The Truthiness and Falsy Object Matrix
explanation: In Python, every object has an implicit boolean value. Falsy values include: None, False, zero in any numeric type (0, 0.0, 0j), empty sequences ("", (), []), and empty mappings ({}).
All other objects evaluate to True (truthy), including custom objects (unless they define __bool__() or __len__() returning 0).
keyRules: Falsy: None, False, 0, 0.0, "", [], (), {}, set()
Truthy: Everything else

codeSnippet.title: Verifying Object Truthiness
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting truth values with the bool() function.
codeSnippet.code:
print("bool(0):", bool(0))
print("bool([]):", bool([]))
print("bool('Hello'):", bool("Hello"))
print("bool([0]):", bool([0]))  # A non-empty list is truthy!
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
bool(0): False
bool([]): False
bool('Hello'): True
bool([0]): True

topics.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation of and / or
explanation: Logical operators "and" and "or" evaluate from left to right and short-circuit: they stop evaluation as soon as the outcome is certain.
Crucially, they do NOT return a boolean True/False; they return the actual operand object that determined the decision!
"x or y" returns x if x is truthy; otherwise it evaluates and returns y (useful for default fallbacks).
keyRules: a or b returns a if truthy, else b
a and b returns a if falsy, else b

codeSnippet.title: Short-Circuit Fallback Values
codeSnippet.description: Using "or" to supply default parameters.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Active configuration: {'timeout': 30, 'debug': False}

topics.title: Pythonic Ternary Conditional Expressions
explanation: Python supports one-line conditional expressions: result = value_if_true if condition else value_if_false.
Unlike C/JavaScript which use "condition ? x : y", Python places the true value first, mimicking natural English grammar.
keyRules: Syntax: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
Both branches must be valid expressions

codeSnippet.title: Ternary Expression in Variable Assignment
codeSnippet.description: Assign values based on inline conditions.
codeSnippet.code:
user_role = "admin"
access_level = 10 if user_role == "admin" else 1
print(f"User '{user_role}' assigned access level: {access_level}")
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: User 'admin' assigned access level: 10

topics.title: Chained Comparison Operators
explanation: Python supports mathematical chained comparisons like "18 <= age < 65".
Under the hood, Python translates this to "18 <= age and age < 65", but evaluates the middle operand "age" only once, preventing redundant computations.
keyRules: Chained comparisons evaluate intermediate expressions once
Works with any comparison operators: <, <=, ==, !=, >=, >

codeSnippet.title: Chained Range Validation
codeSnippet.description: Validating temperature ranges with chained comparisons.
codeSnippet.code:
temperature = 22
is_comfortable = 18 <= temperature <= 25
print(f"Is {temperature}C comfortable?", is_comfortable)

explanation: Python 3.10 introduced structural pattern matching via the "match ... case" syntax (PEP 634).
Unlike traditional switch statements in C/Java that match scalar numbers, Python pattern matching can unpack sequence patterns, mapping patterns, and class patterns.
keyRules: match subject: case pattern:
Underscore (_) acts as wildcard default fallback

keyRules: Syntax: case pattern if condition:

explanation: Deeply nested if-statements (the "Arrow Anti-Pattern") make code hard to read and test.
Idiomatic Python uses early return guard clauses: check for error or edge conditions upfront, exit early, and keep the happy path unindented at the top level.

Keep main business logic at shallow indentation levels

days.title: Loops in Depth: While, For, Enumerate, Zip & Else Clauses
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: While Loops, Iterator Protocol, Range Mechanics, Enumerate, Zip, Loop Control, and The For-Else Pattern
days.overview: Master looping and sequence traversal across 7 distinct topics. Discover how iterables work, avoid indexing counters, zip multiple sequences, and utilize the unique loop else construct.

topics.title: While Loops & Safe State Termination
explanation: While loops execute continuously as long as their condition is truthy.
Always guarantee that loop state advances toward termination to prevent CPU-pegging infinite loops.
keyRules: State must advance toward termination on every cycle
Use while True with explicit break condition for event-driven loops

codeSnippet.title: Halving Algorithm with While Loop
codeSnippet.description: Repeated division until reaching threshold.
codeSnippet.code:
val = 64
steps = 0
while val > 1:
    val = val // 2
    steps += 1
print(f"Steps to reduce to 1: {steps}")
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Steps to reduce to 1: 6

topics.title: The Iterable Contract & For Loops
explanation: In Python, for loops do not use index counters like C (for i=0; i<n; i++). Instead, they iterate directly over any object implementing the Iterable contract (__iter__).
Python calls iter(collection) to obtain an iterator, then repeatedly calls next(iterator) until StopIteration is raised.
keyRules: For loops work over any iterable (lists, tuples, dicts, strings, sets, files)
Direct iteration is cleaner, faster, and avoids off-by-one index bugs

codeSnippet.title: Direct Sequence Iteration
codeSnippet.description: Iterating directly over collection items.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Processing item: APPLE
Processing item: BANANA
Processing item: CHERRY

topics.title: The range() Generator: Memory Efficiency
explanation: In Python 3, range(start, stop, step) is not a list in memory; it is an immutable sequence object that computes elements on-demand in O(1) memory.
range(1_000_000) takes the same 48 bytes of memory as range(10)!
keyRules: range(stop), range(start, stop), range(start, stop, step)
Consumes O(1) memory regardless of upper bound

codeSnippet.title: Range Stepping and Summation
codeSnippet.description: Summing odd numbers via range stride.
codeSnippet.code:
odd_sum = sum(range(1, 20, 2))
print("Sum of odd numbers below 20:", odd_sum)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Sum of odd numbers below 20: 100

topics.title: enumerate() for Clean Index-Value Pairs
explanation: When you need both the item and its index, never write "for i in range(len(items)): item = items[i]".
Use enumerate(iterable, start=0) which yields (index, item) tuples natively.
keyRules: enumerate(items, start=1) supports custom starting index
Eliminates manual index tracking variables

topics.title: Parallel Iteration with zip() & zip_longest()
explanation: zip(*iterables) aggregates elements from multiple collections in lockstep, terminating when the shortest iterable is exhausted.
itertools.zip_longest() continues until the longest collection finishes, filling missing slots with a fillvalue.
keyRules: zip() stops at shortest iterable length
Unpacking zipped pairs: for name, score in zip(names, scores)

codeSnippet.title: Pairing Data Streams with Zip
codeSnippet.description: Combining students and test scores in parallel.
codeSnippet.code:

topics.title: Loop Control: break, continue, and pass
explanation: "break" terminates the innermost loop immediately.
"continue" skips the remainder of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration.
"pass" is a null operation placeholder where syntax requires a statement but no action is needed.
keyRules: break exits loop entirely
continue advances to next iteration immediately

codeSnippet.title: Filtering and Early Termination in Loops

topics.title: The Pythonic for-else Search Pattern
explanation: A loop can have an "else" clause. The else block executes ONLY if the loop finishes naturally without encountering a "break" statement.
This completely eliminates the need for manual boolean search flags like "found = False".
keyRules: Loop else runs if no break was triggered
Ideal for search algorithms with fallback execution

days.title: Functions Architecture: *args, **kwargs, Scope & LEGB Rule
days.subtitle: 7 In-Depth Topics: First-Class Callables, Default Parameter Trap, *args Tuples, **kwargs Dictionaries, Keyword-Only / Positional-Only, Docstrings, and The LEGB Scoping Rule
days.overview: Functions are first-class callable objects. Master flexible parameter unpacking, avoid the infamous mutable default argument bug, and understand how lexical scope resolves names through the LEGB hierarchy across 7 topics.

topics.title: Functions as First-Class Citizens
explanation: In Python, functions are first-class objects: they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, returned from functions, and stored in collections.
A function has attributes like __name__, __doc__, and __annotations__.
keyRules: Functions can be passed and returned like any object
Functions possess introspectable attributes like __name__

codeSnippet.title: Storing and Invoking Functions in a Dispatch Table
codeSnippet.description: Building an operations dictionary with function pointers.
codeSnippet.code:
def add(a, b): return a + b
def multiply(a, b): return a * b

operations = {"+": add, "*": multiply}

op = operations["*"]
print("Result of dispatch multiply(4, 5):", op(4, 5))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Result of dispatch multiply(4, 5): 20

topics.title: The Infamous Mutable Default Parameter Trap
explanation: In Python, default parameter expressions are evaluated ONCE at function definition time, NOT at function call time.
If you write "def append_item(item, target_list=[]):", all function invocations that omit target_list share the EXACT same list instance in memory!
The idiomatic solution: default to None, and create a new empty list inside the function body.
keyRules: Never use mutable containers ([], {}, set()) as default parameters
Use "None" as the default sentinel and initialize inside the body
topics.pitfall: Using "items=[]" in function headers causes shared state mutations across all calls.

codeSnippet.title: Safe Sentinel Default Argument Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Preventing shared list mutations across function calls.
codeSnippet.code:
def add_item(item, collection=None):
    if collection is None:
        collection = []
    collection.append(item)
    return collection

call1 = add_item("First")
call2 = add_item("Second")
print("Call 1 list:", call1)
print("Call 2 list:", call2)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Call 1 list: ['First']
Call 2 list: ['Second']

topics.title: Variable Positional Arguments with *args
explanation: The *args parameter packs any number of positional arguments into a single immutable tuple.
This enables creating flexible functions that accept arbitrary inputs (like print or sum).
keyRules: *args packs variable positional arguments into a tuple
Can be forwarded to other functions using *args unpacking

codeSnippet.title: Arbitrary Argument Multiplier
codeSnippet.description: Accepting variable numbers of arguments with *args.
codeSnippet.code:
def product(*numbers):
    total = 1
    for n in numbers:
        total *= n
    return total

print("product(2, 3, 4) =", product(2, 3, 4))
print("product(5, 10)    =", product(5, 10))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
product(2, 3, 4) = 24
product(5, 10)    = 50

topics.title: Variable Keyword Arguments with **kwargs
explanation: The **kwargs parameter packs all extra keyword arguments into a standard Python dictionary.
This is commonly used in configuration builders and wrapper decorators.
keyRules: **kwargs packs keyword arguments into a dictionary
Can be unpacked into other calls using **kwargs

codeSnippet.title: Building Configuration Dictionaries with **kwargs
codeSnippet.description: Handling arbitrary named parameters.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Created user record: {'id': 101, 'name': 'Alex', 'role': 'Engineer', 'active': True}

topics.title: Positional-Only (/) and Keyword-Only (*) Parameters
explanation: Python 3.8 standardized positional-only parameters using the slash (/) marker. Arguments before "/" cannot be called by keyword.
The asterisk (*) separates positional parameters from keyword-only parameters. Arguments after "*" MUST be called using keyword syntax.
keyRules: def f(pos_only, /, standard, *, kw_only):
Prevents callers from depending on internal positional parameter names

codeSnippet.title: Enforcing Keyword-Only Parameters
codeSnippet.description: Writing robust function signatures with keyword constraints.
codeSnippet.code:
def connect_database(host, port=5432, *, timeout=30, retry=True):
    return f"Connected to {host}:{port} (timeout={timeout}s, retry={retry})"

# timeout and retry MUST be passed as keywords
conn = connect_database("127.0.0.1", timeout=15)
print("Database connection string:", conn)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Database connection string: Connected to 127.0.0.1:5432 (timeout=15s, retry=True)

topics.title: Docstrings, Type Annotations & Introspection
explanation: Python docstrings (PEP 257) are triple-quoted string literals placed as the first statement in a function or class.
Type hints (PEP 484) document parameter and return types for IDE auto-complete and static type checkers like mypy, accessible at runtime via fn.__annotations__.
keyRules: Triple quoted docstrings populate function.__doc__
Type annotations populate function.__annotations__ without enforcing runtime types

codeSnippet.title: Documented and Typed Function
codeSnippet.description: Writing clean, self-documenting functions with type hints.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Discounted total: 85.0
Docstring: Calculates discounted price given a base price and discount rate.

topics.title: Scope Resolution: The LEGB Rule (Local, Enclosing, Global, Builtin)
explanation: When Python encounters a variable name, it searches four scopes in strict order: Local -> Enclosing (nested functions) -> Global (module level) -> Built-in (print, len, range).
To re-bind a variable in an outer enclosing function, use "nonlocal". To re-bind a module-level variable, use "global".
keyRules: L: Local scope inside active function
E: Enclosing scope of enclosing functions (closures)
G: Global scope at module level
B: Built-in namespace with built-in functions and exceptions

codeSnippet.title: LEGB Scope Demonstration with Closures
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating enclosing scope and the nonlocal keyword.
codeSnippet.code:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

c = make_counter()
print("Count 1:", c())
print("Count 2:", c())
print("Count 3:", c())
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Count 1: 1
Count 2: 2
Count 3: 3

keyTakeaways: Functions are first-class callable objects
Never use mutable default arguments; use None as sentinel
*args collects positional arguments; **kwargs collects keyword arguments
LEGB governs scope resolution: Local, Enclosing, Global, Builtin

codeSnippet.title: Complete Ledger Processing Engine
codeSnippet.description: Processing multiple financial transaction strings.
codeSnippet.code:
logs = [
    "TX1:DEPOSIT:500.00",
    "TX2:WITHDRAWAL:120.00",
    "TX3:DEPOSIT:350.50",
    "TX4:FEE:15.00"

        amt = float(amount_str)

questions.question: What happens under the hood when CPython executes a Python script?
options: It is directly compiled to x86/ARM machine code binaries
Source code is parsed into an AST and compiled to bytecode (.pyc), which the PVM executes
It runs purely via line-by-line string regex evaluation with no intermediate representation
It is transpiled to C++ and compiled with GCC
questions.explanation: CPython first parses code into an AST and compiles it into bytecode instructions, which are then interpreted by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM).

questions.question: What is the output of: x = 256; y = 256; print(x is y)?
options: True, because CPython pre-allocates and interns small integers between -5 and 256
False, because every assignment allocates a brand new object in memory
questions.explanation: CPython interns small integers (-5 to 256) at startup; both x and y reference the exact same singleton integer object in memory.

questions.question: What does the slice "Python"[::-1] evaluate to?
questions.explanation: A step of -1 traverses the string backwards from the end to the beginning, reversing the string.

questions.question: Why is defining "def process(items=[])" considered dangerous in Python?
options: Python does not support default lists in function headers
Default parameter values are evaluated once at definition time, so all calls share the same mutable list
It causes a MemoryError on the second call
Default parameters must always be strings or ints
questions.explanation: Because default parameter expressions are evaluated once when the function is defined, the mutable list is shared across all subsequent invocations.

questions.question: When does the "else" clause attached to a "for" loop execute?
options: Whenever the loop terminates via a "break" statement
Only when the iterable was completely empty to begin with
When the loop exhausts normally without encountering a "break" statement
It is invalid syntax and throws a SyntaxError
questions.explanation: In Python, a loop else block runs only if the loop completed naturally without hitting a "break" statement.

days.title: Lists Internals: Dynamic Arrays & Amortized O(1)
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: PyListObject, Over-Allocation Formula, O(n) Pitfalls, Shallow vs Deep Copy, In-Place Mutation, Timsort, and Matrices
days.overview: Python lists are not linked lists! They are dynamic arrays of pointer references. Learn how CPython grows lists in memory, when operations cost O(1) vs O(n), and how Timsort sorts data across 7 comprehensive topics.

topics.title: The PyListObject C Structure
explanation: Under the hood in CPython, a list is represented by the PyListObject structure containing: an ob_refcnt header, an ob_size integer, an allocated capacity integer, and a contiguous array of 64-bit pointers (PyObject**) pointing to items in the heap.
Because pointers are stored contiguously, accessing any item by index (list[i]) takes direct O(1) pointer arithmetic: base_address + i * 8 bytes.
keyRules: Lists store pointers to heap objects, not raw values
Index access list[i] is pure O(1) pointer arithmetic

codeSnippet.title: List Memory Inspection
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting list size and pointer references.
codeSnippet.code:
import sys
items = [10, 20, 30]
print("List object size in bytes:", sys.getsizeof(items))
print("Item at index 1 in O(1):", items[1])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
List object size in bytes: 88
Item at index 1 in O(1): 20

topics.title: The Over-Allocation Growth Formula & Amortized O(1)
explanation: When a list exceeds its current capacity, CPython allocates a larger contiguous buffer and moves the pointers. To prevent doing this on every append, CPython over-allocates extra slots.

The growth pattern is roughly: new_allocated = size + (size >> 3) + (size < 9 ? 3 : 6). This mathematical over-allocation ensures that while occasional reallocations take O(n), append operations cost amortized O(1).
keyRules: append() is amortized O(1)
Over-allocation reserves extra headroom for subsequent additions

codeSnippet.title: Observing Dynamic List Growth
codeSnippet.description: Tracking size increases as items are appended.
codeSnippet.code:
import sys
lst = []
prev_size = sys.getsizeof(lst)
for i in range(10):
    lst.append(i)
    cur_size = sys.getsizeof(lst)
    if cur_size != prev_size:
        print(f"List grew from {prev_size}B to {cur_size}B at length {len(lst)}")
        prev_size = cur_size
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
List grew from 56B to 88B at length 1
List grew from 88B to 120B at length 5
List grew from 120B to 184B at length 9

topics.title: Cost of O(n) List Operations (Insert & Pop at Index 0)
explanation: While appending and popping from the end (list.pop()) are O(1), inserting or removing at index 0 (list.insert(0, val) or list.pop(0)) is O(n) because every single subsequent pointer in the array must shift left or right.
If you need frequent insertions or removals from both ends, use "collections.deque", which is an O(1) double-ended queue.
keyRules: list.append() and list.pop() are O(1)
list.insert(0, x) and list.pop(0) are O(n)
Use collections.deque for FIFO queues

codeSnippet.title: End vs Beginning List Operations
codeSnippet.description: Fast O(1) append/pop vs O(n) beginning insertions.
codeSnippet.code:
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
data.append(6)   # O(1) append at end
last = data.pop() # O(1) pop from end
print("Data after end operations:", data)
print("Popped item:", last)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Data after end operations: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Popped item: 6

topics.title: Shallow Copying vs Deep Copying
explanation: Assignment ("b = a") creates an alias to the same list. Slicing ("b = a[:]") or "b = a.copy()" creates a shallow copy: a new list container, but containing the same inner element references.
If elements are mutable (e.g. nested lists), mutating inner objects in a shallow copy still mutates the original! For fully isolated copies, use copy.deepcopy().
keyRules: list[:] and list.copy() produce shallow copies
copy.deepcopy() recursively duplicates all nested objects

codeSnippet.title: Shallow Copy Aliasing Trap
codeSnippet.description: Observing shared nested objects in shallow copies.
codeSnippet.code:
nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = nested[:]

# Mutating top level is safe
shallow.append([5, 6])
print("Did original list get [5, 6]?", len(nested) == 2)

# Mutating inner list affects both!
shallow[0][0] = 999
print("Did inner item mutate in original?", nested[0][0] == 999)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Did original list get [5, 6]? True
Did inner item mutate in original? True

topics.title: In-Place List Mutation Methods
explanation: Python distinguishes methods that mutate in-place (returning None) from operations that return new lists.
list.sort(), list.reverse(), list.extend(), and list.clear() modify the list in-place and return None. Sliced assignments (list[1:3] = [8, 9]) replace sub-ranges.
keyRules: list.sort() mutates in-place; sorted(list) returns a new sorted list
In-place methods return None to prevent confusing chaining

codeSnippet.title: In-Place List Methods
codeSnippet.description: Mutating lists in place and slicing replacements.
codeSnippet.code:
nums = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9]
nums.sort()
print("Sorted in-place:", nums)
nums.reverse()
print("Reversed in-place:", nums)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Sorted in-place: [1, 2, 5, 8, 9]
Reversed in-place: [9, 8, 5, 2, 1]

topics.title: Timsort Algorithm: Mechanics & Performance
explanation: Python’s sorting algorithm, Timsort (created by Tim Peters in 2002), is a hybrid derived from Merge Sort and Insertion Sort.

Timsort identifies natural contiguous ordered segments ("runs") already present in real-world data and merges them efficiently, achieving O(n) best-case on nearly sorted data and O(n log n) worst-case.
keyRules: Timsort is stable (preserves relative order of equal elements)
Worst case: O(n log n); Best case on ordered data: O(n)

codeSnippet.title: Stable Sorting with Timsort
codeSnippet.description: Sorting tuples stably by multiple keys.
codeSnippet.code:
records = [("Alice", 90), ("Bob", 85), ("Charlie", 90)]
# Stable sort preserves Alice before Charlie
sorted_records = sorted(records, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("Timsort stable results:", sorted_records)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Timsort stable results: [('Alice', 90), ('Charlie', 90), ('Bob', 85)]

topics.title: Multi-Dimensional Matrices & The Multiplier Pitfall
explanation: A common beginner pitfall: creating a 2D matrix with "matrix = [[0] * 3] * 3". This creates 3 pointers to the EXACT SAME list!
Modifying matrix[0][0] = 1 will mutate all 3 rows! The correct idiomatic way is a list comprehension: "[[0 for _ in range(3)] for _ in range(3)]".
keyRules: Never use "[[0] * cols] * rows" (it creates row aliases)
Always use "[[0 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]"
topics.pitfall: Using list multiplication with nested lists replicates the same inner list reference.

codeSnippet.title: Correct 2D Matrix Creation
codeSnippet.description: Building isolated multi-dimensional grid structures.
codeSnippet.code:
rows, cols = 3, 3
matrix = [[0 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]
matrix[0][1] = 7
print("Row 0:", matrix[0])
print("Row 1 (unaffected):", matrix[1])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Row 0: [0, 7, 0]
Row 1 (unaffected): [0, 0, 0]

practiceChallenge.title: Day 8 Challenge: Remove Duplicates Preserving Order
instructions: Write a function remove_duplicates(items) that removes duplicate entries from a list while maintaining original insertion order.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
def remove_duplicates(items):
    # Return unique items in original order
    pass

print(remove_duplicates([1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4]))
hints: Use a helper set to track seen elements in O(1) time.

keyTakeaways: Lists are dynamic arrays of pointers, not linked nodes
Append is amortized O(1); beginning insertions are O(n)
Shallow copies share nested mutable objects
Timsort provides fast, stable O(n log n) sorting

days.title: Tuples, Immutability & Sets
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Tuple Memory Footprint, Sequence Unpacking, Namedtuples, Hashability Contract, Set Hash Tables, Set Theory Algebra, and Frozensets
days.overview: Master immutable sequences and hash tables across 7 topics. Compare tuple memory efficiency against lists, explore sequence unpacking, understand hashability, and execute mathematical set operations.

topics.title: Tuples vs Lists: Memory Footprint & Allocation
explanation: Tuples are immutable fixed-size sequences. Because they can never grow or shrink, CPython allocates the exact amount of memory needed without over-allocation buffers.
CPython also maintains a free list of recycled small tuples to avoid repeated malloc() OS calls, making tuple allocation faster than lists.
keyRules: Tuples consume less memory than lists of equivalent size
Tuples are immutable; items cannot be reassigned or appended

codeSnippet.title: Memory Comparison: Tuple vs List
codeSnippet.description: Comparing sys.getsizeof between tuple and list.
codeSnippet.code:
import sys
t = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
l = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("Tuple memory:", sys.getsizeof(t), "bytes")
print("List memory: ", sys.getsizeof(l), "bytes")
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Tuple memory: 80 bytes
List memory:  104 bytes

topics.title: Sequence Unpacking & The Asterisk Collector (*)
explanation: Python supports tuple and sequence unpacking: a, b = (10, 20).
Extended unpacking uses an asterisk: first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The starred variable captures all remaining elements into a list.
keyRules: Unpacking requires exact matching counts unless * is used
Only one starred expression is permitted per assignment statement

codeSnippet.title: Extended Sequence Unpacking
codeSnippet.description: Capturing head, tail, and middle sequence elements.
codeSnippet.code:
data = [100, 85, 90, 95, 70]
first, *middle, last = data
print("First score:", first)
print("Middle scores:", middle)
print("Last score:", last)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
First score: 100
Middle scores: [85, 90, 95]
Last score: 70

topics.title: Namedtuples for Lightweight Schemas
explanation: collections.namedtuple generates lightweight, memory-efficient tuple subclasses with accessible named fields (e.g. point.x, point.y) rather than numeric indices.
Namedtuples retain complete tuple immutability and compatibility with zero dictionary memory overhead.
keyRules: namedtuple combines tuple efficiency with object attribute readability
Immutable and hashable

codeSnippet.title: Namedtuple Coordinate Modeling
codeSnippet.description: Defining and instantiating namedtuple records.
codeSnippet.code:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple("Point", ["x", "y"])
p = Point(10, 20)
print(f"Point coordinates: x={p.x}, y={p.y}")
print("Indexed access:", p[0])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Point coordinates: x=10, y=20
Indexed access: 10

topics.title: The Hashability Contract (__hash__ and __eq__)
explanation: An object is hashable if it has a hash value that never changes during its lifetime (defines __hash__()) and can be compared to other objects (defines __eq__()).
Mutable collections (lists, dicts, sets) are NOT hashable because modifying their contents would change their hash, corrupting hash tables.
keyRules: Only immutable, hashable objects can be set members or dict keys
Tuples containing mutable elements (e.g. ([1], 2)) are unhashable

codeSnippet.title: Hashability Verification
codeSnippet.description: Verifying hashability of integers, strings, and tuples.
codeSnippet.code:
print("Hash of string 'python':", hash("python") != 0)
print("Hash of tuple (1, 2):", hash((1, 2)) != 0)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Hash of string 'python': True
Hash of tuple (1, 2): True

topics.title: Sets as Key-Only Hash Tables (O(1) Lookups)
explanation: A set is an unordered collection of unique hashable elements implemented as a hash table with dummy values.
Checking membership ("x in my_set") takes average O(1) time complexity, compared to O(n) for a list.
keyRules: Set membership testing is average O(1)
Sets automatically eliminate duplicate items

codeSnippet.title: Instant Set Deduplication and Membership
codeSnippet.description: Rapid membership check and duplicate elimination.
codeSnippet.code:
user_ids = [101, 102, 101, 103, 102, 104]
unique_ids = set(user_ids)
print("Deduplicated unique IDs:", sorted(list(unique_ids)))
print("Is 103 in set? (O(1) lookup):", 103 in unique_ids)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Deduplicated unique IDs: [101, 102, 103, 104]
Is 103 in set? (O(1) lookup): True

topics.title: Set Theory Algebra: Union, Intersection & Difference
explanation: Python sets provide mathematical set operators: Union (|), Intersection (&), Difference (-), and Symmetric Difference (^).
Subsets and supersets can be verified with <= and >=.
keyRules: a & b: Intersection (common to both)
a | b: Union (in either a or b)
a - b: Difference (in a but not in b)
a ^ b: Symmetric difference (in either, but not both)

codeSnippet.title: Set Algebraic Operations
codeSnippet.description: Computing intersections and unions of developer skills.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Common skills: {'docker'}
Combined skills: {'go', 'kubernetes', 'python', 'docker', 'sql'}

topics.title: Frozensets: Immutable Hashable Sets
explanation: Standard sets are mutable and therefore cannot be elements of another set or keys in a dictionary.
Python provides frozenset, which is an immutable, hashable set that can be nested inside other sets or used as dictionary keys.
keyRules: frozenset is immutable and implements __hash__()
Can be stored in sets or used as dict keys

codeSnippet.title: Frozensets as Dictionary Keys
codeSnippet.description: Mapping set relationships in dictionary keys.
codeSnippet.code:
team1 = frozenset(["Alice", "Bob"])
team2 = frozenset(["Charlie", "David"])
project_assignments = {team1: "Project Apollo", team2: "Project Titan"}
print("Team 1 project:", project_assignments[team1])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Team 1 project: Project Apollo

practiceChallenge.title: Day 9 Challenge: Common Skills Identifier
instructions: Given two lists of skills, return the count of skills shared by both using set intersection.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:

    # Return count of common skills

print(count_common_skills(["python", "sql", "git"], ["git", "docker", "python"]))
hints: Convert both lists to sets and find the intersection.

keyTakeaways: Tuples use less memory than lists and are immutable
Extended sequence unpacking (*rest) captures variable lengths
Only hashable objects can be stored in sets or used as dict keys
Sets offer average O(1) membership lookups and set theory operators

days.title: Dictionaries Deep Dive: Compact Hash Tables & Views
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Compact Dict Architecture, Hash Collisions, Safe Key Access, Dynamic Dict Views, Dict Union (|), Insertion Order, and Memory Sizing
days.overview: Dictionaries are the most optimized data structure in Python. Explore the compact table architecture, collision resolution, dynamic views, and dict union operators across 7 topics.

topics.title: The Modern Compact Dict Architecture (Python 3.7+)
explanation: Historically, Python dicts were sparse arrays where 2/3 of slots were empty. Since Python 3.6 (standard in 3.7), dicts use a two-array design: a dense "entries" table and a sparse index table.
Entries are stored densely in the order inserted, reducing memory by 30-40% and preserving insertion order deterministically.
keyRules: Dicts preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+
Compact layout separates sparse indices from dense entries

codeSnippet.title: Dictionary Insertion Order Preservation
codeSnippet.description: Observing deterministic key order.
codeSnippet.code:
d = {}
d["z"] = 1
d["a"] = 2
d["m"] = 3
print("Keys in insertion order:", list(d.keys()))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Keys in insertion order: ['z', 'a', 'm']

topics.title: Hash Collisions & Open Addressing Probing
explanation: When two distinct keys produce the same hash bucket index (a collision), Python uses open addressing with pseudo-random perturbation probing to find the next available slot.
Python randomizes string hash seeds on process startup to prevent Hash DoS attacks.
keyRules: Python uses open addressing, not separate chaining
Hash randomization protects against algorithmic denial-of-service

codeSnippet.title: Custom Object Hash and Equality
codeSnippet.description: Implementing __hash__ and __eq__ for dictionary keys.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Found key in dict? True

topics.title: Safe Key Access: .get(), .setdefault(), and defaultdict
explanation: Accessing a non-existent key via d[key] raises KeyError. Use d.get(key, default) for safe retrieval with a fallback.
d.setdefault(key, default) retrieves the value, inserting default if the key is missing.
collections.defaultdict automatically initializes missing keys using a factory function.
keyRules: d.get(k, default) avoids KeyError
defaultdict(list) initializes empty lists on access

codeSnippet.title: Group By with defaultdict
codeSnippet.description: Grouping items cleanly without manual key existence checks.
codeSnippet.code:
from collections import defaultdict
grouped = defaultdict(list)
words = ["apple", "banana", "apricot", "cherry"]
for w in words:
    grouped[w[0]].append(w)
print("Grouped words by initial:", dict(grouped))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Grouped words by initial: {'a': ['apple', 'apricot'], 'b': ['banana'], 'c': ['cherry']}

topics.title: Dynamic Dictionary Views (.keys, .values, .items)
explanation: In Python 3, d.keys(), d.values(), and d.items() return dynamic view objects, not static lists.
Views reflect changes to the underlying dictionary in real time and support set operations like intersection and union.
keyRules: Dict views are dynamic windows into the dictionary
dict.keys() and dict.items() support set algebra (&, |, -)

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic View Updates
codeSnippet.description: Observing views update when dictionary mutates.
codeSnippet.code:
user = {"name": "Alex", "role": "Dev"}
keys_view = user.keys()
print("Initial keys:", list(keys_view))
user["status"] = "Active"
print("View updated automatically:", list(keys_view))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Initial keys: ['name', 'role']
View updated automatically: ['name', 'role', 'status']

topics.title: Dictionary Union Operators (| and |=) (PEP 584)
explanation: Python 3.9 introduced the dictionary union operator "|". d1 | d2 creates a new merged dictionary with right-hand precedence for overlapping keys.
d1 |= d2 updates d1 in-place.
keyRules: d1 | d2 returns a new merged dictionary
Right-hand operand takes precedence on duplicate keys

codeSnippet.title: Dictionary Merge with Pipe Operator
codeSnippet.description: Merging defaults with custom user configurations.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Merged settings: {'theme': 'dark', 'font_size': 16, 'auto_save': True}

topics.title: Mapping Proxy & Read-Only Dictionaries
explanation: To expose an immutable view of a dictionary (preventing external modification), use types.MappingProxyType.
The proxy reflects updates made to the underlying dict but disallows write operations.
keyRules: MappingProxyType provides a read-only dictionary interface
Protects internal class or module dictionaries from external mutation

codeSnippet.title: Read-Only MappingProxyType
codeSnippet.description: Guarding dictionary attributes against mutation.
codeSnippet.code:
from types import MappingProxyType
internal_data = {"admin_port": 8080}
read_only_view = MappingProxyType(internal_data)
print("Read-only port:", read_only_view["admin_port"])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Read-only port: 8080

topics.title: Dictionary Performance & Memory Profiling
explanation: Dicts require memory for hash tables and sparse indices. Under high volumes (millions of objects), dictionaries can consume significant RAM.
Techniques like __slots__ in classes bypass instance __dict__ overhead, saving 60% memory.
keyRules: Dict lookup is O(1) average time
Use __slots__ to eliminate per-instance __dict__ overhead in classes

codeSnippet.title: Dict Performance Profiling
codeSnippet.description: Measuring speed of dictionary lookups.
codeSnippet.code:
data = {i: i*2 for i in range(1000)}
print("Instant lookup for key 999:", data[999])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Instant lookup for key 999: 1998

instructions: Write a function count_words(sentence) that returns a dictionary mapping each lowercased word to its occurrence count.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
def count_words(sentence):
    # Return frequency dict
    pass

print(count_words("python is great and python is fun"))
hints: Use dict.get(word, 0) + 1 to tally words.

keyTakeaways: Compact dict layout preserves insertion order with low memory footprint
Use .get() and defaultdict to prevent KeyError crashes
Dict views (.keys, .items) support set algebra operations
Merge dicts cleanly using the "|" operator

days.title: Comprehensions Mastery & Generator Expressions
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: List Comprehensions, Filtering Clauses, Ternary Mapping, Dict Comprehensions, Set Comprehensions, Nested Comprehensions, and Lazy Generator Expressions
days.overview: Comprehensions provide concise, declarative transformations. Master list, dict, and set comprehensions, multi-level nesting, and lazy generator expressions across 7 comprehensive topics.

topics.title: List Comprehensions vs Imperative Loops
explanation: A list comprehension builds a new list by executing a dedicated bytecode instruction (LIST_APPEND) at C-speed, avoiding repeated Python-level method lookup overhead.
keyRules: [expression for item in iterable]
Faster and more readable than manual append loops

codeSnippet.title: Squaring Numbers with List Comprehension
codeSnippet.description: Transforming a sequence in one readable line.
codeSnippet.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [x ** 2 for x in numbers]
print("Squares:", squares)

topics.title: Filtering Sequences with Trailing if Clauses
explanation: Placing an "if" at the end of a comprehension filters items before the transformation expression executes.
keyRules: [expr for item in iterable if condition]
Filters out items where condition is falsy

codeSnippet.title: Filtered Even Squares
codeSnippet.description: Selecting and squaring even numbers.
codeSnippet.code:
evens = [x ** 2 for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 0]
print("Even squares:", evens)

topics.title: Conditional Transformations: Inline if-else Expressions
explanation: When you need to transform elements differently based on a condition (not filter them out), place a ternary conditional expression at the FRONT.
keyRules: [val_true if cond else val_false for item in iterable]
Front if-else transforms; trailing if filters

codeSnippet.title: Conditional Transformation Mapping
codeSnippet.description: Labeling numbers as Even or Odd.
codeSnippet.code:
labels = ["Even" if n % 2 == 0 else "Odd" for n in range(1, 6)]
print("Labels:", labels)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Labels: ['Odd', 'Even', 'Odd', 'Even', 'Odd']

topics.title: Dictionary Comprehensions
explanation: Dict comprehensions construct key-value mappings: {k_expr: v_expr for item in iterable}. Frequently used to invert mappings or index records.
keyRules: {key_expr: val_expr for item in iterable}
Keys must be hashable

codeSnippet.title: Inverting a Dictionary Mapping
codeSnippet.description: Swapping keys and values in a single expression.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Inverted mapping: {'Admin': 'Alice', 'Dev': 'Bob', 'Design': 'Charlie'}

topics.title: Set Comprehensions
explanation: Set comprehensions {expr for item in iterable} produce a deduplicated set collection in a single pass.
keyRules: {expr for item in iterable}
Automatically discards duplicate results

codeSnippet.title: Deduplicated Word Lengths
codeSnippet.description: Collecting unique word lengths via set comprehension.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Unique word lengths: {4, 5, 6}

topics.title: Nested Comprehensions & 2D Matrix Flattening
explanation: Comprehensions support nested loops: [item for row in matrix for item in row]. Loops execute in left-to-right order identical to nested for-statements.
keyRules: Left-to-right loop order matches nested imperative loop syntax
Limit nesting to 2 levels to prevent unreadable code

codeSnippet.title: Flattening a 2D Matrix
codeSnippet.description: Transforming a 2D matrix into a 1D sequence.
codeSnippet.code:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
flat = [x for row in matrix for x in row]
print("Flattened list:", flat)

topics.title: Generator Expressions: Lazy O(1) Memory Streams
explanation: Replacing brackets with parentheses (expr for item in iterable) creates a generator expression.
Items are produced lazily on-demand via the iterator protocol without allocating memory for the entire sequence, ideal for sum(), any(), and all().
keyRules: (expr for item in iterable) consumes O(1) memory
Single pass iteration

codeSnippet.title: Generator Expression in Reductions
codeSnippet.description: Summing squares of numbers without allocating a full list.
codeSnippet.code:
total = sum(x * x for x in range(1, 101))
print("Sum of first 100 squares:", total)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Sum of first 100 squares: 338350

practiceChallenge.title: Day 11 Challenge: Filter Even Length Words
instructions: Given a list of words, return a list comprehension containing only the words with an even number of characters, converted to uppercase.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
words = ["code", "python", "developer", "data", "ai"]
# Create even_words comprehension:
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:

print("Even length words:", even_words)
hints: Use [w.upper() for w in words if len(w) % 2 == 0]

keyTakeaways: Comprehensions are faster and more idiomatic than append loops
Trailing if filters; leading if-else transforms
Generator expressions compute lazily in O(1) memory

days.title: Functional Programming: Lambdas, Map, Filter & Closures
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Lambdas, Map & Filter, Custom Key Sorting, Extrema with min/max, functools.reduce, Lexical Closures, and Partial Functions
days.overview: Explore functional programming paradigms in Python across 7 topics. Learn anonymous lambdas, functional pipelines, custom sorting keys, lexical closures, and function currying.

topics.title: Anonymous Functions (Lambdas)
explanation: A lambda is an inline anonymous function: lambda x, y: x + y.
Lambdas are syntactically restricted to a single expression and cannot contain statements or assignments.
keyRules: lambda args: expression
Implicitly returns the value of the evaluated expression

codeSnippet.title: Lambda Expressions
codeSnippet.description: Defining and invoking inline lambdas.
codeSnippet.code:
square = lambda n: n * n
print("Lambda square(6):", square(6))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Lambda square(6): 36

topics.title: Higher-Order Functions: map() and filter()
explanation: map(fn, iterable) applies a function to all items lazily.
filter(predicate, iterable) yields only items where predicate is truthy.
In modern Python, comprehensions are usually preferred for readability.
keyRules: map and filter return lazy iterator objects in Python 3

codeSnippet.title: Map and Filter Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Doubling positive numbers with map and filter.
codeSnippet.code:
numbers = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]
positives = filter(lambda x: x > 0, numbers)
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, positives))
print("Doubled positive numbers:", doubled)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Doubled positive numbers: [2, 4, 6]

topics.title: Custom Sorting Keys with sorted()
explanation: The sorted() function accepts a key parameter: a function that extracts a comparison key from each element.
This allows sorting complex dictionaries, tuples, or objects effortlessly.
keyRules: sorted(data, key=lambda x: ...)
Original collection is not modified

codeSnippet.title: Sorting Dictionaries by Nested Attribute
codeSnippet.description: Sorting employees by salary with lambda key.
codeSnippet.code:
staff = [
    {"name": "Sarah", "salary": 120000},
    {"name": "Mark", "salary": 95000},
    {"name": "Devon", "salary": 140000}
]
sorted_staff = sorted(staff, key=lambda s: s["salary"])
print("Lowest salary staff:", sorted_staff[0]["name"])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Lowest salary staff: Mark

topics.title: Finding Extrema with min() and max() Keys
explanation: min() and max() also accept the key parameter, avoiding sorting when only the single extreme item is required.
keyRules: max(items, key=lambda x: ...) is O(n) compared to O(n log n) for sort

codeSnippet.title: Finding Extreme Elements with Max Key
codeSnippet.description: Extracting highest earner record in O(n).
codeSnippet.code:
staff = [{"name": "Sarah", "salary": 120000}, {"name": "Devon", "salary": 140000}]
top = max(staff, key=lambda s: s["salary"])
print("Top earner:", top["name"])
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Top earner: Devon

topics.title: Cumulative Reductions with functools.reduce
explanation: functools.reduce(func, iterable, initializer) applies a binary function cumulatively to items, reducing a sequence to a single accumulated value.
keyRules: reduce(f, [1, 2, 3]) computes f(f(1, 2), 3)

codeSnippet.title: Factorial Reduction with Reduce
codeSnippet.description: Multiplying sequence elements cumulatively.
codeSnippet.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
product = 1
for n in nums: product *= n
print("Product reduction:", product)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Product reduction: 120

topics.title: Lexical Closures & Enclosed Free Variables
explanation: A closure occurs when a nested inner function retains access to variables from its outer enclosing scope even after the outer function has finished executing.
keyRules: Inner functions capture outer scope variables in __closure__
Enables factory functions and state encapsulation

codeSnippet.title: Closure Multiplier Factory
codeSnippet.description: Generating customized multiplier functions.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: triple(10) = 30

topics.title: Function Currying with functools.partial
explanation: functools.partial freezes a portion of a function’s arguments, returning a new callable with a simpler signature.
keyRules: partial(func, *args, **kwargs) creates specialized callables

codeSnippet.title: Partial Function Application
codeSnippet.description: Pre-filling base arguments for reusable functions.
codeSnippet.code:
def power(base, exponent):

square_fn = lambda x: power(x, 2)
print("square_fn(8) =", square_fn(8))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: square_fn(8) = 64

sorted() with key=lambda allows multi-attribute sorting
Closures capture outer scope references for factory functions

days.title: Error Handling, Custom Exceptions & Context Managers
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: EAFP vs LBYL, Try-Except-Else-Finally, Exception Hierarchy, Raising Exceptions, Custom Exceptions, Context Managers (__enter__/__exit__), and contextlib
days.overview: Write fault-tolerant, resilient code across 7 topics. Learn why Python prefers EAFP over LBYL, master the complete try-except-else-finally architecture, define domain exception classes, and build context managers.

topics.title: Python Philosophy: EAFP vs LBYL
explanation: EAFP ("Easier to Ask for Forgiveness than Permission") assumes operations succeed and catches exceptions if they fail.
LBYL ("Look Before You Leap") tests prerequisites before every call (e.g. if key in dict: val = dict[key]).
EAFP avoids concurrency race conditions (TOCTOU: Time of Check to Time of Use) and executes faster when exceptions are rare.
keyRules: EAFP: Try operation and handle exceptions
Prevents race conditions in file systems and shared state

codeSnippet.title: EAFP Key Retrieval
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating EAFP error mitigation.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Active theme: default-dark

topics.title: The Four-Part Try-Except-Else-Finally Block
explanation: try: Risky code that may throw exceptions.
except Exception: Catches and mitigates specific error types.
else: Executes ONLY if no exception was raised in the try block.
finally: Executes ALWAYS, guaranteeing cleanup even if returns or unhandled errors occur.
keyRules: else isolates code that should run only upon success
finally is guaranteed to execute before returning

codeSnippet.title: Full Try-Except-Else-Finally Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating the complete four-part exception lifecycle.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
[Success] 10 / 2 = 5.0
[Audit] Division calculation completed
[Error] Cannot divide by zero
[Audit] Division calculation completed

topics.title: The Built-in Exception Hierarchy
explanation: All exceptions inherit from BaseException. Standard program exceptions inherit from Exception.
Never write bare "except:" because it intercepts SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and GeneratorExit, making scripts impossible to terminate with Ctrl+C.
keyRules: Catch "except Exception as e:", never bare "except:"
BaseException -> Exception -> ArithmeticError, LookupError, ValueError

codeSnippet.title: Targeting Specific Exception Branches
codeSnippet.description: Catching specific exceptions in order.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Caught ValueError cleanly: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not_a_number'

topics.title: Raising Exceptions & Exception Chaining
explanation: Use "raise ValueError(...)" to reject invalid states.
Python 3 supports exception chaining with "raise NewError() from original_error", preserving the original traceback cause.
keyRules: raise ExceptionClass("message")
raise CustomError from e preserves the root cause

codeSnippet.title: Raising Validation Exceptions
codeSnippet.description: Triggering domain validation errors.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Validation rejected: Age cannot be negative

topics.title: Defining Custom Domain Exception Classes
explanation: Applications should define specific domain exceptions inheriting from Exception to distinguish business rule violations from general Python runtime errors.
keyRules: Custom exceptions should subclass Exception
Add custom metadata attributes in __init__

codeSnippet.title: Custom Business Rule Exception
codeSnippet.description: Authoring and catching custom domain exceptions.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Handled business rule: Cannot withdraw $200; balance is only $50

topics.title: The Context Manager Protocol (__enter__ and __exit__)
explanation: The "with" statement guarantees deterministic resource acquisition and release.
Any class implementing __enter__() and __exit__(exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) conforms to the Context Manager Protocol.
keyRules: __enter__() initializes the resource and returns the bound target
__exit__() executes cleanup and can suppress exceptions by returning True

[Session] Connected to database

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of checking membership ("x in container") for a set vs a list with n elements?
questions.explanation: Sets are implemented as hash tables allowing O(1) average lookup, whereas lists require a linear scan of O(n).

questions.question: Why cannot a standard Python list be used as a key in a dictionary?
options: Lists are mutable and do not implement __hash__()
Dictionaries only permit strings as keys
CPython limits key types to integers and floats
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable and their hash must remain constant throughout their lifetime. Lists are mutable and unhashable.

questions.question: What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
options: There is no difference; they are exact aliases
A list comprehension builds the full collection eagerly in memory; a generator expression yields items lazily on demand
List comprehensions can only process numbers
questions.explanation: Generator expressions are evaluated lazily one element at a time, making them memory-efficient for large sequences.

questions.question: What is the result of [x.upper() for x in ["py", "go"] if len(x) > 2]?
questions.explanation: Both "py" and "go" have a length of 2, so the condition len(x) > 2 is False for both items, resulting in an empty list [].

questions.question: In a try/except/else/finally block, when does the "else" block execute?
options: Whenever an exception is caught and handled
Only if no exception was raised in the try block
Always, immediately before the finally block
Only if an unhandled fatal error occurred
questions.explanation: The else block in exception handling executes exclusively when the try block completes successfully without raising any exceptions.
