days.title: OOP Foundations: Classes, Instances & Namespaces
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Class vs Instance, The self Parameter, Instantiation Lifecycle, __dict__ Namespaces, Class Attributes, Bound Methods, Dynamic Patching
days.overview: In Python, classes are first-class objects instantiated by the metaclass `type`. Understand how instance state differs from class state, how method binding works, and how Python stores attributes in hash tables across 7 detailed topics.

topics.title: Class Objects vs Instance Objects
explanation: A class in Python is an actual runtime object (an instance of `type`). When Python executes a `class` statement, it evaluates the body into a namespace dictionary and creates a class object in memory.

Instances are distinct heap objects that hold a reference to their class via `__class__`. When you access an attribute on an instance, Python first checks the instance namespace, then the class namespace, and finally the inheritance hierarchy.
keyRules: Classes are instances of `type`
Instances reference their creator class via `obj.__class__`

codeSnippet.title: Class vs Instance Identity
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting the types and identities of classes and their instances.
codeSnippet.code:
class Engine:
    cylinders = 4

v8 = Engine()
print("Class object type:", type(Engine))
print("Instance object type:", type(v8))
print("Instance points back to class:", v8.__class__ is Engine)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Class object type: <class 'type'>
Instance object type: <class 'Engine'>
Instance points back to class: True

topics.title: The self Parameter & Explicit Receiver
explanation: Unlike languages with implicit `this`, Python explicitly passes the target instance as the first parameter to methods, conventionally named `self`.
When calling `obj.method(x)`, Python translates it into `Class.method(obj, x)`. This explicit receiver makes Python methods ordinary functions when accessed through the class.
keyRules: Method call `obj.drive(50)` is syntactic sugar for `Car.drive(obj, 50)`
`self` is not a keyword, but a universal PEP 8 convention

codeSnippet.title: Demonstrating Explicit self Passing
codeSnippet.description: Calling methods both via instance syntax and explicit class function syntax.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Tesla says beep!
Tesla says beep!

topics.title: The Instantiation Lifecycle: __new__ vs __init__
explanation: Creating an object is a two-step process: `__new__` allocates the object in memory, and `__init__` initializes its state.
`__new__(cls, ...)` is a static method that returns a new instance of `cls`. Once `__new__` returns the instance, Python invokes `__init__(self, ...)` to populate attributes.
keyRules: `__new__` is the constructor (allocates memory and returns object)
`__init__` is the initializer (configures state on existing object)
Singleton patterns and immutable subclassing override `__new__`

codeSnippet.title: Tracing Object Creation Lifecycle
codeSnippet.description: Printing execution order of __new__ and __init__.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
1. __new__ allocating memory for class: Lifecycle
2. __init__ initializing state for: ProductionServer

topics.title: Instance and Class Namespaces via __dict__
explanation: Every standard Python object stores its writable attributes in an internal dictionary called `__dict__`.
Modifying `self.x = 10` is functionally equivalent to writing `self.__dict__["x"] = 10`. Because attributes live in a hash table, lookups are fast O(1).
keyRules: `instance.__dict__` holds instance-specific attributes
`Class.__dict__` holds class attributes and functions

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Object __dict__ Dictionaries
codeSnippet.description: Directly inspecting the underlying dictionary storing object state.
codeSnippet.code:
class User:
    role = "Standard"
    def __init__(self, username, email):
        self.username = username
        self.email = email

u = User("alice", "alice@example.com")
print("Instance __dict__:", u.__dict__)
print("Class role in u.__class__.__dict__:", "role" in User.__dict__)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Instance __dict__: {'username': 'alice', 'email': 'alice@example.com'}
Class role in u.__class__.__dict__: True

topics.title: Class Attributes vs Instance Shadowing
explanation: Class attributes are shared across all instances. If you read `instance.attr`, and `attr` is not in `instance.__dict__`, Python reads it from `Class.__dict__`.
However, assigning `instance.attr = value` does NOT mutate the class attribute! It creates a new key in `instance.__dict__`, shadowing the class attribute for that instance alone.
keyRules: Reading falls back from instance to class
Writing to `instance.attr` creates an instance attribute (shadowing)
Mutable class attributes (like lists) mutated in-place affect ALL instances

codeSnippet.title: Attribute Shadowing Demonstration
codeSnippet.description: Showing how assigning to an instance shadows the shared class variable.
codeSnippet.code:
class Node:
    status = "healthy"

n1 = Node()
n2 = Node()
print("Initial status:", n1.status, n2.status)

n1.status = "degraded"  # Shadows class attribute in n1 only
print("After n1 mutation:", n1.status, n2.status)
print("Node class status remains:", Node.status)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Initial status: healthy healthy
After n1 mutation: degraded healthy
Node class status remains: healthy

topics.title: Bound Methods vs Unbound Functions
explanation: When a function defined inside a class is accessed through an instance, Python invokes the descriptor protocol to create a `bound method` object.
A bound method bundles the underlying function pointer with the target instance (`__self__`). When called, it automatically injects `__self__` as the first argument.
keyRules: `Class.method` is a standard function
`instance.method` is a bound method bound to that instance

codeSnippet.title: Bound vs Unbound Method Introspection
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting method object binding and __self__ references.
codeSnippet.code:
class Greeter:
    def greet(self):
        return "Hello"

g = Greeter()
print("Class function:", Greeter.greet)
print("Bound method:", g.greet)
print("Bound instance is g:", g.greet.__self__ is g)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Class function: <function Greeter.greet at ...>
Bound method: <bound method Greeter.greet of <Greeter object at ...>>
Bound instance is g: True

topics.title: Dynamic Attribute Binding & Monkey Patching
explanation: Because Python namespaces are open mutable dictionaries, you can attach new attributes and functions to existing instances or classes at runtime.
Attaching a method directly to an instance requires using `types.MethodType` so that `self` is properly bound.
keyRules: Classes can be modified at runtime (monkey patching)
Direct instance methods require `types.MethodType` for binding

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic Method Binding with MethodType
codeSnippet.description: Binding a new method to a specific instance at runtime.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Pinged 192.168.1.1 successfully

practiceChallenge.title: Build a Self-Registering Service Registry
instructions: Create a class `Service` with a class-level list `registry`.
In `__init__`, append `self` to `Service.registry`.
Implement a class method or function to return active service names.
practiceChallenge.starterCode:
class Service:
    registry = []
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        # TODO: Register instance
        pass

s1 = Service("Auth")
s2 = Service("Billing")
print("Registered count:", len(Service.registry))
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:

    registry = []
    def __init__(self, name):

        Service.registry.append(self)

s1 = Service("Auth")

keyTakeaways: Classes are heap objects created by type.
self is an explicit instance receiver.
__new__ allocates; __init__ configures.
Instance attributes shadow class attributes on assignment.

days.title: Encapsulation, Descriptors & Memory Optimization
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Public vs Protected, Private Name Mangling, The @property Decorator, Getters/Setters/Deleters, Descriptor Protocol, Memory Savings with __slots__, Read-Only Validation
days.overview: Master data hiding and attribute interception in Python. Discover the difference between convention and name mangling, how descriptors intercept attribute access, and how __slots__ eliminates dict overhead across 7 comprehensive topics.

topics.title: Protected Attributes & Single Underscore Convention
explanation: Python does not have enforced `private` keywords. By convention established in PEP 8, an attribute prefixed with a single underscore (e.g. `_internal_state`) is protected: an indicator that it is private implementation detail and not part of public API.
Tools, IDEs, and linters warn against accessing `_protected` attributes from outside the class hierarchy, but Python runtime permits it.
keyRules: Single underscore `_name` is an API convention for protected access
Enforced by linters and code reviews, not by runtime exception

codeSnippet.title: Single Underscore Convention
codeSnippet.description: Distinguishing between public interface and protected internals.
codeSnippet.code:
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance):
        self.owner = owner          # Public
        self._balance = balance      # Protected internal state

acc = BankAccount("Alice", 1000)
print("Public owner:", acc.owner)
print("Internal balance:", acc._balance)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Public owner: Alice
Internal balance: 1000

topics.title: Double Underscore & Name Mangling
explanation: Attributes prefixed with two leading underscores (and at most one trailing underscore), like `__secret`, trigger Python name mangling.
The compiler automatically rewrites the attribute name in `__dict__` to `_ClassName__secret`. This is designed to prevent unintended attribute collisions in subclasses, not for cryptography.
keyRules: `__name` is transformed to `_ClassName__name` in `__dict__`
Prevents accidental override by child classes
Can still be accessed via the mangled name if deliberately needed

codeSnippet.title: Name Mangling in Action
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting mangled attribute names in instance __dict__.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Keys in __dict__: ['_Vault__secret_key']
Access via mangled name: top-secret-99

topics.title: The @property Decorator: Managed Attributes
explanation: The `@property` decorator turns a method into a managed attribute getter. Callers access it with simple dotted syntax (`obj.area`), but under the hood, your function runs.
This enables you to refactor simple attributes into computed properties without breaking client code contracts.
keyRules: Access managed attributes like fields: `circle.area` without parens `()`
Executes custom logic dynamically upon every read

codeSnippet.title: Computed Property with @property
codeSnippet.description: Exposing dynamic calculations as clean attribute access.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Computed area: 20

topics.title: Property Setters and Deleters for Validation
explanation: You can attach setter and deleter functions to a property using `@prop_name.setter` and `@prop_name.deleter`.
This allows you to enforce strict business validation rules (e.g., non-negative temperature, email format) whenever an assignment `obj.prop = val` occurs.
keyRules: Define setter using `@<property_name>.setter`
Raise `ValueError` or `TypeError` on invalid assignment
Enforces encapsulation while preserving clean Pythonic syntax

codeSnippet.title: Validated Property Setter
codeSnippet.description: Enforcing boundary constraints during attribute assignment.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Temperature: 25
Updated temperature: 30

topics.title: The Descriptor Protocol: __get__, __set__, and __delete__
explanation: The descriptor protocol is the underlying machinery powering `@property`, `@classmethod`, `@staticmethod`, and ORMs like Django and SQLAlchemy.

A descriptor is any object defining `__get__(self, instance, owner)`, `__set__(self, instance, value)`, or `__delete__(self, instance)`. Data descriptors (defining both get and set) take precedence over the instance dictionary.
keyRules: Descriptor must be attached as a CLASS attribute, not instance attribute
`__get__` receives both the instance and the owner class

codeSnippet.title: Custom NonNegative Number Descriptor
codeSnippet.description: Building a reusable descriptor that validates numeric fields.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Validated price and stock: 49 100

topics.title: Memory Optimization with __slots__
explanation: By default, Python instances store attributes in an open `__dict__`, which consumes significant heap memory (around 150+ bytes per instance).

By defining `__slots__ = ("x", "y")`, you instruct Python to allocate a fixed-size compact C struct array of pointers instead of a dynamic dictionary, slashing instance memory footprint by 60-70% and accelerating attribute lookups.
keyRules: `__slots__` prevents creation of `__dict__` and `__weakref__` by default
Instances cannot have arbitrary new attributes assigned at runtime
Ideal for high-volume objects (millions of records, particles, vectors)

codeSnippet.title: Memory Savings with __slots__
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating that slotted instances have no __dict__ attribute.
codeSnippet.code:
class SlottedPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = SlottedPoint(10, 20)
print("Has __dict__?:", hasattr(p, "__dict__"))
print("Coordinates:", p.x, p.y)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Has __dict__?: False
Coordinates: 10 20

topics.title: Read-Only and Cached Attributes
explanation: A property without a setter is inherently read-only: trying to reassign `obj.prop = 5` raises `AttributeError: can't set attribute`.
Python 3.8+ introduced `@functools.cached_property`, which executes an expensive computation once on first access and stores the result directly in `instance.__dict__` for subsequent O(1) lookups.
keyRules: Omitting setter creates an immutable property
`cached_property` caches expensive results without custom boilerplate

codeSnippet.title: Read-Only Property Protection
codeSnippet.description: Showing how read-only properties prevent accidental mutations.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Current env: production
Assignment blocked: AttributeError

keyTakeaways: Single underscore is convention; double underscore triggers name mangling.
@property enables getters, setters, and deleters with dot-syntax.
Descriptors power properties, methods, and ORMs.
__slots__ removes __dict__ to minimize memory usage.

days.title: Inheritance, Polymorphism & Abstract Base Classes
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Single Inheritance, Method Overriding, super() Fundamentals, Polymorphic Dispatch, Abstract Classes (abc.ABC), Protocols & Duck Typing, Mixin Design Pattern
days.overview: Design extensible systems using inheritance and polymorphism. Learn when to subclass, how abstract base classes enforce interface contracts, and how Python leverages structural duck typing across 7 detailed topics.

topics.title: Single Inheritance & Base Class Hierarchy
explanation: Inheritance allows a subclass to inherit attributes and methods from a parent class using the syntax `class Child(Parent):`.
Every user-defined class in Python 3 implicitly inherits from the root `object` class, gaining default implementations of `__repr__`, `__eq__`, and `__hash__`.
keyRules: All Python classes inherit from `object`
Subclasses automatically inherit methods from base classes

topics.title: Method Overriding & Behavior Specialization
explanation: A subclass can redefine a method inherited from its parent. When that method is called on a child instance, Python finds and executes the child's version first.
Overriding allows specialized domain behavior without modifying the original base class code (Open-Closed Principle).
keyRules: Child method definition overrides base method with the same name
Base implementation remains intact for instances of the base class

topics.title: Using super() to Extend Base Implementations
explanation: Often you do not want to completely discard the parent's method, but rather extend it with extra initialization or teardown.
`super()` delegates method calls to the next class in the Method Resolution Order (MRO). In single inheritance, `super().__init__(...)` ensures parent constructor logic runs reliably.
keyRules: `super().method(*args)` invokes parent implementation
Prevents duplicating parent attribute assignments

topics.title: Polymorphic Dispatch & Uniform Interfaces
explanation: Polymorphism enables treating different specialized classes through the exact same interface without type checks or `switch` statements.
A function can accept any object with a `.render()` or `.execute()` method and run it transparently.
keyRules: Call methods uniformly without inspecting explicit type
Replaces rigid `if isinstance(x, ...)` branching

topics.title: Abstract Base Classes with abc.ABC & @abstractmethod
explanation: Python's `abc` module lets you define formal interface contracts. A class inheriting from `abc.ABC` with at least one `@abstractmethod` cannot be directly instantiated.
Subclasses MUST override and implement all abstract methods; if they do not, Python raises a `TypeError` at instantiation time.
keyRules: Subclasses of ABC cannot be instantiated until all abstract methods are implemented
Guarantees API compliance at startup

topics.title: Protocols and Structural Duck Typing
explanation: Python is famously duck-typed ("If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck").
With Python 3.8+ `typing.Protocol`, you can define structural subtyping without requiring explicit inheritance. An object satisfies the protocol simply by implementing the matching signatures.
keyRules: Protocols enable static type checking of duck typing
No need to explicitly subclass the Protocol

topics.title: The Mixin Design Pattern
explanation: A Mixin is a specialized class intended to provide standalone behavior to other classes through multiple inheritance, without being instantiated on its own.
Mixins encourage code reuse across unrelated class hierarchies (e.g. `JSONSerializableMixin`, `LoggingMixin`).
keyRules: Mixins should not have their own `__init__` state
Place mixin classes first in inheritance list

days.title: Multiple Inheritance, C3 Linearization & MRO
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Multiple Inheritance Syntax, The Diamond Problem, The C3 Linearization Rules, Inspecting __mro__, Cooperative super() Chaining, Kwargs Forwarding in MRO, Anti-Patterns
days.overview: Conquer Python's most sophisticated inheritance mechanics: the C3 Linearization Algorithm. Understand how Python resolves the diamond problem deterministically and why cooperative super() calls are essential across 7 in-depth topics.

interactiveDiagram.title: The Diamond Problem & C3 MRO Linearization
interactiveDiagram.caption: Class D inherits from B and C, which both inherit from A. C3 Linearization guarantees D -> B -> C -> A -> object with monotonic ordering.

topics.title: Multiple Inheritance Syntax and Mechanics
explanation: Python allows a class to inherit from multiple parent classes: `class D(B, C):`.
This enables rich behavioral composition, but introduces challenges when parents declare methods with identical signatures.
keyRules: Classes can specify multiple parents in comma-separated list
Order of declaration in the class header matters

codeSnippet.title: Multiple Inheritance Declaration
codeSnippet.description: Declaring a class that inherits methods from two distinct base classes.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Can read: reading data
Can write: writing data

topics.title: The Diamond Problem & Ambiguity
explanation: The Diamond Problem occurs when class `D` inherits from `B` and `C`, and both `B` and `C` inherit from root class `A`.

If both `B` and `C` override a method from `A`, which implementation should `D` execute? Without a strict algorithm, resolution order is ambiguous and can lead to subtle bugs or duplicated calls to `A`.
keyRules: Occurs when two base classes share a common ancestor
Naive depth-first search would evaluate A before C, violating subclass precedence

codeSnippet.title: Diamond Problem Topology
codeSnippet.description: Defining diamond hierarchy classes A, B, C, D.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: D resolves ping() to: B

topics.title: The C3 Linearization Algorithm
explanation: Python uses the C3 Linearization Algorithm (introduced in Python 2.3) to produce a monotonic Method Resolution Order (MRO).

The 3 core constraints of C3 are: (1) Children precede parents, (2) Parent order in class definition is preserved, (3) Monotonicity: if A precedes B in one class MRO, A must precede B in any subclass MRO.
keyRules: Children always precede parents
Left-to-right definition order is strictly maintained
Incompatible hierarchies raise `TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order`

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Class MRO
codeSnippet.description: Printing the exact linearized tuple of classes for D.

class A: pass
class B(A): pass
class C(A): pass
class D(B, C): pass

print("Linearized MRO for D:")
for cls in D.__mro__:
    print(" ->", cls.__name__)

topics.title: Cooperative super() Chaining
explanation: `super()` does NOT call the parent class! It calls the NEXT class in the instance MRO.

In multiple inheritance, `super()` enables cooperative multiple inheritance: every method calls `super().method()`, causing execution to traverse the entire diamond without duplicating calls or skipping classes.
keyRules: super() delegates to the next class in `type(self).__mro__`
Every participating class must call `super()` to sustain the chain

codeSnippet.title: Cooperative Chain Execution
codeSnippet.description: Tracing method execution through all diamond ancestors.

topics.title: Kwargs Forwarding Across Cooperative __init__
explanation: When classes in a cooperative MRO require different constructor parameters, methods must accept `**kwargs` and pass remaining keyword arguments forward to `super().__init__(**kwargs)`.
The terminal class (`object.__init__`) accepts zero arguments, so all custom keyword arguments must be consumed by the chain before reaching `object`.
keyRules: Consume needed params with `kwargs.pop('key')` and pass `**kwargs` forward
Prevents missing argument or unexpected argument TypeErrors

topics.title: Inconsistent MRO Conflicts
explanation: If you attempt to define an inheritance topology that violates the C3 constraints (such as asking Python to place class X before Y, while an ancestor demands Y before X), Python halts at class definition time.
It will raise a `TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases`.
keyRules: C3 detects cyclic or conflicting ordering constraints at class creation
Fix by harmonizing base class order or decoupling hierarchy

topics.title: Composition vs Multiple Inheritance Tradeoffs
explanation: While multiple inheritance is powerful for mixins and frameworks, deeply nested diamond hierarchies are notoriously hard to reason about.
The Gang of Four principle "Favor object composition over class inheritance" is standard Python practice: store helper components as attributes instead of inheriting them.
keyRules: Composition is easier to test and mock than deep inheritance
Use mixins for orthogonal, stateless capabilities

codeSnippet.title: Composition Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Composing distinct components into a cohesive service.

keyTakeaways: C3 Linearization computes a deterministic, monotonic MRO.
super() delegates to the next class in MRO, not the syntactic parent.
Kwargs forwarding enables diverse cooperative constructors.
Prefer composition for business logic; reserve mixins for cross-cutting concerns.

days.title: Dunder Magic Methods & Operator Overloading
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: __str__ vs __repr__, Comparison Dunders, Arithmetic Overloading, Emulating Containers (__getitem__), Callable Instances (__call__), Context Protocol (__enter__/__exit__), Hashability (__hash__)
days.overview: Transform custom classes into first-class Python citizens. Learn how special double-underscore methods emulate numbers, sequences, mappings, context managers, and callable functions across 7 deep topics.

topics.title: __repr__ vs __str__: Representations for Developers vs Users
explanation: `__repr__` is intended for developers and debugging: it should ideally return an unambiguous string that could recreate the object (e.g. `Vector(3, 4)`).
`__str__` is intended for end users and human-readable output (e.g. `Vector at (3, 4)`). If `__str__` is missing, Python falls back to `__repr__`.
keyRules: Always implement `__repr__` first
`__repr__` should be unambiguous; `__str__` should be readable

codeSnippet.title: __repr__ and __str__ Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Defining distinct developer and user representations.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
repr(v): Vector(3, 4)
str(v): (3, 4)

topics.title: Arithmetic Operator Overloading (__add__, __mul__)
explanation: Python maps binary operators directly to dunder methods: `+` calls `__add__`, `*` calls `__mul__`, and `-` calls `__sub__`.
To support operations where your custom class is on the right side of a standard type (e.g., `3 * vector`), implement reflected methods like `__rmul__`.
keyRules: `a + b` invokes `a.__add__(b)`
If `__add__` returns `NotImplemented`, Python attempts `b.__radd__(a)`

codeSnippet.title: Vector Arithmetic Overloading
codeSnippet.description: Implementing __add__ and __mul__ on custom vector class.

topics.title: Rich Comparison Methods (__eq__, __lt__, functools.total_ordering)
explanation: Python provides 6 rich comparison dunders: `__eq__`, `__ne__`, `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, and `__ge__`.
Instead of manually coding all 6, decorating your class with `@functools.total_ordering` and defining `__eq__` plus just one ordering dunder (`__lt__`) automatically derives the rest.
keyRules: Default `__eq__` compares memory identity (`is`), not value equivalence
`@total_ordering` synthesizes `<=`, `>`, `>=` from `==` and `<`

codeSnippet.title: Total Ordering Comparisons
codeSnippet.description: Deriving full comparison suite with functools.total_ordering.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
t1 < t2: True
t2 > t1: True
t1 <= t2: True

topics.title: Emulating Containers: __len__, __getitem__, __contains__
explanation: By implementing the sequence protocol methods, your custom object can be indexed with brackets `obj[i]`, measured with `len(obj)`, and checked with `in`.
Supporting slice objects in `__getitem__` allows custom collections to slice just like native lists.
keyRules: `len(x)` calls `x.__len__()`
`x[i]` calls `x.__getitem__(i)`
`item in x` calls `x.__contains__(item)`

topics.title: Callable Instances with __call__
explanation: Defining `__call__(self, *args, **kwargs)` makes an instance callable just like a regular function: `obj(*args)`.
This is the idiomatic way to create stateful function objects, custom decorators, and parameterized pipelines.
keyRules: `obj()` delegates to `obj.__call__()`
Callable instances retain persistent state across invocations

codeSnippet.title: Stateful Accumulator with __call__
codeSnippet.description: Invoking object instances as functions.

topics.title: Context Management Protocol: __enter__ and __exit__
explanation: The `with` statement calls `__enter__` upon entering the block and guarantees `__exit__` runs when exiting, even if exceptions are raised.
`__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)` receives exception details. If `__exit__` returns `True`, the exception is suppressed; if it returns `None` or `False`, it propagates.
keyRules: `__enter__` returns the resource bound by `as var`
`__exit__` handles cleanup and error suppression

codeSnippet.title: Custom Timer Context Manager
codeSnippet.description: Measuring execution duration using enter and exit dunders.
codeSnippet.code:
import time

class Benchmark:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"Block finished in {self.elapsed:.4f}s")
        return False

with Benchmark():
    total = sum(i for i in range(100000))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Block finished in 0.0...s

topics.title: Hashability and Immutability: __hash__ and __eq__
explanation: For an object to be used as a dictionary key or set element, it must be hashable: its hash value must never change during its lifetime.
If you override `__eq__`, Python automatically sets `__hash__ = None` to prevent bugs. To make it hashable again, implement `__hash__` using an immutable tuple of attributes.
keyRules: Equal objects must have equal hash values: `a == b ==> hash(a) == hash(b)`
Never hash mutable attributes

days.title: Dataclasses, Type Hints & Metaprogramming
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: @dataclass Decorator, Field Defaults & default_factory, Frozen Immutable Dataclasses, Type Annotations & Generics, Runtime Introspection (inspect/getattr), __init_subclass__, Metaclasses with type
days.overview: Modernize Python code with declarative data classes, static type hints, and metaprogramming hooks. Eliminate boilerplate and enforce class contracts at compile and runtime across 7 topics.

topics.title: The @dataclass Decorator: Automatic Boilerplate Generation
explanation: Python 3.7 introduced `@dataclass` in the standard library. It automatically generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`, and ordering methods based on type annotations.
It eliminates hundreds of lines of repetitive boilerplate while preserving standard Python class semantics.
keyRules: Fields require type annotations to be recognized by dataclass
Generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__` by default

codeSnippet.title: Clean Model with @dataclass
codeSnippet.description: Defining structured data models with automatic representations.
codeSnippet.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Transaction:
    sender: str
    recipient: str
    amount: float

t = Transaction("Alice", "Bob", 250.75)
print(t)
print("Equality check:", t == Transaction("Alice", "Bob", 250.75))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Transaction(sender='Alice', recipient='Bob', amount=250.75)
Equality check: True

topics.title: Field Customization and default_factory
explanation: Standard default values for mutable types (like `tags: list = []`) are forbidden in dataclasses because lists are shared singletons across all instances.
Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=list)` to guarantee that each new instance receives its own freshly allocated list or dictionary.
keyRules: Never use mutable literals as default values
`field(default_factory=...)` creates fresh instances

codeSnippet.title: Using field(default_factory=...) with Dataclasses
codeSnippet.description: Safe mutable default initialization in dataclasses.
codeSnippet.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class UserProfile:
    username: str
    badges: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

u1 = UserProfile("alice")
u1.badges.append("Pioneer")
u2 = UserProfile("bob")
print("Alice badges:", u1.badges)
print("Bob badges:", u2.badges)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Alice badges: ['Pioneer']
Bob badges: []

topics.title: Immutable Dataclasses (frozen=True)
explanation: Adding `@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes the instance read-only. Any attempt to modify an attribute after instantiation raises `FrozenInstanceError`.
Frozen dataclasses also automatically generate a `__hash__` method, making them immediately safe to use as dictionary keys or set elements.
keyRules: `frozen=True` prevents in-place mutation
Frozen dataclasses are automatically hashable if their fields are hashable

codeSnippet.title: Frozen Dataclass Immutability
codeSnippet.description: Enforcing immutable value objects with frozen=True.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Mutation blocked: FrozenInstanceError
Safe in set: 1

topics.title: Modern Type Annotations and Generics
explanation: Modern Python (3.9+) supports built-in generic types (`list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, `tuple[int, ...]`) directly without importing from `typing`.
For parameterized functions and generic classes, use `TypeVar` and `Generic[T]` to enforce consistent types across inputs and outputs.
keyRules: Use built-in types for generics (`list[int]`, `dict[str, Any]`)
Union types with pipe syntax: `int | str | None`

topics.title: Runtime Introspection with getattr, setattr & inspect
explanation: Python allows inspecting and manipulating objects dynamically at runtime using `getattr()`, `setattr()`, `hasattr()`, and `inspect`.
This forms the backbone of serialization frameworks, CLI argument parsers, and dependency injection containers.
keyRules: `getattr(obj, name, default)` safely retrieves attributes
`setattr(obj, name, val)` modifies attributes dynamically

topics.title: Subclass Hooking with __init_subclass__
explanation: Python 3.6 introduced `__init_subclass__`, which provides an elegant hook for parent classes to intercept and configure subclasses when they are defined.
It replaces complex metaclasses for 90% of subclass registration, validation, and schema configuration use cases.
keyRules: `__init_subclass__` runs automatically when a child class is created
Can accept custom class keyword arguments: `class Child(Parent, plugin_name="v1"):`

codeSnippet.title: Automatic Plugin Registration with __init_subclass__
codeSnippet.description: Registering child plugins automatically upon class definition.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Registered plugins: ['pdf', 'image']

topics.title: Metaclasses with type: The Class Factories
explanation: Just as objects are instances of classes, classes are instances of metaclasses. The default metaclass is `type`.
By subclassing `type` and overriding `__new__(mcs, name, bases, namespace)`, you can intercept and modify class creation itself, enforcing attributes or transforming methods before the class exists.
keyRules: `class MyClass(metaclass=MyMeta):` defines custom metaclass
Use sparingly: "Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about"

Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults.

days.title: Iterators, Generators & The Yield Protocol
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Iterable vs Iterator Protocol, __iter__ and __next__, StopIteration Mechanics, Generator Functions & yield, Generator Expressions Memory Profile, Bidirectional Generators (.send()), Delegation with yield from
days.overview: Master Python's lazy evaluation engine. Understand how iterators traverse data without indexing, how generators execute on-demand with minimal memory, and how yield from delegates across 7 in-depth topics.

topics.title: Iterable vs Iterator Protocol
explanation: An `Iterable` is any object that can return an iterator via `iter(obj)` (implements `__iter__`). Examples: list, tuple, dict, str.
An `Iterator` is an object that represents a stream of data; it implements `__next__()` to return successive items, and `__iter__()` returning itself.
keyRules: `iter(iterable)` returns an iterator
`next(iterator)` returns the next value or raises `StopIteration`

codeSnippet.title: Iterating Manually with iter() and next()
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting iterable and iterator objects under the hood.
codeSnippet.code:
items = [10, 20]
it = iter(items)
print("Iterator object:", type(it))
print("First item:", next(it))
print("Second item:", next(it))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Iterator object: <class 'list_iterator'>
First item: 10
Second item: 20

topics.title: Custom Iterator Class Implementation
explanation: To build a custom iterator, define a class with `__iter__` (returning `self`) and `__next__`.
When the sequence ends, `__next__` MUST raise `StopIteration`. The `for` loop catches this exception automatically to cleanly terminate the loop.
keyRules: `__iter__` returns self
`__next__` updates state and returns value, raising `StopIteration` when complete

codeSnippet.title: Countdown Iterator Class
codeSnippet.description: Building a stateful iterator that raises StopIteration.

topics.title: Generator Functions and the yield Statement
explanation: Any function containing the `yield` keyword is a generator function. Calling it does NOT run the code; it returns a generator object.

When `next()` is called on the generator, execution advances until hitting `yield`. The yielded value is returned, and the function's execution frame (local variables and instruction pointer) is frozen in memory until the next request.
keyRules: yield pauses execution and preserves local variables in the frame
Calling generator function returns a generator object without running yet

codeSnippet.title: Lazy Fibonacci Generator
codeSnippet.description: Generating infinite sequences lazily with yield.

topics.title: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions Memory Comparison
explanation: List comprehensions `[x for x in data]` build the entire collection in memory upfront, taking megabytes or gigabytes for large sequences.

Generator expressions `(x for x in data)` evaluate one item at a time lazily on demand. Their memory footprint is tiny and constant O(1), regardless of whether they process 10 items or 10 billion items.
keyRules: Parentheses `(x for x in ...)` create generator expressions
Memory usage is constant O(1) regardless of sequence length

codeSnippet.title: Memory Footprint Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Comparing memory sizes of list vs generator expression.
codeSnippet.code:
import sys

list_comp = [x * 2 for x in range(10000)]
gen_exp = (x * 2 for x in range(10000))

print("List size in bytes:", sys.getsizeof(list_comp))
print("Generator size in bytes:", sys.getsizeof(gen_exp))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
List size in bytes: 85176
Generator size in bytes: 200

topics.title: Bidirectional Generators: Communicating with .send()
explanation: Generators are not just data producers—they can also receive data dynamically from callers using the `.send(value)` method.
Inside the generator, `val = yield output` receives whatever the caller passed into `.send(val)`. This enables coroutines and state machine programming.
keyRules: Must prime the generator first with `next(gen)` or `gen.send(None)`
Enables bidirectional data flow between caller and generator

codeSnippet.title: Running Average Coroutine with .send()
codeSnippet.description: Sending dynamic values into a running generator.
codeSnippet.code:
def running_average():
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    avg = None
    while True:
        val = yield avg
        if val is None: break
        total += val
        count += 1
        avg = total / count

avg_gen = running_average()
next(avg_gen)  # Prime
print("Avg after 10:", avg_gen.send(10))
print("Avg after 20:", avg_gen.send(20))
print("Avg after 30:", avg_gen.send(30))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Avg after 10: 10.0
Avg after 20: 15.0
Avg after 30: 20.0

topics.title: Delegation with yield from
explanation: Python 3.3 introduced `yield from subgenerator()`, establishing a direct transparent bidirectional pipeline between the outer caller and an inner subgenerator.
It forwards values, exceptions, and the subgenerator's return value automatically, eliminating verbose manual forwarding loops.
keyRules: `yield from iterable` delegates value production
Captures subgenerator `return value` into a variable: `result = yield from subgen()`

codeSnippet.title: Subgenerator Delegation with yield from
codeSnippet.description: Flattening nested iterables cleanly using yield from.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Merged stream: [1, 2, 'a', 'b', True]

topics.title: Generator Pipelines: Composable Data Processing
explanation: Generators can be chained together in pipelines, resembling Unix pipes (`cat log | grep ERROR | cut`).
Each generator processes data on-the-fly and yields it to the next step, allowing petabyte-scale data stream processing with minuscule memory consumption.
keyRules: Compose small, single-responsibility generator stages
Data streams through the stages without accumulating in RAM

codeSnippet.title: Data Stream Processing Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Chaining generators for filtering and transforming logs.

instructions: Write a generator function `batch(iterable, size)`.
Yield lists of items up to `size` elements each.
Yield the final partial batch if items remain.

keyTakeaways: Iterables implement __iter__; iterators implement __next__ and __iter__.
yield pauses function execution, maintaining local frame state.
Generators enable infinite sequences with O(1) memory footprint.
yield from transparently connects callers to subgenerators.

quiz.title: Week 3 Qualifying Exam: OOP & Advanced Architecture
quiz.description: Score 80% or higher to unlock Week 4: Concurrency, Asyncio & Production Engineering.

questions.question: Which method in Python is the actual object constructor responsible for allocating memory before state initialization?
questions.explanation: __new__ is the static constructor method that allocates memory and returns a fresh instance. __init__ merely initializes state on an already created instance.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of the C3 Linearization Algorithm in Python?
options: To compress bytecode files into .pyc binaries
To compute a deterministic, monotonic Method Resolution Order (MRO) for multiple inheritance
To optimize garbage collection cycles for cyclic references
To convert dynamically typed functions into static C extensions
questions.explanation: C3 Linearization guarantees a deterministic, monotonic Method Resolution Order preserving subclass precedence and local declaration order across multiple inheritance diamond hierarchies.

questions.question: What happens to the internal memory layout of an instance when a class defines `__slots__ = ("x", "y")`?
options: The class becomes read-only and immutable
The __dict__ hash table is eliminated and attributes are stored in a compact pointer array
All attributes are stored in a shared global class dictionary
Attributes x and y are converted to 64-bit C floats
questions.explanation: __slots__ disables the default instance __dict__, saving substantial memory by storing attributes in fixed-offset C pointer slots.

questions.question: In the Descriptor protocol, which condition defines a "Data Descriptor"?
options: Defining only __get__ without any other dunders
questions.explanation: A Data Descriptor defines both __get__ and __set__ (and/or __delete__). Data descriptors take precedence over the instance dictionary during attribute lookup.

questions.question: Why does a generator expression `(x * 2 for x in range(1_000_000))` consume virtually identical memory to `(x * 2 for x in range(10))`?
options: Because Python caches all integer values in a global table
Because generators evaluate lazily on-demand without storing the entire sequence in memory
Because range() allocates in CPU registers instead of heap memory
Because the Python compiler optimizes generator expressions to C while-loops
questions.explanation: Generators yield values on-the-fly and preserve only the current frame state, achieving constant O(1) memory consumption regardless of stream length.

days.title: Decorators, Closures & Functional Metaprogramming
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Lexical Scoping & Closures, Decorator Anatomy, functools.wraps, Decorators with Arguments, Class-Based Decorators, Decorator Stacking Order, Practical Caching & Rate Limiting
days.overview: Decorators are one of Python's signature design powers. Learn how lexical closures capture state, how to write clean higher-order functions, and how to preserve function metadata across 7 in-depth topics.

topics.title: Lexical Scoping and Closures
explanation: A closure is a function that retains access to variables in its enclosing lexical scope even after that outer scope has finished execution.
Python achieves this via cell objects in `func.__closure__`. If you need to reassign a variable in an outer non-global scope, use the `nonlocal` keyword.
keyRules: Closures capture free variables from enclosing parent functions
Use `nonlocal` to modify an enclosing variable instead of creating a local one

codeSnippet.title: Closure State Retention
codeSnippet.description: Creating a stateful closure using lexical scoping and nonlocal.
codeSnippet.code:
def make_counter(start=0):
    count = start
    def step():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return step

c1 = make_counter(10)
print("Step 1:", c1())
print("Step 2:", c1())
print("Closure cells:", len(c1.__closure__))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Step 1: 11
Step 2: 12
Closure cells: 1

topics.title: The Anatomy of a Python Decorator
explanation: A decorator is simply a callable that takes a function as an argument and returns a replacement callable.
The `@decorator` syntax is pure syntactic sugar: writing `@my_dec` before `def foo():` is exactly equivalent to `foo = my_dec(foo)`.
keyRules: `@dec` is syntactic sugar for `fn = dec(fn)`
Wrappers typically accept `*args, **kwargs` and return the result

topics.title: Preserving Metadata with functools.wraps
explanation: When a function is wrapped, its `__name__`, `__doc__`, and `__annotations__` are replaced by the wrapper's attributes by default, breaking introspection and debuggers.
Decorating the wrapper with `@functools.wraps(func)` copies over all identity attributes and sets `__wrapped__` to point directly to the original function.
keyRules: Always decorate inner wrappers with `@functools.wraps(func)`
Preserves docstrings, function names, and signature introspection

topics.title: Decorators with Arguments (3-Layer Factory)
explanation: If a decorator requires parameters (e.g., `@retry(max_attempts=3)`), you need a 3-layer function factory.
Layer 1 accepts decorator arguments; Layer 2 accepts the target function; Layer 3 is the inner wrapper that executes the actual calls.
keyRules: A decorator with arguments is a function that RETURNS a decorator
Requires 3 nested functions or a class-based approach

topics.title: Class-Based Decorators with __call__
explanation: Instead of nested functions, you can implement decorators as classes by implementing `__init__(self, func)` and `__call__(self, *args, **kwargs)`.
Class decorators are particularly well-suited for stateful decorators, such as execution call counters, memoization tables, or circuit breakers.
keyRules: `__init__` receives the decorated function
`__call__` executes on every function invocation

codeSnippet.title: Call Counter Class Decorator

codeSnippet.expectedOutput: query_db was invoked 3 times

topics.title: Decorator Stacking and Evaluation Order
explanation: When multiple decorators are applied to a single function, they are evaluated bottom-to-top (inside-out).
keyRules: Decorators are applied from bottom-to-top at definition time
Outer wrappers execute first during function calls

codeSnippet.title: Tracing Decorator Stacking Order
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating inside-out wrapping order.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Rendered HTML: Decorators Stacked!

topics.title: Production Caching with functools.lru_cache
explanation: Python's standard library provides `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)`: a high-performance Least Recently Used memoization decorator.
It caches function outputs based on input arguments, turning exponential recursive algorithms (like naive Fibonacci $O(2^n)$) into linear $O(n)$ computations.
keyRules: Arguments to lru_cache functions must be hashable
Use `lru_cache(maxsize=None)` for unbounded caching

codeSnippet.title: High-Speed Memoization with lru_cache
codeSnippet.description: Accelerating recursive computation using lru_cache.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
fib(35) computed instantly: 9227465
Cache info: CacheInfo(hits=33, misses=36, maxsize=64, currsize=36)

Print elapsed seconds with 4 decimal places.
Use `@functools.wraps` to preserve function identity.

import time

@dec is syntactic sugar for fn = dec(fn).

days.title: File I/O, Serialization & Pathlib
days.subtitle: 7 Topics: Context Managed File I/O, Text vs Binary Buffers, Modern Paths with pathlib, JSON Parsing & Custom Encoders, CSV DictReader/DictWriter, Security Risks of Pickle, Binary Packing with struct
days.overview: Interact reliably with storage and network data streams. Learn how context managers prevent file descriptor leaks, how pathlib replaces legacy os.path, and how to safely serialize structured data across 7 comprehensive topics.

topics.title: Deterministic File I/O with Context Managers
explanation: Operating systems allocate a finite pool of file descriptors. Failing to close files can cause system descriptor starvation, buffer flushes to be skipped, or file locking errors.
The `with open("file.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:` construct guarantees the file descriptor is closed and buffers are flushed immediately upon leaving the block.
keyRules: Always specify `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly for text files
Always use `with` statements for automatic resource cleanup

codeSnippet.title: Context-Managed File Writing and Reading
codeSnippet.description: Safely writing and reading data using open context managers.
codeSnippet.code:
import io

# Simulating file stream with io.StringIO
stream = io.StringIO()
stream.write("Log Entry: System started\nStatus: Operational")
stream.seek(0)

for line in stream:
    print("Read:", line.strip())
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Read: Log Entry: System started
Read: Status: Operational

topics.title: Text vs Binary Mode (UTF-8 Encodings vs Raw Bytes)
explanation: In text mode (`"r"`), Python decodes raw bytes into Unicode `str` objects according to an encoding (like UTF-8) and translates platform newline conventions (`\r\n` to `\n`).
In binary mode (`"rb"`), Python reads raw `bytes` objects without modification, essential for images, audio, network packets, and compiled formats.
keyRules: Text mode returns `str`; binary mode returns `bytes`
Encoding errors occur when byte sequences cannot be decoded to UTF-8

codeSnippet.title: Text vs Raw Bytes Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting string encoding to UTF-8 byte representations.
codeSnippet.code:
message = "Python 🐍"
byte_data = message.encode("utf-8")
print("String:", message, "type:", type(message))
print("Raw bytes:", byte_data, "length:", len(byte_data))
print("Decoded back:", byte_data.decode("utf-8"))
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
String: Python 🐍 type: <class 'str'>
Raw bytes: b'Python \xf0\x9f\x90\x8d' length: 11
Decoded back: Python 🐍

topics.title: Modern Filesystem Navigation with pathlib
explanation: Python 3.4 introduced `pathlib`, providing object-oriented filesystem paths that replace clunky `os.path` string manipulations.
Path objects support operator overloading with the `/` slash operator for platform-independent path joining (`path / "subdir" / "file.txt"`).
keyRules: Use `/` operator to join paths cleanly across OSes
Methods `.exists()`, `.is_file()`, `.read_text()`, `.suffix` provide unified access

codeSnippet.title: Pathlib Operations
codeSnippet.description: Constructing and inspecting path objects.
codeSnippet.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("/var/log/app/service.log")
print("File name:", p.name)
print("File stem:", p.stem)
print("Extension:", p.suffix)
print("Parent folder:", p.parent.name)
joined = Path("home") / "developer" / "code"
print("Joined path:", joined)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
File name: service.log
File stem: service
Extension: .log
Parent folder: app
Joined path: home/developer/code

topics.title: JSON Serialization & Custom JSONEncoders
explanation: The `json` module translates Python data structures to JSON strings (`dumps`) and vice versa (`loads`).

Standard types (dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans) serialize automatically. Non-standard types (like `datetime`, `UUID`, or custom classes) require a custom `JSONEncoder` subclass or `default` serializer function.
keyRules: `json.dumps(obj)` serializes to string; `json.loads(str)` deserializes
Pass `default=callable` to handle custom objects like datetimes

codeSnippet.title: Custom Object JSON Serialization
codeSnippet.description: Serializing non-standard types using custom default function.

topics.title: Structured Tabular Data with CSV DictReader and DictWriter
explanation: Python's `csv` module includes `DictReader` and `DictWriter` for reading and writing CSV rows mapped directly to dictionaries keyed by header column names.
This avoids brittle index-based column lookups (`row[3]`) and automatically accommodates reordered CSV columns.
keyRules: `csv.DictReader` parses rows into `{column: value}` dicts
`csv.DictWriter` requires explicit `fieldnames` and `writeheader()`

codeSnippet.title: Reading CSV into Dictionaries with DictReader
codeSnippet.description: Parsing CSV data streams into structured dictionaries.
codeSnippet.code:
import csv
import io

csv_data = "id,name,role\n101,Alice,Engineer\n102,Bob,Architect"
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(csv_data))
for row in reader:
    print(f"User {row['id']}: {row['name']} ({row['role']})")
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
User 101: Alice (Engineer)
User 102: Bob (Architect)

topics.title: Serialization Security: The Risks of pickle
explanation: Python's `pickle` module can serialize arbitrary Python objects. However, unpickling untrusted data is a severe security vulnerability: `pickle.loads()` can execute arbitrary shell commands via `__reduce__` exploit payloads.
Rule of thumb: Never unpickle untrusted data from network requests. Prefer JSON, Protocol Buffers, or message packs for untrusted inputs.
keyRules: `pickle` is not secure against erroneous or maliciously constructed data
Use JSON or protobufs for untrusted network payloads

codeSnippet.title: Pickle Serialization Warning
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating safe standard serialization alternatives to pickle.
codeSnippet.code:
import json

# Safe serialization contract for distributed services
safe_data = {"user_id": 481, "role": "admin"}
payload = json.dumps(safe_data)
print("Safe portable JSON payload:", payload)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Safe portable JSON payload: {"user_id": 481, "role": "admin"}

topics.title: Binary Packing & Unpacking with struct
explanation: For binary wire protocols, file headers, and low-level C interoperability, the `struct` module packs Python values into compact byte sequences matching C struct layouts.
Format specifiers like `>I` (big-endian 32-bit uint) or `<h` (little-endian 16-bit signed short) allow byte-exact network parsing.
keyRules: `struct.pack(fmt, *args)` converts Python values into bytes
`struct.unpack(fmt, bytes)` decodes bytes back into a tuple

codeSnippet.title: Binary Packing with struct
codeSnippet.description: Packing network header integers into raw bytes.
codeSnippet.code:
import struct

# Format: > (big-endian) I (4-byte unsigned int) H (2-byte unsigned short)
packet = struct.pack(">IH", 1024, 80)
print("Packed bytes:", packet, "byte size:", len(packet))
unpacked = struct.unpack(">IH", packet)
print("Unpacked values:", unpacked)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Packed bytes: b'\x00\x00\x04\x00\x00P' byte size: 6
Unpacked values: (1024, 80)

practiceChallenge.title: Serialize and Deserialize a User Registry to JSON
instructions: Create a dictionary of 2 users with names and scores.
Convert the dictionary to a formatted JSON string using `json.dumps(indent=2)`.
Parse the string back using `json.loads()` and verify the data.

import json

users = {"u1": {"name": "Alice", "score": 95}, "u2": {"name": "Bob", "score": 88}}
encoded = json.dumps(users, indent=2)
print("JSON String:\n" + encoded)
decoded = json.loads(encoded)
print("Decoded user 1 score:", decoded["u1"]["score"])
