days.title: JavaScript Core Fundamentals from Scratch
days.subtitle: Data types, memory models, let/const, coercion, and operators
days.overview: Begin programming in JavaScript from the absolute ground up. Understand primitives vs references, variable declaration scopes, truthiness, strict equality, and control flow.

topics.title: JavaScript Primitive Data Types vs Objects
explanation: JavaScript has 7 primitive types: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `bigint`.
Primitives are immutable and passed by value. Everything else is an `object` (arrays, functions, plain objects, dates), which are mutable and passed by reference.

codeSnippet.title: Value vs Reference in JavaScript
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating how primitives copy by value while objects copy references.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
a is: 42
user1 role is: Tech Lead

topics.pitfall: Assigning an object to a new variable does not clone it; modifying `user2` mutates `user1`. Use `{ ...user1 }` or `structuredClone(user1)` for copies.

quickCheck.question: Which of the following is NOT a JavaScript primitive data type?
quickCheck.explanation: Arrays are objects (instances of Array.prototype) in JavaScript; string, number, and boolean are primitives.

topics.title: Variable Declarations: const vs let vs var
explanation: `const` declares block-scoped variables that cannot be reassigned (prefer this by default).
`let` declares block-scoped variables that can be reassigned (e.g. loop counters).
`var` is function-scoped, hoisted with `undefined`, and can be re-declared; avoid `var` in modern JavaScript.

codeSnippet.title: Block Scope with const and let
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating temporal dead zone and block scoping.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Counter is: 1

topics.pitfall: `const` prevents variable reassignment, but does NOT make object properties immutable. Properties inside a `const obj = {}` can still be modified.

quickCheck.question: What happens when you declare a variable with const obj = { age: 20 } and then run obj.age = 21?
options: The mutation succeeds because const protects the reference, not the object properties
quickCheck.explanation: const binds the reference; mutating internal properties of an object or array is completely legal unless Object.freeze() is used.

topics.title: Strict Equality (===) vs Loose Equality (==) & Type Coercion
explanation: `===` (strict equality) checks both value and type without coercion.
`==` (loose equality) attempts implicit type conversion before comparison, leading to notorious bugs like `0 == false` (true) and `"" == 0` (true).
Always use `===` and `!==` in professional code.

codeSnippet.title: Strict vs Loose Equality Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Comparing type coercion behavior.
codeSnippet.code:
console.log('5' == 5);   // true (Loose: coerced string to number)
console.log('5' === 5);  // false (Strict: string is not number)

console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false

console.log(0 === false);        // false
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
true
false
true
false
false

topics.pitfall: Using loose equality `==` can cause security flaws in authentication checks (e.g. comparing string tokens to empty arrays or numbers).

quickCheck.question: What is the result of expression ("42" === 42)?
quickCheck.explanation: Strict equality requires both the value and the type to match. A string never strictly equals a number.

topics.title: Truthiness, Falsiness & The 8 Falsy Values
explanation: In JavaScript conditions (`if`, ternary), values are coerced to booleans.

There are exactly 8 falsy values in JavaScript: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy (including empty arrays `[]` and empty objects `{}`!).

codeSnippet.title: Testing Truthiness of Common Values
codeSnippet.description: Checking boolean conversion of empty structures and falsy values.
codeSnippet.code:
const checkTruth = (val) => Boolean(val);

console.log('"" is:', checkTruth(""));         // false (empty string is falsy)
console.log('0 is:', checkTruth(0));           // false
console.log('null is:', checkTruth(null));     // false
console.log('[] is:', checkTruth([]));         // true! (Empty array is truthy)
console.log('{} is:', checkTruth({}));         // true! (Empty object is truthy)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
"" is: false
0 is: false
null is: false
[] is: true
{} is: true

topics.pitfall: Checking `if (items)` to see if an array has elements fails because `[]` is truthy! Check `if (items.length > 0)` instead.

quickCheck.question: Is an empty array [] in JavaScript truthy or falsy?
quickCheck.explanation: All objects in JavaScript (including empty arrays [] and empty objects {}) evaluate to truthy.

topics.title: Logical Operators: Short-Circuiting (&&, ||, and ??)
explanation: `&&` returns the first falsy operand, or the last operand if all are truthy.
`||` returns the first truthy operand, or the last operand if all are falsy.
`??` (Nullish Coalescing) returns the right-hand operand ONLY if left is `null` or `undefined` (unlike `||`, it does NOT replace `0` or `""`).

codeSnippet.title: Comparing || (OR) with ?? (Nullish Coalescing)
codeSnippet.description: Handling zero and empty string default values safely.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Using ||: 10
Using ??: 0

topics.pitfall: Using `||` for default settings replaces valid inputs like `0`, `false`, or `""`. Always prefer `??` for default configurations.

quickCheck.question: What does expression (false ?? true) evaluate to?
quickCheck.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator ?? only triggers for null and undefined. false is defined, so false is returned.

topics.title: Control Flow: if-else, switch, and Ternary Operator
explanation: Control flow structures direct code execution based on boolean conditions.
The ternary operator `condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse` provides an inline expression ideal for returning UI states in React or template strings.

codeSnippet.title: Ternary Expressions vs Switch Statements
codeSnippet.description: Clean concise conditional evaluation.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Badge: 🛡️ Administrator
Access level: 3

topics.pitfall: Never nest multiple ternary operators deeper than 2 levels; it damages code readability. Use a function with early returns instead.

quickCheck.question: What is the main advantage of the ternary operator over an if statement?
options: It is faster on the CPU
It is an expression that yields a value and can be embedded inline
It does not require a condition
quickCheck.explanation: Ternaries are expressions, meaning they evaluate directly to a value that can be assigned to a variable or returned from a function.

topics.title: Loops: for, for...of, and while
explanation: Use standard `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` when you need numeric indices.
Use `for (const item of array)` for clean iteration over iterable values (arrays, sets, maps).
Use `for...in` ONLY for iterating over object keys (not arrays).

codeSnippet.title: Iterating Collections with for...of
codeSnippet.description: Modern clean iteration over an array of student records.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Learned skill: HTML5
Learned skill: CSS3
Learned skill: JavaScript
Learned skill: Node.js

topics.pitfall: Do not use `for...in` on arrays; it iterates over property keys (as strings) and may enumerate non-numeric prototype properties.

quickCheck.question: Which loop construct is recommended for cleanly iterating directly over array values?
quickCheck.explanation: for...of iterates over iterable values (elements of an array) directly.

topics.title: Functions: Declarations vs Expressions vs Arrow Functions
explanation: Function declarations `function fn() {}` are hoisted with their complete implementation.
Arrow functions `const fn = () => {}` do not bind their own `this`, `arguments`, or `super`, making them the modern standard for callbacks, closures, and React components.

codeSnippet.title: Arrow Functions and Concise Bodies
codeSnippet.description: Implicit returns and lexical this scoping.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Tax on $100: 8
Add 5 + 7: 12
Double 21: 42

topics.pitfall: Arrow functions do not have their own `this` keyword; do not use them as object methods when you need `this` to refer to the host object.

quickCheck.question: What happens to this inside an arrow function?
options: It refers to the global window object always
It is lexically bound from the surrounding enclosing scope
It creates a new this object
quickCheck.explanation: Arrow functions capture this lexically from the scope in which they were defined.

practiceChallenge.title: Build a Safe Shopping Cart Tax & Total Calculator
instructions: Declare a cart array containing items with name and price.
Calculate total price using a loop or reduce.
Apply nullish coalescing to support optional discount codes.
Format and return the final receipt string.
hints: Use discountPercent ?? 0 so that if discountPercent is undefined, it safely defaults to 0.
Sum up item.price for each item in the cart.

keyTakeaways: Primitives copy by value; objects and arrays copy by memory reference.
Always use const by default and let when reassignment is needed; avoid var.
Use strict equality === and nullish coalescing ?? to avoid coercion bugs.

days.title: Modern JavaScript ES6+, Arrays, Async & Promises
days.subtitle: Destructuring, rest/spread, map/filter/reduce, Promises, and async/await
days.overview: Master the idioms of modern JavaScript: destructuring arrays and objects, spread/rest operators, functional array transformations (map, filter, reduce), and asynchronous programming with Promises and async/await.

topics.title: Object & Array Destructuring
explanation: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables in a single expressive line.
Supports default values, renaming aliases, and nested object extraction.

codeSnippet.title: Object and Array Destructuring in Action
codeSnippet.description: Extracting data with defaults and property aliases.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
johndoe is a Full Stack Engineer with status active
Coords: 37.7749 -122.4194

topics.pitfall: Destructuring properties from `null` or `undefined` throws an immediate TypeError. Use optional chaining `user?.profile` when data may be absent.

quickCheck.question: How do you rename a property key while destructuring const user = { first: "Jane" }?
quickCheck.explanation: The colon syntax { originalKey: newVariableName } extracts and renames the property in JavaScript destructuring.

topics.title: Spread (...) and Rest (...) Operators
explanation: The Spread operator (`...`) expands an iterable into individual elements (used for shallow-cloning objects, merging arrays, passing arguments).
The Rest parameter (`...args`) gathers multiple remaining function arguments into an array.

codeSnippet.title: Cloning and Merging with Spread
codeSnippet.description: Immutable object updates and rest parameter gathering.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Original theme: light
Updated theme: dark
Sum: 100

topics.pitfall: Spread performs a SHALLOW copy; nested objects still share memory references. Mutating `updatedUser.nested.prop` will mutate `originalUser.nested.prop`.

quickCheck.question: What is the key difference between spread and rest operators?
options: Spread unpacks elements; rest collects multiple elements into a single array
Spread is for numbers only; rest is for strings only
Rest cannot be used in functions
quickCheck.explanation: Spread expands elements outward; rest collects incoming arguments into an array.

topics.title: Array Transformations: map() and filter()
explanation: `map()` creates a new array populated with the results of calling a provided function on every element in the calling array.
`filter()` creates a shallow copy of a portion of an array containing only elements that pass the predicate test.
Both are pure functions that do not mutate the original array.

codeSnippet.title: Chaining filter() and map()
codeSnippet.description: Filtering active students and formatting names.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Honor Roll: [ 'ALEX', 'TAYLOR' ]

topics.pitfall: Do not use `map()` when you do not intend to use the returned array; use `forEach()` or `for...of` for side effects.

quickCheck.question: Does array.filter() mutate the source array in place?
options: No, it returns a new array containing only matching elements
Only if wrapped in a function
quickCheck.explanation: filter() is immutable and returns a new array, leaving the original array intact.

topics.title: The Swiss Army Knife: Array.prototype.reduce()
explanation: `reduce()` executes a user-supplied reducer callback function on each element of the array, passing the return value from the calculation on the preceding element.
Can compute sums, build lookup dictionaries/maps, flatten structures, and count frequencies in a single pass.

codeSnippet.title: Building a Lookup Dictionary with reduce()
codeSnippet.description: Transforming an array of records into an indexed O(1) object lookup.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Product p2 is: Mouse

topics.pitfall: Always provide an explicit initial value to `reduce(callback, initialValue)`; omitting it causes the first element to become the initial accumulator, leading to bugs on empty arrays.

quickCheck.question: What happens if you call array.reduce() without an initialValue on an empty array []?
options: Throws a TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
quickCheck.explanation: Calling reduce on an empty array without an initialValue throws a fatal TypeError.

topics.title: Understanding Promises: Pending, Fulfilled & Rejected
explanation: A `Promise` is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value.
A promise exists in one of three states: `pending` (initial), `fulfilled` (resolved with value), or `rejected` (failed with reason).
Handle promises with `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()`.

codeSnippet.title: Creating and Consuming a Promise
codeSnippet.description: Simulating an asynchronous database query.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Fetched user: Jordan

topics.pitfall: Uncaught promise rejections crash Node.js processes and log noisy warnings in browsers. Always attach `.catch()` or use `try/catch`.

quickCheck.question: Once a Promise transitions from pending to fulfilled, can it be changed to rejected?
options: No, a promise settles only once and becomes immutable thereafter
quickCheck.explanation: Promises are immutable once settled; they cannot transition from fulfilled to rejected or vice versa.

topics.title: Modern Async / Await Syntax & Error Handling
explanation: `async/await` is syntactic sugar over Promises that allows writing asynchronous code with clean synchronous structure.
Any function marked `async` automatically returns a Promise. The `await` keyword pauses execution of the async function until the Promise settles.

codeSnippet.title: Clean Asynchronous Workflow with try/catch
codeSnippet.description: Fetching and handling errors with async/await.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Loading metrics...
Metrics loaded successfully: 1420
Metrics loading sequence completed.

topics.pitfall: Forgetting `await` before a promise causes the variable to store the Promise object itself instead of the resolved data value.

quickCheck.question: What does a function prefixed with the async keyword always return?
quickCheck.explanation: Every async function automatically wraps its return value in a resolved Promise.

topics.title: Concurrent Async Operations: Promise.all() vs Promise.allSettled()
explanation: Running independent asynchronous requests sequentially with `await req1; await req2;` causes an unnecessary network waterfall.
`Promise.all([p1, p2])` executes requests concurrently and fails fast if any reject. `Promise.allSettled([p1, p2])` waits for all to finish, returning an array of statuses.

codeSnippet.title: Concurrent Execution with Promise.all
codeSnippet.description: Executing multiple network requests in parallel.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Concurrent results: 2 students, 28 lessons

topics.pitfall: If one promise in `Promise.all()` rejects, the entire batch rejects immediately, discarding results from all successful promises. Use `Promise.allSettled()` if partial success is acceptable.

quickCheck.question: When should you choose Promise.allSettled() over Promise.all()?
options: When you need one rejection to cancel everything
When you want all promises to finish and inspect both fulfilled and rejected results individually
When you only have one promise
quickCheck.explanation: Promise.allSettled never rejects early; it waits for all promises to resolve or reject and returns detailed status objects.

topics.title: DOM Querying, Event Listeners & Event Delegation
explanation: Use `document.querySelector()` and `document.querySelectorAll()` to locate elements using modern CSS selectors.
Event Delegation attaches a single listener to a parent container to manage events from hundreds of dynamic child elements using `event.target`, optimizing memory usage.

codeSnippet.title: High-Performance Event Delegation
codeSnippet.description: Listening for clicks on a list of buttons with a single parent handler.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Deleted record ID: 42

topics.pitfall: Attaching individual event listeners to 1,000 table rows consumes huge memory and causes memory leaks when rows are re-rendered; always delegate.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary memory advantage of event delegation?
options: It attaches one listener to a common ancestor instead of hundreds of listeners on child nodes
quickCheck.explanation: Event delegation leverages event bubbling to handle actions on multiple children with a single parent listener.

practiceChallenge.title: Build an Async Data Pipeline with Filter and Map
instructions: Create an async function processOrders(ordersPromise) that awaits an array of orders.
Filter out orders with status !== "completed".
Calculate total revenue and extract an array of customer emails.
hints: Use await ordersPromise to resolve the promise first.
Use reduce to sum the order amounts.

keyTakeaways: Destructuring and spread syntax write concise, immutable, readable transformations.
Array methods map, filter, and reduce are pure functions that avoid mutation side effects.
async/await provides clean synchronous appearance with full non-blocking asynchronous power.

days.title: Git & GitHub from Scratch: Init, Staging, Commit & Push
days.subtitle: Version control models, repository initialization, branching, remotes, and pull requests
days.overview: Master Git and GitHub from the absolute basics: how distributed version control works, initializing repositories, staging areas, atomic commits, branching, merging, and pushing to remote GitHub repositories.

topics.title: What is Version Control & The Three Trees of Git
explanation: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks snapshots of your files over time, allowing you to restore history, branch off experiments, and collaborate securely.

Git organizes local work into Three Trees (states): 1) Working Directory (untracked/modified files), 2) Staging Area / Index (prepared for commit), 3) Git Repository (.git folder with permanent immutable commit snapshots).

codeSnippet.title: Checking Git Working Tree Status
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting working directory vs staging index.
codeSnippet.code:
# Check the current status of working directory & staging area
git status

# Inspect differences between working directory and staging index
git diff
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit: ...

topics.pitfall: Do not confuse Git (the local CLI version control tool) with GitHub (the cloud-hosted collaboration platform). You can use Git entirely offline without GitHub.

quickCheck.question: What are the three local states/trees of Git?
options: Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), and Repository (.git history)
quickCheck.explanation: Git tracks changes across the Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), and the permanent commit Repository.

topics.title: Initializing a Repository & Global User Configuration
explanation: Before committing, Git must know your identity for commit attribution.
`git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"` set this identity.
`git init` creates a hidden `.git` directory in the project root, turning the folder into a Git repository.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring Git and Initializing a Repo
codeSnippet.description: First-time setup commands on any new developer machine.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Set global identity (used in all future commits)
git config --global user.name "Alex Rivera"
git config --global user.email "alex@developer.io"

# 2. Set default branch name to 'main'
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# 3. Initialize a new local repository in current folder
git init
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Initialized empty Git repository in /project/.git/

topics.pitfall: Never run `git init` inside your home directory `~` or an existing parent Git repository; only run it in project root directories.

quickCheck.question: What hidden folder does git init create in your project root?
quickCheck.explanation: git init creates the .git directory containing all commit objects, branch references, and version history.

topics.title: The .gitignore File: Protecting Secrets and Node Modules
explanation: The `.gitignore` file tells Git which files or directories to ignore and never track.
Crucially, you must NEVER commit sensitive credentials (`.env`), API keys, build artifacts (`/dist`, `/build`), or heavy package dependencies (`node_modules/`).

codeSnippet.title: Essential .gitignore for Web Projects
codeSnippet.description: Standard rules safeguarding secrets and vendor packages.
codeSnippet.code:
# Dependency packages (rebuilt via npm install)
node_modules/

# Environment secrets and API keys (CRITICAL)
.env
.env.local
*.pem

# Build output directories
dist/
build/
.next/

# OS metadata
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Protected files are automatically ignored by git status

topics.pitfall: If you accidentally commit a `.env` file with secret keys and push it to GitHub, changing the file in a new commit does NOT delete it from Git history! The secret is compromised and must be revoked immediately.

quickCheck.question: Why should node_modules/ and .env always be listed in .gitignore?
options: node_modules is massive and easily re-installed, while .env contains secret credentials that should never be public
quickCheck.explanation: node_modules contains thousands of vendor files, and .env contains private API keys that must never be exposed.

topics.title: Staging & Atomic Commits: git add & git commit
explanation: `git add <file>` moves changes from the working directory into the staging area.
`git commit -m "message"` captures an immutable snapshot of all currently staged files.
Write atomic commits: each commit should accomplish one logical, cohesive unit of work with a descriptive imperative message (e.g. "feat: add user login form validation").

codeSnippet.title: Staging Files and Creating Commits
codeSnippet.description: Moving changes through staging to permanent history.
codeSnippet.code:
# Stage a single file
git add src/App.tsx

# Stage all modified and new files
git add .

# Create a conventional atomic commit
git commit -m "feat: add responsive navbar with theme toggle"

# View commit history
git log --oneline -n 5
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: [main 9a4e21c] feat: add responsive navbar with theme toggle

topics.pitfall: Avoid vague commit messages like "fix stuff" or "update". Follow Conventional Commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `docs:`, `test:`.

quickCheck.question: What does git add . do?
options: Commits all files directly to GitHub
Stages all modified and new files in the current directory and subdirectories
quickCheck.explanation: git add . stages all modified, untracked, and deleted files in the current workspace into the staging area.

topics.title: Git Branching: Feature Isolation & git checkout / switch
explanation: Branches are lightweight movable pointers to commits. They allow you to develop features in complete isolation without breaking the stable `main` branch.
Use `git switch -c <branch-name>` (or `git checkout -b <branch-name>`) to create and switch to a new branch.

codeSnippet.title: Creating and Switching Branches
codeSnippet.description: Isolating feature development on a dedicated branch.
codeSnippet.code:
# Create and switch to a new feature branch
git switch -c feature/user-authentication

# List all local branches (active branch marked with *)
git branch

# Work, stage, and commit on the feature branch
git add src/auth/
git commit -m "feat(auth): implement jwt token generation"

# Switch back to the main branch
git switch main
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Switched to a new branch 'feature/user-authentication'

topics.pitfall: Never build complex experimental features directly on `main`; always branch off so unfinished code does not compromise production.

quickCheck.question: What modern Git command creates a new branch and immediately switches to it?
quickCheck.explanation: git switch -c <name> (or git checkout -b <name>) creates the branch and checks it out in one step.

topics.title: Merging Branches & Resolving Merge Conflicts
explanation: `git merge <branch>` integrates changes from the specified branch into your current active branch.

A Fast-Forward merge occurs if `main` has no new commits. If both branches modified the same lines of code, Git pauses and marks a Merge Conflict with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` for manual resolution.

codeSnippet.title: Merging a Feature Branch into Main
codeSnippet.description: Standard merge sequence from main branch.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Switch to the target branch (main)
git switch main

# 2. Merge the completed feature branch
git merge feature/user-authentication

# 3. Clean up the merged branch after success
git branch -d feature/user-authentication
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Updating 3c8e102..9a4e21c
Fast-forward
 src/auth.ts | 48 ++++++++++

topics.pitfall: When resolving merge conflicts, never leave Git conflict markers (`<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`) inside your source code; delete the markers after picking the correct code.

quickCheck.question: What happens when two branches have modified the exact same line of code and are merged?
options: Git flags a merge conflict and requests manual resolution of the conflicting lines
Git picks the first commit automatically
quickCheck.explanation: Git cannot guess which change is correct, so it halts the merge and inserts conflict markers for the developer to resolve.

topics.title: Remote Repositories: Connecting to GitHub & git push
explanation: A remote is a common repository hosted on the internet (such as GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket).
`git remote add origin <url>` connects your local repo to the remote.
`git push -u origin main` pushes your local commits to GitHub and sets up upstream tracking.

codeSnippet.title: Connecting Local Repo to GitHub Remote
codeSnippet.description: Publishing local commits to remote GitHub repository.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Add remote alias named 'origin'
git remote add origin https://github.com/developer/fullstack-academy.git

# 2. Verify configured remotes
git remote -v

# 3. Push commits to GitHub and link upstream (-u)
git push -u origin main

# Subsequent pushes simply require:
git push
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Branch 'main' set up to track remote branch 'main' from 'origin'.

topics.pitfall: Never use `git push --force` on shared team branches like `main` or `develop`; it overwrites commit history on the server and breaks teammates working copies.

quickCheck.question: What does the -u flag do in git push -u origin main?
options: Sets upstream tracking so future git push and git pull commands do not require typing origin main
quickCheck.explanation: -u sets the default upstream remote and branch for the current branch, enabling bare "git push" thereafter.

topics.title: Pull Requests (PRs), Code Reviews & GitHub Collaboration Workflow
explanation: In professional software teams, developers never push directly to `main`.
Instead, you push your feature branch to GitHub (`git push -u origin feature/my-feature`), open a Pull Request (PR), solicit peer code reviews, pass automated CI checks, and merge via GitHub.

codeSnippet.title: The Professional Team Git Workflow
codeSnippet.description: Step-by-step summary of the industry standard GitHub workflow.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Ensure local main is synchronized
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create isolated feature branch
git switch -c feat/checkout-api

# 3. Make changes, stage, and commit
git add .
git commit -m "feat(api): implement stripe payment intent handler"

# 4. Push feature branch to GitHub
git push -u origin feat/checkout-api

# 5. Open Pull Request on GitHub UI -> Review -> Merge!
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Total 5 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0)
To https://github.com/developer/app.git

topics.pitfall: Always run `git pull origin main` before creating or finalizing a feature branch to ensure you are building on the latest code.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of a GitHub Pull Request (PR)?
options: To download files to your computer
To propose code changes from a feature branch, review diffs, run tests, and merge into main
quickCheck.explanation: A Pull Request is a collaborative discussion and review process for proposing changes before merging into production.
