days.title: Relational Databases & SQL from Scratch: PostgreSQL
days.subtitle: Tables, primary keys, foreign keys, SELECT, JOINs, indexing, and ACID transactions
days.overview: Master relational databases from zero. Learn how Structured Query Language (SQL) operates, create tables with data types, enforce data integrity with primary and foreign keys, write multi-table INNER/LEFT JOINs, and execute atomic transactions.

topics.title: What is a Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)?
explanation: An RDBMS stores structured data in tables consisting of rows (records) and columns (attributes). Tables relate to each other through keys.
PostgreSQL is the gold standard open-source enterprise RDBMS, renowned for robust ACID compliance, advanced indexing, and rich data types (JSONB, UUID, timestamps).

codeSnippet.title: Connecting to PostgreSQL via CLI (psql)
codeSnippet.description: Basic PostgreSQL connection and version inspection.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: PostgreSQL 16.2 on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu

topics.pitfall: Do not store relational structured data in flat JSON files; flat files lack concurrency controls, crash under simultaneous writes, and require O(N) full scans.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary language used to manage and query relational databases like PostgreSQL?
quickCheck.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for querying and manipulating relational databases.

topics.title: Creating Tables, Data Types & Primary Keys
explanation: `CREATE TABLE` defines the schema: column names, data types (`VARCHAR`, `INT`, `BOOLEAN`, `TIMESTAMP`, `UUID`), and constraints.
Every table MUST have a `PRIMARY KEY` (a unique identifier for each row, such as `BIGSERIAL` or `UUID`).

codeSnippet.title: Creating Students Table Schema
codeSnippet.description: Table definition with constraints and primary key.
codeSnippet.code:
CREATE TABLE students (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  enrolled_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE
);
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
CREATE TABLE
Table "students" created with primary key and unique email constraint

topics.pitfall: Never use plain text without length limits or validation for emails; always add `UNIQUE NOT NULL` to prevent duplicate accounts.

quickCheck.question: What constraint guarantees that no two rows in a table share the exact same identifier?
quickCheck.explanation: PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each record in a database table, enforcing uniqueness and non-nullability.

topics.title: Relationships & Foreign Keys: One-to-Many & Many-to-Many
explanation: A `FOREIGN KEY` creates a link between two tables, referencing the primary key of another table.
One-to-Many (1:N): One course has many modules. The `modules` table contains `course_id REFERENCES courses(id)`.
Many-to-Many (N:M): Students can enroll in multiple courses, and courses have multiple students. Modeled via a Junction Table (`enrollments`).

codeSnippet.title: Junction Table Modeling Many-to-Many Relationship
codeSnippet.description: Creating enrollments table linking students and courses.
codeSnippet.code:
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  course_id BIGINT REFERENCES courses(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  enrolled_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE,
  completed BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id) -- Composite Primary Key
);
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
CREATE TABLE
Composite primary key junction table linking students and courses

topics.pitfall: Always specify `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE RESTRICT` on foreign keys so you control what happens when parent records are deleted.

quickCheck.question: How is a Many-to-Many relationship implemented between two tables in a relational database?
options: By storing an array of IDs in a text column
By creating a Junction (Join) Table containing foreign keys referencing both tables
Relational databases cannot model many-to-many relationships
quickCheck.explanation: A junction table with foreign keys referencing both primary tables cleanly models many-to-many relationships.

topics.title: SQL CRUD Queries: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE & DELETE
explanation: `INSERT INTO table (cols) VALUES (vals) RETURNING *` inserts records.
`SELECT cols FROM table WHERE cond ORDER BY col LIMIT n` reads filtered data.
`UPDATE table SET col = val WHERE cond` modifies matching rows.
`DELETE FROM table WHERE cond` removes rows.

codeSnippet.title: Standard SQL CRUD Operations
codeSnippet.description: Inserting, reading, updating, and deleting rows safely.
codeSnippet.code:
-- 1. Insert and return created record
INSERT INTO students (name, email) 
VALUES ('Taylor Smith', 'taylor@dev.io')
RETURNING id, name, enrolled_at;

-- 2. Query with filter and ordering
SELECT id, name, email 
FROM students 
WHERE is_active = TRUE 
ORDER BY enrolled_at DESC 
LIMIT 10;

-- 3. Safe update with WHERE condition
UPDATE students 
SET is_active = FALSE 
WHERE id = 42;
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
INSERT 0 1
Returned newly created row with generated ID

topics.pitfall: NEVER execute `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause! Omitting `WHERE` will update or wipe out EVERY single row in your entire table!

quickCheck.question: What catastrophic error occurs if you run DELETE FROM students; without a WHERE clause?
options: It deletes the first row only
It permanently deletes EVERY record in the students table
quickCheck.explanation: Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE and DELETE apply to every single row in the target table.

topics.title: Mastering SQL JOINs: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
explanation: `INNER JOIN` returns only rows that have matching values in both tables.
`LEFT JOIN` returns all rows from the left table, plus matched rows from the right table (unmatched columns are populated with `NULL`).

codeSnippet.title: Joining Students and Completed Quizzes
codeSnippet.description: LEFT JOIN including students even if they have not taken any quizzes yet.
codeSnippet.code:
SELECT 
  s.id AS student_id,
  s.name,
  s.email,
  q.week_number,
  COALESCE(q.score, 0) AS quiz_score
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN quiz_submissions q ON s.id = q.student_id
WHERE s.is_active = TRUE;
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Combined result set displaying student info alongside optional quiz scores

topics.pitfall: Using `INNER JOIN` when you should use `LEFT JOIN` will silently hide students who have not yet submitted a quiz from your reports!

quickCheck.question: What is returned by a LEFT JOIN for rows in the left table that have no matching records in the right table?
options: Those rows are excluded from the result set
Those rows are included with NULL values for all columns from the right table
The query fails with an error
quickCheck.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves all rows from the left table, filling in NULL for missing right-table columns.

topics.title: Database Indexing: B-Tree Indexes & EXPLAIN ANALYZE
explanation: Without an index, querying `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '...'` performs a Sequential Scan: scanning every row on disk (O(N) time). On 10 million rows, this takes seconds.
A B-Tree Index creates a sorted balanced search tree (O(log N) lookup time), reducing query duration from 3,000ms to 2ms. Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to inspect query plans.

codeSnippet.title: Creating an Index and Analyzing Execution Plan
codeSnippet.description: Optimizing search performance with B-tree index.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Index Scan using idx_students_email (cost=0.29..8.30 rows=1 width=72) (actual time=0.042ms)

topics.pitfall: Do not index every single column; indexes consume disk space and slow down `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` operations because every index must be updated on write.

quickCheck.question: What SQL command shows the execution plan, cost estimate, and actual execution time in milliseconds for a query?
quickCheck.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and displays the execution plan with real millisecond timings.

topics.title: ACID Properties & Database Transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK)
explanation: ACID guarantees financial and mission-critical reliability: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (rules enforced), Isolation (concurrent operations do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
Transactions bundle multiple queries together: if any query fails, `ROLLBACK` undoes all prior steps, leaving the database clean.

codeSnippet.title: Executing an Atomic Transfer Transaction
codeSnippet.description: Safely transferring balance between accounts.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
COMMIT
Both updates committed atomically; money is never created or lost

topics.pitfall: Executing multi-step operations (like charging a credit card and unlocking a course) without a database transaction risks leaving your database in a corrupt, half-finished state if a crash occurs midway.

quickCheck.question: What does Atomicity in ACID mean for a multi-query database transaction?
options: All statements within the transaction succeed together, or if any fails, all changes are rolled back completely (All or Nothing)
Only one user can use the database
quickCheck.explanation: Atomicity ensures that all modifications in a transaction are treated as a single indivisible unit: either all succeed or none do.

topics.title: Connection Pooling: pg.Pool & Managing Server Concurrency
explanation: Establishing a new TCP/TLS connection to PostgreSQL takes 50-100ms and spawns an operating system process on the database host.
A Connection Pool (`pg.Pool`) maintains a pre-warmed set of reusable connections (e.g. 10-20 connections). Requests borrow a connection, run their query, and return it to the pool in 1ms.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring pg.Pool in Node.js
codeSnippet.description: Reusing database connections across HTTP requests.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Executing parameterized query: SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = $1

topics.pitfall: Creating a new client connection on every single HTTP request (`new Client()`) will quickly exhaust PostgreSQL maximum connection limit (`max_connections = 100`) and crash your server.

quickCheck.question: Why should a backend server use a Connection Pool (pg.Pool) instead of opening a new database connection on every HTTP request?
options: Opening new connections is slow and quickly exhausts PostgreSQL connection limits; a pool reuses existing open connections efficiently
quickCheck.explanation: Connection pools maintain a pool of open connections that are reused across requests, dramatically improving speed and throughput.

practiceChallenge.title: Design a Normalized Course & Enrollment Database Schema
instructions: Write SQL to create a courses table (id, title, weeks, created_at).
Create a students table (id, name, email, unique).
Create an enrollments junction table with foreign keys referencing both tables and composite primary key.
Add an index on students(email).
practiceChallenge.starterCode: -- Write SQL schema definitions here
hints: Use REFERENCES table(id) ON DELETE CASCADE for foreign keys.
Define PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id) on the junction table.

keyTakeaways: PostgreSQL delivers robust ACID-compliant relational data management.
Use Primary Keys to uniquely identify rows and Foreign Keys to enforce referential integrity.
Always use B-Tree indexes on lookup columns and connection pools in Node.js applications.

days.title: ORMs & Modern Data Modeling: Prisma ORM & Migrations
days.subtitle: Schema definition, declarative data modeling, migrations, type-safe queries, and seeding
days.overview: Master modern Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) with Prisma. Define data models declaratively in schema.prisma, run database migrations, query databases with 100% static type safety in TypeScript, and seed initial test datasets.

topics.title: Why Use an ORM? Raw SQL vs Type-Safe Data Mapping
explanation: Writing raw SQL strings (`"SELECT * FROM users"`) inside JavaScript provides zero compile-time type safety. If you rename a database column, TypeScript cannot warn you, causing runtime crashes.
An Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) maps database tables to typed TypeScript objects. Prisma generates fully typed query methods (`prisma.user.findMany()`) directly from your schema file.

codeSnippet.title: Raw SQL Strings vs Type-Safe Prisma Queries
codeSnippet.description: Comparing brittle string queries with autocomplete-backed ORM calls.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Full compile-time type safety and instant autocomplete on database queries

topics.pitfall: Do not use ORMs blindly for complex statistical aggregation queries where a hand-optimized raw SQL query performs 10x faster.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of Prisma ORM over writing raw SQL strings in TypeScript?
options: Prisma generates 100% type-safe query clients with autocomplete matching your database schema
quickCheck.explanation: Prisma generates a typed client from your schema, catching database query mismatches at compile time.

topics.title: The schema.prisma File: Models, Relations & Attributes
explanation: The `schema.prisma` file is the declarative single source of truth for your database models and connection.
You define models with fields, types, and attributes: `@id`, `@default(autoincrement())`, `@unique`, `@updatedAt`, and `@relation`.

codeSnippet.title: Declarative Model Definition in schema.prisma
codeSnippet.description: Declaring Course and Lesson models with 1:N relation.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Declarative schema mapping models, relations, and cascade deletion rules

topics.pitfall: Always define the relation on both sides of the model in `schema.prisma`; Prisma will report a schema validation error if the opposing relation field is missing.

quickCheck.question: What Prisma attribute automatically updates a timestamp field whenever a record is modified?
quickCheck.explanation: @updatedAt automatically manages timestamp updates on record mutation in Prisma.

topics.title: Database Migrations with prisma migrate dev
explanation: Database schemas evolve over time as features are added (adding columns, renaming tables).
`npx prisma migrate dev --name <migration_name>` compares your `schema.prisma` against your database, generates a version-controlled SQL migration file, and applies it to your database.

codeSnippet.title: Running Database Migrations via CLI
codeSnippet.description: Generating and applying SQL migrations.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Update schema.prisma with new fields
# 2. Run migration command
npx prisma migrate dev --name add_quiz_submission_model

# Output generated in prisma/migrations/20261024_add_quiz_submission_model/migration.sql:
# CREATE TABLE "QuizSubmission" ( ... );

# 3. In production CI/CD, apply migrations without generating new ones:
npx prisma migrate deploy
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Your database is now in sync with your schema.
Generated Prisma Client.

topics.pitfall: Never manually edit existing migration files that have already been applied to production; create a new migration instead.

quickCheck.question: What command applies pending migrations safely in a production deployment environment?
quickCheck.explanation: prisma migrate deploy applies pending migrations safely in production without prompting or generating new files.

topics.title: CRUD Queries with Prisma Client
explanation: Prisma Client provides expressive query methods for all CRUD operations: `findUnique`, `findFirst`, `findMany`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, and `upsert`.
All methods return native Promises that resolve to strongly typed objects.

codeSnippet.title: Executing Typed CRUD Queries with Prisma Client
codeSnippet.description: Creating and querying records with filtering.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Queries executed type-safely

topics.pitfall: Do not instantiate `new PrismaClient()` inside every route handler function. In Node/Next.js/Express, maintain a single global singleton instance to avoid exhausting connection pools.

quickCheck.question: Why should PrismaClient be instantiated as a singleton rather than created inside each route handler?
options: Each PrismaClient instance creates its own database connection pool; creating new instances on every request exhausts connections
Prisma is only for single-user apps
quickCheck.explanation: Each PrismaClient instance manages its own connection pool, so instantiating multiple clients exhausts database connections.

topics.title: Eager Loading & Nested Relations with include and select
explanation: The N+1 Query Problem occurs when you fetch a list of 50 courses, and then run 50 separate queries to fetch the lessons for each course (51 queries total!).
Prisma solves this with the `include` option: `prisma.course.findMany({ include: { days: true } })` fetches courses and their related lessons in a single optimized JOIN/batch query.

codeSnippet.title: Fetching Related Data with include and select
codeSnippet.description: Eager loading nested relations in one efficient query.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Complete nested course tree loaded in a single performant database trip

topics.pitfall: Avoid using `include` blindly on massive tables (like including all 50,000 comments on a post); use pagination on nested relations.

quickCheck.question: How do you prevent the N+1 query problem when loading parent-child relations with Prisma?
options: Use the include option to fetch related records in a single optimized query
Run a for loop with individual queries
quickCheck.explanation: The include option instructs Prisma to batch or join related records, eliminating N+1 sequential round-trips.

topics.title: Database Transactions in Prisma ($transaction)
explanation: Prisma supports atomic transactions using `prisma.$transaction([op1, op2])` (sequential array) or interactive transactions `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... })`.
If any step within the transaction fails or throws an error, all operations rollback automatically.

codeSnippet.title: Interactive Transaction with Prisma $transaction
codeSnippet.description: Enrolling student and creating payment record atomically.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Enrollment and student count updated atomically within single transaction

topics.pitfall: Never execute slow external HTTP calls (like calling Stripe API) INSIDE a database transaction block; keep database transactions as short as possible to prevent holding table locks.

quickCheck.question: What happens to changes made within a prisma.$transaction block if an error is thrown?
options: Successful operations are kept, failed ones are skipped
The entire transaction is automatically aborted and all changes are rolled back
quickCheck.explanation: If any error occurs inside $transaction, Prisma executes a ROLLBACK, undoing all queries in the block.

topics.title: Automated Database Seeding (prisma/seed.ts)
explanation: Spinning up a fresh development environment requires initial data: sample courses, days, quizzes, and default admin users.
Prisma provides automated seeding via `prisma/seed.ts` configured in `package.json`. Running `npx prisma db seed` populates the database deterministically.

codeSnippet.title: Automated Seed Script Pattern in TypeScript
codeSnippet.description: Populating initial curriculum data via seed script.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Seeding initial curriculum data...
Database seeding finished successfully!

topics.pitfall: Use `upsert` (update if exists, insert if not) rather than plain `create` in seed scripts so running the seed command multiple times does not throw unique constraint violations.

quickCheck.question: Why is upsert preferred over create when writing database seed scripts?
options: upsert is idempotent: if the record already exists, it updates it instead of throwing a unique constraint error
quickCheck.explanation: upsert allows seed scripts to be executed repeatedly without crashing due to duplicate key errors.

topics.title: Prisma Studio: Visual Database GUI in the Browser
explanation: Inspecting data in terminals can be tedious.

`npx prisma studio` launches a local visual web interface at `http://localhost:5555`. It allows viewing, filtering, editing, and deleting records across all database tables with an intuitive spreadsheet-style GUI.

codeSnippet.title: Launching Prisma Studio Web Interface
codeSnippet.description: Starting local visual database browser.
codeSnippet.code:
# Launch visual database interface in local browser
npx prisma studio

# Output:
# Prisma Studio is up on http://localhost:5555
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Prisma Studio is up on http://localhost:5555

topics.pitfall: Do not expose Prisma Studio on public production ports without strict password protection and firewall rules.

quickCheck.question: What does npx prisma studio provide to developers?
options: A local browser-based GUI to visually explore, filter, and edit database records
quickCheck.explanation: Prisma Studio is a visual browser GUI for inspecting and modifying database models and records.

practiceChallenge.title: Define a Complete Full-Stack Academy Prisma Schema
instructions: Create Course model with id (cuid), title, and relation to Module.
Create Module model with weekNumber, title, and relation to DayLesson.
Create DayLesson model with dayNumber, title, and relation to SubTopic.
Configure CASCADE deletion across all parent-child relationships.
practiceChallenge.starterCode: // Write complete schema.prisma models
hints: Use @relation(fields: [...], references: [...], onDelete: Cascade).
Use @id @default(cuid()) for unique primary keys.

keyTakeaways: Prisma ORM provides 100% type-safe database queries synchronized with your schema.
Use prisma migrate dev to version-control schema changes and apply migrations.
Use include to eliminate N+1 queries and upsert for idempotent seed scripts.

days.title: NoSQL Databases & In-Memory Caching: MongoDB & Redis
days.subtitle: Document stores, JSON collections, Redis key-value caching, TTL, and cache invalidation
days.overview: Explore non-relational data architectures. Understand when to choose document stores (MongoDB) over relational databases, model flexible nested JSON documents, and implement lightning-fast in-memory caching with Redis (TTL, cache-aside pattern).

topics.title: SQL vs NoSQL: Relational Tables vs Document Stores
explanation: Relational (SQL): Rigid predefined schemas, strict tabular structure, ACID transactions, and JOINs. Ideal for financial ledgers, user accounts, and relational systems.

NoSQL (Document/MongoDB): Dynamic schema, hierarchical JSON/BSON documents, high write scalability, and horizontal sharding. Ideal for polymorphic catalogs, IoT telemetry, and rapidly evolving payloads.

codeSnippet.title: Relational Tables vs MongoDB Document Structure
codeSnippet.description: Comparing normalized tables with embedded document hierarchy.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Rich nested JSON document stored directly in a single document collection

topics.pitfall: Do not use MongoDB if your domain requires complex relational JOINs across dozens of normalized entities; SQL is far superior for relational queries.

quickCheck.question: What format does MongoDB use to store documents on disk?
quickCheck.explanation: MongoDB stores documents in BSON, a binary-encoded serialization of JSON that supports additional types (like Date and ObjectId).

topics.title: Embedding vs Referencing in Document Databases
explanation: Embedding: nesting related data inside a single document (e.g. embedding 7 subtopics inside a day lesson document). Eliminates JOINs, allowing atomic reads of the entire hierarchy in one disk seek.
Referencing: storing ObjectIds of separate documents (normalized). Preferred when child collections grow unboundedly (like millions of log entries).

codeSnippet.title: Embedding Subtopics inside Lesson Document
codeSnippet.description: One-to-few relationship modeled via embedded array.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Entire lesson and nested topics retrieved in a single O(1) query

topics.pitfall: Beware of MongoDB 16MB document size limit. Never embed unbounded arrays (like infinite chat messages) inside a single parent document.

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum single document size limit in MongoDB?
quickCheck.explanation: MongoDB enforces a 16MB BSON document size limit to preserve high RAM and disk performance.

topics.title: What is Redis? In-Memory Key-Value Architecture
explanation: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an ultra-fast, in-memory key-value data store.
Because data resides in physical RAM rather than disk drives, Redis operations execute in sub-millisecond speeds (100,000+ operations per second).
Used for caching database queries, storing user sessions, rate-limit counters, and real-time leaderboards.

codeSnippet.title: Basic Redis CLI Operations
codeSnippet.description: Setting and getting keys with expiration TTL.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Set key with value
SET course:fs:title "Full Stack Web Development"

# 2. Get key value (sub-millisecond!)
GET course:fs:title

# 3. Set key with Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration of 60 seconds
SETEX cache:stats 60 '{"activeStudents": 1420}'

# 4. Check remaining TTL in seconds
TTL cache:stats
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
"Full Stack Web Development"
OK
(integer) 58

topics.pitfall: RAM is significantly more expensive than disk storage; do not store gigabytes of cold static assets in Redis. Use Redis for hot, frequently accessed data.

quickCheck.question: Why are read and write operations in Redis orders of magnitude faster than PostgreSQL?
options: Redis stores data directly in system RAM (in-memory) rather than performing persistent disk I/O
quickCheck.explanation: RAM read/write speeds are thousands of times faster than magnetic or SSD persistent disk reads.

topics.title: The Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) Pattern
explanation: The Cache-Aside pattern is the standard caching strategy:
1) When a request arrives, check Redis first (`Cache Hit`). If found, return immediately without touching the database!
2) If key is not in Redis (`Cache Miss`), query PostgreSQL, write the result into Redis with a TTL, and return to the client.

codeSnippet.title: Implementing the Cache-Aside Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Checking Redis before querying primary database.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Subsequent requests served instantly from RAM in under 1ms

topics.pitfall: Always set a Time-To-Live (`TTL`) when caching in Redis; otherwise, the cache will grow unbounded and run out of RAM.

quickCheck.question: What is a "Cache Hit" in the Cache-Aside pattern?
options: When the requested data is found already stored in the fast in-memory cache, avoiding a database query
quickCheck.explanation: A Cache Hit occurs when the requested record exists in the fast cache, delivering instant responses.

topics.title: Cache Invalidation: The Hard Problem in Computer Science
explanation: "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." — Phil Karlton
When data is updated in the database (`UPDATE course SET title = ...`), the Redis cache becomes stale and out-of-sync.
Strategies: 1) TTL (passive expiration), 2) Write-Through / Invalidate-on-Write (explicitly call `redis.del(cacheKey)` whenever an update mutation runs).

codeSnippet.title: Invalidating Cache on Data Mutation
codeSnippet.description: Purging stale cache upon database update.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Stale cache purged, guaranteeing fresh data on subsequent reads

topics.pitfall: Updating the database without clearing the corresponding Redis cache key means users will continue seeing outdated stale data until the TTL expires.

quickCheck.question: What should you do to the Redis cache key when a user updates their profile in the database?
options: Delete or update the cache key immediately (Invalidate on write)
quickCheck.explanation: Invalidating or updating the cache upon data mutation ensures clients immediately receive fresh data.

topics.title: Redis Data Structures: Hashes, Lists, Sets & Sorted Sets
explanation: Redis is not just a plain string store; it provides rich native data structures:
Strings (text/JSON), Hashes (objects like `HSET user:1 name "Alex"`), Lists (queues with `LPUSH/RPOP`), Sets (unique items `SADD`), and Sorted Sets (leaderboards with scores `ZADD`).

codeSnippet.title: High-Performance Leaderboard with Sorted Sets (ZSET)
codeSnippet.description: O(log N) ranking of top students by quiz score.
codeSnippet.code:
# Add students and scores to leaderboard
ZADD leaderboard:week1 95 "alex"
ZADD leaderboard:week1 100 "taylor"
ZADD leaderboard:week1 88 "jordan"

# Retrieve top 3 students sorted highest to lowest score
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:week1 0 2 WITHSCORES

# Output:
# 1) "taylor" (100)
# 2) "alex"   (95)
# 3) "jordan" (88)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: O(log N) leaderboard sorted instantly in memory

topics.pitfall: Do not parse and re-stringify entire JSON arrays for simple queue or set operations; use native Redis Lists (`LPUSH/RPOP`) and Sets (`SADD/SMEMBERS`).

quickCheck.question: Which Redis data structure is ideal for implementing real-time gaming or quiz score leaderboards?
quickCheck.explanation: Sorted Sets maintain elements ordered by floating-point score, providing instant ranking lookups.

topics.title: Distributed Session Storage with Redis
explanation: If you deploy your backend across 3 server instances (load balanced), storing session memory inside Node.js `MemoryStore` means a user logging into Server 1 will appear logged out when the balancer directs them to Server 2.
Pointing `express-session` or token blocklists to a centralized Redis cluster shares session state across all server instances seamlessly.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring Redis Session Store in Express
codeSnippet.description: Centralized session state across distributed clusters.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Sessions accessible across all cluster nodes without memory leaks

topics.pitfall: Never use the default `MemoryStore` for `express-session` in production; it leaks memory and fails in multi-process/multi-server deployments.

quickCheck.question: Why is the default in-memory session store unusable when running multiple backend server instances?
options: Because memory is not shared between server instances; a request routed to a different instance will lose the session
Because memory stores are too fast
quickCheck.explanation: Separate server processes do not share RAM; a central store like Redis is required for shared sessions.

topics.title: Database Architecture Decision Matrix: Choosing the Right Storage Tier
explanation: Production enterprise systems use Polyglot Persistence: using multiple specialized storage engines together:
PostgreSQL: Core transactional source of truth (Users, Orders, Billing, Relational models).
Redis: Ephemeral fast caching, rate limiting, pub/sub messaging, and sessions.
MongoDB / S3: Flexible documents, unstructured payloads, and static media files.

codeSnippet.title: Polyglot Architecture Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Combining PostgreSQL, Redis, and Object Storage.
codeSnippet.code:
# PostgreSQL: Primary Source of Truth (ACID, Financial, Relations)
# Redis: Caching Tier (Sub-millisecond reads, Session store, Rate limit)
# S3 / GCS: Cloud Object Storage (Video lessons, Avatars, PDF Certificates)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Balanced full-stack architecture leveraging the strengths of each storage tier

topics.pitfall: Trying to force one single database engine to do everything (e.g. using relational SQL as an in-memory cache or using Redis as a 500GB primary database) leads to severe performance degradation.

quickCheck.question: What is Polyglot Persistence in software architecture?
options: Using only one database for everything
Using different database technologies to handle different data storage needs based on their strengths
quickCheck.explanation: Polyglot persistence leverages the optimal database engine (SQL, Redis, S3) for each specific data requirement.

practiceChallenge.title: Implement a Cached API Endpoint with Cache-Aside & Invalidation
instructions: Create a mock Redis cache and PostgreSQL database.
Build getCourseStats(id) implementing the cache-aside pattern with 60-second TTL.
Build updateCourseStats(id, updates) that modifies the database and invalidates the cache.
Verify that updates clear the cache.
practiceChallenge.starterCode: // Write complete cache-aside and invalidation implementation
hints: Check mockRedis before reading mockDb.
Call mockRedis.delete on mutation to invalidate.

keyTakeaways: Document databases (MongoDB) excel at hierarchical, polymorphic JSON data.
Redis delivers sub-millisecond in-memory speeds for caching, sessions, and leaderboards.
Always implement the Cache-Aside pattern with TTL and invalidate on write.

days.title: Full-Stack Integration: Connecting React Frontend to Node/DB Backend
days.subtitle: API client abstraction, TanStack Query, optimistic UI, and error boundaries
days.overview: Bridge the gap between client and server. Wire up your React frontend to your Express backend: building an API client abstraction with Axios/Fetch, managing server caching with TanStack React Query, executing optimistic UI updates, and catching errors with Error Boundaries.

topics.title: The Unified Full-Stack Architecture Blueprint
explanation: A production full-stack application connects a client layer (React, Tailwind CSS, TypeScript), a network boundary (HTTP/REST, JSON, HTTPS, CORS), a server layer (Node.js, Express, Middleware, Zod, JWT), and a data layer (PostgreSQL, Prisma, Redis).
Keeping interfaces typed and consistent across the boundary ensures end-to-end type safety.

codeSnippet.title: End-to-End Type Sharing Across Frontend & Backend
codeSnippet.description: Shared types package or directory imported by client and server.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: End-to-end contract synchronization preventing client-server discrepancies

topics.pitfall: Do not define different shapes of the same data model independently in frontend and backend code; share types via a shared directory or monorepo package.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of sharing TypeScript interfaces between frontend and backend?
options: It eliminates the need for a database
Any change to the backend API response contract will immediately flag type errors in frontend components during compilation
quickCheck.explanation: Shared type contracts ensure frontend components and backend endpoints stay perfectly synchronized at compile time.

topics.title: Building a Centralized API Client with Fetch & Axios
explanation: Never scatter raw `fetch("http://localhost:3000/api/...")` calls across 30 different React components.
Create a centralized `apiClient` that automatically attaches the base URL, handles `Authorization: Bearer <token>` headers, sets JSON content headers, and intercepts 401 errors for auto-redirect.

codeSnippet.title: Type-Safe Centralized API Client Wrapper
codeSnippet.description: Centralized fetch wrapper handling base URL and error parsing.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Clean, centralized network abstraction used across all React views

topics.pitfall: Do not hardcode `http://localhost:3000` inside your API client; use relative paths `/api` or environment variables `import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE` so it works in production.

quickCheck.question: Why should you use relative paths (e.g. /api/users) or environment variables instead of hardcoding http://localhost:3000?
options: Because localhost:3000 only exists on your local laptop; in production, the code runs on cloud domains with HTTPS
quickCheck.explanation: Hardcoding localhost will break in production where the app runs on a public domain.

topics.title: Server State Management with TanStack React Query
explanation: TanStack Query (React Query) replaces fragile `useEffect` data fetching.
It provides `useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })`: automatic caching, loading and error states, background re-fetching on window focus, and deduplication of simultaneous requests.

codeSnippet.title: Declarative Data Fetching with useQuery
codeSnippet.description: Zero boilerplate loading, error, and cached data states.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Automatic caching, background re-fetching, and declarative UI states

topics.pitfall: Do not duplicate React Query data into local `useState`; let React Query serve as the single source of truth for all remote server state.

quickCheck.question: What does staleTime: 60000 do in TanStack React Query?
options: Considers data fresh for 60 seconds, skipping background network re-fetches during that window
quickCheck.explanation: staleTime specifies the duration data is considered fresh before a background re-fetch is triggered.

topics.title: Optimistic UI Updates: Zero-Latency User Interactions
explanation: In standard apps, clicking "Complete Day" makes the UI wait 300ms for the server to reply before changing the icon.

Optimistic UI immediately updates the client screen assuming success. If the server request fails, it rolls back to previous state and displays an error toast, giving users a blazing fast, native-feeling UI.

codeSnippet.title: Optimistic State Toggle Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Immediate local UI update with server error rollback.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Instantaneous UI feedback with reliable error rollback protection

topics.pitfall: Always preserve a rollback snapshot before applying an optimistic update so you can restore the exact previous state if the network fails.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary user experience advantage of Optimistic UI updates?
options: Zero-latency perception: UI responds immediately to user clicks without waiting for network round-trips
quickCheck.explanation: Optimistic UI makes interactions feel instantaneous by updating the interface before the server response returns.

topics.title: Handling Errors Gracefully: React Error Boundaries
explanation: By default, if an unhandled JavaScript error occurs inside any component render, React unmounts the entire application tree, leaving the user with a blank white screen.
An Error Boundary is a React component that catches JavaScript errors anywhere in its child component tree and displays a graceful fallback UI.

codeSnippet.title: React Error Boundary Component
codeSnippet.description: Catching runtime render errors and presenting recovery screen.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Catches runtime exceptions and prevents full-page whiteout crashes

topics.pitfall: Error boundaries catch errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. They do NOT catch errors in asynchronous event handlers (use `try/catch` there).

quickCheck.question: What happens if a child component throws an unhandled error during render without an Error Boundary?
options: React unmounts the entire application tree, leaving the user with a blank white screen
quickCheck.explanation: Uncaught render errors cause React to unmount the entire component tree to avoid corrupt UI state.

topics.title: Vite Proxy: Seamless Local Full-Stack Development
explanation: In development, Vite frontend runs on `http://localhost:5173` and Express backend runs on `http://localhost:3000`. Direct requests trigger CORS errors.
Vite built-in development proxy (`vite.config.ts`) proxies all `/api` requests from Vite to Express, eliminating CORS issues during development completely.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring Vite Development Proxy
codeSnippet.description: Forwarding /api calls to backend server transparently.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Frontend fetch("/api/courses") routes cleanly to Express port 3000 without CORS

topics.pitfall: Vite proxy only runs during local development (`npm run dev`). In production, configure reverse proxy in Nginx/Vercel or serve static assets from Express.

quickCheck.question: What problem does the Vite dev server proxy solve during local development?
options: It eliminates CORS errors by forwarding /api requests directly to the backend server behind the same origin
quickCheck.explanation: The proxy forwards requests to the backend server seamlessly from the same origin, bypassing browser CORS restrictions.

topics.title: Full-Stack Form Submissions: React Hook Form & Zod Resolver
explanation: Combining React Hook Form with Zod (`@hookform/resolvers/zod`) shares your backend validation schema directly with the frontend form.
Forms validate instantly on the client as users type, while the identical schema validates on the Express server upon submission.

codeSnippet.title: Shared Zod Schema in React Hook Form
codeSnippet.description: Single validation schema powering client and server forms.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Client form immediately highlights invalid inputs matching backend rules

topics.pitfall: Do not duplicate validation regular expressions in React; import the exact same Zod schema used on the backend.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary advantage of using a Zod resolver in React Hook Form?
options: It allows using the exact same Zod validation schema across both frontend forms and backend API routes
It eliminates the need for passwords
quickCheck.explanation: Using the same schema on frontend and backend guarantees identical validation rules and eliminates code duplication.

topics.title: Telemetry & Full-Stack Health Checks (/api/health)
explanation: Every production web service must expose an unauthenticated `/api/health` or `/livez` endpoint.

Cloud load balancers and container orchestrators (Kubernetes, AWS ECS) poll this endpoint every 10 seconds: if it returns `200 OK`, traffic is routed; if the database is down or memory exhausted, it fails over.

codeSnippet.title: Production Health Check Endpoint in Express
codeSnippet.description: Verifying database connectivity and uptime.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"status":"healthy","uptime":1420,"checks":{"database":"connected"}}

topics.pitfall: Never protect `/api/health` behind authentication; load balancers cannot authenticate and will mark your server unhealthy.

quickCheck.question: Why must the /api/health endpoint be publicly accessible without authentication?
options: Because cloud load balancers and orchestrators must poll it anonymously to determine if the server is healthy
To let hackers test the server
Because health checks do not support JSON
quickCheck.explanation: Automated infrastructure load balancers require unauthenticated access to monitor node vitality.

practiceChallenge.title: Wire Up an End-to-End Course Progress Toggle Flow
instructions: Create a client-side function toggleDay(dayNum) that updates local state optimistically.
Send POST /api/progress/toggle with the day number.
Revert state and show an alert if the network call rejects.
Add a /api/health endpoint.

hints: Store previous state array before setting optimistic state.
Revert to previous in catch block.

keyTakeaways: Centralize API client requests to handle base URLs, auth headers, and errors consistently.
Use Optimistic UI updates to provide instant native-feeling responsiveness.
Always expose an unauthenticated /api/health endpoint for cloud load balancers.

days.title: Advanced Git & GitHub Collaboration: PRs, Rebase & Conflicts
days.subtitle: Git branching models, interactive rebase, pull requests, code reviews, and resolving conflicts
days.overview: Level up your version control to senior software engineering standards. Master trunk-based development vs Gitflow, interactive rebase (git rebase -i) to squash messy commit histories, resolving gnarly merge conflicts, and conducting professional GitHub code reviews.

topics.title: Git Branching Strategies: Trunk-Based Development vs Gitflow
explanation: Gitflow: Long-lived branches (`develop`, `release`, `hotfix`, `feature`). Feature branches live for weeks, causing painful "merge hell" when integrating.

Trunk-Based Development: Modern industry standard. Developers merge small, short-lived feature branches (< 1-2 days) frequently into `main` (the trunk), backed by automated CI tests and feature flags.

codeSnippet.title: Trunk-Based Workflow Commands
codeSnippet.description: Fast, short-lived branch creation and synchronization.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Pull latest trunk (main)
git switch main
git pull --rebase origin main

# 2. Create small, focused feature branch
git switch -c feat/navbar-theme-toggle

# 3. Commit atomic changes
git commit -am "feat: add light and dark mode toggle"

# 4. Push and open PR within 24 hours
git push -u origin feat/navbar-theme-toggle
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Short-lived branch ready for rapid peer review and automated CI merge

topics.pitfall: Letting feature branches linger for weeks without pulling changes from `main` guarantees massive, painful merge conflicts.

quickCheck.question: What is the core principle of Trunk-Based Development compared to Gitflow?
options: Developers merge small, short-lived branches frequently into the main trunk, avoiding long-lived branch divergence
quickCheck.explanation: Trunk-Based Development emphasizes short-lived branches merged quickly into main to prevent merge conflicts.

topics.title: Git Merge vs Git Rebase: Linear vs Historical Graph
explanation: `git merge` creates a new "Merge Commit" that ties two histories together, preserving exact branch history but cluttering the commit log with "Merge branch..." noise.
`git rebase` lifts your branch commits and replays them one-by-one on top of the target branch tip, creating a clean, perfectly linear project history without merge commits.

codeSnippet.title: Rebasing a Feature Branch onto Latest Main
codeSnippet.description: Replaying commits on top of updated upstream main.
codeSnippet.code:
# Switch to feature branch
git switch feat/auth-service

# Rebase commits on top of the latest main branch
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# History is now linear: [main commits] -> [your feature commits]
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/auth-service

topics.pitfall: THE GOLDEN RULE OF REBASE: Never rebase a public shared branch (like `main` or `develop`)! Rebasing rewrites commit SHA hashes and breaks teammates repositories. Only rebase your local private feature branches.

quickCheck.question: What is the Golden Rule of Git Rebase?
options: Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repository and have been pushed to a shared public branch
quickCheck.explanation: Rebasing rewrites commit hashes; doing so on shared branches corrupts teammates Git histories.

topics.title: Interactive Rebase: Squashing Messy Commits (git rebase -i)
explanation: During local feature development, developers create messy exploratory commits: "wip", "fix typo", "testing again", "oops".
Before submitting a Pull Request, run `git rebase -i HEAD~4` to Squash multiple trivial commits into a single cohesive, beautifully documented commit.

codeSnippet.title: Interactive Rebase Command and Editor Commands
codeSnippet.description: Squashing 3 exploratory commits into one clean commit.
codeSnippet.code:
# Interactively rebase the last 3 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# In the interactive editor:
# pick 3a1b4c5 feat: scaffold registration endpoint
# squash 7e8f9a0 fix typo in email validator
# squash 1c2d3e4 clean up console logs
# (Saves and prompts for a single unified commit message!)
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: [detached HEAD 9a4e21c] feat: implement registration endpoint with email validation

topics.pitfall: Do not panic if you make a mistake during rebase; `git rebase --abort` immediately restores your branch to its exact state before you started rebasing.

quickCheck.question: What command immediately cancels an ongoing interactive rebase and returns your repository to its original state?
quickCheck.explanation: git rebase --abort stops the rebase operation and resets the working branch to where it started.

topics.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts Confidently
explanation: When two commits modify the exact same line of code in different ways, Git halts and inserts conflict markers:
`<<<<<<< HEAD` (your current branch code), `=======` (separator), `>>>>>>> branch` (incoming branch code).
To resolve: inspect both changes, choose the correct combination, delete the conflict markers, stage with `git add`, and continue.

codeSnippet.title: Anatomy and Resolution of a Merge Conflict
codeSnippet.description: Editing conflict markers in source code.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Conflict resolved, file staged with git add, and merge continued

topics.pitfall: Accidentally leaving a `<<<<<<< HEAD` marker inside your file will cause immediate syntax errors when the code compiles.

quickCheck.question: What should you do with the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers when resolving a merge conflict?
options: Leave them for the browser to parse
Delete all marker lines completely after selecting the desired code
quickCheck.explanation: Conflict markers are temporary visual aids inserted by Git and must be removed before staging the resolved file.

topics.title: Git Cherry-Pick: Selectively Transplanting a Single Commit
explanation: `git cherry-pick <commit-hash>` applies the changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch directly onto your current branch, without merging the whole branch.
Invaluable for extracting a single critical hotfix or isolated feature from an incomplete branch.

codeSnippet.title: Cherry-Picking a Hotfix Commit to Main
codeSnippet.description: Transplanting a single commit SHA directly onto main.
codeSnippet.code:
# Find the commit hash on experimental branch
git log experimental-branch --oneline -n 3
# Output: e4a81c2 fix: patch critical auth token expiration

# Switch to main and cherry-pick only that specific commit!
git switch main
git cherry-pick e4a81c2
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
[main 91b2c4e] fix: patch critical auth token expiration
 1 file changed, 4 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

topics.pitfall: Cherry-picking creates a duplicate commit with a new SHA hash; overusing cherry-picking instead of clean merging can lead to duplicated commit histories.

quickCheck.question: What does git cherry-pick <hash> do?
options: Applies the exact changes from a specific commit onto your current branch
quickCheck.explanation: Cherry-pick takes the patch introduced by a single commit and applies it on top of the currently checked out branch.

topics.title: The Safety Net: git reflog and Recovering "Lost" Commits
explanation: In Git, it is almost impossible to truly lose committed work.
`git reflog` (reference log) records every time HEAD was updated (commits, checkouts, rebases, resets).
Even if you run `git reset --hard` and accidentally delete your work, `git reflog` shows the commit hash, allowing you to restore it instantly via `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`.

codeSnippet.title: Rescuing Deleted Commits with Reflog
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting reflog and restoring state after accidental reset.
codeSnippet.code:
# View history of all past HEAD pointer movements
git reflog

# Output:
# 3b4e1a2 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1 (Accidental deletion!)
# 9f8c2b1 HEAD@{1}: commit: feat: complete database integration (Lost commit!)

# Restore the lost commit instantly:
git reset --hard 9f8c2b1
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
HEAD is now at 9f8c2b1 feat: complete database integration
Lost work completely restored!

topics.pitfall: Reflog only tracks committed work or staged states; uncommitted, unstaged modifications in your working directory cannot be recovered if wiped with `git checkout -- .`. Commit often!

quickCheck.question: What tool allows developers to find and recover commits that were accidentally deleted via git reset --hard?
quickCheck.explanation: git reflog tracks every movement of HEAD, providing an immutable audit trail to recover discarded commits.

topics.title: Conducting Professional Pull Request Code Reviews on GitHub
explanation: Code review is a collaborative quality gate, not an interrogation.
Effective reviewers check: architectural soundness, edge cases, test coverage, security vulnerabilities (un-sanitized inputs), and maintainability.
Use GitHub Suggestion blocks (```suggestion) so authors can apply one-click fixes directly in the PR diff.

codeSnippet.title: GitHub Suggestion Block in Markdown Review
codeSnippet.description: Providing executable one-click code suggestions in PR comments.
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Collaborative code review with actionable, one-click patch application

topics.pitfall: Avoid nitpicking purely stylistic formatting (tabs vs spaces); automate formatting with Prettier and ESLint in CI so human reviewers focus on architecture and logic.

quickCheck.question: What should automated CI linters (ESLint/Prettier) handle instead of human code reviewers?
options: Stylistic formatting, semicolon rules, and indentation nitpicks
quickCheck.explanation: Formatting and style enforcement should be 100% automated so engineers focus on logic, architecture, and edge cases.

topics.title: GitHub Branch Protection Rules & Required Status Checks
explanation: In enterprise repositories, developers are forbidden from pushing directly to `main`.

GitHub Branch Protection Rules enforce: 1) Require a Pull Request before merging, 2) Require at least 1-2 approving peer reviews, 3) Require all automated CI checks (linting, tests, build) to pass green.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring Branch Protection Safeguards
codeSnippet.description: Enforcing merge criteria on production branches.
codeSnippet.code:
# GitHub Repository Settings -> Branches -> Add rule: "main"
# [X] Require a pull request before merging
#     [X] Require approvals: 1
#     [X] Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
# [X] Require status checks to pass before merging
#     [X] Require branches to be up to date before merging
#     Status checks: "test", "build", "lint"
# [X] Do not allow bypassing the above settings
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Production branch permanently protected against accidental or broken pushes

topics.pitfall: Never disable branch protection to push a quick emergency fix; emergency fixes are the most likely to introduce critical regressions.

quickCheck.question: What does a GitHub Branch Protection Rule requiring "status checks to pass before merging" prevent?
options: Prevents merging PRs whose automated tests, linting, or build checks have failed
Prevents anyone from reading the code
quickCheck.explanation: Required status checks block PRs with failing automated test suites from merging into production.

practiceChallenge.title: Simulate Interactive Rebase and Conflict Resolution
instructions: Create a git repository with an initial commit on main.
Create two branches: feature-a and feature-b modifying the same file line.
Merge feature-a into main.
Attempt to merge feature-b, observe conflict markers, resolve, and commit.
practiceChallenge.starterCode: # Write bash commands to simulate conflict resolution
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
git init
echo "version = 1" > config.txt
git add config.txt
git commit -m "chore: initial version"

git switch -c feature-a
echo "version = 2 (feature-a)" > config.txt
git commit -am "feat: bump version to 2"

git switch main
git switch -c feature-b
echo "version = 3 (feature-b)" > config.txt
git commit -am "feat: bump version to 3"

# Merge feature-a into main
git switch main
git merge feature-a

# Merge feature-b -> CONFLICT!
git merge feature-b || true

# Resolve conflict
echo "version = 3 (resolved)" > config.txt
git add config.txt
git commit -m "merge: resolve version conflict between feature-a and feature-b"
git log --oneline -n 4
hints: Both branches modify config.txt, creating conflict on merge.
Overwrite config.txt with resolved version and stage with git add.

keyTakeaways: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches minimizes painful merge conflicts.
Use interactive rebase (git rebase -i) to squash messy commits before submitting PRs.
Protect production branches using GitHub Branch Protection Rules requiring peer approvals and green CI checks.

days.title: Containerization with Docker: Dockerfile, Images & Docker Compose
days.subtitle: OS containers, Dockerfile instructions, multi-stage builds, and multi-container composition
days.overview: Eliminate the "it works on my machine" problem forever. Master containerization with Docker: understand containers vs virtual machines, write optimized multi-stage Dockerfiles for Node.js and React, manage environment variables, and orchestrate multi-container apps (Node + PostgreSQL + Redis) using Docker Compose.

topics.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines: The Docker Revolution
explanation: Virtual Machines (VMs) virtualize physical hardware, running a complete guest Operating System (several gigabytes, slow boots, heavy CPU/RAM overhead).

Docker Containers virtualize the OS kernel. Containers share the host OS kernel and run as isolated processes with their own filesystem, environment variables, and networking (megabytes, sub-second boot).

codeSnippet.title: Verifying Docker CLI and Running Hello-World
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting Docker daemon and running first test container.
codeSnippet.code:
# Verify Docker installation
docker --version

# Run official hello-world container
docker run hello-world

# List active running containers
docker ps
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Hello from Docker! This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.

topics.pitfall: Do not confuse Docker Images with Containers. An Image is a read-only blueprint (class); a Container is a live, running instance of an image (object).

quickCheck.question: What is the fundamental architectural difference between Docker containers and Virtual Machines (VMs)?
options: Containers share the host OS kernel and run as lightweight isolated user-space processes; VMs package a full guest OS on virtual hardware
quickCheck.explanation: Containers share the host operating system kernel, making them lightweight and fast compared to full VMs.

topics.title: The Anatomy of a Dockerfile: Core Instructions
explanation: A `Dockerfile` is a text document containing instructions to build a Docker image.

Core instructions: `FROM` (base image), `WORKDIR` (working directory), `COPY` (transfer files into container), `RUN` (execute shell commands during build), `EXPOSE` (document port), `CMD` (default runtime command).

codeSnippet.title: Standard Node.js Dockerfile
codeSnippet.description: Containerizing a Node.js Express server.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Base Image: Lean Node 22 Alpine Linux
FROM node:22-alpine

# 2. Set container working directory
WORKDIR /app

# 3. Copy package manifests first for optimal layer caching!
COPY package*.json ./

# 4. Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 5. Copy remaining application source code
COPY . .

# 6. Expose HTTP port
EXPOSE 3000

# 7. Start server process
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Step 1/7 : FROM node:22-alpine
Successfully tagged my-backend:latest

topics.pitfall: Copying source code before `package.json` (`COPY . .` before `RUN npm install`) invalidates Docker layer cache every time you change a line of code, forcing slow re-installations of node_modules!

quickCheck.question: Why should COPY package*.json ./ and RUN npm install precede COPY . . in a Dockerfile?
options: To take advantage of Docker layer caching: if dependencies did not change, Docker reuses the cached layer and skips npm install
quickCheck.explanation: Docker caches layers sequentially. Copying package manifests first prevents unnecessary npm re-installations on code changes.

topics.title: The .dockerignore File: Keeping Images Lean and Secure
explanation: Just like `.gitignore`, `.dockerignore` prevents copying unwanted, sensitive, or heavy files into the Docker build context.
Always exclude `node_modules/` (let container build its own Linux binaries), `.env` (prevents baking secrets into image layers!), `.git/`, and build artifacts.

codeSnippet.title: Essential .dockerignore Configuration
codeSnippet.description: Preventing secret leakage and bloat in container builds.
codeSnippet.code:
# Ignore local machine dependencies
node_modules/

# NEVER bake secrets into image layers! (CRITICAL SECURITY)
.env
.env.*

# Ignore version control metadata
.git/
.gitignore

# Ignore local build logs
npm-debug.log*
dist/
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Clean build context transferred to Docker daemon

topics.pitfall: If you omit `.dockerignore` and have a `.env` with AWS or database keys, running `COPY . .` will bake your secrets into the public Docker image layer history!

quickCheck.question: Why should .env files be strictly excluded in .dockerignore?
options: Because copying .env bakes private secrets into image layers that anyone pulling the image can inspect and steal
quickCheck.explanation: Docker image layers are inspectable; embedding .env exposes secrets to anyone with access to the image.

topics.title: Multi-Stage Docker Builds for High-Performance Production Images
explanation: A naive build leaves TypeScript compilers, build tools, devDependencies, and test runners in the final production image (bloating images to 1.5GB).

Multi-Stage Builds use multiple `FROM` statements: Stage 1 ("builder") compiles TypeScript and builds React; Stage 2 ("runner") copies ONLY the compiled output into a pristine Alpine runtime image (reducing image size to 50MB!).

codeSnippet.title: Multi-Stage Dockerfile for React SPA with Nginx
codeSnippet.description: Compiling React in Node and serving via ultra-light Nginx.
codeSnippet.code:
# --- STAGE 1: Build Frontend Assets ---
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build # Outputs compiled static files to /app/dist

# --- STAGE 2: Lightweight Production Nginx Server ---
FROM nginx:alpine
# Copy compiled HTML/JS/CSS from builder stage
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Final production image size shrunk from 1.2GB down to 23MB!

topics.pitfall: Leaving build-time devDependencies and TypeScript compilers in production containers increases image attack surface and deployment transfer times.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary advantage of Multi-Stage Docker Builds?
options: Allows separating build tools from runtime environments, creating tiny, secure, stripped-down production images
quickCheck.explanation: Multi-stage builds leave compilers and devDependencies behind, copying only final artifacts to the production image.

topics.title: Managing Containers: build, run, exec, stop & logs
explanation: Essential Docker CLI commands for daily engineering:

`docker build -t my-app .` (builds image), `docker run -p 3000:3000 -d my-app` (runs container detached with port mapping), `docker logs -f <id>` (follows logs), `docker exec -it <id> sh` (opens interactive shell inside container).

codeSnippet.title: Docker Lifecycle CLI Commands
codeSnippet.description: Building, running, inspecting, and debugging containers.
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Build image with tag 'fullstack-api'
docker build -t fullstack-api:v1 .

# 2. Run container in background (-d) mapping host port 8080 to container 3000
docker run -d -p 8080:3000 --name api-service fullstack-api:v1

# 3. Stream live server logs
docker logs -f api-service

# 4. Open bash shell inside running container for debugging
docker exec -it api-service sh

# 5. Stop and remove container
docker stop api-service && docker rm api-service
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Container started with port forwarding 8080 -> 3000

topics.pitfall: Remember port mapping `-p <host_port>:<container_port>`. If your app listens on 3000 inside the container, running `-p 8080:3000` makes it accessible at `localhost:8080` on your laptop.

quickCheck.question: In docker run -p 8080:3000 my-image, what does 8080 represent?
options: The port on the host machine where external requests arrive
quickCheck.explanation: The format is -p <hostPort>:<containerPort>. 8080 is the port opened on the host machine.

topics.title: Multi-Container Orchestration with Docker Compose
explanation: Real-world full-stack applications require multiple coordinated services (Node backend + PostgreSQL database + Redis cache).
`docker-compose.yml` declares all services, their environment variables, networks, and persistent storage volumes in a single file. Running `docker compose up` boots the entire stack in one command.

codeSnippet.title: Full-Stack docker-compose.yml Configuration
codeSnippet.description: Orchestrating Node.js, PostgreSQL, and Redis together.
codeSnippet.code:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://dev:pass@db:5432/app
      - REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      - db
      - cache

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: dev
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  postgres_data:
codeSnippet.expectedOutput:
Network fullstack_default Created
Container db Started
Container cache Started
Container api Started

topics.pitfall: Notice that inside Docker Compose, services communicate using their service name as the host! The API connects to PostgreSQL at `db:5432`, NOT `localhost:5432`.

quickCheck.question: How do containers in the same docker-compose.yml network address each other?
options: By their service name (e.g. host "db" or "cache")
quickCheck.explanation: Docker Compose creates a shared bridge network where service names act as automatic DNS hostnames.

topics.title: Persistent Storage: Docker Named Volumes
explanation: Containers are ephemeral: when a container is deleted (`docker rm`), any files written inside its filesystem vanish forever.

Docker Volumes (`volumes: [ "postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data" ]`) mount dedicated storage outside the container filesystem directly on the host machine, preserving database records across container restarts and upgrades.

codeSnippet.title: Managing Docker Named Volumes
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting persistent storage volumes.
codeSnippet.code:
# List active Docker volumes
docker volume ls

# Inspect physical host mount path
docker volume inspect postgres_data

# Back up volume data
docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/db_backup.tar.gz /data
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Data persisted safely on host drive surviving container destruction

topics.pitfall: Running a PostgreSQL database container without a mounted volume means destroying the container destroys your entire database permanently!

quickCheck.question: Why must databases running inside Docker containers use Docker Volumes?
options: Because container filesystems are ephemeral; volumes persist database files on the host disk even when containers are deleted
quickCheck.explanation: Volumes ensure data persistence beyond the ephemeral lifecycle of individual container instances.

topics.title: Container Security: Non-Root Users & Least Privilege
explanation: By default, processes inside containers run as the Linux `root` superuser (UID 0). If an attacker breaches the application via remote code execution, they gain root access within the container and potentially the host.
Production Dockerfiles must switch to a non-root user (e.g. `USER node`) after installation, adhering to the principle of least privilege.

codeSnippet.title: Enforcing Non-Root Execution in Dockerfile
codeSnippet.description: Switching process execution to unprivileged node user.
codeSnippet.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .

# Change ownership of application directory to 'node' user
RUN chown -R node:node /app

# Switch to unprivileged non-root user (SECURITY REQUIREMENT)
USER node

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Container processes execute with restricted unprivileged node user credentials

topics.pitfall: Never run production containers as `root`; always declare `USER node` (or equivalent unprivileged user).

quickCheck.question: Why should production Dockerfiles declare USER node to run as a non-root user?
options: To enforce the principle of least privilege, preventing an attacker who breaches the app from gaining root superuser capabilities
quickCheck.explanation: Running as non-root limits the damage of security vulnerabilities by restricting process permissions.

practiceChallenge.title: Build a Multi-Stage Dockerfile with Non-Root Security
instructions: Create a 2-stage Dockerfile: builder stage compiles TypeScript with devDependencies.
Runner stage uses node:22-alpine, copies dist/ and production node_modules.
Set USER node for non-root execution.
Expose port 3000 and declare CMD.
practiceChallenge.starterCode: # Write multi-stage production Dockerfile
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
# Stage 1: Build
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: Production Runner
FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
RUN chown -R node:node /app
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
hints: Use AS builder and AS runner.
Copy compiled output using COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist.

keyTakeaways: Containers virtualize OS processes, ensuring identical execution across local dev and production clouds.
Multi-stage Docker builds shrink image sizes by 95% and remove build-time attack surfaces.
Use Docker Compose to orchestrate multi-container apps (Node + PostgreSQL + Redis) with named volumes.

days.title: Production Deployment & Publishing: CI/CD, Cloud Hosting & SSL
days.subtitle: GitHub Actions, automated test pipelines, Vercel/Render deployment, SSL certificates, and monitoring
days.overview: Cross the finish line: publish your full-stack application to the world! Automate Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) with GitHub Actions, deploy static frontends to Vercel/Netlify, deploy Dockerized backend APIs to Render/Fly.io/AWS, configure custom domains with SSL, and monitor errors with Sentry.

topics.title: What is CI/CD? Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment
explanation: Continuous Integration (CI): automatically builds code, runs linters, and executes automated test suites on every GitHub push and Pull Request, catching bugs before merging.
Continuous Deployment (CD): automatically packages passing code into Docker containers and deploys them to production cloud servers without manual intervention.

codeSnippet.title: Visualizing the Automated CI/CD Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Git push triggers automated testing, building, and deployment.
codeSnippet.code:
# Step 1: Developer pushes commit to GitHub
# Step 2: GitHub Actions triggers CI runner in cloud
#   ├── Run ESLint (npm run lint)
#   ├── Run Unit Tests (npm test)
#   └── Run Production Build (npm run build)
# Step 3: If all pass -> CD automatically deploys to Production Cloud!
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Automated pipeline guarantees only verified, tested code reaches production

topics.pitfall: Never deploy to production manually by dragging files via FTP or running commands on live servers; manual deployments are prone to human error and lack audit trails.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary role of Continuous Integration (CI)?
options: Automatically test and validate code changes on every commit before they merge into the production codebase
quickCheck.explanation: CI automatically executes builds and tests on every push, ensuring changes do not break existing features.

topics.title: Building a CI Pipeline with GitHub Actions (.github/workflows)
explanation: GitHub Actions workflows are declared in YAML files inside `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
You define events (`on: [push, pull_request]`), environments (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`), matrix strategies (testing on Node 20 and 22), and steps.

codeSnippet.title: Production GitHub Actions CI Workflow (ci.yml)
codeSnippet.description: Automated linting, testing, and building pipeline.
codeSnippet.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: Full Stack CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js 22
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run ESLint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run Test Suite
        run: npm test

      - name: Verify Production Build
        run: npm run build
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: GitHub Actions checks pass: All jobs finished successfully (Green checkmark!)

topics.pitfall: Use `npm ci` (clean install) instead of `npm install` in CI pipelines; `npm ci` strictly honors `package-lock.json` and fails if dependencies drift.

quickCheck.question: Why should npm ci be used in CI/CD pipelines instead of npm install?
options: npm ci is faster and strictly installs exact versions from package-lock.json without modifying it
npm install does not work on Linux
quickCheck.explanation: npm ci performs an automated clean install directly against the lockfile, guaranteeing reproducible builds.

topics.title: Deploying Frontend Single-Page Apps to Vercel / Netlify / Cloudflare Pages
explanation: Static Single-Page Apps (React, Vite, HTML/CSS/JS) do not require a heavy Node.js server to serve them. Deploying them to global Edge CDNs (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare) provides sub-50ms latency worldwide.
Connect your GitHub repository: on every push to `main`, the CDN runs `npm run build`, uploads `/dist` to global edge servers, and generates unique Preview URLs for every Pull Request.

codeSnippet.title: Deploying to Vercel via CLI
codeSnippet.description: Deploying production build to edge network.
codeSnippet.code:
# Install Vercel CLI
npm i -g vercel

# Deploy preview build
vercel

# Deploy directly to live production domain
vercel --prod

# Output:
# Inspect: https://vercel.com/dev/fullstack-app
# Production: https://fullstack-academy.vercel.app [320ms]
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Production: https://fullstack-academy.vercel.app

topics.pitfall: Remember to configure the SPA redirect rewrite in `vercel.json` (`{ "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }] }`) to prevent 404s when users refresh nested routes!

quickCheck.question: What is a major advantage of deploying static React SPAs to Edge CDNs (Vercel/Cloudflare Pages)?
options: Static assets are replicated across hundreds of global edge data centers, delivering sub-50ms loading times worldwide
It replaces the need for a backend
It allows running Python scripts directly in CSS
It is free for all enterprise banks
quickCheck.explanation: Edge CDNs cache static assets geographically close to users worldwide, minimizing network latency.

topics.title: Deploying Backend Node APIs & Databases to Render / Railway / Fly.io
explanation: Backend servers require persistent compute environments to listen on ports and connect to databases.

Platforms like Render, Railway, and Fly.io connect to your GitHub repo, automatically detect your Dockerfile or `package.json`, provision a managed PostgreSQL database, inject environment variables, and manage zero-downtime rolling deploys.

codeSnippet.title: Configuring Render Blueprint (render.yaml)
codeSnippet.description: Infrastructure as code for backend and managed PostgreSQL database.
codeSnippet.code:
# render.yaml Blueprint
services:
  - type: web
    name: fullstack-api
    runtime: node
    plan: starter
    buildCommand: npm ci && npx prisma migrate deploy
    startCommand: node src/server.js
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_ENV
        value: production
      - key: DATABASE_URL
        fromDatabase:
          name: fullstack-db
          property: connectionString

databases:
  - name: fullstack-db
    plan: starter
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: Infrastructure provisioned: Node service + Managed PostgreSQL connected

topics.pitfall: Never configure managed databases with public internet access without IP whitelisting or SSL enforcement (`sslmode=require`).

quickCheck.question: Why must npx prisma migrate deploy be executed during backend deployment before the server starts?
options: To apply any pending schema changes to the production database so the server code and database tables match
Prisma requires it to turn on
quickCheck.explanation: Running migrations during deployment ensures the database schema is updated to support the new application code.

topics.title: Custom Domains, DNS Records & Free Automated SSL/TLS (Let's Encrypt)
explanation: To use your own domain (`academy.io`), configure DNS records at your domain registrar:
1) A Record: maps `@` (root domain) to your server IP address (e.g. `76.76.21.21`).
2) CNAME Record: maps `www` to your hosting alias (e.g. `cname.vercel-dns.com`).
Modern cloud platforms automatically provision free, auto-renewing SSL/TLS certificates via Let's Encrypt, securing connections via HTTPS.

codeSnippet.title: Verifying SSL/TLS Certificate and HTTPS Redirection
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting live SSL certificate parameters.
codeSnippet.code:
# Verify HTTPS TLS handshake and certificate issuer
curl -I https://academy.io

# Output:
# HTTP/2 200
# date: Fri, 24 Oct 2026 12:00:00 GMT
# content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
# strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: HTTP/2 200 OK with Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) enforced

topics.pitfall: DNS propagation can take up to 24 hours (governed by DNS TTL). Set your TTL low (300 seconds) prior to cutover to minimize waiting time.

quickCheck.question: Which DNS record type is used to alias a subdomain (like www.example.com) to another hostname?
quickCheck.explanation: A CNAME (Canonical Name) record aliases one domain name to another canonical hostname.

topics.title: Managing Production Secrets & Environment Variables
explanation: Production secrets (`DATABASE_URL`, `JWT_SECRET`, `STRIPE_KEY`) must NEVER be in your code or git history.
Inject them via your cloud platform dashboard (Vercel Project Settings / Render Environment / AWS Secrets Manager) or encrypted secret management tools (Infisical, Doppler).

codeSnippet.title: Adding Secrets via GitHub CLI for CI/CD
codeSnippet.description: Injecting encrypted repository secrets for automated workflows.
codeSnippet.code:
# Set encrypted repository secret using GitHub CLI
gh secret set DATABASE_URL --body "postgres://prod_user:secret_pass@db.cloud.com/app"
gh secret set JWT_SECRET --body "super_secret_high_entropy_random_key_64_bytes"

# Workflows access them securely: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
codeSnippet.expectedOutput: ✓ Set secret DATABASE_URL for developer/fullstack-app

topics.pitfall: Never echo or print environment variables in build scripts or logs (`console.log(process.env)`); this leaks production secrets into public CI build logs!

explanation: In production, when a user encounters a crash, you cannot open their Chrome console. Without observability, bugs remain invisible.
Sentry captures unhandled exceptions in real time across both frontend and backend, recording stack traces, user breadcrumbs, browser versions, and alerts you via Slack/email.
