practiceChallenge.title: Author a Production GitHub Actions CI/CD Pipeline
instructions: Write a complete GitHub Actions YAML workflow named deploy.yml.
Trigger on push to main branch.
Define jobs for test (lint, test, build) and deploy (simulated deploy step).
Ensure deploy only runs if test passes (needs: test).
practiceChallenge.starterCode: # Write complete GitHub Actions deploy.yml workflow
practiceChallenge.solutionCode:
name: Production CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy to Cloud Provider
        run: echo "Deploying verified build to production cloud..."
hints: Use needs: test on the deploy job so it waits for testing to pass.
Use uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with cache: npm.

It runs 10 operating systems at once

days.title: Compilation Pipeline, Types & Fast I/O
days.subtitle: Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker, primitive types & std::cin/cout mechanics
days.overview: Understand how C++ source code transforms into bare-metal machine instructions. Learn the 4 compilation phases, exact type sizes, fixed-width integers, fast I/O optimization, and the core anatomy of a C++ translation unit.

topics.title: The 4-Stage C++ Compilation Pipeline
explanation: C++ does not run on a virtual machine or interpreter. It compiles directly to native processor instructions through 4 distinct stages: Preprocessing, Compilation, Assembly, and Linking.

In the Preprocessor stage (`cpp` / `-E`), macro directives starting with `#` (#include, #define, #ifdef) are textually expanded. Header files are copied directly into the source file to form a Translation Unit.

The Compiler (`-S`) analyzes the AST, performs semantic checking, optimizes intermediate representation, and produces assembly code. The Assembler (`-c`) translates assembly into binary machine object files (`.o` / `.obj`). Finally, the Linker resolves external symbols, stitches object files with the standard library (`libstdc++`/`libc++`), and outputs the final ELF or PE binary executable.
keyRules: Each .cpp file is compiled independently as a single Translation Unit.
Header files (.h / .hpp) contain declarations; implementation files (.cpp) contain definitions.
One Definition Rule (ODR): An entity cannot have multiple conflicting definitions in a program.

codeSnippet.title: Compilation Pipeline Commands & Verification
codeSnippet.description: Shell commands for inspecting intermediate compilation stages in GCC/Clang
codeSnippet.code:
# 1. Preprocess only (expands macros & includes) -> main.i
g++ -E main.cpp -o main.i

# 2. Compile to assembly language -> main.s
g++ -S main.cpp -o main.s

# 3. Assemble into machine object file -> main.o
g++ -c main.cpp -o main.o

# 4. Link object files into final executable binary
g++ main.o -o program
./program

topics.pitfall: Placing function definitions with bodies in headers without `inline` causes Linker error LNK2005 / duplicate symbol definitions.

quickCheck.question: Which stage of the C++ compilation pipeline resolves external function calls across different object files?
quickCheck.explanation: The Linker is responsible for resolving unresolved external symbol references and combining multiple object files into the final executable.

topics.title: Primitive Types, Sizes & Fixed-Width Integers
explanation: C++ primitive types have platform-dependent sizes guaranteed only by minimum ranges in the standard (e.g. `int` is at least 16 bits, typically 32 bits on modern x86_64).

For cross-platform systems programming and binary protocol serialization, always include `<cstdint>` and use exact-width types: `int8_t`, `int16_t`, `int32_t`, `int64_t`, and unsigned counterparts `uint8_t`, `uint32_t`, `uint64_t`.
`size_t` is the standard unsigned integer type for object sizes and array indexing, matching the native word size of the CPU architecture (64-bit on 64-bit systems).
keyRules: sizeof(char) is always guaranteed to be 1 byte by definition in the C++ standard.
Use uint8_t for raw byte manipulation, uint32_t for 32-bit words, uint64_t for large counters.
size_t is unsigned; subtracting a larger size_t from a smaller one wraps to a massive positive number (underflow).

codeSnippet.title: Exact Width Integers & Type Sizes
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting exact byte allocations with sizeof() and <cstdint>

topics.pitfall: Comparing signed `int` with unsigned `size_t` causes implicit conversion to unsigned, turning negative numbers into huge positive values.

quickCheck.question: What header must be included to use fixed-width types like int32_t and uint64_t?
quickCheck.explanation: <cstdint> declares exact-width integer types such as int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, and int64_t.

topics.title: High-Performance Fast I/O & Stream Synchronization
explanation: By default, C++ streams (`std::cin` / `std::cout`) maintain synchronization with C runtime standard I/O buffers (`stdin` / `stdout`). This synchronization allows mixing `printf` and `std::cout`, but causes heavy function-call overhead.
In competitive programming, game engines, and low-latency servers, you disable this sync via `std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);`.
Additionally, `std::cin` is tied to `std::cout` by default, flushing `cout` before every input operation. Untying them with `std::cin.tie(nullptr);` eliminates redundant flushes.
keyRules: Call std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); std::cin.tie(nullptr); at the beginning of main().
Avoid std::endl because it flushes the OS buffer; use "\n" for newline without flushing.

codeSnippet.title: Fast I/O Setup Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Uncoupling C synchronization for microsecond stream throughput

topics.pitfall: Using `std::endl` in loops forces a hardware flush on every iteration, destroying I/O throughput.

quickCheck.question: Why is "\n" preferred over std::endl in high-throughput C++ applications?
options: std::endl causes an automatic buffer flush, which is slow
std::endl does not emit a newline character
\n is only supported on Linux systems
quickCheck.explanation: std::endl inserts a newline AND explicitly flushes the stream buffer, causing an expensive write system call.

topics.title: Variable Initialization: Uniform Braced Initialization (`{}`)
explanation: C++ historically had multiple conflicting initialization syntaxes: copy initialization (`int x = 5;`), direct initialization (`int x(5);`), and aggregate initialization.
C++11 introduced Uniform Braced Initialization (`int x{5};` or `int x = {5};`). It works consistently across primitives, structs, arrays, and STL containers.
Crucially, braced initialization strictly prevents narrowing conversions (e.g. implicitly converting `double` to `int` or `long long` to `int` without warning).
keyRules: Prefer braced initialization `int val{42};` as default in modern C++.
`double d = 3.14; int x{d};` produces a compilation error because it truncates data.

codeSnippet.title: Uniform Braced Initialization vs Narrowing
codeSnippet.description: Safe initialization preventing precision truncation bugs at compile time

topics.pitfall: Using parentheses for object construction can trigger the "Most Vexing Parse", where the compiler interprets an object declaration as a function signature.

quickCheck.question: What happens when you compile `int x{3.99};` in modern C++?
options: The compiler emits an error for narrowing conversion
x silently truncates to 3 without warning
quickCheck.explanation: Braced initialization enforces compile-time safety by rejecting narrowing conversions that lose precision.

topics.title: `constexpr`, `consteval` & Compile-Time Evaluation
explanation: `const` specifies runtime immutability (the value cannot be modified after initialization).

`constexpr` specifies compile-time computability: expressions and functions marked `constexpr` can be evaluated by the compiler during compilation, embedding constant results directly into the binary without any runtime CPU cost.
C++20 introduced `consteval` (immediate functions), which MUST execute at compile time; if the argument is not a compile-time constant, compilation fails immediately.
keyRules: Use constexpr for mathematical constants, lookup tables, and pure calculation functions.
constexpr functions can execute at compile time OR runtime depending on their arguments.
consteval functions ONLY execute at compile time; calling them with runtime variables errors.

codeSnippet.title: Zero-Cost Compile-Time Factorial & Math
codeSnippet.description: Computing values at compile time with constexpr and consteval

topics.pitfall: Marking a function `constexpr` does not guarantee it runs at compile time unless its return value is assigned to a `constexpr` variable or template parameter.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary difference between const and constexpr?
options: const ensures runtime immutability; constexpr can compute the value at compile time
constexpr can only be used with floating-point numbers
const is evaluated by the linker, constexpr by the assembler
const variables can be modified inside functions
quickCheck.explanation: const means read-only at runtime; constexpr requires that the expression can be evaluated at compile time.

topics.title: Type Inference with `auto` & `decltype`
explanation: C++11 introduced automatic type deduction via `auto`. The compiler deduces the exact type from the initializing expression at compile time with zero runtime overhead.
`auto` strips references (`&`) and top-level `const` by default. To preserve them, specify `const auto&` or `auto&`.
`decltype(expr)` extracts the exact declared type of an expression without evaluating it, essential for generic templates and forwarding return types.
keyRules: Use auto when types are obvious from context (e.g., auto iter = vec.begin();).
Use const auto& when iterating over containers to avoid expensive element copies.
auto x = 5; deduces int. auto& ref = x; deduces int&.

codeSnippet.title: auto Deduction Rules & const auto&
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating reference decay and preserving qualifiers with auto

topics.pitfall: Iterating with `for (auto item : container)` makes an expensive copy of every element on each step; use `for (const auto& item : container)` instead.

quickCheck.question: If `const int x = 10;`, what is the deduced type of `auto y = x;`?
quickCheck.explanation: Plain `auto` strips top-level const and references. `y` is deduced as a mutable `int` copy.

topics.title: Scoped Enumerations: `enum class` vs Legacy `enum`
explanation: Legacy C-style `enum Color { Red, Green, Blue };` exports its enumerators into the enclosing scope, creating global naming collisions. It also implicitly converts to integer.
Modern C++ `enum class Color { Red, Green, Blue };` is strongly typed and strongly scoped. Enumerator names must be qualified (`Color::Red`) and do not implicitly convert to integers.
You can also specify the underlying storage type (e.g. `enum class PacketType : uint8_t { ... };`) for precise network and memory layout control.
keyRules: Always use enum class instead of plain enum.
Use static_cast<int>(val) if you explicitly need the numeric integer value.
Specify the underlying integer type (uint8_t, uint16_t) to save memory.

codeSnippet.title: Scoped enum class with Fixed Underlying Type
codeSnippet.description: Preventing namespace pollution and ensuring type safety

topics.pitfall: Plain `enum` values collide when two enums in the same file have a member with the same name (e.g. `Status::OK` vs `Http::OK`).

quickCheck.question: Why is `enum class` preferred over traditional C-style `enum`?
options: It prevents namespace pollution and prevents implicit conversion to int
It compiles faster than legacy enum
It can only store string values
quickCheck.explanation: enum class values are scoped to their type (Color::Red) and require explicit casting to integers, preventing bugs.

topics.title: Anatomy of a Production Translation Unit & Capstone Day 1
explanation: A production C++ file cleanly combines header guards (`#pragma once`), standard includes, custom namespace encapsulation, and the `int main()` entry point.

Namespaces (`namespace Engine { ... }`) prevent global symbol collisions in large codebases. Never write `using namespace std;` in header files because it pollutes every file that includes that header.
Returning `0` from `main()` indicates successful execution to the operating system; C++ implicitly appends `return 0;` if omitted from `main()`.
keyRules: Use #pragma once at the top of headers as the industry-standard header guard.
Never place "using namespace std;" in header files.
Encapsulate domain code inside your own project namespace.

codeSnippet.title: Production C++ Program Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Structured translation unit with namespaces and clean entry point

topics.pitfall: Placing `using namespace std;` in a header file forces that namespace on every translation unit that includes it, breaking compilation with ambiguous symbols.

quickCheck.question: Where should `using namespace std;` strictly NEVER be placed?
quickCheck.explanation: Including `using namespace std;` in a header leaks the entire standard namespace into every source file that includes it.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 1 Capstone: Memory-Sized Network Packet Header
instructions: Define an enum class PacketType with underlying type uint8_t containing: SYN=1, ACK=2, DATA=3, FIN=4.
Create a struct PacketHeader with exact-width types: uint32_t sequenceId, PacketType type, and uint16_t payloadLength.
Verify that sizeof(PacketHeader) and sizeof(PacketType) match expectations.
hints: Remember to specify : uint8_t after enum class PacketType.
Use static_cast<int>(header.type) when printing with std::cout.

keyTakeaways: C++ compiles through 4 distinct stages: Preprocessor, Compiler, Assembler, and Linker.
Always use <cstdint> fixed-width integer types for predictable memory layout.
Braced initialization prevents accidental data truncation via narrowing conversion errors.
constexpr evaluates math and data structures at compile time with zero runtime CPU cost.

days.title: Pointers from Scratch: Addresses & Pointer Arithmetic
days.subtitle: The address-of operator (&), dereferencing (*), null pointers & contiguous pointer traversal
days.overview: Demystify the central mechanism of C++: pointers. Master memory addresses, pointer syntax, null pointer safety with nullptr, pointer arithmetic across contiguous buffers, and void pointers.

topics.title: Memory Addresses & The Address-of Operator (`&`)
explanation: Every variable stored in memory resides at a unique physical or virtual address (typically expressed as a hexadecimal number like `0x7ffee4b2891c`).
The address-of operator `&` retrieves the memory address of any lvalue variable.
A pointer is simply a variable whose stored value is the memory address of another variable.
keyRules: int* ptr = &x; declares ptr as a pointer to an integer.
The size of any pointer depends on CPU architecture: 4 bytes on 32-bit systems, 8 bytes on 64-bit systems, regardless of what type it points to.

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Memory Addresses
codeSnippet.description: Printing variable addresses and pointer memory footprints

topics.pitfall: Confusing the address-of operator `&` with the bitwise AND operator `&`.

quickCheck.question: What is the size of a pointer to a char (`char*`) on a 64-bit operating system?
quickCheck.explanation: On a 64-bit architecture, ALL pointers occupy 8 bytes because they hold a 64-bit memory address.

topics.title: Dereferencing Pointers (`*`) & Indirect Mutation
explanation: Dereferencing a pointer using the unary `*` operator accesses the value residing at the target memory address.
Reading `*ptr` fetches the pointed-to value. Writing `*ptr = newValue;` modifies the target variable indirectly.
The pointer type (e.g. `int*` vs `double*`) informs the compiler how many bytes to read/write starting from that memory address.
keyRules: *ptr reads or writes the value at the destination address.
Dereferencing an uninitialized or wild pointer leads to undefined behavior or segmentation fault.

codeSnippet.title: Dereferencing & Indirect Mutation
codeSnippet.description: Mutating variables through pointers

topics.pitfall: Dereferencing a dangling pointer whose target has been destroyed causes silent memory corruption.

quickCheck.question: What does `*p = 100;` do if `p` points to variable `x`?
options: Changes the memory address stored in p to 100
Creates a new pointer with value 100
quickCheck.explanation: Dereferencing `p` accesses `x` directly, mutating `x` to 100.

topics.title: The `nullptr` Literal vs Legacy `NULL` / `0`
explanation: In C and pre-C++11, null pointers were represented by the macro `NULL` or the literal integer `0`. This caused subtle bugs when calling overloaded functions.
C++11 introduced `nullptr`, a keyword of type `std::nullptr_t`. It implicitly converts to any pointer type, but NEVER converts to an integer.
Always initialize pointers that do not yet have a target to `nullptr`.
keyRules: Always initialize pointers: int* ptr = nullptr; instead of leaving them uninitialized.
Always check if (ptr != nullptr) before dereferencing.

codeSnippet.title: nullptr Safety & Overload Disambiguation
codeSnippet.description: Why nullptr is strictly typesafe compared to legacy 0/NULL

topics.pitfall: Passing `NULL` to overloaded functions can invoke the `int` overload instead of the pointer overload because `NULL` is `#define NULL 0`.

quickCheck.question: What is the type of the `nullptr` literal in C++11 and later?
quickCheck.explanation: nullptr has its own unique, typesafe type: std::nullptr_t.

topics.title: Pointer Arithmetic & Memory Offsets
explanation: Adding an integer `k` to a pointer `ptr + k` does not add `k` bytes; it advances the address by `k * sizeof(*ptr)` bytes.
For example, if `int* p = 0x1000;`, then `p + 1` evaluates to `0x1004` (since `sizeof(int) == 4`).
Subtracting two pointers pointing to elements in the same array yields the number of elements between them, represented by `std::ptrdiff_t`.
keyRules: Pointer arithmetic is only defined within the bounds of an array (plus one past the end).
ptr++ advances to the next contiguous element.
ptr2 - ptr1 computes element distance, not raw byte distance.

codeSnippet.title: Pointer Arithmetic Across Contiguous Arrays
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating stride progression based on sizeof(T)

topics.pitfall: Performing pointer arithmetic outside the allocated bounds of an array causes Undefined Behavior.

quickCheck.question: If `double* p = (double*)0x2000;` and `sizeof(double) == 8`, what is `p + 2`?
quickCheck.explanation: p + 2 adds 2 * sizeof(double) = 16 bytes = 0x10 in hex. 0x2000 + 0x10 = 0x2010.

topics.title: Pointers and Array Decay
explanation: In C++, the name of a raw array decays implicitly into a pointer to its first element (`&arr[0]`) when passed to functions or assigned to pointers.
However, a raw array retains its total size (`sizeof(arr) == N * sizeof(T)`) within its declaring scope, whereas a decayed pointer only has `sizeof(ptr) == 8`.
Bracket indexing `arr[i]` is syntactic sugar for `*(arr + i)`.
keyRules: arr[i] is identical to *(arr + i).
Passing raw arrays to functions strips size information; pass size separately or use std::span / std::array.

codeSnippet.title: Array Decay vs sizeof Preservation
codeSnippet.description: Comparing raw array scope vs decayed function parameter pointer

topics.pitfall: Trying to compute the number of elements in a function parameter array using `sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0])` calculates `8 / 4 = 2` on 64-bit systems instead of true array length.

quickCheck.question: Why does passing an array to a function `void foo(int arr[])` cause array decay?
options: The array parameter decays into a pointer `int*` to its first element
The array elements are copied onto the stack
The array is automatically converted to std::vector
The compiler throws an error unless std::array is used
quickCheck.explanation: Function parameter `int arr[]` is adjusted by the compiler to `int* arr`, losing the original array size.

topics.title: `void*` (Generic Pointers) & Static Casts
explanation: A `void*` is a pointer to an untyped memory address. It can store the address of any object without an explicit cast.
Because `void` has no size, you CANNOT dereference or perform pointer arithmetic on a `void*`.
To access the underlying data, you must cast it back to a typed pointer using `static_cast<T*>()` or `reinterpret_cast<T*>()`.
keyRules: void* cannot be dereferenced directly (*p is illegal).
Use static_cast<TargetType*>(voidPtr) to restore type information.
Widely used in low-level memory managers, callbacks, and OS APIs.

codeSnippet.title: Generic void* and static_cast
codeSnippet.description: Safely handling untyped memory addresses

topics.pitfall: Casting a `void*` to the wrong pointer type causes undefined behavior and garbage data reads.

quickCheck.question: Can you dereference a `void*` pointer directly (`*ptr`)?
options: No, because the compiler does not know the size or type of the object
Yes, it defaults to a 1-byte char read
quickCheck.explanation: void has an incomplete type with unknown size, making direct dereferencing illegal.

topics.title: Pointer to Pointer (`T**`) & Dynamic 2D Arrays
explanation: A pointer to a pointer stores the address of another pointer. Syntax: `int** ptrToPtr;`.
Pointer-to-pointer is commonly used for dynamic 2D matrices, modifying pointers inside functions, and handling arrays of string pointers (`char* argv[]`).
Each level of `*` dereferences one indirection level: `**pp` accesses the underlying integer.
keyRules: *pp yields the address of the intermediate pointer.
**pp yields the actual value.
In modern C++, prefer flat 1D vectors with row-major indexing: index = row * cols + col.

codeSnippet.title: Pointer-to-Pointer Indirection
codeSnippet.description: Two levels of indirection and value access

topics.pitfall: Allocating 2D arrays as arrays of pointers (`new int*[rows]`) scatters rows across the heap, destroying CPU cache locality compared to contiguous flat buffers.

quickCheck.question: If `p` is an `int*`, what is the type of `&p`?
quickCheck.explanation: Taking the address of an `int*` yields a pointer to a pointer to int: `int**`.

topics.title: Pointer Safety Guidelines & Day 2 Capstone
explanation: Pointers provide maximum performance and hardware control, but improper usage causes the majority of security vulnerabilities (use-after-free, buffer overflows, null dereference).
Adhere to three defensive rules: (1) Always initialize to `nullptr`; (2) Always null-check before dereference; (3) Set freed pointers to `nullptr` immediately after deletion.
In Days 3 and 10, we will learn how modern references and smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`) automate these protections.
keyRules: Rule 1: Never leave a pointer uninitialized.
Rule 2: Never return a pointer to a local stack variable.
Rule 3: Set deleted pointers to nullptr.

codeSnippet.title: Defensive Pointer Traversal Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Safe sequential array traversal using pointer arithmetic

topics.pitfall: Returning the address of a local stack variable: `int* getPtr() { int x = 10; return &x; }` causes catastrophic undefined behavior because the stack frame is destroyed on return.

quickCheck.question: What happens if a function returns `&x` where `x` is a local stack variable?
options: It returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory (undefined behavior)
The compiler promotes x to the heap automatically
quickCheck.explanation: Local stack variables are popped when the function returns, leaving a dangling pointer.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 2 Capstone: In-Place Array Reversal via Pointer Arithmetic
instructions: Implement a function `void reverseArray(int* start, int* end)` where `start` points to the first element and `end` points to the last element.
Use two pointers (`left` moving forward, `right` moving backward) and swap values until they meet.
Do NOT use bracket notation `arr[i]`; use only pointer dereferencing and arithmetic.
hints: The loop condition should be `while (start < end)`.
Increment `start++` and decrement `end--` inside the loop.

keyTakeaways: A pointer stores the memory address of an object; dereferencing (*) accesses the value.
Always use `nullptr` instead of `0` or `NULL` for typesafe pointer initialization.
Pointer arithmetic advances by `sizeof(T)` bytes per step, not 1 byte.
Never return the address of a local stack variable.

days.title: References, Const Correctness & Value Semantics
days.subtitle: Lvalue references, re-binding impossibility, const references & pointer-to-const vs const-pointer
days.overview: Learn the power of C++ references: aliases that never require null-checking. Understand const-correctness from left-to-right reading rules and pass-by-const-reference for zero-copy performance.

topics.title: Lvalue References (`&`) as Variable Aliases
explanation: A reference is an alias for an existing object. Syntax: `int& ref = original;`.
Unlike pointers, a reference MUST be initialized at creation time. It cannot be null, and it CANNOT be rebound to refer to a different object later.
Any operation applied to `ref` is applied directly to the original object.
keyRules: References cannot be null: no null checks required.
References cannot be rebound: assigning ref = other changes original value, not alias binding.
References do not have their own address; &ref returns the address of the target object.

codeSnippet.title: Reference Alias Semantics
codeSnippet.description: Direct variable aliasing without pointer syntax

topics.pitfall: Trying to re-bind a reference with `ref = other;` does NOT point the reference to `other`; it assigns the value of `other` into the original variable.

quickCheck.question: Can a C++ reference be rebound to refer to a different variable after initialization?
options: No, references can never be rebound
quickCheck.explanation: References are permanent aliases established at initialization; they cannot be rebound to refer to another object.

topics.title: Pass-by-Const-Reference (`const T&`) for Zero-Copy
explanation: Passing large objects (strings, vectors, custom structs) by value copies the entire memory footprint onto the stack, destroying throughput.
Passing by `const T&` passes a lightweight memory address (8 bytes on 64-bit) while guaranteeing to the caller that the function will NOT mutate the object.
Fundamental rule of C++ API design: Pass cheap primitives (int, double, pointers, std::string_view) by value; pass non-trivial objects by `const T&`.
keyRules: Rule of thumb: sizeof(T) <= 2 * sizeof(void*) -> pass by value; larger -> pass by const T&.
const references can bind to temporary rvalue literals (e.g. const std::string& s = "hello";).

codeSnippet.title: Pass-by-Value vs Pass-by-Const-Reference
codeSnippet.description: Eliminating deep buffer clones in function arguments

topics.pitfall: Passing small primitive types (like `int` or `float`) by `const int&` is actually SLOWER than passing by value because it adds pointer indirection overhead.

quickCheck.question: Why is `const std::string&` preferred over `std::string` in function parameters?
options: It avoids an expensive heap copy of the string contents
It makes the string mutable inside the function
It converts the string to a C-string
quickCheck.explanation: Passing by const reference passes only a memory address, avoiding heap allocation and deep buffer copying.

topics.title: Pointer to Const vs Const Pointer (Clockwise / Spiral Rule)
explanation: Understanding `const` placement with pointers is critical in C++.
`const int* ptr` (or `int const* ptr`): Pointer to CONST data. The target integer CANNOT be modified through `ptr`, but `ptr` can be pointed to another address.
`int* const ptr`: CONST pointer to mutable data. The target integer can be modified, but `ptr` itself CANNOT be changed to point elsewhere.
`const int* const ptr`: CONST pointer to CONST data. Neither the pointer address nor the target data can be changed.
keyRules: Read type declarations from right to left starting at the identifier.
const to the left of * = data is const.
const to the right of * = pointer address is const.

codeSnippet.title: Deciphering Const Pointers
codeSnippet.description: Target immutability vs pointer address immutability

topics.pitfall: Accidentally using `int* const` instead of `const int*` when you intended to protect the data from mutation.

quickCheck.question: What is immutable in `const int* p`?
options: The integer data pointed to by p
The memory address stored in p
Both the data and the address
quickCheck.explanation: Because const appears before the asterisk, the pointed-to int value is read-only.

topics.title: Const Member Functions in Classes
explanation: In C++, member functions that do not mutate member variables should be marked with trailing `const`: `int getScore() const { return score; }`.
Within a `const` member function, all member variables are treated as `const`, and `this` has type `const MyClass* const`.
Const member functions are required so that callers holding a `const MyClass&` can invoke them.
keyRules: Mark all getters and inspection methods as const.
A const object or const reference can ONLY invoke const member functions.
Use mutable keyword only for caching/mutex primitives that do not affect observable state.

codeSnippet.title: Const Member Function Declaration
codeSnippet.description: Enabling inspection on const object instances

topics.pitfall: Omitting `const` on a getter prevents it from being called whenever the object is passed by `const&`, causing cascading compilation errors.

quickCheck.question: What happens if you try to call a non-const member function on a `const` object reference?
options: Compilation error: non-const method cannot be called on a const object
The const qualifier is automatically stripped
quickCheck.explanation: The compiler prevents calling non-const methods on const objects to enforce const-correctness.

topics.title: Const Casting & The `mutable` Keyword
explanation: The `mutable` keyword allows a class member variable to be modified even inside `const` member functions.
This is strictly intended for internal implementation details that do not alter the logical state of the object, such as `std::mutex` locks or memoization caches.
`const_cast<T*>` or `const_cast<T&>` removes constness. However, modifying an object that was originally declared `const` via `const_cast` is UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR.
keyRules: Use mutable exclusively for mutexes, thread locks, and internal cache counters.
Never cast away const with const_cast to modify truly const data.

codeSnippet.title: Thread-Safe Mutable Access Counter
codeSnippet.description: Using mutable for internal access logging in const methods

topics.pitfall: Using `const_cast` to modify an object in read-only memory (ROM/Flash or .rodata section) results in a hardware memory fault crash.

quickCheck.question: When is using the `mutable` keyword on a class member variable justified?
options: For internal implementation details like mutexes and caches that do not affect logical state
To allow any function to delete the object
quickCheck.explanation: mutable is specifically designed for thread locks, memoization, and debug statistics that do not change logical observable state.

topics.title: Structured Binding Declarations (C++17)
explanation: C++17 introduced structured bindings (`auto [x, y] = pair;`), allowing simultaneous decomposition of tuples, pairs, structs, and fixed arrays into individual named aliases.
Syntax: `auto [a, b, c] = myStruct;` copies members; `const auto& [a, b, c] = myStruct;` binds const references without copying.
Extensively used when iterating over key-value maps: `for (const auto& [key, value] : myMap)`.
keyRules: Use const auto& [k, v] when iterating over std::map to prevent pair copying.
Works seamlessly on public aggregate structs without boilerplate getter methods.

codeSnippet.title: Structured Bindings with Structs & Maps
codeSnippet.description: Clean tuple and struct unpacking in C++17

topics.pitfall: Writing `auto [x, y]` creates copies of all fields; remember `auto& [x, y]` if you intend to modify the original struct fields.

quickCheck.question: What C++ standard version introduced structured bindings (`auto [x, y] = ...`)?
quickCheck.explanation: Structured bindings were officially standardized in C++17.

topics.title: References vs Pointers Comparison Matrix
explanation: Both pointers and references achieve indirection and pass-by-address, but have distinct design constraints.
References: Must be initialized, cannot be null, cannot be rebound, access members with `.`, cleaner syntax.
Pointers: Can be uninitialized/null, can be rebound to new targets, support pointer arithmetic, access members with `->`.
keyRules: Use references by default for parameters and return types.
Use pointers when optionality (nullability) or rebinding is genuinely required.
Use smart pointers (std::unique_ptr) when managing ownership of dynamic memory.

codeSnippet.title: Side-by-Side: Reference vs Pointer Usage
codeSnippet.description: Contrasting syntax, nullability, and access semantics

topics.pitfall: Returning a reference to a local stack variable produces a dangling reference, identically dangerous to a dangling pointer.

quickCheck.question: When should a pointer be chosen over a reference for a function parameter?
options: When the argument is optional and can be `nullptr`
quickCheck.explanation: Pointers represent nullable/optional semantics; references guarantee a non-null target.

topics.title: Day 3 Capstone: Const-Correct Financial Transaction Ledger
explanation: Synthesizing Day 3 concepts into a realistic banking transaction engine.
Demonstrating const-correct getters, pass-by-const-reference, structured bindings, and mutable audit trail logging.
Clean architecture separates mutable command operations from read-only query operations.
keyRules: Command-Query Separation: Mutation methods modify state; query methods are const.
All non-trivial parameters passed via const reference.

codeSnippet.title: Production Const-Correct Account Class
codeSnippet.description: Complete class implementing full const correctness

topics.pitfall: Failing to declare query methods const makes them unusable on const account instances.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of const-correctness across a large C++ codebase?
options: It provides compile-time guarantees against unintended state mutations and documents API intent
It eliminates the need for header files
It forces all functions to be inlined
quickCheck.explanation: Const-correctness enables the compiler to enforce immutability rules, preventing whole classes of mutation bugs at compile time.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 3 Capstone: Safe Buffer Viewer Class
instructions: Create a class `BufferViewer` that holds a `const int* data` and `size_t size`.
Implement const member functions `size()`, `get(size_t index)`, and `print()` that traverse the buffer without modifying it.
Verify that a const instance of `BufferViewer` can call all member functions.
hints: Make sure all public inspection functions end with the `const` keyword.
Store the pointer as `const int* m_data`.

keyTakeaways: References are permanent aliases that cannot be null or rebound.
Pass large objects by `const T&` for zero-copy performance and caller safety.
Read pointer declarations right-to-left: `const int*` = const data; `int* const` = const address.
Mark all non-mutating class methods `const` so const references can call them.

days.title: Stack vs Heap Memory: `new` / `delete` Mechanics
days.subtitle: Virtual address space layout, stack frames, heap fragmentation & memory leak prevention
days.overview: Understand the physical anatomy of computer memory in C++: the code segment, data segment, BSS, stack, and heap. Learn dynamic memory allocation with new/delete, array new[]/delete[], and the origins of memory leaks.

topics.title: Process Virtual Memory Layout (Text, Data, BSS, Stack, Heap)
explanation: When an OS executes a C++ binary, it assigns it a Virtual Address Space partitioned into distinct segments.
Text Segment: Read-only machine instructions. Data Segment: Initialized global and static variables. BSS: Zero-initialized global/static data.
Stack: Fast, LIFO memory managed automatically by the CPU. Allocations happen by simply moving the Stack Pointer register (`%rsp`).
Heap: Dynamic memory allocated at runtime via the OS memory allocator (`brk`/`mmap` via `malloc`/`new`). Slower, but persists across function calls until explicitly freed.
keyRules: Stack allocations are instantaneous (single instruction subtract on %rsp).
Heap allocations require searching free lists, thread locks, and system calls.
Stack grows downward on x86; Heap grows upward toward the stack.

codeSnippet.title: Comparing Stack vs Heap Addresses
codeSnippet.description: Observing opposite memory address spaces for stack and heap variables

topics.pitfall: Allocating massive buffers on the stack (e.g. `int huge[10000000];`) exceeds the OS stack limit (typically 8MB on Linux) and causes immediate Stack Overflow segmentation fault.

quickCheck.question: What segment of memory is managed automatically by the CPU stack pointer register?
quickCheck.explanation: The stack is managed automatically by CPU push/pop and stack pointer adjustments.

topics.title: Dynamic Allocation with `new` and `delete`
explanation: The `new` operator performs two distinct tasks: (1) Allocates raw bytes from the free store (heap); (2) Invokes the constructor to initialize the object.
The `delete` operator performs the reverse: (1) Invokes the destructor to clean up resources; (2) Returns memory back to the heap allocator.
Calling `delete` on a pointer does NOT erase the pointer itself; it only frees the pointed-to memory. The pointer becomes a "dangling pointer" unless set to `nullptr`.
keyRules: Every single `new` must have exactly one corresponding `delete`.
Deleting nullptr is completely safe and performs no operation (no-op).
Always set ptr = nullptr immediately after delete ptr.

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic Heap Allocation and Deletion
codeSnippet.description: Safe allocation, dereference, and cleanup pattern

topics.pitfall: Double deletion (`delete p; delete p;`) corrupts heap allocator metadata and crashes the application with a double-free error.

quickCheck.question: What happens if you execute `delete p;` when `p == nullptr`?
options: Nothing: deleting nullptr is guaranteed to be a safe no-op in C++
quickCheck.explanation: The C++ standard explicitly mandates that deleting a nullptr is a safe no-op.

topics.title: Dynamic Array Allocation: `new[]` and `delete[]`
explanation: Allocating a contiguous array on the heap requires the array new syntax: `int* arr = new int[size];`.
To free dynamic arrays, you MUST use `delete[] arr;` with empty square brackets.
Using single `delete arr;` on an array allocated with `new[]` causes Undefined Behavior because it only calls the destructor for element 0 and corrupts the allocator array-cookie metadata.
keyRules: Match operators strictly: new -> delete; new[] -> delete[].
In modern C++, prefer std::vector<T> over raw new[] for dynamic arrays.

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic Array Allocation with new[] / delete[]
codeSnippet.description: Allocating and freeing dynamic contiguous buffers

topics.pitfall: Calling `delete arr;` instead of `delete[] arr;` on an array of objects leaves elements 1 through N-1 un-destructed and leaks memory.

quickCheck.question: Which operator must be used to free memory allocated with `int* buf = new int[50];`?
quickCheck.explanation: Allocations made with `new[]` must be matched with `delete[]`.

topics.title: Memory Leaks & Detection Tools (Valgrind & ASan)
explanation: A memory leak occurs when heap memory is allocated with `new`, but the pointer pointing to it is overwritten or goes out of scope before calling `delete`.
Over time, uncollected memory exhausts system RAM, causing the operating system OOM killer to terminate the process.
Modern C++ developers detect leaks using AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address -g`) built into GCC/Clang or Valgrind (`valgrind --leak-check=full ./program`).
keyRules: Compile with -fsanitize=address during development and continuous integration.
Never reassign a pointer holding heap memory without deleting the existing allocation first.

codeSnippet.title: Enabling AddressSanitizer (ASan) in GCC/Clang
codeSnippet.description: Compile flags for automated memory leak and out-of-bounds detection
codeSnippet.code:
# Compile with AddressSanitizer enabled
g++ -std=c++20 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address main.cpp -o app_asan

# Run binary - ASan will report exact file & line number of any leak
./app_asan

topics.pitfall: Reassigning a pointer in a loop without deleting: `for (...) { ptr = new Node(); }` creates thousands of unreclaimable leaked heap objects.

quickCheck.question: What compiler flag enables AddressSanitizer in GCC and Clang?
quickCheck.explanation: -fsanitize=address embeds memory validation instrumentation directly into the compiled binary.

topics.title: Dangling Pointers & Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities
explanation: A dangling pointer points to a memory address that has already been deallocated by `delete`.
Attempting to read or write through a dangling pointer is a "Use-After-Free" (UAF) vulnerability—one of the most severe security exploits in computer science.
Because the OS may reallocate that same memory address to a different subsystem, writing through a dangling pointer silently overwrites unrelated application state.
keyRules: Set pointers to nullptr immediately after deletion: delete ptr; ptr = nullptr;
Never share raw ownership across multiple loose pointers without clear lifetime semantics.

codeSnippet.title: Neutralizing Dangling Pointers
codeSnippet.description: Preventing Use-After-Free bugs with immediate nullptr assignment

topics.pitfall: Having two pointers `p1` and `p2` pointing to the same heap object. If you `delete p1;`, `p2` becomes a dangling pointer without any indication.

quickCheck.question: What is a "Use-After-Free" (UAF) vulnerability?
options: Accessing or writing to a memory address that has already been deallocated
Allocating more memory than physical RAM
Using a stack variable before initializing it
quickCheck.explanation: UAF occurs when code dereferences a pointer that points to deallocated heap storage.

topics.title: Placement `new` & Explicit Destructor Invocation
explanation: Standard `new` allocates memory and constructs. "Placement new" constructs an object at a PRE-ALLOCATED memory address without requesting memory from the OS.
Syntax: `#include <new>; new (memoryAddress) MyClass(args);`.

Extensively used in high-performance custom memory pools, game engines, and `std::vector` internals. Objects constructed via placement new MUST have their destructor called explicitly: `objPtr->~MyClass();`.
keyRules: Placement new requires #include <new>.
Never call delete on a placement-new object; explicitly invoke its destructor objPtr->~Type().

codeSnippet.title: Placement new on Pre-Allocated Buffer
codeSnippet.description: Constructing objects in pre-allocated memory pools

topics.pitfall: Calling `delete p;` on an object constructed with placement new in a stack buffer crashes the program because `arena` was never allocated on the heap.

quickCheck.question: How do you destroy an object that was constructed via placement new?
options: It is destroyed automatically by the OS
quickCheck.explanation: Placement new objects do not own the underlying memory, so only the destructor must be called explicitly.

topics.title: Memory Alignment & `alignof` / `alignas`
explanation: Modern CPUs do not read individual bytes from memory; they read in 32-bit, 64-bit, or 128-bit aligned words. Accessing misaligned data causes multi-cycle penalties or hardware bus errors.
`alignof(T)` queries the byte alignment required by type `T`.
`alignas(N)` forces a variable or struct to be aligned to an N-byte boundary (e.g. `alignas(64)` for cache-line alignment to avoid false sharing in multithreading).
keyRules: alignof(T) is typically equal to sizeof(T) for fundamental types.
alignas(64) aligns data to CPU L1 cache lines (prevents cache thrashing).

codeSnippet.title: Querying and Enforcing Alignment
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting hardware alignment with alignof and alignas

topics.pitfall: Specifying an alignment smaller than the natural alignment of the type is illegal and rejected by the compiler.

quickCheck.question: What operator queries the alignment requirement of a type in C++?
quickCheck.explanation: alignof(T) returns the alignment in bytes required for instances of type T.

topics.title: Day 4 Capstone: Manual Dynamic IntVector Buffer
explanation: Synthesizing Day 4 concepts by constructing a bare-metal dynamic integer array with resizing capabilities.
Demonstrates `new[]`, copying elements, `delete[]` of old buffers, capacity doubling, and pointer updating.
This forms the foundational mechanics behind `std::vector`.
keyRules: Always allocate new capacity first before freeing old buffer.
Delete the old buffer with delete[] to prevent memory leaks during resize.

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic Array Resizing Engine
codeSnippet.description: Manual heap reallocation and buffer copy

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to free the old buffer with `delete[] m_data` when growing the array leaks the old buffer forever.

quickCheck.question: When resizing a dynamic array, why must the new buffer be allocated before deleting the old buffer?
options: So that existing data can be copied from the old buffer into the new buffer
Because the operating system requires it
Because delete[] only works on empty buffers
quickCheck.explanation: You must copy existing elements into the newly allocated buffer before releasing the old memory.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 4 Capstone: Dynamic String Buffer with Zero Leaks
instructions: Create a class `HeapBuffer` that dynamically allocates a `char*` array on the heap in its constructor.
Provide methods to write and read characters.
Ensure the destructor frees the buffer with `delete[]` and sets the pointer to nullptr.
hints: Allocate with `m_buffer = new char[m_capacity];`.
Free in destructor with `delete[] m_buffer;`.

keyTakeaways: The stack is managed automatically by the CPU; the heap is managed manually via `new`/`delete`.
Always pair `new` with `delete`, and `new[]` with `delete[]`.
AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`) is the industry standard for discovering leaks at runtime.
Always set deleted pointers to `nullptr` to prevent dangerous Use-After-Free vulnerabilities.

days.title: Arrays, C-Strings & Modern `std::string_view`
days.subtitle: Buffer layouts, null-terminators, string_view zero-copy slicing & bounds safety
days.overview: Master low-level strings and contiguous memory. Compare legacy null-terminated C-strings (`char*`), `std::string`, and C++17 `std::string_view` for zero-allocation substring and string parameter performance.

topics.title: Null-Terminated C-Strings (`char*` & `\0`)
explanation: In C and low-level C++, a string is an array of characters terminated by a null byte (`'\0'`, ASCII value 0).
String literals like `"Hello"` have type `const char[6]` (5 characters plus the implicit trailing `'\0'`).
Functions in `<cstring>` (`strlen`, `strcpy`, `strcmp`) walk the buffer until they encounter the null byte.
keyRules: A char buffer holding N characters requires an array size of at least N + 1 bytes.
strlen() counts characters up to (but not including) the null terminator; complexity is O(N).

codeSnippet.title: Null Terminator Verification
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting string literal null bytes and lengths

topics.pitfall: Omitting the null terminator when building manual char arrays causes `strlen` and `printf` to keep reading past the buffer into neighboring memory until hitting random zero bytes.

quickCheck.question: What is the sizeof the string literal `"Data"` in C++?
quickCheck.explanation: "Data" contains 4 characters plus the implicit null terminator `\0`, totaling 5 bytes.

topics.title: Buffer Overflows & Safe String Manipulation
explanation: Legacy C functions (`strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, `gets`) do not perform bounds checking and write past the end of allocated buffers.
Buffer overflows can overwrite stack return addresses, allowing attackers to hijack execution flow (arbitrary code execution).
Modern C++ replaces these functions with `std::string`, `std::string_view`, and bounded functions like `strncpy` or `snprintf`.
keyRules: Never use gets() or unbounded strcpy().
Prefer std::string for owning strings and std::string_view for non-owning views.

codeSnippet.title: Bounded Safe String Operations
codeSnippet.description: Using snprintf for size-guaranteed string formatting

topics.pitfall: Using `strncpy` does not guarantee null-termination if the source string exceeds the destination buffer length.

quickCheck.question: Why are functions like `strcpy` considered dangerous in security audits?
options: They do not verify destination buffer capacity, causing buffer overflows
They allocate heap memory without freeing it
quickCheck.explanation: strcpy writes until finding a null terminator in the source, overflowing destination buffers if the source is too large.

topics.title: `std::string` Architecture & Small String Optimization (SSO)
explanation: `std::string` manages dynamic heap allocation, reallocations, and null-termination automatically.
Small String Optimization (SSO): Most standard library implementations include an internal inline stack buffer (typically 15 to 22 bytes) inside the `std::string` struct itself.
If the string length is within this threshold, NO heap allocation occurs. Only long strings trigger dynamic heap memory allocation.
keyRules: Strings shorter than ~15-22 characters enjoy zero heap allocation overhead due to SSO.
std::string is an RAII object that cleans up its own memory automatically when it goes out of scope.

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting std::string Footprint and SSO
codeSnippet.description: Examining sizeof(std::string) and heap bypass

topics.pitfall: Assuming `std::string` is always heap-allocated; for small tokens and IDs, SSO makes it as fast as a stack char array.

quickCheck.question: What is Small String Optimization (SSO) in C++ standard libraries?
options: Storing short strings inside an internal inline buffer to avoid heap allocations
quickCheck.explanation: SSO stores strings smaller than ~15-22 bytes directly inside the string object on the stack.

topics.title: Modern `std::string_view` (C++17 Zero-Copy Views)
explanation: C++17 introduced `std::string_view`, a lightweight non-owning view of a sequence of characters.
Internally, it consists of only two fields: a `const char* pointer` and a `size_t length` (total 16 bytes on 64-bit systems).
Passing `std::string_view` accepts string literals, `const char*`, and `std::string` with zero memory allocation and zero buffer copying.
keyRules: Pass std::string_view by value (it is only 16 bytes).
std::string_view does NOT own the memory; the underlying string must outlive the view.
string_view is NOT guaranteed to be null-terminated; do not pass view.data() to functions expecting a null-terminated C-string.

codeSnippet.title: std::string_view Parameter and Substring Slicing
codeSnippet.description: Zero-allocation slicing and universal string handling

topics.pitfall: Creating a `std::string_view` from a temporary `std::string`: `std::string_view sv = std::string("temp");` leaves `sv` dangling immediately after the line ends.

quickCheck.question: What are the internal members of a `std::string_view`?
options: A pointer to character data and a size length
A vector of chars and a capacity
A reference counter and an address
quickCheck.explanation: std::string_view is simply a pointer (`const char*`) and a size (`size_t`), making it 16 bytes on 64-bit.

topics.title: `std::array<T, N>`: Zero-Overhead Fixed-Size Arrays
explanation: C-style raw arrays decay to pointers and lack standard container interfaces.
`std::array<T, N>` is a thin wrapper over a C-style stack array with zero overhead in memory or execution time.
It provides `.size()`, bounds-checked `.at(i)`, iterators (`begin()`/`end()`), and does not implicitly decay to a raw pointer.
keyRules: Prefer std::array<T, N> over raw C arrays for fixed-size buffers.
arr.at(i) throws std::out_of_range if index is out of bounds; arr[i] is unchecked for maximum speed.

codeSnippet.title: std::array Usage & Bounds Checking
codeSnippet.description: Typesafe fixed-size arrays with standard iterator support

topics.pitfall: Using `std::array` for massive collections (like 1,000,000 elements) allocates on the stack, causing stack overflow; use `std::vector` for large collections.

quickCheck.question: Does `std::array<int, 10>` allocate memory on the heap?
options: No, it allocates entirely on the stack with zero heap overhead
quickCheck.explanation: std::array is an aggregate stack structure with zero heap overhead.

topics.title: Modern `std::span<T>` (C++20 Contiguous Views)
explanation: C++20 introduced `std::span<T>`, generalizing `std::string_view` to ANY contiguous sequence of elements (raw array, `std::array`, or `std::vector`).
`std::span<T>` provides a non-owning view of contiguous memory. It replaces legacy function signatures like `void process(int* arr, size_t size)` with `void process(std::span<int> data)`.
It can be read-only (`std::span<const T>`) or read-write (`std::span<T>`).
keyRules: Pass std::span by value.
Accepts C arrays, std::array, and std::vector seamlessly without template bloat.

codeSnippet.title: C++20 std::span Universal Array Views
codeSnippet.description: Accepting vectors, arrays, and buffers with one unified signature

topics.pitfall: Like `std::string_view`, `std::span` does not own the memory; modifying the size of a referenced `std::vector` (causing reallocation) invalidates the span.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary role of `std::span<T>` in modern C++20?
options: To provide a lightweight, non-owning view over any contiguous sequence of elements
quickCheck.explanation: std::span provides a standardized non-owning view over arrays, vectors, and memory buffers.

topics.title: Memory Operations: `std::memcpy`, `std::memmove` & `std::memset`
explanation: In low-level systems programming, `<cstring>` memory routines provide hardware-accelerated byte-level manipulation.
`std::memset(dest, val, count)` fills a block of memory with a specific byte pattern (e.g. zeroing a buffer).
`std::memcpy(dest, src, count)` performs ultra-fast byte copying using SIMD registers, but requires that `dest` and `src` memory regions DO NOT OVERLAP.
`std::memmove(dest, src, count)` safely handles overlapping memory buffers by utilizing an intermediate buffer if needed.
keyRules: Use std::memcpy only when buffers are guaranteed not to overlap.
Use std::memmove if buffers might overlap (e.g. shifting elements within the same array).
Only use memcpy/memmove on Trivially Copyable types; never use on types with non-trivial constructors/destructors.

codeSnippet.title: High-Speed Byte Copying & Zeroing
codeSnippet.description: Direct byte memory manipulation with memset and memcpy

topics.pitfall: Using `std::memcpy` on non-trivially copyable objects (like `std::string` or `std::vector`) corrupts their internal pointers and triggers double-free crashes.

quickCheck.question: When must `std::memmove` be used instead of `std::memcpy`?
options: When the source and destination memory regions may overlap
quickCheck.explanation: std::memmove is required when source and destination buffers overlap to prevent data corruption.

topics.title: Day 5 Capstone: Zero-Copy HTTP Request Header Parser
explanation: Synthesizing Day 5 concepts by building a zero-copy HTTP header line parser using `std::string_view`.
Demonstrates finding delimiters (`: `), slicing into key and value string views without allocating a single byte on the heap.
Highlights the microsecond throughput advantages of C++ systems programming.
keyRules: Parse and slice strings using string_view::substr and string_view::find.
Zero heap allocations during line tokenization.

codeSnippet.title: Zero-Allocation HTTP Header Parser
codeSnippet.description: Slicing HTTP request lines with std::string_view

topics.pitfall: Storing `std::string_view` in an object that outlives the raw network buffer from which it was sliced causes dangling pointer reads.

quickCheck.question: How many dynamic heap allocations occur when `std::string_view::substr()` is called?
quickCheck.explanation: substr on a string_view merely adjusts a pointer and size, performing zero dynamic heap allocations.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 5 Capstone: Safe String Truncator & Sanitizer
instructions: Write a function `std::string_view trimPrefix(std::string_view input, std::string_view prefix)` that checks if `input` starts with `prefix`.
If it does, return the sliced view without the prefix; otherwise return the original view.
Verify that zero allocations occur during this operation.
hints: Use input.substr(0, prefix.length()) to compare the starting characters.
Return input.substr(prefix.length()) to remove the prefix.

keyTakeaways: C-strings require a null terminator (`\0`); forgetting it causes buffer overruns.
Small String Optimization (SSO) makes short `std::string` instances stack-allocated.
`std::string_view` (16 bytes) provides zero-copy slicing for read-only string parameters.
Use `std::array` instead of C raw arrays for fixed-size stack buffers.

days.title: Functions: Value vs Ref, Overloading & Inlining
days.subtitle: Pass semantics, return-value optimization (RVO), inline functions & function pointers
days.overview: Master the full depth of C++ functions: parameter pass mechanisms, function overloading, default arguments, inline expansion, name mangling, Return Value Optimization (RVO/NRVO), and raw function pointers.

topics.title: Parameter Passing Matrix: Value vs Pointer vs Reference
explanation: Pass-by-value (`void f(int x)`): Creates an independent copy. Changes inside the function do NOT affect the caller.
Pass-by-reference (`void f(int& x)`): Passes an alias. The function can mutate the caller variable directly.
Pass-by-const-reference (`void f(const BigData& x)`): Passes an address without copying, but forbids mutation.
Pass-by-pointer (`void f(int* x)`): Explicit address passing with optional nullability.
keyRules: Primitives (<= 16 bytes): Pass by value.
Objects (> 16 bytes, e.g. structs, strings): Pass by const reference.
Output parameters (mutation needed): Pass by non-const reference or return a struct.

codeSnippet.title: Function Parameter Passing Variations
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating value, reference, and const reference mechanics

topics.pitfall: Passing large collections like `std::vector<int>` by value in recursion triggers exponential cloning and exhausts CPU memory.

quickCheck.question: When should a parameter be passed by `const T&`?
options: When the object is non-trivial/large and the function only needs to read it
When the function needs to modify the original object
When the argument is an integer
quickCheck.explanation: const T& avoids copy overhead while guaranteeing that the function will not modify the caller object.

topics.title: Return Value Optimization (RVO) & Copy Elision
explanation: Historically, returning a large object by value required copying it from the function stack frame to the caller stack frame.
Modern C++ compilers perform Return Value Optimization (RVO) and Named RVO (NRVO): the compiler constructs the object directly in the memory location allocated for the caller variable.
Since C++17, RVO is MANDATORY by the language standard, guaranteeing zero-copy return by value.
keyRules: Feel free to return large objects (vectors, strings) by value; RVO guarantees zero copy overhead.
Do not wrap return statements in std::move(x) when returning local variables; it prevents RVO.

codeSnippet.title: Guaranteed Copy Elision (C++17)
codeSnippet.description: Returning objects by value with zero copies via RVO

topics.pitfall: Writing `return std::move(localObj);` disables NRVO and degrades performance.

quickCheck.question: What is guaranteed by C++17 regarding Return Value Optimization (RVO)?
options: Copy elision is mandatory when returning an unnamed prvalue temporary
Functions cannot return objects larger than 64 bytes
RVO is only enabled with -O3 optimization
quickCheck.explanation: C++17 formalized copy elision as a core language rule, completely eliminating copy/move operations for prvalue returns.

topics.title: Function Overloading & Name Mangling
explanation: C++ allows multiple functions to share the exact same name as long as their parameter signatures (number or types of arguments) differ.

To allow the linker to distinguish between overloaded functions with identical names, C++ compilers perform "Name Mangling" (encoding parameter types into the binary symbol name, e.g. `_Z3addii` for `add(int, int)`).
To interface with C libraries or disable name mangling, wrap function declarations in `extern "C" { ... }`.
keyRules: Functions CANNOT be overloaded based on return type alone.
extern "C" disables name mangling so C code and dynamic linkers can locate the symbol.

codeSnippet.title: Function Overloading & extern "C"
codeSnippet.description: Overloaded signatures and C ABI linkage compatibility

topics.pitfall: Attempting to overload two functions where the only difference is the return type: `int f();` and `double f();` is a compilation error.

quickCheck.question: Why is `extern "C"` used when exporting C++ functions for use in C or shared libraries?
options: It disables C++ name mangling, preserving the exact function symbol name
It converts C++ code to C source code
It makes the function run in kernel mode
quickCheck.explanation: extern "C" instructs the compiler to emit C linkage without name mangling.

topics.title: `inline` Functions & Linker Rules
explanation: The `inline` keyword originally suggested that the compiler replace function calls with the function body itself to eliminate call overhead.
In modern C++, compilers inline functions automatically based on cost models regardless of the keyword.

The true modern meaning of `inline` is an ODR (One Definition Rule) directive: it permits a function or variable to be defined in a header file included by multiple translation units without linker "multiple definition" errors.
keyRules: Functions defined entirely inside class definitions are implicitly inline.
Free functions defined in headers must be marked inline to avoid linker collisions.

codeSnippet.title: Header-Safe inline Function Definition
codeSnippet.description: Preventing LNK2005 multiple definition errors across translation units

topics.pitfall: Placing a non-inline function body in a header file included in more than one `.cpp` file causes duplicate symbol linker errors.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary modern purpose of the `inline` keyword on free functions in headers?
options: To allow the function definition to appear in multiple translation units without ODR violations
To force the CPU to execute the function in parallel
To allocate the function on the stack
quickCheck.explanation: inline tells the linker that multiple identical definitions across translation units should be merged into a single implementation.

topics.title: Function Pointers & Callback Architecture
explanation: Functions reside in the executable code segment (text) and have memory addresses.
A function pointer stores the address of a function, allowing functions to be passed as arguments, stored in arrays, and invoked dynamically at runtime.
Syntax: `ReturnType (*ptrName)(ParamTypes) = &functionName;`.
keyRules: int (*op)(int, int) declares op as a function pointer accepting two ints and returning int.
Invoking: (*op)(2, 3) or simply op(2, 3).

codeSnippet.title: Function Pointers as Algorithm Callbacks
codeSnippet.description: Customizing transformation logic via raw function pointers

topics.pitfall: Forgetting parentheses in function pointer declarations: `int* func(int)` declares a function returning `int*`, whereas `int (*func)(int)` declares a pointer to a function.

quickCheck.question: What does `void (*callback)(int);` declare?
options: A pointer to a function that accepts an int and returns void
A function that returns a void pointer
quickCheck.explanation: The parentheses around `(*callback)` bind the asterisk to the identifier, declaring a function pointer.

topics.title: Default Arguments & Evaluation Constraints
explanation: C++ functions can provide default parameter values: `void log(std::string msg, int level = 1);`.
Default arguments MUST be specified on trailing parameters only (all parameters following a defaulted parameter must also have defaults).
Default arguments are evaluated at the call site at compile time. In multi-file projects, specify default arguments in the header declaration, NEVER in the `.cpp` definition.
keyRules: Default arguments must appear on the rightmost parameters.
Declare defaults in header files only; redefining defaults in the implementation causes a redefinition error.

codeSnippet.title: Trailing Default Arguments Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Declaring fallback values for flexible function invocation

topics.pitfall: Placing default arguments in both the header declaration and the `.cpp` function definition causes a compiler error for redefinition of default parameter.

quickCheck.question: Where should default argument values be specified in a multi-file C++ project?
options: In both the header and implementation files
quickCheck.explanation: Callers must see default arguments at compile time from the included header file.

topics.title: Lambdas (`[](){}`): Anonymous Inline Functions
explanation: C++11 introduced lambda expressions, allowing ad-hoc anonymous functions to be defined directly at the call site.
Syntax: `[capture-clause](parameters) -> return-type { body }`.
The capture clause controls access to outer variables: `[]` (no capture), `[&]` (capture all by reference), `[=]` (capture all by value/copy), or explicit `[x, &y]`.
keyRules: Lambdas without captures decay implicitly to raw function pointers.
Use [&] with caution; capturing a local variable by reference in a lambda that outlives the scope causes a dangling reference.

codeSnippet.title: Modern C++ Lambdas and Captures
codeSnippet.description: Defining inline anonymous callable objects

topics.pitfall: Capturing references `[&]` into a lambda stored asynchronously or in a callback leads to accessing destroyed stack variables when invoked later.

quickCheck.question: What does the capture clause `[=]` do in a C++ lambda?
options: Captures all enclosing local variables by value (copy)
quickCheck.explanation: [=] creates copies of any enclosing variables referenced inside the lambda.

topics.title: Day 6 Capstone: Pluggable Event Dispatcher System
explanation: Synthesizing Day 6 function paradigms into a pluggable event dispatch mechanism.
Demonstrating function pointers, lambdas, pass-by-const-reference, and cleanly structured callback architectures.
Forms the foundation of game event loops, UI event handlers, and network packet dispatchers.
keyRules: Store callable listeners cleanly.
Pass event payload by const reference to avoid copying.

codeSnippet.title: Pluggable Event Dispatch Engine
codeSnippet.description: Event listener pattern using function pointers

topics.pitfall: Attempting to assign a stateful lambda (with captures) to a raw function pointer `void (*)(const Event&)` fails compilation because stateful lambdas are structs with fields, not bare function pointers.

quickCheck.question: Can a lambda with captures (e.g. `[x](int a){...}`) be converted to a raw function pointer (`int(*)(int)`)?
options: No, only capture-less lambdas `[]` can decay to raw function pointers
Only if x is an integer
quickCheck.explanation: Lambdas with captures have internal state and cannot be represented by a simple raw function pointer address.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 6 Capstone: Generic Math Pipeline with Function Pointers
instructions: Create a function `int transform(int value, int (*fn)(int))` that applies a transformation function to an integer.
Define two transformation functions: `doubleVal(int x)` (returns x * 2) and `squareVal(int x)` (returns x * x).
Test `transform` with both functions and output the results.
hints: The function pointer signature is `int (*fn)(int)`.
Pass the function names `doubleVal` and `squareVal` as arguments.

keyTakeaways: Pass cheap primitives by value; pass non-trivial objects by `const T&`.
Modern C++17 guarantees Return Value Optimization (RVO) for zero-copy return-by-value.
Name mangling encodes parameter types into symbol names; use `extern "C"` for C linkage.
Lambdas without captures decay cleanly to raw function pointers.

days.title: Week 1 Synthesis: Custom Stack Memory Arena & Qualifying Exam
days.subtitle: Building a bare-metal linear bump allocator, memory alignment & Week 1 qualifying assessment
days.overview: Synthesize all of Week 1 into a high-performance linear Memory Arena Allocator. Understand how game engines, embedded systems, and HFT systems achieve microsecond allocations by bypassing malloc/free with pre-allocated memory buffers.

topics.title: The Problem with General-Purpose `malloc` / `new`
explanation: General-purpose allocators (`malloc`/`new`) must handle arbitrary allocation sizes, concurrent threads, and unpredictable lifetimes.
To do this, they maintain free-lists, perform locks, search for best-fit blocks, and incur OS system call overhead (`brk`/`mmap`).
In game engines and high-frequency trading (HFT), calling `new` thousands of times per frame causes frame drops and heap fragmentation.
keyRules: malloc() has unpredictable execution latency and causes heap fragmentation.
Custom allocators provide deterministic O(1) allocation times.

codeSnippet.title: Latency of Dynamic Heap Allocation
codeSnippet.description: Why systems engineers replace new/delete in hot paths

topics.pitfall: Calling `new` inside high-frequency real-time audio threads or rendering loops causes audio glitches and frame rate stutter.

quickCheck.question: Why do game engines and financial trading systems avoid frequent `new`/`delete` calls in hot loops?
options: General heap allocation has non-deterministic latency and causes memory fragmentation
delete cannot be called more than 100 times
quickCheck.explanation: Dynamic heap allocation involves thread locks and free-list searches that introduce non-deterministic execution spikes.

topics.title: Linear Bump Allocator (Arena) Architecture
explanation: A Memory Arena pre-allocates a single large contiguous block of memory (e.g. 1MB or 64MB) upfront at application startup.
To allocate `N` bytes, it simply increments an offset pointer (a "bump pointer") by `N` bytes. This is an $O(1)$ single-cycle pointer addition.
Individual deallocations are no-ops. When a frame or request finishes, the entire arena is reset back to offset 0 in a single instruction.
keyRules: Allocation cost: O(1) pointer addition.
Deallocation cost: O(1) setting offset = 0 for the entire batch.
Eliminates fragmentation and guarantees 100% cache locality.

codeSnippet.title: Linear Arena Mechanics Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Concept diagram of memory arena bump pointer
codeSnippet.code:
/*
  [==================== PRE-ALLOCATED ARENA BUFFER ====================]
  |  Alloc 1 (64B)  |  Alloc 2 (128B) |  Alloc 3 (32B)  |   Free Space... |
  ^                                                     ^
  Base Address                                      Offset (Bump Pointer)
  
  Resetting the entire arena: offset = 0; // Instant 0-cycle deallocation!
*/

topics.pitfall: Freeing individual objects inside a linear arena is impossible; all objects in an arena share the same lifetime.

quickCheck.question: What is the algorithmic time complexity of allocating memory in a linear bump allocator arena?
quickCheck.explanation: A bump allocator simply adds the requested byte size to its current offset, which is an O(1) single-cycle operation.

topics.title: Memory Alignment Padding in Custom Allocators
explanation: If you bump the pointer by an arbitrary number of bytes (e.g. 3 bytes), the next allocation will land on an unaligned address, degrading CPU performance.
Custom allocators round the current offset UP to the nearest multiple of the required alignment before advancing.
The formula: `alignedOffset = (offset + (alignment - 1)) & ~(alignment - 1);`.
keyRules: Always align allocations to alignof(T) or max_align_t (typically 8 or 16 bytes).
Bitwise rounding mask: (x + 7) & ~7 rounds up to the next 8-byte boundary.

codeSnippet.title: Bitwise Memory Alignment Formula
codeSnippet.description: Aligning addresses to CPU word boundaries using bit manipulation

topics.pitfall: Failing to align allocations can trigger CPU bus error traps on ARM and RISC architectures that forbid unaligned memory reads.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of alignment padding in a custom memory allocator?
options: To ensure every allocation starts at an address divisible by the type alignment requirement
quickCheck.explanation: Alignment padding guarantees that data starts on hardware-friendly memory boundaries for fast CPU cache access.

topics.title: Implementing the `MemoryArena` Class
explanation: Constructing the full C++ `MemoryArena` class.
Maintains a heap-allocated byte buffer `char* m_buffer`, total `m_capacity`, and current `m_offset`.
Provides a templated `alloc<T>(size_t count)` method that handles alignment, bounds checks, and returns a typed pointer `T*`.
keyRules: Constructor allocates raw buffer: new char[capacity].
Destructor frees buffer: delete[] m_buffer.
reset() sets m_offset = 0.

codeSnippet.title: The Complete MemoryArena Class Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Production-ready linear bump allocator in modern C++

topics.pitfall: Overrunning the arena buffer without checking `newOffset > m_capacity` causes heap memory corruption.

quickCheck.question: How does a memory arena free all allocated memory at the end of a frame?
options: By resetting its internal offset pointer back to 0
By calling free() on every individual object
quickCheck.explanation: The entire arena is reclaimed instantaneously by resetting the offset counter to 0.

topics.title: Constructing Objects in Arena Memory via Placement `new`
explanation: The `allocate()` method returns raw uninitialized bytes.
To create real C++ objects with active constructors inside the arena, we combine the arena with placement new.
Template helper: `template <typename T, typename... Args> T* create(Args&&... args)`.
keyRules: Use placement new: new (rawMemory) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
Constructs objects directly in the arena without general heap overhead.

codeSnippet.title: Arena Object Construction Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Combining arena allocation with placement new for zero-overhead objects

topics.pitfall: Constructing objects that hold external resources (like file handles or network sockets) in an arena requires calling their destructors before calling arena.reset().

quickCheck.question: Why is placement new needed when allocating objects in a custom memory arena?
options: Because arena allocation only reserves raw bytes; placement new executes the constructor
Because C++ forbids pointers to arenas
To convert C++ code to C
quickCheck.explanation: The arena reserves raw memory bytes; placement new initializes the object state by executing its constructor at that address.

topics.title: Benchmarking Arena vs Standard Heap Allocator
explanation: Benchmarking 1,000,000 allocations in standard `new` vs a custom `MemoryArena`.
Standard `new` takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds due to heap bookkeeping and synchronization.
The linear arena completes 1,000,000 allocations in single-digit milliseconds, delivering an order-of-magnitude throughput improvement.
keyRules: Arena throughput is bounded only by memory bandwidth, not CPU allocator algorithms.
Cache locality is vastly superior because allocations are strictly contiguous.

codeSnippet.title: Arena Allocation Benchmark Simulation
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating contiguous cache locality and allocation throughput

topics.pitfall: Using an arena for objects with long, staggered, independent lifetimes causes memory bloat because memory cannot be reclaimed until the whole arena resets.

quickCheck.question: Why is a linear memory arena faster than standard `new`/`delete`?
options: It avoids free-list searches and locks, performing allocations in a single pointer addition
It uses graphics cards for allocation
quickCheck.explanation: A bump allocator eliminates heap search overhead and fragmentation, advancing a single memory pointer.

topics.title: Week 1 Review & Architecture Checklist
explanation: Reviewing the core pillars of Week 1:
1. Types & Sizes: Fixed-width `<cstdint>` integers, braced initialization `{}` preventing narrowing.
2. Pointers: Addresses `&`, dereferencing `*`, typesafe `nullptr`, pointer arithmetic strides.
3. References: Un-rebindable aliases, pass-by-`const T&`, const member methods.
4. Memory Management: Stack vs Heap, `new`/`delete` matching `new[]`/`delete[]`, leak detection via ASan.
5. Strings & Views: `std::string` SSO vs zero-copy `std::string_view`.
keyRules: Clean mental model: Variables hold values; pointers hold addresses; references are aliases.
Const-correctness is non-negotiable in production C++.

codeSnippet.title: Week 1 Syntax Verification Matrix
codeSnippet.description: Consolidated verification of all Week 1 core syntax rules

topics.pitfall: Neglecting const correctness early in a project leads to painful refactoring when integrating with standard library algorithms.

quickCheck.question: Which of the following causes Undefined Behavior in C++?
options: Passing a const reference to a function
quickCheck.explanation: Calling delete on an already freed pointer causes heap metadata corruption and undefined behavior.

topics.title: Week 1 Qualifying Exam Readiness
