The exam tests: Compilation stages, exact type sizes, pointer arithmetic byte math, const rules, delete vs delete[], and string_view semantics.
Take the exam when ready or retake it to reinforce your systems engineering foundations.
keyRules: Passing score: 80% (4 out of 5 questions correct).
Unlocks Week 2: Object-Oriented Programming, RAII, Smart Pointers & Move Semantics.

codeSnippet.title: Week 1 Exam Gateway Kicker
codeSnippet.description: Readiness checklist for module advancement

topics.pitfall: Rushing into Object-Oriented design without mastering pointers and memory will cause confusion when implementing copy/move constructors in Week 2.

quickCheck.question: What is required to unlock Week 2 of the C++ Systems Academy?
options: Score at least 80% on the Week 1 Qualifying Exam (or enable Dev Mode)
Install Clang compiler on your local machine
Read the entire ISO C++ specification
quickCheck.explanation: Passing the qualifying quiz with >= 80% verifies competency and unlocks Week 2.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 7 Capstone Project: Working Linear Memory Arena
instructions: Implement a complete `ArenaAllocator` with a fixed buffer size of 256 bytes.
Implement `void* allocate(size_t bytes)` that advances a bump pointer.
Implement `void reset()` that clears the allocated count back to 0.
Allocate space for 3 integer variables, assign them values, and print them out.
hints: Use a static char buffer `char m_buffer[256];` inside the class.
Cast the allocated void pointer to `int*` with `static_cast<int*>()`.

keyTakeaways: Memory Arenas provide microsecond O(1) allocation and O(1) bulk reset.
Always handle memory alignment when building low-level custom allocators.
Placement new constructs objects in pre-allocated buffers without requesting memory from the OS.
Week 1 establishes the bedrock of C++ memory control: pointers, references, and hardware layouts.

quiz.title: Week 1 Qualifying Exam: C++ Memory & Pointer Architecture
quiz.description: Score at least 80% (4/5 correct) to unlock Week 2: OOP, RAII, Smart Pointers & Move Semantics.

questions.question: Which tool in the C++ compilation pipeline resolves external function definitions across multiple object files?
questions.explanation: The Linker stitches together compiled object files and libraries, resolving cross-module symbols.

questions.question: If `int* ptr = (int*)0x1000;` on an x86_64 system where `sizeof(int) == 4`, what is `ptr + 3`?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic increments by 3 * sizeof(int) = 12 bytes = 0x0C in hex. 0x1000 + 0x0C = 0x100C.

questions.question: Why is `const std::string&` preferred over `std::string` when passing a string parameter for inspection?
options: It passes by address, eliminating an expensive deep heap copy of the string buffer
It converts the string to upper-case automatically
It allows the function to modify the caller string
It is required by the C++ preprocessor
questions.explanation: Passing by const reference avoids cloning the string buffer onto the stack or heap.

questions.question: What happens if you free an array allocated with `int* a = new int[20];` using single `delete a;`?
options: Undefined Behavior: only element 0 is destructed and heap allocator metadata is corrupted
The compiler converts it to delete[] automatically
It emits a compile-time warning and works normally
questions.explanation: Allocations made with `new[]` must be matched with `delete[]`. Mismatched delete invokes Undefined Behavior.

questions.question: What is the memory size of `std::string_view` on a 64-bit architecture?
options: 16 bytes (8 bytes for pointer + 8 bytes for length)
Dynamically sized depending on string length
questions.explanation: std::string_view is a non-owning slice containing a const char* pointer (8 bytes) and a size_t length (8 bytes).

days.title: Classes, Encapsulation & Destructor Mechanics
days.subtitle: Constructors, member initializer lists, explicit keyword, destructor ordering & encapsulation
days.overview: Understand the mechanics of C++ classes. Learn member initializer lists, the explicit keyword preventing accidental type coercion, deterministic destructor ordering, and class vs struct distinctions.

topics.title: Class vs Struct: Default Visibility & Intent
explanation: In C++, `class` and `struct` are virtually identical under the hood, with only one difference: default member and inheritance visibility.
In a `struct`, members and base classes are `public` by default. In a `class`, members and base classes are `private` by default.
Convention: Use `struct` for Passive Data Objects (Plain Old Data / aggregates); use `class` when enforcing invariants through private state and public member functions.
keyRules: struct default: public. class default: private.
Both support constructors, destructors, methods, inheritance, and templates identically.

codeSnippet.title: Class vs Struct Visibility
codeSnippet.description: Comparing default member accessibility in C++

topics.pitfall: Relying on default visibility without explicit `public:` or `private:` labels makes code ambiguous for team maintenance.

quickCheck.question: What is the ONLY difference between `class` and `struct` in C++?
options: Default member and inheritance visibility (struct is public, class is private)
Classes can have virtual functions, structs cannot
Structs are allocated on the stack, classes on the heap
quickCheck.explanation: In C++, struct and class are identical except that members of struct default to public, while members of class default to private.

topics.title: Member Initializer Lists vs Assignment in Constructor Body
explanation: Constructing a class occurs in two distinct phases: (1) Base classes and member variables are initialized; (2) The constructor body `{ ... }` executes.
Initializing members in the constructor body first calls their default constructor and then calls their copy assignment operator, doing double work.
Member Initializer Lists (`MyClass() : m_val(5) {}`) construct the member directly in-place with its final value with ZERO redundant work.
keyRules: Always use member initializer lists instead of body assignments.
Members are ALWAYS initialized in the order they are declared in the class definition, NOT the order they appear in the initializer list.
const members and reference members MUST be initialized via member initializer lists.

codeSnippet.title: Member Initializer List Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Direct in-place member initialization

topics.pitfall: Listing members in a different order in the initializer list than declared in the class triggers compiler warnings and can cause subtle bugs if one member relies on another during construction.

quickCheck.question: In what order are class member variables initialized in C++?
options: In the order they are declared in the class definition
In the order they appear in the constructor initializer list
quickCheck.explanation: The C++ standard mandates that members are always initialized in the exact order they are declared inside the class header.

topics.title: The `explicit` Keyword: Preventing Unintended Conversions
explanation: In C++, any constructor that can be called with a single argument acts as an implicit conversion operator by default.
For example, `String s = "hello";` or passing `42` to a function expecting `MyContainer` will silently construct a temporary object.
Adding the `explicit` keyword (`explicit MyClass(int size);`) disables implicit conversion, requiring callers to explicitly invoke the constructor.
keyRules: Mark all single-argument constructors `explicit` by default.
Only omit `explicit` if implicit conversion is an intentional, idiomatic design goal.

codeSnippet.title: explicit Constructor Defense
codeSnippet.description: Preventing dangerous implicit conversions

topics.pitfall: Omitting `explicit` on a constructor like `Vector(int size)` allows `Vector v = 50;` which looks like assigning a number instead of creating a 50-element vector.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of marking a single-argument constructor `explicit`?
options: To prevent the compiler from performing implicit type conversions
To allocate the object on the heap
quickCheck.explanation: `explicit` prevents the compiler from using the constructor to silently convert one type into another.

topics.title: Deterministic Destructor Mechanics & Reverse Destruction Order
explanation: Unlike garbage-collected languages (Java/Python/Go) where finalizers run at unpredictable times or never, C++ guarantees deterministic destruction.
When an object leaves scope, its destructor `~ClassName()` is called IMMEDIATELY.

Destruction order is strictly the exact REVERSE of construction order: local stack variables are destroyed in reverse order of declaration; class members are destroyed in reverse order of declaration; derived class destructors run before base class destructors.
keyRules: Destruction is strictly LIFO (Last In, First Out).
Destructors take no arguments and return no values.
Destructors must NEVER throw exceptions; if an exception escapes a destructor during stack unwinding, std::terminate() crashes the program.

codeSnippet.title: LIFO Destruction Order Demonstration
codeSnippet.description: Observing exact reverse destructor sequencing

topics.pitfall: Throwing an exception inside a destructor while an existing exception is propagating causes `std::terminate()` to kill the process immediately.

quickCheck.question: In what order are local stack objects destroyed when leaving a block scope?
options: Reverse order of construction (LIFO: Last In, First Out)
Random order based on garbage collector availability
quickCheck.explanation: C++ guarantees strict LIFO destruction: the last constructed object is the first to be destroyed.

topics.title: Defaulted (`= default`) and Deleted (`= delete`) Methods
explanation: C++11 introduced `= default` and `= delete` for explicit compiler-generated special member control.
`= default` instructs the compiler to generate the standard implementation of a constructor, copy constructor, or destructor.
`= delete` explicitly disables a method or constructor. If any code attempts to invoke a deleted function, compilation fails with a clear message (e.g. making an object non-copyable).
keyRules: Use = delete to make classes non-copyable (e.g. FileHandle, ThreadLock).
Use = default to restore the compiler-generated default constructor when custom constructors exist.

codeSnippet.title: Non-Copyable Class Pattern with = delete
codeSnippet.description: Preventing accidental object cloning at compile time

topics.pitfall: Using legacy pre-C++11 patterns (making copy constructor private without definition) produces link-time errors instead of immediate compile-time errors.

quickCheck.question: How do you make a class non-copyable in modern C++?
options: Mark the copy constructor and copy assignment operator with `= delete`
Inherit from std::noncopyable in C++98 only
quickCheck.explanation: Deleting the copy constructor and copy assignment operator (`= delete`) explicitly forbids copy operations.

topics.title: Delegating Constructors (C++11)
explanation: Before C++11, if multiple constructors shared common initialization logic, developers had to write private `init()` helper functions.
C++11 allows a constructor to delegate to another constructor of the same class in its member initializer list.
Syntax: `MyClass(int x) : MyClass(x, "default_tag") {}`.
keyRules: The delegating constructor must be the ONLY item in the initializer list.
After the delegated constructor finishes, the delegating constructor body executes.

codeSnippet.title: Delegating Constructor Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Consolidating construction logic across overloaded constructors

topics.pitfall: Creating circular constructor delegation (`A() : B() {}` and `B() : A() {}`) causes a compile-time recursion error.

quickCheck.question: What is the syntax for a constructor delegating to another constructor of the same class?
options: ClassName(args) : ClassName(other_args) {} in the initializer list
quickCheck.explanation: A constructor delegates by calling the target constructor in its member initializer list.

topics.title: Static Members & Static Member Functions
explanation: A `static` member variable belongs to the class itself, not to individual instances. Only ONE shared copy exists across all instances in the entire program.
Non-inline static variables must be defined outside the class in a `.cpp` file (or marked `inline static` in C++17).
`static` member functions do not have a `this` pointer and can only access static members or other static functions.
keyRules: In C++17: inline static int sharedCounter = 0; can be declared directly in the header.
Static member functions can be called without an instance: MathUtils::clamp(val, min, max);

codeSnippet.title: Modern inline static Member Variables (C++17)
codeSnippet.description: Shared class-level state without separate .cpp definitions

topics.pitfall: Omitting `inline` on a static member variable in a header file triggers duplicate symbol definition linker errors when included in multiple `.cpp` files.

quickCheck.question: Do `static` member functions have access to the `this` pointer?
options: No, because static functions belong to the class and have no instance
quickCheck.explanation: Static member functions operate without an object instance, so no `this` pointer exists.

topics.title: Day 8 Capstone: Thread-Safe State Machine Class
explanation: Synthesizing Day 8 concepts into an industrial state machine class.
Demonstrating private state, member initializer list, explicit constructor, const inspection methods, and deterministic destructor cleanup.
Highlights the power of robust encapsulation in systems software.
keyRules: Encapsulate transitions inside validateAndTransition() method.
Enforce clean lifecycle logging in constructor and destructor.

codeSnippet.title: Production State Machine Class Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Encapsulated state machine with deterministic lifecycle

topics.pitfall: Leaving state uninitialized leads to random garbage states on creation.

quickCheck.question: What is guaranteed about destructor execution when an object goes out of scope?
options: It runs immediately and deterministically at the exact moment scope ends
It runs whenever the garbage collector has idle cycles
It is postponed until application termination
It only runs if memory is low
quickCheck.explanation: C++ guarantees deterministic destruction: destructors execute immediately when their scope closes.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 8 Capstone: Non-Copyable Resource Handle
instructions: Create a class `FileDescriptor` that takes an `int fd` in its constructor.
Mark the constructor `explicit`.
Delete the copy constructor and copy assignment operator using `= delete`.
Implement a destructor that logs closing the file descriptor.
hints: Mark the constructor `explicit FileDescriptor(int fd)`.
Add `FileDescriptor(const FileDescriptor&) = delete;`.

keyTakeaways: Prefer member initializer lists over body assignments to avoid redundant construction.
Always mark single-argument constructors `explicit` to prevent implicit conversions.
Destruction is strictly deterministic and follows LIFO (reverse construction) order.
Use `= delete` to declare non-copyable resource handles.

days.title: The RAII Philosophy: Automatic Resource Management
days.subtitle: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, exception safety, scope-bound resource management
days.overview: Understand RAII, the single most important design pattern in C++. Learn how binding resource ownership to object lifetime guarantees leak-free management of memory, file handles, mutexes, and sockets—even in the presence of runtime exceptions.

topics.title: The Core Tenet of RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
explanation: RAII (invented by Bjarne Stroustrup) ties the lifecycle of a resource (heap memory, file handles, sockets, database transactions, mutexes) to the lifetime of an automatic (stack) object.
Acquisition happens in the constructor: If acquisition fails, the constructor throws an exception, and the object is never created.
Release happens in the destructor: When the object leaves scope for ANY reason (normal return, break, or thrown exception), the destructor runs immediately and frees the resource.
keyRules: Never manage raw resources directly in business logic.
Wrap every resource inside an RAII wrapper object.
Stack unwinding during exceptions guarantees destructors are called.

codeSnippet.title: Classic RAII File Wrapper Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Guaranteed file closure even when early returns occur

topics.pitfall: Managing resources manually with open() and close() calls leads to leaks whenever early returns or exceptions bypass the close() call.

quickCheck.question: When is a resource released in the RAII pattern?
options: Automatically inside the destructor when the wrapper object goes out of scope
Only when the operating system shuts down
quickCheck.explanation: RAII guarantees automatic resource release inside the destructor when the stack object leaves scope.

topics.title: Stack Unwinding & Exception Safety Guarantees
explanation: When an exception is thrown in C++, the runtime performs "Stack Unwinding": walking back up the call stack frame by frame.
During stack unwinding, EVERY fully constructed stack object has its destructor invoked automatically.
C++ defines 4 Exception Safety Levels: (1) No-throw guarantee (`noexcept`); (2) Strong guarantee (commit or rollback); (3) Basic guarantee (no leaks, valid state); (4) No guarantee.
keyRules: Without RAII, any thrown exception causes catastrophic resource leaks.
Mark functions noexcept if they are guaranteed never to throw (critical for move constructors and destructors).

codeSnippet.title: Stack Unwinding with RAII
codeSnippet.description: Observing automatic destructor calls during exception propagation

topics.pitfall: Allocating raw heap memory with `new` before throwing an exception guarantees that `delete` will be skipped, causing an irrecoverable memory leak.

quickCheck.question: What happens to local stack objects when an exception propagates up the call stack?
options: Their destructors are called in reverse order during stack unwinding
They remain in memory until the program terminates
Their memory is immediately wiped without calling destructors
Stack unwinding causes a segmentation fault
quickCheck.explanation: Stack unwinding systematically calls the destructors of all local objects in the unwound stack frames.

topics.title: `std::lock_guard` & Scoped Mutex Management
explanation: In multithreaded programming, locking a `std::mutex` manually with `mtx.lock()` and `mtx.unlock()` is error-prone (forgetting to unlock on early returns or exceptions causes permanent deadlocks).
`std::lock_guard<std::mutex>` is the quintessential standard RAII wrapper for synchronization.
It locks the mutex in its constructor and unlocks it automatically in its destructor.
keyRules: Never call mutex.unlock() manually; always use std::lock_guard or std::scoped_lock.
C++17 std::scoped_lock can lock multiple mutexes simultaneously without risk of deadlock.

codeSnippet.title: Deadlock-Free Thread Locking with RAII
codeSnippet.description: Automated mutex lock and unlock via std::lock_guard

topics.pitfall: Calling `mtx.lock()` manually before a function that can throw leaves the mutex permanently locked, deadlocking all other threads.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of `std::lock_guard` over manual `mutex.lock()` and `mutex.unlock()`?
options: It guarantees the mutex is unlocked even if an exception or early return occurs
It makes code run on multiple CPUs simultaneously
It converts the mutex to an atomic integer
quickCheck.explanation: By using RAII, lock_guard guarantees unlock upon scope exit regardless of return path or exceptions.

topics.title: Custom RAII Scope Guard / Defer Pattern
explanation: Sometimes you need to execute ad-hoc cleanup logic without writing an entire dedicated class.
A Scope Guard (or `defer` idiom, popularized by Go/Zig) accepts an arbitrary lambda and executes it in its destructor.
Invaluable for legacy C API integration, resetting temporary state, or restoring terminal display modes.
keyRules: Store the callable lambda inside the guard class.
The destructor executes the lambda upon exiting the block scope.

codeSnippet.title: Custom ScopeGuard Defer Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Executing arbitrary cleanup lambdas via RAII

topics.pitfall: Letting an exception throw out of a ScopeGuard destructor terminates the program; ensure cleanup lambdas are noexcept.

quickCheck.question: What does a ScopeGuard or `defer` pattern guarantee?
options: That a specified cleanup function will execute whenever the current scope exits
That code runs in a background thread
That all heap allocations are doubled
That memory is allocated on the GPU
quickCheck.explanation: A ScopeGuard wraps a callable action in a destructor, guaranteeing execution on scope exit.

topics.title: RAII Across Standard Library Components
explanation: Modern C++ is built entirely on RAII:
`std::vector<T>`: RAII wrapper over dynamic heap arrays.
`std::string`: RAII wrapper over dynamic char buffers.
`std::fstream`: RAII wrapper over OS file handles.
`std::unique_ptr<T>`: RAII wrapper over single-owner heap pointers.
`std::jthread` (C++20): RAII wrapper over OS threads that joins automatically on destruction.
keyRules: Embrace the standard library RAII types to avoid writing manual memory management.
If you write "delete" in modern C++, you are likely violating RAII best practices.

codeSnippet.title: Standard Library RAII in Action
codeSnippet.description: Zero manual deletes across vectors and file streams

topics.pitfall: Manually calling `.close()` on `std::fstream` or `.clear()` before vector destruction is redundant noise; RAII handles it automatically.

quickCheck.question: Why does modern C++ rarely require writing explicit `delete` calls?
options: Standard library containers and smart pointers manage heap memory through RAII destructors
C++ added a mandatory garbage collector in C++20
The compiler converts delete into a syntax warning
All variables are now stored on the stack
quickCheck.explanation: Modern RAII wrappers (`std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`, `std::string`) release memory automatically in their destructors.

topics.title: The "Rule of Zero": The Peak of RAII Design
explanation: The "Rule of Zero" states: If a class does not directly manage raw resources, it should define ZERO custom special member functions (no custom destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, or move assignment).
By using standard RAII members (`std::string`, `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr`), the compiler-generated special members will automatically do the right thing.
Classes with Rule of Zero are simpler, bug-free, and maintain maximum performance.
keyRules: Prefer Rule of Zero whenever possible.
Only write custom destructors in low-level resource wrapper classes.

codeSnippet.title: The Rule of Zero Class Design
codeSnippet.description: Flawless resource management without writing a single destructor

topics.pitfall: Writing unnecessary empty destructors `~MyClass() {}` suppresses the compiler from generating automatic move constructors, degrading performance.

quickCheck.question: What is the "Rule of Zero" in C++ software engineering?
options: Classes that compose RAII member types should avoid defining custom destructors or copy/move operations
No class can have more than zero base classes
quickCheck.explanation: The Rule of Zero advises delegating resource management to standard RAII member types so no custom special members are needed.

topics.title: Exception-Safe Transaction Pattern with Commit / Rollback
explanation: Using RAII to implement the Strong Exception Safety Guarantee.
An `AutoRollback` RAII object assumes failure by default. If an exception occurs, its destructor rolls back the transaction.
If all steps succeed, calling `commit()` or `dismiss()` disarms the rollback guard, cementing the changes.
keyRules: Assume failure on initialization.
Call guard.dismiss() only at the very end of the safe path.

codeSnippet.title: Transaction Rollback Guard Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Automatic rollback on exception using RAII dismiss guard

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to disarm the rollback guard on the success path causes unintentional rollbacks when exiting the function.

quickCheck.question: How does an RAII rollback guard ensure the Strong Exception Guarantee?
options: It automatically reverts changes in its destructor if commit() was never called due to an exception
It re-runs the code until it succeeds
It creates a backup of the hard drive
quickCheck.explanation: If an exception unwinds the stack before commit(), the destructor executes rollback logic automatically.

topics.title: Day 9 Capstone: RAII POSIX Socket Wrapper
explanation: Synthesizing Day 9 concepts into an industrial network socket descriptor wrapper.
Guarantees that socket descriptors are closed, prevents double-close errors, and demonstrates non-copyable RAII resource management.
Forms the backbone of production high-performance web servers.
keyRules: Encapsulate raw OS integer file descriptors inside an RAII class.
Strictly delete copy constructor and copy assignment.

codeSnippet.title: Production RAII Socket Wrapper Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Leak-proof socket management conforming to RAII standards

topics.pitfall: Copying raw socket wrappers without unique ownership leads to closing the same OS file descriptor twice.

quickCheck.question: Why should RAII wrappers over OS file descriptors be non-copyable by default?
options: To prevent two wrapper instances from closing the same underlying file descriptor twice
Because the operating system forbids copying
quickCheck.explanation: If two objects hold the same raw OS file descriptor, both destructors would close it, causing double-close errors.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 9 Capstone: RAII Benchmark Stopwatch Timer
instructions: Create a class `ExecutionTimer` that records `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now()` in its constructor.
In its destructor, compute the elapsed milliseconds and print the timing benchmark.
Test it by wrapping a computationally intensive loop.
hints: Store start time in `m_startTime = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();`.
Calculate duration in destructor with `std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>`.

keyTakeaways: RAII guarantees automatic resource release in destructors upon leaving scope.
Stack unwinding during exceptions ensures destructors are reliably called.
The Rule of Zero advises composing standard RAII members instead of writing custom destructors.
Never manage raw mutexes or file handles manually; use scoped RAII guards.

days.title: Smart Pointers: `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr` & `weak_ptr`
days.subtitle: Exclusive ownership, reference-counted shared ownership & breaking cyclic reference leaks
days.overview: Eliminate raw pointer bugs with C++11 smart pointers. Master std::unique_ptr for exclusive zero-overhead ownership, std::shared_ptr for reference-counted ownership, std::make_unique/make_shared, and std::weak_ptr for breaking cyclic memory leaks.

topics.title: `std::unique_ptr<T>`: Exclusive Zero-Overhead Ownership
explanation: `std::unique_ptr<T>` owns and manages a heap object exclusively. Exactly ONE `unique_ptr` owns the target at any time.
When the `unique_ptr` goes out of scope, it automatically deletes the owned object.
Zero overhead: `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>) == sizeof(T*)` (exactly 8 bytes on 64-bit). It has zero memory or execution cost compared to a raw pointer.
keyRules: unique_ptr cannot be copied (copy constructor is deleted).
unique_ptr CAN be moved (ownership transferred via std::move).
Always prefer unique_ptr by default for dynamic heap allocations.

codeSnippet.title: std::unique_ptr Exclusive Ownership
codeSnippet.description: Zero-overhead automatic heap deletion upon scope exit

topics.pitfall: Attempting to copy a `unique_ptr` will fail compilation; transfer ownership using `std::move(ptr)` instead.

quickCheck.question: What is the memory size overhead of `std::unique_ptr<T>` compared to a raw pointer `T*`?
options: Zero overhead (same size as raw pointer: 8 bytes on 64-bit)
quickCheck.explanation: std::unique_ptr is a zero-cost abstraction with identical memory size and runtime speed to a raw pointer.

topics.title: `std::make_unique<T>` (C++14): Exception Safety & Efficiency
explanation: Never construct a unique pointer with raw `new`: `std::unique_ptr<T>(new T())` is an anti-pattern.
Always use `std::make_unique<T>(args...)` (standardized in C++14).
It provides clean syntax without repeating the type name and eliminates potential memory leaks if an exception is thrown in another argument of a multi-parameter function call.
keyRules: Use auto ptr = std::make_unique<T>(constructor_args...);
Eliminates raw "new" from modern application codebases.

codeSnippet.title: Factory Pattern with std::make_unique
codeSnippet.description: Clean exception-safe heap allocation syntax

topics.pitfall: Using `new` inside a function call like `foo(std::unique_ptr<A>(new A()), std::unique_ptr<B>(new B()))` can leak if evaluation order throws an exception between the allocations.

quickCheck.question: Why is `std::make_unique<T>()` preferred over `std::unique_ptr<T>(new T())`?
options: It provides exception safety and eliminates redundant type declarations
It allows unique_ptr to be copied
It runs faster on 32-bit systems only
quickCheck.explanation: make_unique provides complete exception safety and cleaner syntax without mentioning the type twice.

topics.title: `std::shared_ptr<T>`: Reference-Counted Shared Ownership
explanation: `std::shared_ptr<T>` allows multiple owners to share ownership of a single heap object.
Internally, it manages a heap-allocated "Control Block" containing: (1) Strong Reference Count; (2) Weak Reference Count; (3) Custom deleter (if any).
Copying a `shared_ptr` atomically increments the strong reference count. When any `shared_ptr` is destroyed, it decrements the count. When the count drops to ZERO, the managed object is deleted.
keyRules: Reference count increments/decrements are atomic (thread-safe).
Memory size of shared_ptr is 16 bytes (pointer to object + pointer to control block).
Use shared_ptr only when true shared, multi-owner lifetime is necessary.

codeSnippet.title: std::shared_ptr Reference Counting
codeSnippet.description: Tracking use_count() across multiple sharing owners

topics.pitfall: Using `shared_ptr` by default everywhere introduces atomic reference-counting cache line thrashing and control block overhead; use `unique_ptr` unless shared ownership is strictly required.

quickCheck.question: When is the object managed by a `std::shared_ptr` destroyed?
options: When the strong reference count drops to zero
When the first shared_ptr goes out of scope
quickCheck.explanation: The managed object is deleted when the last shared_ptr owner is destroyed (use_count() reaches 0).

topics.title: `std::make_shared<T>`: Single-Allocation Optimization
explanation: Creating a shared pointer via `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T())` performs TWO separate heap allocations: (1) for the object `T`; (2) for the internal Control Block.
`std::make_shared<T>(args...)` performs a single contiguous heap allocation combining both the object `T` and the Control Block into one contiguous memory chunk.
Result: Halves heap allocation count and significantly improves CPU cache locality.
keyRules: Always use std::make_shared<T>() instead of shared_ptr<T>(new T()).
Single heap allocation for both object and control block.

codeSnippet.title: std::make_shared Combined Memory Layout
codeSnippet.description: Single allocation for control block and object payload
codeSnippet.code:
/*
  std::shared_ptr<T>(new T()) -> 2 Heap Allocations:
  [Alloc 1: Object T]  <--- Separate Memory Block --->  [Alloc 2: Control Block]

  std::make_shared<T>()       -> 1 Contiguous Allocation:
  [=== Combined Heap Allocation: Control Block (16B) | Object T ===]
*/

topics.pitfall: Because `make_shared` combines the control block and object in one allocation, if a `weak_ptr` outlives all `shared_ptr`s, the memory for the object cannot be released back to the OS until all `weak_ptr`s are also destroyed.

quickCheck.question: How many heap allocations are performed by `std::make_shared<T>()`?
quickCheck.explanation: make_shared allocates both the control block and the object in a single unified heap allocation.

topics.title: Cyclic References & Memory Leaks with `shared_ptr`
explanation: If Object A holds a `std::shared_ptr<B>` to Object B, and Object B holds a `std::shared_ptr<A>` to Object A, a "Cyclic Reference" (reference cycle) is formed.
Even when all external pointers go out of scope, both objects have `use_count() == 1` because they hold each other.
Neither destructor is EVER called, causing an irrecoverable memory leak in production.
keyRules: Cyclic shared_ptr relationships cause permanent memory leaks.
Break cycles by converting one direction of the relationship into a std::weak_ptr.

codeSnippet.title: Cyclic Reference Memory Leak Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating how circular shared_ptr causes destructors to never run

topics.pitfall: Using `shared_ptr` for parent-child tree relationships (child points to parent via shared_ptr) creates circular reference leaks.

quickCheck.question: What occurs when two objects hold `std::shared_ptr` references to each other?
options: A circular reference leak occurs where neither object is ever destructed
The compiler detects it and throws an error
The program crashes with stack overflow
quickCheck.explanation: Both objects maintain a non-zero reference count on each other, preventing destruction.

topics.title: `std::weak_ptr<T>`: Non-Owning Observer & Cycle Breaker
explanation: `std::weak_ptr<T>` is a non-owning smart pointer that observes an object managed by `std::shared_ptr`.
It does NOT increment the strong reference count, completely breaking cyclic memory leaks.
To access the object, you must call `wp.lock()`, which returns a temporary `std::shared_ptr`. If the object was already destroyed, `lock()` safely returns `nullptr`.
keyRules: Use weak_ptr for child-to-parent pointers, caches, and observer patterns.
Always check if (auto sp = wp.lock()) before dereferencing.

codeSnippet.title: Breaking Cycles with std::weak_ptr
codeSnippet.description: Safe non-owning observer with lock() promotion

topics.pitfall: Dereferencing a `weak_ptr` directly is impossible (`*wp` is illegal); you must call `wp.lock()` to obtain a temporary `shared_ptr`.

quickCheck.question: How do you access the object pointed to by a `std::weak_ptr`?
options: Cast it to a raw pointer
quickCheck.explanation: Calling `lock()` safely verifies if the object is still alive and returns a shared_ptr.

topics.title: Custom Deleters in Smart Pointers
explanation: By default, smart pointers invoke `delete` when freeing their managed target.
You can supply a Custom Deleter (a lambda, functor, or function pointer) to manage non-memory resources like C file handles (`std::fclose`), database connections, or GPU handles.
`std::unique_ptr<T, Deleter>` encodes the deleter type in its template signature; `std::shared_ptr<T>` uses type erasure so the deleter type is not part of the pointer type.
keyRules: unique_ptr deleter type is in template: std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)>.
shared_ptr deleter is passed as a constructor argument without affecting its type.

codeSnippet.title: Custom Deleter for C File Handles
codeSnippet.description: Wrapping legacy C resources inside std::unique_ptr

topics.pitfall: Supplying a stateful functor as a deleter to `unique_ptr` increases the size of the pointer struct.

quickCheck.question: Can `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr` manage non-memory resources like file handles?
options: Yes, by supplying a custom deleter function or lambda
No, they only support C++ objects allocated with new
quickCheck.explanation: Custom deleters allow smart pointers to manage any resource with cleanup APIs (like fclose, close, sqlite3_close).

topics.title: Day 10 Capstone: LRU Cache Element Graph with Smart Pointers
explanation: Synthesizing Day 10 smart pointers into a robust graph structure.
Demonstrating `std::unique_ptr` for node ownership, `std::weak_ptr` for observer references, and zero memory leaks under AddressSanitizer.
The foundational design pattern for game scenegraphs and caching systems.
keyRules: Use unique_ptr for parent -> child hierarchy.
Use weak_ptr for child -> parent back-pointers.

codeSnippet.title: SceneGraph Node Hierarchy Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Parent-child hierarchy using unique_ptr and weak_ptr

topics.pitfall: Storing a `shared_ptr` back to parent inside `child->parent` creates a cycle that permanently leaks the entire scene tree.

quickCheck.question: In a tree or scenegraph, what smart pointer type should child nodes use to point to their parent?
options: std::weak_ptr to avoid circular reference memory leaks
quickCheck.explanation: Using `std::weak_ptr` for parent back-pointers breaks the cycle, allowing the tree to be cleaned up naturally.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 10 Capstone: Factory Function Returning std::unique_ptr
instructions: Create a struct `Task` with fields `int id` and `std::string title`.
Implement a factory function `std::unique_ptr<Task> createTask(int id, const std::string& title)`.
Call `createTask` and store the result in a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Task>>`.
hints: Use `std::make_unique<Task>(id, title)` inside the factory function.
Iterate over the vector using `const auto& task` because `unique_ptr` cannot be copied.

keyTakeaways: `std::unique_ptr` is the zero-overhead default choice for exclusive heap ownership.
Always use `std::make_unique` (C++14) and `std::make_shared` (C++11).
Use `std::weak_ptr` to observe `std::shared_ptr` without forming circular reference leaks.
Smart pointers support custom deleters for managing non-memory resources (like C file handles).

days.title: Operator Overloading & C++20 Spaceship Operator (`<=>`)
days.subtitle: Arithmetic, stream << / >>, subscript [], and the C++20 Three-Way Comparison Spaceship operator
days.overview: Make custom classes behave like native primitives. Master arithmetic operators (+, -, *), stream insertion/extraction (<<, >>), subscript ([]), function call (()), and the modern C++20 Three-Way Comparison ("spaceship") operator (<=>).

topics.title: Operator Overloading Foundations & Syntax
explanation: Operator overloading allows custom types to use built-in C++ operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `==`, `[]`, etc.).
Operators can be overloaded as member functions (left-hand operand is `*this`) or non-member friend functions (both operands passed as parameters).
Rule of Symmetry: Binary operators that should treat both operands equally (e.g. `a + b` allowing `complex + 5` and `5 + complex`) should be implemented as non-member functions.
keyRules: You cannot create new operator symbols; only existing C++ operators can be overloaded.
You cannot change operator precedence or arity (binary remains binary).
Never overload &&, ||, or comma operators because overloading breaks short-circuit evaluation.

codeSnippet.title: Vector2D Arithmetic Operator Overloading
codeSnippet.description: Overloading operator+ for mathematical vector addition

topics.pitfall: Overloading `operator&&` or `operator||` disables compiler short-circuit evaluation, forcing both expressions to evaluate and causing subtle bugs.

quickCheck.question: Can you invent brand new operator symbols (such as `**` for exponentiation) in C++?
options: No, only existing C++ operators can be overloaded
quickCheck.explanation: The C++ standard restricts operator overloading strictly to existing predefined operator tokens.

topics.title: Stream Insertion (`<<`) & Extraction (`>>`) Operators
explanation: To allow printing an object with `std::cout << myObj;`, you must overload `operator<<`.
Because the left-hand operand is `std::ostream&`, this operator MUST be a non-member function.
Signature: `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const MyClass& obj);` returning `os` by reference to enable chaining (`std::cout << a << b;`).
keyRules: Must be a non-member function; declare as friend if private access is required.
Always return ostream& by reference to support stream chaining.

codeSnippet.title: Stream Insertion operator<< Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Enabling direct std::cout printing for custom types

topics.pitfall: Returning `void` or `std::ostream` by value from `operator<<` breaks stream chaining like `std::cout << a << b;`.

quickCheck.question: Why must `operator<<` for printing be implemented as a non-member function?
options: Because the left-hand operand is `std::ostream&`, not the custom class instance
quickCheck.explanation: The left-hand side of `std::cout << obj` is `std::cout` (an ostream), so it cannot be a member of `obj`.

topics.title: Subscript Operator (`[]`): Read & Write Access
explanation: The subscript operator `operator[]` provides array-like bracket indexing for custom collections and matrices.
Idiomatic design requires TWO overloads:
(1) Non-const overload returning `T&` (allows assignment: `buf[0] = 42;`);
(2) Const overload returning `const T&` (allows inspection on const objects: `int x = constBuf[0];`).
keyRules: Always provide both const and non-const overloads of operator[].
operator[] MUST be implemented as a class member function.

codeSnippet.title: Dual Subscript Overloads Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Supporting mutable and read-only bracket indexing

topics.pitfall: Providing only a non-const `operator[]` prevents indexing any `const MyContainer&` object.

quickCheck.question: Why should a container provide both `T& operator[](size_t)` and `const T& operator[](size_t) const`?
options: To allow mutation on non-const instances and read-only access on const instances
quickCheck.explanation: The non-const version allows write access, while the const overload allows reading from const container references.

topics.title: Function Call Operator (`operator()`) & Functors
explanation: A class that overloads the function call operator `operator()` is called a "Functor" (function object).
Unlike raw functions, functors can maintain internal state across multiple invocations.
Extensively used as predicates in STL algorithms (`std::sort`, `std::find_if`) and is the underlying mechanism that compilers use to implement lambdas.
keyRules: operator() can take any number of arguments and return any type.
Functor state persists between invocations.

codeSnippet.title: Stateful Functor Class
codeSnippet.description: Function call operator operator() maintaining running state

topics.pitfall: Assuming functors are slower than function pointers; functors are actually faster because compiler inlines their `operator()` directly.

quickCheck.question: What is a "functor" in C++?
options: A class or struct that overloads `operator()` so its instances can be called like functions
A mathematical function that cannot fail
quickCheck.explanation: A functor is an object with an overloaded `operator()`, allowing it to be invoked with function call syntax.

topics.title: The C++20 Three-Way Comparison "Spaceship" Operator (`<=>`)
explanation: Historically, implementing full comparison required writing 6 separate boilerplate operators: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.
C++20 introduced the Three-Way Comparison Operator `<=>` (the "spaceship" operator).
Writing `auto operator<=>(const MyClass&) const = default;` generates ALL SIX relational comparison operators automatically using member-by-member lexicographical comparison!
keyRules: auto operator<=>(const MyClass&) const = default; generates <, <=, >, >= automatically.
It returns std::strong_ordering (less, equal, greater) for integers/pointers.
You also default operator==: bool operator==(const MyClass&) const = default;.

codeSnippet.title: C++20 Spaceship Operator <=> Generation
codeSnippet.description: Single-line generation of all 6 relational comparison operators

topics.pitfall: Comparing floating-point values returns `std::partial_ordering` because `NaN` is unordered (NaN is neither less, equal, nor greater than any number).

quickCheck.question: What does `auto operator<=>(const MyClass&) const = default;` provide in C++20?
options: Generates all relational comparison operators (<, <=, >, >=) automatically
quickCheck.explanation: The spaceship operator `<=>` automatically generates relational comparisons based on member-wise lexicographical order.

topics.title: Comparison Ordering Categories: `strong_ordering` vs `partial_ordering`
explanation: C++20 categorizes comparisons into three distinct ordering categories:
`std::strong_ordering`: Absolute equivalence (if `a == b`, then `f(a) == f(b)`). Used for integers, strings.
`std::weak_ordering`: Equivalence without identical substitution (e.g. case-insensitive string comparison where `"abc"` and `"ABC"` are equivalent).
`std::partial_ordering`: Some values cannot be compared (e.g. `NaN` in floating-point numbers `float`/`double`).
keyRules: Integers produce strong_ordering.
Floating-point types (float, double) produce partial_ordering due to NaN.
Custom spaceship operators return the strongest ordering supported by all members.

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting C++20 Comparison Ordering Results
codeSnippet.description: Differentiating strong ordering from partial ordering with NaN

topics.pitfall: Assuming `double` comparison returns `std::strong_ordering`; it returns `std::partial_ordering` because of `std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN()`.

quickCheck.question: Why do floating point types (`double`) return `std::partial_ordering` with `<=>`?
options: Because NaN (Not a Number) cannot be compared to any number
Because floating point operations are non-deterministic
quickCheck.explanation: NaN cannot be less, greater, or equal to any value, requiring partial ordering.

topics.title: Compound Assignment (`+=`) vs Binary Operator (`+`) Pattern
explanation: Best practice in C++ operator design: Implement compound assignment `operator+=` as a member function first, and implement binary `operator+` in terms of it.
`MyClass& operator+=(const MyClass& rhs)` modifies `*this` in-place and returns `*this` by reference.
Then `MyClass operator+(MyClass lhs, const MyClass& rhs)` takes `lhs` by value, invokes `lhs += rhs;`, and returns `lhs` (leveraging RVO).
keyRules: operator+= is a member returning T&.
operator+ is a non-member returning T by value, implemented via +=.
Guarantees consistency and eliminates duplicated arithmetic logic.

codeSnippet.title: Canonical += and + Operator Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Reusing compound assignment for clean binary addition

topics.pitfall: Implementing `+` and `+=` independently can cause divergence where `a + b` gives a different result than `a += b`.

quickCheck.question: What is the canonical best practice for implementing binary `operator+` in C++?
options: Implement member `operator+=` first, then implement non-member `operator+` by reusing `+=`
Always declare both as friend functions
quickCheck.explanation: Implementing `+` in terms of `+=` prevents code duplication and ensures semantic consistency.

explanation: Synthesizing Day 11 concepts into a complete FixedPoint decimal numeric class.
Demonstrating arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`), stream insertion (`<<`), spaceship comparison (`<=>`), and compound assignments.
Used heavily in financial trading and physics engines to avoid floating-point binary rounding errors.
keyRules: Store scaled integer internally.
Provide full suite of mathematical and relational operators.

codeSnippet.description: Custom numeric type with complete operator overloading

topics.pitfall: Returning a local object by reference from `operator+` produces a dangling reference crash; always return by value.

quickCheck.question: What return type should binary `operator+` have?
quickCheck.explanation: Binary `operator+` creates a new result object, which must be returned by value (leveraging RVO).

instructions: Create a class `ComplexNumber` with `double real` and `double imag`.

days.title: Inheritance, Virtual Functions & VTable Internals
days.subtitle: Dynamic polymorphism, virtual destructors, vptr & vtable layout, override & final keywords
days.overview: Understand how runtime polymorphism is implemented under the hood in C++. Learn how the compiler constructs Virtual Method Tables (vtables) and embeds virtual table pointers (vptr) in class memory, why virtual destructors are mandatory, and how to use the override and final keywords.

topics.title: Inheritance & Access Specifiers (`public`, `protected`, `private`)
explanation: C++ supports three modes of inheritance: `public`, `protected`, and `private`.
`public` inheritance represents an "is-a" relationship (Subclass is a BaseClass) and is the cornerstone of object-oriented polymorphism.
`protected` members are accessible inside derived classes, but inaccessible to outside callers.
`private` inheritance represents "implemented-in-terms-of" and hides base class methods from the outside interface.
keyRules: Use public inheritance for polymorphic subtyping.
Prefer composition ("has-a") over private inheritance whenever possible.

codeSnippet.title: Public Inheritance and Protected Members
codeSnippet.description: Base and derived class access relationships

topics.pitfall: Omitting the `public` keyword in class inheritance (`class Dog : Animal`) defaults to `private` inheritance, making base methods inaccessible.

quickCheck.question: What is the default inheritance access specifier for a `class` if omitted (`class B : A`)?
quickCheck.explanation: For `class`, default inheritance is private. For `struct`, default inheritance is public.

topics.title: Virtual Functions & Runtime Dynamic Dispatch
explanation: By default, function calls in C++ use Static Binding: the compiler resolves which function to call based on the compile-time pointer type.
Prefixing a member function with `virtual` enables Dynamic Dispatch: the function call is resolved at RUNTIME based on the actual concrete type of the object.
Allows treating derived instances uniformly through base class pointers (`Base* ptr = new Derived(); ptr->render();`).
keyRules: virtual functions enable runtime polymorphic method invocation.
Dynamic dispatch only occurs when invoking methods through pointers (Base*) or references (Base&).

codeSnippet.title: Static Binding vs Virtual Dynamic Dispatch
codeSnippet.description: Observing runtime polymorphic dispatch through base pointer

topics.pitfall: Calling a virtual function by value (`Shape s = Circle(); s.draw();`) causes "Object Slicing", stripping derived data and calling `Shape::draw()`.

quickCheck.question: What keyword enables dynamic runtime dispatch for a member function in C++?
quickCheck.explanation: The `virtual` keyword instructs the compiler to use dynamic dispatch via the virtual method table.

topics.title: The Mandatory Virtual Destructor Rule
explanation: CRITICAL RULE: Any class designed to be a polymorphic base class MUST declare its destructor `virtual`: `virtual ~Base() = default;`.
If a derived object is deleted through a base class pointer (`Base* ptr = new Derived(); delete ptr;`) and the base destructor is NOT virtual, ONLY the base destructor runs.
The derived class destructor is completely skipped, causing memory leaks and resource corruption.
keyRules: Rule: If a class has at least one virtual function, its destructor MUST be virtual.
virtual ~Base() = default; ensures complete bottom-to-top destruction.

codeSnippet.title: Virtual Destructor Defense
codeSnippet.description: Ensuring derived destructors run during polymorphic deletion

topics.pitfall: Deleting a derived instance through a non-virtual base pointer causes Undefined Behavior and skips derived class cleanup.

quickCheck.question: Why MUST a base class with virtual functions declare a `virtual` destructor?
options: To ensure derived class destructors are called when deleting through a base pointer
Because the C++ compiler requires all destructors to be virtual
quickCheck.explanation: A virtual destructor ensures that deleting an object via a base pointer executes derived destructors first.

topics.title: VTable and VPtr Memory Layout Internals
explanation: How does the machine actually implement virtual functions?
For every class with virtual functions, the compiler creates a static table of function pointers called the VTable (Virtual Method Table).
Inside every object instance of that class, the compiler invisibly injects an 8-byte pointer called the `vptr` (Virtual Pointer) pointing to that class's VTable.
Calling `ptr->draw()` compiles to: `ptr->vptr[INDEX_OF_DRAW](ptr)`.
keyRules: A class with virtual functions increases in size by sizeof(void*) = 8 bytes due to vptr.
Virtual function invocation costs one pointer indirection (vptr lookup), which is negligible (~1-2 nanoseconds).

codeSnippet.title: VTable and vptr Size Verification
codeSnippet.description: Observing the 8-byte vptr injection inside an object

topics.pitfall: Adding virtual functions to lightweight mathematical structs (like `Vector3`) inflates their size from 12 bytes to 24 bytes and breaks flat memory cache performance.

quickCheck.question: What hidden member is injected into an object instance when its class defines virtual functions?
options: A vptr (virtual pointer) pointing to the class vtable
A copy of the entire vtable
quickCheck.explanation: The compiler injects a single 8-byte `vptr` per object pointing to the shared class VTable.

topics.title: The `override` & `final` Keywords (C++11)
explanation: Prior to C++11, typos in derived class function signatures (e.g. `void draw(int x)` instead of `void draw(long x)`) silently created a brand new function instead of overriding.
`override`: Directs the compiler to verify that a base virtual function with the EXACT same signature exists. If not, compilation fails.
`final`: Forbids a virtual function from being overridden further by derived classes, or forbids an entire class from being inherited (`class Leaf final : public Base`).
keyRules: Always mark overriding member functions with the override keyword.
Use final to allow compiler "devirtualization" optimizations.

codeSnippet.title: Using override and final
codeSnippet.description: Compile-time verification of polymorphic overriding

topics.pitfall: Omitting `override` allows signature mismatches (like missing `const`) to silently fail to override the base class function.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of the `override` specifier in modern C++?
options: It instructs the compiler to verify that the method overrides an exact base virtual function
It forces the function to be inline
quickCheck.explanation: The override keyword triggers compile-time checks, ensuring signatures match base class virtual methods.

topics.title: Pure Virtual Functions & Abstract Interfaces
explanation: A Pure Virtual Function has no implementation in the base class and ends with `= 0`: `virtual void execute() = 0;`.
A class with at least one pure virtual function is an "Abstract Class". It CANNOT be instantiated directly.
Abstract classes define pure interfaces (contracts) in C++, identical to interfaces in Java/TypeScript or traits in Rust.
keyRules: virtual ReturnType method() = 0; declares a pure virtual function.
Derived classes must implement all pure virtual functions to become concrete instantiable types.

codeSnippet.title: Pure Abstract Interface Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Defining strict contracts with pure virtual functions

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to provide an implementation for even a single pure virtual function makes the derived class abstract, preventing instantiation.

quickCheck.question: What makes a C++ class an "Abstract Class"?
options: Having at least one pure virtual function (`= 0`)
quickCheck.explanation: Any class containing at least one pure virtual function (`= 0`) is an abstract class that cannot be instantiated.

topics.title: Multiple Inheritance & The Diamond Problem (`virtual` Inheritance)
explanation: C++ allows a class to inherit from multiple base classes (`class Worker : public Employee, public Student`).
The Diamond Problem: If classes B and C inherit from A, and class D inherits from both B and C, class D contains TWO independent copies of class A, causing symbol ambiguity and wasted memory.
Solution: Use Virtual Inheritance (`class B : virtual public A` and `class C : virtual public A`). Class D will now share a single unified instance of A.
keyRules: Virtual inheritance ensures only one instance of the common base class is included.
Multiple inheritance of pure abstract interfaces does NOT cause the diamond problem.

codeSnippet.title: Resolving Diamond Problem with virtual Inheritance
codeSnippet.description: Sharing a single base instance in diamond hierarchies

topics.pitfall: Omitting `virtual` in diamond inheritance leads to compiler error: `request for member 'x' is ambiguous`.

quickCheck.question: How does C++ solve the Diamond Problem in multiple inheritance?
options: Using `virtual public Base` inheritance to ensure only one instance of the common base exists
quickCheck.explanation: Virtual inheritance ensures that the most-derived class contains only a single shared copy of the base class.

topics.title: Day 12 Capstone: Extensible Game Renderer Pipeline
explanation: Synthesizing Day 12 concepts into an industrial extensible game rendering engine.
Demonstrating abstract base interfaces (`IRenderable`), virtual destructors, `override`, `final`, vtable dispatch, and `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<IRenderable>>`.
Forms the foundational architecture of real-world graphics and simulation software.
keyRules: Polymorphic collections must store pointers (unique_ptr<Base>), never values.
Storing values in `std::vector<Base>` causes object slicing.

codeSnippet.title: Polymorphic Renderer Pipeline Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Rendering diverse game entities through base interface pointers

topics.pitfall: Storing concrete derived objects in `std::vector<IRenderable>` by value slices off all derived state.

quickCheck.question: What occurs if you attempt to store polymorphic derived objects by value in `std::vector<BaseClass>`?
options: Object Slicing: derived member variables and virtual behavior are sliced off
The compiler throws a memory leak error
The vector automatically converts to pointers
quickCheck.explanation: Object slicing occurs when a derived object is copied into a base value, truncating derived members.

instructions: Create an abstract class `AudioOscillator` with a pure virtual method `float generateSample(float time) = 0` and a virtual destructor.

Always make base class destructors `virtual` to prevent resource leaks.
The VTable and vptr (8 bytes) facilitate runtime method resolution.

days.title: Move Semantics, Rvalues (`&&`) & The Rule of 5
days.subtitle: Value categories (lvalue/rvalue), move constructors, std::move cast, and the Rule of 3/5/0
days.overview: Master the performance revolution of C++11: Move Semantics. Understand lvalues vs rvalues, rvalue references (T&&), stealing heap buffers instead of deep copying, the mechanics of std::move, and the authoritative Rule of 5.

topics.title: Value Categories: Lvalues vs Rvalues Explained
explanation: Every expression in C++ has two properties: a type and a value category.

Lvalue (locator value): An expression that has an identifiable memory address and persists beyond a single expression (e.g. named variables `int x = 5;`, `ptr`, `arr[0]`). You can take its address with `&`.

Rvalue (read value / temporary): A temporary expression that does NOT have a persistent name or address, about to be destroyed at the end of the statement (e.g. literals `42`, temporary calculations `x + y`, function return temporaries `std::string("temp")`).
keyRules: If you can take its address with & -> It is an Lvalue.
If it is a temporary value about to expire -> It is an Rvalue.

codeSnippet.title: Identifying Lvalues vs Rvalues
codeSnippet.description: Testing expressions for addressability and lifetime

topics.pitfall: Attempting to bind a non-const lvalue reference `int& ref = 42;` fails compilation because 42 is an rvalue.

quickCheck.question: Which of the following is an Lvalue?
quickCheck.explanation: A named variable has an identifiable memory address and outlives the current statement, making it an lvalue.

topics.title: Rvalue References (`T&&`): Binding to Temporaries
explanation: C++11 introduced Rvalue References, declared with two ampersands: `T&&`.
While a traditional reference `T&` can only bind to lvalues, an rvalue reference `T&&` binds EXCLUSIVELY to expiring rvalue temporaries.
Binding to an rvalue signals to the program: "This object is temporary and about to die; you can safely steal its internal heap resources instead of copying them."
keyRules: T& binds to mutable lvalues.
const T& can bind to both lvalues and rvalues.
T&& binds exclusively to rvalues.

codeSnippet.title: Rvalue Reference Binding Rules
codeSnippet.description: Contrasting lvalue and rvalue reference binding

topics.pitfall: A named rvalue reference variable (e.g. `int&& r = 42;`) is itself an LVALUE inside the function because it has a name and address!

quickCheck.question: What does the `T&&` syntax represent in C++11 and later?
quickCheck.explanation: Two ampersands `T&&` denote an rvalue reference, binding to temporary values for move semantics.

topics.title: The `std::move` Cast: Unconditional Cast to Rvalue
explanation: Contrary to its name, `std::move` DOES NOT MOVE ANYTHING at runtime. It emits zero machine instructions!
`std::move(x)` is simply a compile-time static cast: `static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(x)`.
It tells the compiler: "Treat this named variable as an rvalue temporary, enabling the move constructor to steal its resources."
keyRules: std::move does not move anything; it casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference.
After calling std::move(x), x is left in a "valid but unspecified" state (usually empty). Do not read from it.

codeSnippet.title: Stealing Heap Buffers with std::move
codeSnippet.description: Zero-copy pointer transfer between strings via std::move

topics.pitfall: Reading or dereferencing an object after it has been moved-from leads to undefined or unexpected behavior.

quickCheck.question: What does `std::move` actually do at runtime?
options: Nothing: it is a compile-time cast to an rvalue reference that generates 0 CPU instructions
It copies memory bytes in a background thread
quickCheck.explanation: std::move is purely a compile-time cast to an rvalue reference, enabling the move constructor.

topics.title: Move Constructor & Move Assignment Operator
explanation: A Copy Constructor duplicates memory: `MyClass(const MyClass& other)`.
A Move Constructor steals pointers: `MyClass(MyClass&& other) noexcept`. It shallow-copies the internal heap pointer and sets `other.ptr = nullptr;`.
The Move Assignment Operator `MyClass& operator=(MyClass&& other) noexcept` releases its current resource, steals the other's pointer, and nullifies the other.
keyRules: Move operations MUST be marked noexcept so STL containers (like std::vector) will use them during reallocation.
Always set the moved-from object pointers to nullptr so its destructor does not free the stolen memory.

codeSnippet.title: Move Constructor & Move Assignment Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Properly stealing raw pointers and nullifying moved-from object

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to set `other.data = nullptr` in the move constructor causes a catastrophic double-free crash when `other` leaves scope.

quickCheck.question: Why MUST move constructors be marked `noexcept` in modern C++?
options: So that `std::vector` will move elements during reallocation instead of copying them
Because the compiler refuses to compile without noexcept
To speed up CPU clock frequency
quickCheck.explanation: std::vector checks `std::is_nothrow_move_constructible` to preserve the strong exception guarantee; without noexcept, it falls back to copying.

topics.title: The Rule of 3 vs The Rule of 5
explanation: C++98 "Rule of Three": If a class defines a custom Destructor, Copy Constructor, or Copy Assignment Operator, it almost certainly needs to define all THREE.

C++11 "Rule of Five": With the advent of move semantics, if you define any of the big three, you must explicitly declare all FIVE special member functions: (1) Destructor; (2) Copy Constructor; (3) Copy Assignment; (4) Move Constructor; (5) Move Assignment.
If you declare a custom destructor or copy operation, the compiler SUPPRESSES the automatic generation of move constructors.
keyRules: Rule of 5: Destructor, Copy Ctor, Copy Assign, Move Ctor, Move Assign.
Rule of 0: Prefer using RAII members and defining none of the 5.

codeSnippet.title: The Full Rule of 5 Template
codeSnippet.description: Complete boilerplate for managing a raw resource in C++

topics.pitfall: Defining a custom destructor without declaring move operations forces the compiler to perform slow deep copies when returning from functions.

quickCheck.question: What are the 5 special member functions in the "Rule of Five"?
options: Destructor, Copy Constructor, Copy Assignment, Move Constructor, Move Assignment
Static constructor, Private constructor, Copy, Move, Virtual destructor
quickCheck.explanation: The Rule of 5 covers the destructor plus both copy and move variations of constructors and assignments.

topics.title: The Copy-and-Swap Idiom: Strong Exception Safety in 1 Line
explanation: Writing separate copy and move assignment operators involves repetitive boilerplate, self-assignment checks, and exception vulnerabilities.
The Copy-and-Swap Idiom implements both copy and move assignment in a single operator: `MyClass& operator=(MyClass other)` taking parameter BY VALUE.
Inside, it simply swaps member pointers using `swap(*this, other);`. The parameter is constructed cleanly (via copy or move), and the destructor of `other` frees the old memory on scope exit!
keyRules: Pass by value: operator=(MyClass other).
Swap members with non-throwing friend swap(a, b) noexcept.
Provides the Strong Exception Guarantee automatically.

codeSnippet.title: Copy-and-Swap Assignment Idiom
codeSnippet.description: Unified exception-safe assignment operator using swap

topics.pitfall: Passing by reference `const MyClass&` to the Copy-and-Swap operator breaks the idiom; the argument MUST be taken by value.

quickCheck.question: Why does the Copy-and-Swap assignment operator take its argument by value (`MyClass other`)?
options: So the compiler automatically invokes the copy constructor for lvalues or the move constructor for rvalues
Because references are forbidden in assignment operators
quickCheck.explanation: Taking by value delegates allocation and copying to the constructor, handling both copy and move uniformly.

topics.title: Universal References & `std::forward` (Perfect Forwarding Preview)
explanation: In template contexts, `T&&` with type deduction is NOT an rvalue reference; it is a "Forwarding Reference" (Universal Reference).
`std::forward<T>(arg)` preserves the exact value category (lvalue or rvalue) of the argument passed by the caller, enabling perfect forwarding in templates and constructors.
keyRules: std::move casts unconditionally to rvalue.
std::forward casts conditionally: preserves lvalue if caller passed lvalue, rvalue if caller passed rvalue.
Essential for factory functions like std::make_unique.

codeSnippet.title: std::forward Perfect Forwarding Preview
codeSnippet.description: Preserving value categories in generic forwarding wrappers

topics.pitfall: Using `std::move` inside a generic forwarding function turns every argument into an rvalue, destroying caller variables even when they passed an lvalue.

quickCheck.question: What is the key difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`?
options: std::move casts unconditionally to rvalue; std::forward preserves original lvalue/rvalue category
std::forward copies memory; std::move deletes it
std::move is C++98; std::forward is C++20
quickCheck.explanation: std::move is an unconditional cast to rvalue, whereas std::forward conditionally preserves the argument category.

explanation: Synthesizing Day 13 concepts into an empirical performance benchmark.
Demonstrating the difference between a 10MB memory reallocation clone vs an instantaneous 0-cycle pointer transfer.
Move semantics is the reason C++ standard containers achieve unmatched data pipeline throughput.
keyRules: Moving transfers ownership of a pointer in O(1) single-cycle time regardless of buffer size.
Copying scales linearly O(N) with the buffer size.

codeSnippet.description: Contrasting O(N) buffer cloning with O(1) move pointer swap

quickCheck.explanation: Moving a vector simply copies 3 internal pointers (begin, end, capacity) and sets the old pointers to null in O(1) time.

keyTakeaways: Lvalues have persistent addresses; Rvalues are expiring temporaries.
`std::move` is a compile-time cast to an rvalue reference that generates 0 CPU instructions.
Move constructors steal pointers in $O(1)$ time and MUST be marked `noexcept`.
Follow the Rule of 5 whenever managing a raw resource.

days.title: Week 2 Capstone: Building a Custom `std::vector` & Exam
days.subtitle: Complete dynamic array class with Rule of 5, RAII, iterators & Module 2 qualifying exam
days.overview: Synthesize all of Week 2 by constructing a full production-grade custom dynamic vector class (`CustomVector<T>`). Implement the Rule of 5, dynamic geometric capacity doubling, placement new, and pass the Week 2 Qualifying Assessment.

topics.title: Architecture of a Production Vector Container
explanation: A production vector maintains three pointers:
1. `m_data`: Pointer to the start of allocated heap storage.
2. `m_size`: Number of currently constructed, active elements.
3. `m_capacity`: Total number of elements the buffer can hold before requiring reallocation.
This 3-pointer architecture achieves amortized $O(1)$ `push_back()`.
keyRules: Capacity represents allocated memory; Size represents initialized objects.
Never access memory past m_size, even if within m_capacity.

codeSnippet.title: Vector 3-Pointer Anatomy
codeSnippet.description: Standard memory layout of dynamic vector containers
codeSnippet.code:
/*
  [==================== HEAP ALLOCATED BUFFER ====================]
  |  Item 0  |  Item 1  |  Item 2  |  Item 3  |  Uninitialized Capacity... |
  ^                                           ^                            ^
  m_data                                  m_size                      m_capacity
*/

topics.pitfall: Confusing `size()` with `capacity()`; writing to index `[size]` without resizing causes undefined behavior.

quickCheck.question: What is the difference between vector `size` and vector `capacity`?
options: Size is the number of active constructed elements; Capacity is the total allocated buffer space
Capacity is in bytes, size is in bits
quickCheck.explanation: Size counts valid objects currently in the vector; capacity counts how many elements can fit before reallocation is needed.

topics.title: Geometric Reallocation Strategy (Amortized $O(1)$ Push Back)
explanation: If a vector grew by 1 element on every `push_back()`, inserting $N$ elements would require $O(N^2)$ copies and reallocations.
By doubling capacity geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...) or multiplying by 1.5x, reallocations become rare exponential events.
The aggregate cost of $N$ insertions is $O(N)$, resulting in an amortized $O(1)$ cost per insertion.
keyRules: Geometric growth (typically 1.5x or 2x) guarantees amortized O(1) push_back.
Linear growth causes disastrous O(N^2) insertion slowdowns.

codeSnippet.title: Geometric Capacity Doubling Logic
codeSnippet.description: Calculating amortized O(1) growth thresholds

topics.pitfall: Reallocating the vector invalidates all existing raw pointers and iterators referencing its elements.

quickCheck.question: What is the amortized time complexity of `push_back()` in `std::vector`?
quickCheck.explanation: Because capacity doubles exponentially, the average cost across all insertions is O(1) constant time.

Ensure move constructor is marked noexcept.

quickCheck.question: Why does `reallocate()` use `std::move(m_data[i])` instead of copying?
options: To transfer element resources efficiently without cloning
Because copying is illegal in templates
To avoid deleting the old buffer
quickCheck.explanation: Moving elements during reallocation avoids cloning heap buffers for types like strings or sub-vectors.

topics.title: Iterator Support: `begin()` and `end()` for Range-Based For Loops
explanation: How does C++ enable range-based for loops: `for (const auto& item : myVector)`?
The compiler simply looks for `.begin()` and `.end()` methods that return pointers or iterator objects supporting `*`, `++`, and `!=`.
For contiguous arrays, raw pointers `T*` are already valid Random Access Iterators!
keyRules: T* begin() { return m_data; }
T* end() { return m_data + m_size; }
Enables standard STL algorithms and range-for loops automatically.

codeSnippet.title: Enabling Range-Based For Loops on Custom Containers
codeSnippet.description: Adding begin() and end() pointer iterators

topics.pitfall: Returning `data + size - 1` from `end()` is an off-by-one error; `end()` must point ONE PAST the last valid element.

quickCheck.question: Where must `end()` point in standard C++ iterator semantics?
options: One position past the last valid element
quickCheck.explanation: C++ iterators use half-open ranges `[begin, end)`, where `end` points one past the final element.

topics.title: `reserve()` vs `resize()`: Avoiding Reallocation Overhead
explanation: `vec.reserve(N)`: Pre-allocates memory capacity for at least $N$ elements without constructing any objects (`size` remains unchanged). Use this when you know the approximate element count in advance to eliminate ALL intermediate reallocations.
`vec.resize(N)`: Actually changes the `size` of the vector to $N$, default-constructing new elements if growing, or destroying elements if shrinking.
keyRules: Always call vec.reserve(estimatedCount) before a heavy insertion loop.
reserve() changes capacity; resize() changes size.

codeSnippet.title: reserve() Eliminating Reallocations
codeSnippet.description: Zeroing allocation overhead with pre-reserved capacity

topics.pitfall: Calling `reserve()` and then using bracket indexing `vec[0] = 5;` without calling `push_back()` causes undefined behavior because `size` is still 0.

quickCheck.question: What is the effect of calling `vec.reserve(500)` on an empty `std::vector`?
options: Capacity becomes at least 500, but size remains 0
quickCheck.explanation: reserve() only allocates raw capacity space without constructing objects; size remains 0.

topics.title: `emplace_back()` vs `push_back()`: In-Place Construction
explanation: `push_back(obj)` requires creating a temporary object and then moving or copying it into the vector buffer.
`emplace_back(args...)` uses variadic templates and placement new to construct the object directly IN-PLACE inside the vector's pre-allocated capacity.
Eliminates temporary object construction and move operations entirely.
keyRules: Use emplace_back when passing constructor arguments.
If you already have a constructed object, push_back(std::move(obj)) is identical.

codeSnippet.title: emplace_back In-Place Construction
codeSnippet.description: Constructing directly inside vector buffer without temporaries

topics.pitfall: Using `emplace_back(Employee(101, "role"))` defeats the purpose of emplace because a temporary object is still constructed.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary performance benefit of `emplace_back()` over `push_back()`?
options: It constructs the object directly in the vector buffer, eliminating temporaries and moves
It runs in a background thread
quickCheck.explanation: emplace_back forwards constructor arguments directly to placement new inside the vector buffer.

topics.title: Week 2 Architectural Synthesis & Mastery Checklist
explanation: Consolidating all Week 2 pillars:
1. OOP Encapsulation: Member initializer lists, `explicit`, and deterministic LIFO destruction.
2. RAII: Automatic resource ownership tied to stack scopes, stack unwinding exception safety.
3. Smart Pointers: `unique_ptr` (exclusive, 0 overhead), `shared_ptr` (atomic ref count), `weak_ptr` (cycle breaker).
4. Operator Overloading: Canonical `+=` / `+`, stream `<<`, bracket `[]`, and C++20 `<=>`.
5. Polymorphism: `virtual` functions, mandatory virtual destructors, vtables, `override` and `final`.
6. Move Semantics: Rvalue references `&&`, `std::move` cast, and the Rule of 5.
keyRules: Follow the Rule of Zero as primary default; use Rule of Five when wrapping raw handles.
Never delete through a base pointer without a virtual destructor.

codeSnippet.title: Week 2 Synthesis Verification Matrix
codeSnippet.description: Verifying modern C++ OOP and ownership practices

topics.pitfall: Mixing manual `new`/`delete` with smart pointers leads to double-free crashes or memory leaks.

quickCheck.question: Which smart pointer should be used by default in modern C++ when dynamic allocation is needed?
quickCheck.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` provides zero-cost, exclusive ownership and should be the default choice.

topics.title: Week 2 Qualifying Assessment Gateway
explanation: To unlock Week 3 (Templates, Generic Programming, C++20 Ranges & STL Mastery), you must pass the Week 2 Qualifying Exam with >= 80%.
The assessment verifies: RAII destruction, virtual destructor necessity, smart pointer selection, copy vs move semantics, and vtable mechanics.
Advance to Week 3 to master the generic programming engine of C++.
keyRules: Passing score: 80% (4 out of 5 questions correct).
Unlocks Week 3: Templates, Concepts, STL Algorithms & C++20 Ranges.

codeSnippet.title: Week 2 Exam Gateway Kicker
codeSnippet.description: Readiness checklist for Week 3 template advancement

topics.pitfall: Rushing past move semantics and smart pointers will make understanding STL containers and move-only types in Week 3 difficult.

quickCheck.question: What is required to unlock Week 3 of the C++ Systems Academy?
options: Score at least 80% on the Week 2 Qualifying Exam (or enable Dev Mode)
quickCheck.explanation: Achieving >= 80% on the Week 2 quiz certifies competency and unlocks Week 3.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 14 Capstone Project: Production Move-Only UniquePointer Class
instructions: Implement your own simplified `UniquePtr<T>` class from scratch.
Store a raw pointer `T* m_ptr`.
Implement destructor that calls `delete m_ptr`.
Delete the copy constructor and copy assignment operator.
Implement move constructor and move assignment operator marked `noexcept`.
Overload `operator*` and `operator->`.
hints: In move constructor and move assignment, set `other.m_ptr = nullptr;`.
Delete copy operations with `= delete;`.

keyTakeaways: A vector uses a 3-pointer architecture to achieve amortized $O(1)$ push_back.
`reserve()` pre-allocates capacity to eliminate reallocation overhead in hot loops.
Iterators are half-open ranges `[begin, end)` that enable modern range-based for loops.
