Week 2 establishes professional object lifecycles: RAII, smart pointers, and move semantics.

quiz.title: Week 2 Qualifying Exam: OOP, RAII & Move Semantics
quiz.description: Score at least 80% (4/5 correct) to unlock Week 3: Templates, Concepts, Modern C++20 & STL Mastery.

questions.question: Why must base class destructors be declared `virtual` in polymorphic hierarchies?
options: To ensure derived class destructors are invoked when deleting an object through a base pointer
To allocate the class on the heap
To allow member variables to be private
questions.explanation: Without a virtual destructor, deleting via a base pointer only calls the base destructor, leaking derived class resources.

questions.question: What is the runtime cost of moving a `std::vector` or `std::string` using `std::move`?
options: O(1) constant time: it only swaps internal pointers, generating zero element allocations
O(N) linear time proportional to vector size
It depends on the CPU clock speed
questions.explanation: Move semantics performs a shallow pointer transfer in O(1) time regardless of how many elements the container holds.

questions.question: What smart pointer should be used to break cyclic reference memory leaks between `std::shared_ptr` nodes?
questions.explanation: std::weak_ptr is a non-owning observer that does not increment the strong reference count, breaking reference cycles.

questions.question: What does `auto operator<=>(const MyClass&) const = default;` generate in C++20?
options: All six relational comparison operators (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) using member-wise comparison
questions.explanation: Defaulting the three-way comparison spaceship operator generates the full suite of comparison operators automatically.

questions.question: Why should move constructors always be marked `noexcept`?
options: So standard containers like `std::vector` will move elements during reallocation instead of deep copying them
Because the compiler refuses to compile move constructors without noexcept
questions.explanation: std::vector will only move elements during growth if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies to preserve exception safety.

modules.title: Templates, Generic Programming, C++20 Concepts & STL
modules.theme: Compile-Time Code Generation, Modern Type Constraints & STL Architecture
modules.description: Master C++ generic programming: function and class templates, Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD), SFINAE vs C++17 if constexpr, C++20 Concepts and Constraints, STL containers and algorithms, and pipeline views.
modules.imageAlt: C++ generic programming and compile-time template instantiation visualization

days.title: Function & Class Templates, CTAD (C++17)
days.subtitle: Type parameters, template instantiation, header-only template definitions & argument deduction
days.overview: Understand compile-time metaprogramming with templates. Learn how the compiler generates concrete specialized functions from generic blueprints, template parameter deduction, and modern C++17 Class Template Argument Deduction.

topics.title: The Blueprint Philosophy: Compile-Time Code Generation
explanation: Templates in C++ are not functions or classes; they are blueprints instructing the compiler on how to generate concrete functions or classes.
When you write `template <typename T> T max(T a, T b)`, the compiler emits ZERO binary instructions until you actually call `max(3, 5)` or `max(1.2, 3.4)`.

This process is called "Template Instantiation": the compiler stamps out an exact copy of the function with `T` substituted by `int` or `double`, optimizing it with zero runtime polymorphism overhead.
keyRules: Templates have ZERO runtime overhead compared to hand-written type-specific code.
Template definitions MUST reside in header files because the compiler needs the full source code to instantiate them at compile time in each translation unit.

codeSnippet.title: Function Template Instantiation
codeSnippet.description: Generic function blueprint generating type-specific code

topics.pitfall: Placing template function definitions in a `.cpp` file causes linker "unresolved external symbol" errors because other `.cpp` files cannot see the template body during instantiation.

quickCheck.question: Where must template function and class definitions reside in a multi-file project?
options: In header files (.h / .hpp) so any translation unit can instantiate them
quickCheck.explanation: Compilers instantiate templates at the point of call, requiring full template definitions to be visible in included headers.

topics.title: Template Argument Deduction & Explicit Specification
explanation: When calling a function template, the compiler automatically deduces the template type parameters from the argument types passed.
If arguments have conflicting types (e.g. `findMax(4, 5.5)` where one is `int` and one is `double`), deduction fails because `T` is ambiguous.
You can resolve ambiguity by explicitly specifying the type parameter: `findMax<double>(4, 5.5)`, or by using multiple template parameters (`template <typename T, typename U>`).
keyRules: Deduction fails if multiple arguments deduce conflicting types for the same T.
Explicitly specify types with angle brackets: func<TargetType>(args).

codeSnippet.title: Resolving Type Deduction Ambiguity
codeSnippet.description: Explicit template arguments vs multi-type parameters

topics.pitfall: Relying on implicit conversion in template functions without explicit angle brackets: template deduction does not perform automatic type promotion.

quickCheck.question: What happens when you call `template <typename T> void f(T a, T b)` with `f(10, 3.14)`?
options: Compilation error: type deduction fails due to ambiguous candidates (int vs double)
quickCheck.explanation: Template type deduction does not perform implicit conversions when deducing the same type parameter T.

topics.title: Class Templates: Generic Data Structures
explanation: Class templates allow writing generic containers (like `std::vector<T>`, `std::optional<T>`, `Pair<K, V>`).
Member functions defined outside the class template must also include the template header: `template <typename T> void MyClass<T>::method()`.
Every unique combination of template arguments creates an entirely distinct class type in memory.
keyRules: Pair<int, string> and Pair<double, double> are two completely independent types.
Class templates can accept multiple type and non-type parameters.

codeSnippet.title: Generic KeyValuePair Class Template
codeSnippet.description: Defining and instantiating generic data structures

topics.pitfall: Static member variables inside a class template are shared ONLY among instances with the exact same template arguments.

quickCheck.question: Are `std::vector<int>` and `std::vector<double>` related in the type system?
options: No, they are two completely distinct, unrelated types generated at compile time
Yes, they inherit from a common VectorBase class
They share the same static members
quickCheck.explanation: Class templates generate independent, distinct concrete classes for each unique type parameter.

topics.title: Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD) in C++17
explanation: Prior to C++11/C++17, instantiating a class template required repeating the type in angle brackets: `std::pair<int, std::string> p(1, "one");`. Helper functions like `std::make_pair(1, "one")` were created to deduce types.
C++17 introduced CTAD (Class Template Argument Deduction): The compiler deduces class template types directly from constructor arguments!
Now you write simply: `std::pair p(1, "one");` or `std::lock_guard lock(mtx);`.
keyRules: CTAD deduces template parameters from constructor arguments automatically.
You can write custom Deduction Guides: `MyType(const char*) -> MyType<std::string>;`.

codeSnippet.title: CTAD in Action (C++17)
codeSnippet.description: Constructing template classes without angle brackets

topics.pitfall: CTAD cannot deduce types if default constructors are called without arguments; `std::vector vec;` is illegal (must write `std::vector<int> vec;`).

quickCheck.question: What C++ standard introduced Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD)?
quickCheck.explanation: CTAD was standardized in C++17, eliminating redundant angle brackets when constructing objects.

topics.title: Non-Type Template Parameters (NTTP)
explanation: Templates can accept values (constants) as parameters in addition to types.
Examples: `template <typename T, size_t N> class FixedStack;` (how `std::array<T, N>` is implemented).
C++20 expanded Non-Type Template Parameters to accept floating-point numbers (`double`), structural literal classes, and lambda objects.
keyRules: NTTP arguments must be compile-time constants (constexpr).
Used to create statically-sized buffers with zero heap allocation.

codeSnippet.title: Non-Type Template Parameters for Statically Sized Stack
codeSnippet.description: Embedding capacity constants directly into template types

topics.pitfall: `StaticRingBuffer<int, 32>` and `StaticRingBuffer<int, 64>` are two completely different types; you cannot assign one to the other.

quickCheck.question: What is a Non-Type Template Parameter (NTTP)?
options: A template parameter that is a compile-time constant value (like an integer size) rather than a type
A template that cannot be compiled
quickCheck.explanation: NTTPs accept compile-time values (integers, pointers, sizes) rather than types.

topics.title: Default Template Arguments
explanation: Like function parameters, template parameters can have default values: `template <typename T = int, size_t N = 16> class Buffer;`.
If the caller omits arguments, the defaults are substituted automatically.
Extensively used across the STL: `std::vector<T, Allocator = std::allocator<T>>`.
keyRules: Default template arguments can appear on class templates and function templates.
Parameters with defaults must be trailing parameters.

codeSnippet.title: Default Template Parameters Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Configuring default types and sizes in class templates

topics.pitfall: Writing `CoordinateVector` without empty angle brackets `<>` when defaults exist was illegal pre-C++17 (C++17 CTAD allows it if constructors exist).

quickCheck.question: Can template parameters have default values in C++?
options: Yes, both class and function templates can define default type and non-type parameters
No, only function parameters can have defaults
quickCheck.explanation: C++ fully supports default template arguments for both types and non-type constants.

topics.title: Variadic Templates (`typename... Args`) & Parameter Packs
explanation: C++11 introduced Variadic Templates, allowing templates to accept an arbitrary number of arguments: `template <typename... Args>`.
`Args...` is a "Template Parameter Pack"; `args...` is a "Function Parameter Pack".
In C++11/14, packs were unpacked using recursive template instantiation. In C++17, "Fold Expressions" allow unpacking in a single expressive line: `(... + args)`.
keyRules: sizeof...(Args) queries the number of arguments in the pack at compile time.
C++17 Fold expressions: (... + args) sums all arguments.

codeSnippet.title: Variadic Templates & C++17 Fold Expressions
codeSnippet.description: Summing arbitrary numbers of arguments in one line

topics.pitfall: Attempting to index directly into a parameter pack like `args[2]` is illegal; packs must be unpacked via fold expressions or `std::tuple`.

quickCheck.question: What operator syntax represents a template parameter pack in C++?
quickCheck.explanation: The ellipsis `typename... Args` declares a variadic template parameter pack.

topics.title: Day 15 Capstone: Generic Thread-Safe Object Pool
explanation: Synthesizing Day 15 concepts into an industrial Generic Object Pool container.
Demonstrating class templates, variadic constructor forwarding, placement new, and zero heap reallocation during hot gameplay loops.
Massively utilized in high-performance networking and game development.
keyRules: Pre-allocate capacity in template class.
Return generic pointers/references for high throughput.

codeSnippet.title: Generic Object Pool Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Template object pool for zero-allocation recycling

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to clear or reset the state of a recycled object before putting it back into the pool leaks stale data across operations.

quickCheck.question: What is the purpose of a Generic Object Pool in performance-critical software?
options: To reuse pre-allocated objects, avoiding expensive dynamic new/delete operations in hot loops
quickCheck.explanation: Object pools recycle existing objects to eliminate runtime heap allocation latencies.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 15 Capstone: Generic Array Statistics Calculator
instructions: Create a template function `T calculateSum(const T* arr, size_t count)`.
Create a template function `T calculateMax(const T* arr, size_t count)`.
Test both functions with an array of `int` and an array of `double`.
hints: Initialize `total = 0;` and `maxVal = arr[0];`.
Use standard for loops up to `count`.

keyTakeaways: Templates are compile-time code generation blueprints with zero runtime overhead.
Template definitions must be placed in header files for instantiation visibility.
C++17 CTAD deduces class template parameters automatically from constructor arguments.
Variadic templates with C++17 fold expressions unpack argument lists in one expressive line.

days.title: Template Specialization, SFINAE & `if constexpr`
days.subtitle: Full & partial specialization, type traits (<type_traits>), SFINAE and C++17 if constexpr
days.overview: Master advanced compile-time branching. Learn full and partial template specialization, standard type traits (<type_traits>), SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error), and the modern C++17 compile-time if constexpr statement.

topics.title: Full (Explicit) Template Specialization
explanation: Sometimes the generic implementation of a template is inefficient or incorrect for a specific type (e.g. `char*` needing `strcmp` instead of `==`, or `bool` needing bit-packing).
Full Specialization allows providing a completely custom implementation for a specific type.
Syntax: `template <> class Container<bool> { ... };` (empty angle brackets signal specialization).
keyRules: Full specialization uses template <> with empty parameter list.
The specialized class can have completely different members and implementations from the primary template.

codeSnippet.title: Full Template Specialization for const char*
codeSnippet.description: Customizing comparison logic for raw C-strings

topics.pitfall: Omitting the `template <>` header when defining a full specialization generates a compiler error.

quickCheck.question: What header precedes a full template specialization definition?
quickCheck.explanation: `template <>` with empty angle brackets denotes an explicit/full specialization.

topics.title: Partial Template Specialization
explanation: Partial Specialization customizes a template for a SUBSET of types (e.g. all pointer types `T*`, all vectors `std::vector<T>`, or fixing 1 of 2 parameters).
Function templates CANNOT be partially specialized in C++ (only overloaded); Class templates CAN be partially specialized.
Syntax: `template <typename T> class Container<T*> { ... };`.
keyRules: Only class templates support partial specialization.
To specialize functions partially, delegate to a class template or use function overloading.

codeSnippet.title: Partial Specialization for All Pointer Types
codeSnippet.description: Custom handling for all pointer types T*

topics.pitfall: Trying to partially specialize a function template `template <typename T> void f<T*>()` fails compilation; use function overloading instead.

quickCheck.question: Can free function templates be partially specialized in standard C++?
options: No, only class templates can be partially specialized (functions should be overloaded)
quickCheck.explanation: The C++ standard explicitly disallows partial specialization of function templates; developers use function overloading instead.

topics.title: Type Traits Library (`<type_traits>`)
explanation: C++11 introduced `<type_traits>`, a compile-time metadata reflection library.
Traits query properties of types at compile time: `std::is_integral<T>::value`, `std::is_pointer<T>::value`, `std::is_trivially_copyable<T>::value`.
C++14/17 added clean variable template aliases ending in `_v`: `std::is_integral_v<T>` and type transformations ending in `_t`: `std::remove_reference_t<T>`.
keyRules: Query properties with std::is_xxx_v<T> (returns constexpr bool).
Transform types with std::remove_xxx_t<T> (returns type).

codeSnippet.title: Querying Type Traits at Compile Time
codeSnippet.description: Inspecting types with modern _v and _t type traits

topics.pitfall: Using legacy `std::is_integral<T>::value` instead of C++17 `std::is_integral_v<T>` adds unnecessary verbosity.

quickCheck.question: What header provides compile-time type reflection traits like `std::is_integral_v`?
quickCheck.explanation: <type_traits> contains all standardized compile-time type introspection and transformation templates.

topics.title: Modern Compile-Time Branching: `if constexpr` (C++17)
explanation: In standard `if (condition)`, all branches must compile successfully even if the condition is known at compile time.
C++17 introduced `if constexpr (compile_time_condition)`: The compiler evaluates the boolean expression at compile time and DISCARDS the untaken branch entirely.
Code in the discarded branch is not instantiated, allowing different code paths for completely incompatible types without SFINAE boilerplate!
keyRules: Condition must be a compile-time boolean constant expression.
Replaces 90% of legacy SFINAE and enable_if hacks with clean readable code.

codeSnippet.title: if constexpr Compile-Time Branching
codeSnippet.description: Discarding incompatible branch instantiations cleanly in C++17

topics.pitfall: Using regular `if` instead of `if constexpr` causes compilation failure because `*val` fails to compile for non-pointer types like `int`.

quickCheck.question: Why does `if constexpr` succeed where a regular `if` would fail when dereferencing `*val`?
options: The compiler completely discards and does not instantiate the untaken branch
quickCheck.explanation: `if constexpr` discards the untaken branch at compile time, skipping instantiation for incompatible types.

topics.title: SFINAE: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
explanation: SFINAE is a fundamental C++ rule: If substituting a template argument results in an invalid type or expression during overload resolution, the compiler does NOT emit an error; it simply removes that candidate from the overload set.
Historically implemented via `std::enable_if_t<Condition, ReturnType>`.
Allows conditionally enabling or disabling functions based on whether a type supports specific operations.
keyRules: Invalid substitution silently discards the candidate function.
If all candidates are discarded, a "no matching function call" error is emitted.

codeSnippet.title: SFINAE with std::enable_if_t
codeSnippet.description: Conditionally enabling function templates using SFINAE

topics.pitfall: SFINAE error messages can be notoriously cryptic when compiler output exceeds hundreds of lines of substitution failures.

quickCheck.question: What does SFINAE stand for in C++ metaprogramming?
options: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
quickCheck.explanation: SFINAE guarantees that an invalid template substitution drops the candidate from overload resolution without a compilation error.

topics.title: `decltype` & `std::declval` for Expression SFINAE
explanation: Expression SFINAE tests whether an expression (e.g. `a + b` or `obj.serialize()`) is valid for type `T`.
`std::declval<T>()` allows creating a fictitious reference to type `T` in an unevaluated expression without needing a constructor.
`decltype(std::declval<T>().size())` extracts the return type of `.size()`, validating if the method exists.
keyRules: std::declval<T>() can ONLY be used inside unevaluated operands (like sizeof or decltype).
Enables detecting whether a class has specific member methods.

codeSnippet.title: Detecting Member Function via decltype
codeSnippet.description: Checking for .size() method using unevaluated declval

topics.pitfall: Calling `std::declval<T>()` in an evaluated runtime context causes a compilation error; it is strictly an unevaluated type helper.

quickCheck.question: Can `std::declval<T>()` be called at runtime in executable code?
options: No, it can ONLY be used in unevaluated contexts like `decltype` and `sizeof`
Yes, it returns a default-constructed object
quickCheck.explanation: std::declval cannot be called at runtime; it exists solely to yield a fictitious reference in unevaluated type expressions.

topics.title: Template Template Parameters (`template <typename> class C`)
explanation: A template parameter can itself be a template! Syntax: `template <template <typename> class Container, typename T>`.
This allows writing generic algorithms that accept container templates themselves (e.g. `std::vector`, `std::list`) parameterized on any type `T`.
Forms the architecture behind container adapters like `std::stack` and `std::queue`.
keyRules: Enables decoupling container topology from element payload type.
C++17 allows template <template <typename...> class C>.

codeSnippet.title: Template Template Parameter Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Accepting container templates as generic parameters

topics.pitfall: STL containers take default allocator parameters; forgetting to account for the allocator template parameter in pre-C++17 template template signatures causes template matching errors.

quickCheck.question: What is a Template Template Parameter?
options: A template parameter that is itself a template blueprint
quickCheck.explanation: Template template parameters accept a generic template (like `std::vector`) rather than a concrete type (like `std::vector<int>`).

topics.title: Day 16 Capstone: Zero-Copy Binary Serializer Engine
explanation: Synthesizing Day 16 concepts into a high-performance binary serializer.
Demonstrating compile-time branching with `if constexpr`: fast `memcpy` for trivially copyable types vs custom element iteration for complex types.
Delivers maximum theoretical throughput for network and disk serialization.
keyRules: Use std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T> to branch at compile time.
Trivially copyable types serialize in a single direct memcpy byte copy.

codeSnippet.title: High-Performance Serializer with if constexpr
codeSnippet.description: Optimizing serialization via compile-time type introspection

topics.pitfall: Using `std::memcpy` on non-trivially copyable objects like `std::string` or `std::shared_ptr` corrupts internal pointers.

quickCheck.question: What trait identifies types that can be safely copied using raw `std::memcpy`?
quickCheck.explanation: Types satisfying `std::is_trivially_copyable_v` have no complex copy logic and can be serialized via bitwise byte copying.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 16 Capstone: Generic Formatter with if constexpr
instructions: Write a template function `std::string formatItem(T value)`.
Using `if constexpr`, if `T` is a pointer, print `*value` (or "nullptr" if null).
If `T` is a boolean, print "true" or "false".
Otherwise, use `std::to_string(value)`.
hints: Use `if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T>)`.
Use `else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, bool>)`.

keyTakeaways: Full specialization customizes a template for an exact type; partial specialization customizes for a subset of types.
`if constexpr` (C++17) evaluates at compile time and discards untaken branches completely.
SFINAE discards invalid overload candidates silently during template deduction.
`<type_traits>` provides compile-time type introspection for building adaptive zero-cost algorithms.

days.title: STL Sequence Containers: Memory & Complexity
days.subtitle: vector, deque, list, forward_list, array & contiguous vs node-based memory cache analysis
days.overview: Master the fundamental sequential containers of the Standard Template Library. Analyze their algorithmic complexity ($O(1)$ vs $O(N)$), iterator invalidation rules, memory topologies, and hardware cache performance.

topics.title: The STL Sequential Containers Taxonomy
explanation: The Standard Template Library partitions sequence containers into two primary memory topologies:
1. Contiguous Memory: `std::vector` (dynamic array), `std::array` (fixed stack array), `std::deque` (segmented chunks). Optimal CPU cache prefetching.
2. Node-Based Memory: `std::list` (doubly-linked list), `std::forward_list` (singly-linked list). Scattered heap allocations, high memory pointer overhead, poor cache locality.
keyRules: Default container of choice: std::vector.
Only use std::list if frequent insertions in the middle without iterator invalidation are required.

codeSnippet.title: Comparing Sequence Container Initializations
codeSnippet.description: Declaring and initializing contiguous vs node-based containers

topics.pitfall: Using `std::list` assuming it is faster for insertions; in reality, traversing a linked list is 10x-50x slower than `std::vector` due to CPU cache misses.

quickCheck.question: Which container should be the default choice in C++ for sequential collections?
quickCheck.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup and the C++ standard mandate `std::vector` as the default container due to CPU cache locality.

topics.title: `std::deque`: Segmented Dynamic Buffer Architecture
explanation: `std::deque` (Double-Ended Queue) provides $O(1)$ fast insertion and deletion at BOTH the front and back.
Unlike `std::vector`, a deque does NOT store elements in a single contiguous array. Instead, it manages a center index table of fixed-size chunks (e.g. 512-byte pages).
Inserting at the front or back never requires moving existing elements; it simply allocates a new chunk if the current chunk is full.
keyRules: push_front() and push_back() are both O(1).
Elements are indexed in O(1): deq[i] involves two pointer dereferences (index table + chunk).
Memory is not contiguous: cannot pass deq.data() to C APIs expecting a raw array.

codeSnippet.title: std::deque O(1) Push Front & Back
codeSnippet.description: Bi-directional insertion without full reallocation

topics.pitfall: Assuming deque elements are contiguous in memory; taking `&deq[0]` and incrementing the pointer will crash when crossing chunk boundaries.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of `push_front()` in `std::deque` versus `std::vector`?
options: std::deque is O(1); std::vector is O(N) because all elements must be shifted
quickCheck.explanation: deque allocates an independent front chunk in O(1), whereas vector must shift all N elements rightward.

topics.title: `std::list` & `std::forward_list`: Node Mechanics
explanation: `std::list` is a doubly-linked list (each node has `prev`, `next`, and payload). Each node requires 16 bytes of pointer overhead on 64-bit systems.
`std::forward_list` is a singly-linked list (each node has only `next` pointer). It has minimum memory overhead and no `.size()` method ($O(1)$ space, no size tracking).
Key Advantage: Inserting or splicing elements into any iterator position takes $O(1)$ pointer rewiring and NEVER invalidates iterators to other elements.
keyRules: Iterator stability: Pointers and references to list elements remain valid even after insertions/deletions elsewhere.
No random access: list[i] is NOT supported; traversing to index i takes O(N).

codeSnippet.title: std::list Splicing & Iterator Stability
codeSnippet.description: O(1) node splicing without element copying

topics.pitfall: Using `std::list` for small primitive elements (like `char` or `int`): a 4-byte `int` requires 24 bytes per node (600% memory bloat) due to 16-byte pointers and 8-byte alignment.

quickCheck.question: Does inserting an element into `std::list` invalidate iterators pointing to other existing elements?
options: No, iterators to other nodes remain completely valid
quickCheck.explanation: Node-based containers guarantee iterator stability; existing node memory addresses never change.

topics.title: Iterator Invalidation Rules Matrix
explanation: Iterator Invalidation is one of the most common causes of crashes in C++: an iterator becomes dangling when the container reallocates or shifts elements.
`std::vector`: Reallocation invalidates ALL iterators and references; insertion/deletion without reallocation invalidates iterators at or after the modification point.
`std::deque`: Insertion at ends invalidates iterators, but references to elements remain valid! Insertion in middle invalidates all.
`std::list`: Insertions and deletions NEVER invalidate iterators to other nodes.
keyRules: Modifying a vector during a loop invalidates your loop iterator.
Use the return value of vec.erase(it) to advance safely: it = vec.erase(it);.

codeSnippet.title: Safe Element Eradication Pattern (Erase-Remove)
codeSnippet.description: Safely deleting elements during container traversal

topics.pitfall: Calling `vec.erase(it); ++it;` increments an invalidated iterator, leading to an immediate segmentation fault.

quickCheck.question: What does `vector.erase(it)` return in C++?
options: An iterator pointing to the element immediately following the removed element
quickCheck.explanation: erase() returns an iterator to the new location of the element that followed the erased element.

topics.title: Cache Locality: Hardware Prefetching vs Pointer Chasing
explanation: Modern CPUs fetch memory into L1/L2/L3 caches in 64-byte Cache Lines.
`std::vector` stores elements sequentially. When the CPU loads element 0, it automatically prefetches elements 1 through 15 into L1 cache for free ($~1$ cycle access).

`std::list` scatters nodes across random heap addresses. Each node access requires waiting for a RAM access ($~200$ CPU cycles). In benchmarks, iterating over `std::vector` is up to 50x faster than `std::list`.
keyRules: Contiguous arrays are hardware-friendly; linked lists cause cache line misses.
Always favor cache-friendly structures over theoretically lower big-O pointer structures.

codeSnippet.title: Memory Cache Line Visualizer
codeSnippet.description: Contiguous 64-byte cache line layout vs fragmented pointer nodes
codeSnippet.code:
/*
  std::vector (Sequential Cache Line):
  [ 64-Byte L1 Cache Line: Int 0 | Int 1 | Int 2 | Int 3 | Int 4 ... ] -> 100% Cache Hits!

  std::list (Fragmented Heap Nodes):
  [Node @ 0x1A00] ------(200 cycle RAM miss)------> [Node @ 0x9B40] -> Cache Thrashing!
*/

topics.pitfall: Choosing linked lists based on theoretical $O(1)$ middle insertion when in practice finding the insertion point takes $O(N)$ slow cache-miss traversals.

quickCheck.question: Why is `std::vector` significantly faster than `std::list` in practice even when Big-O suggests equal or worse complexity?
options: Vector elements reside contiguously in memory, enabling CPU hardware cache prefetching
Vector is compiled by the operating system kernel
quickCheck.explanation: Contiguous memory allows the CPU cache prefetcher to load adjacent elements into L1 cache ahead of execution.

topics.title: Container Adapters: `std::stack`, `std::queue`, `std::priority_queue`
explanation: Container Adapters do not manage memory directly; they wrap an underlying sequence container and expose a restricted interface.
`std::stack` (LIFO): Defaults to wrapping `std::deque` (provides `push`, `pop`, `top`).
`std::queue` (FIFO): Defaults to wrapping `std::deque` (provides `push`, `pop`, `front`, `back`).
`std::priority_queue` (Max Heap): Defaults to wrapping `std::vector` (provides `push`, `pop`, `top` in $O(\log N)$ time).
keyRules: Container adapters do not expose iterators.
You can customize the underlying container: std::stack<int, std::vector<int>> st;

codeSnippet.title: Container Adapter Usage Patterns
codeSnippet.description: Stack and Queue adapter interfaces

topics.pitfall: Attempting to iterate over a `std::stack` with a range-based for loop fails compilation; adapters hide internal iterators by design.

quickCheck.question: What is the default underlying container used by `std::stack` and `std::queue`?
quickCheck.explanation: Both stack and queue default to `std::deque` because it avoids massive reallocations while supporting fast end operations.

topics.title: Modern `std::erase` & `std::erase_if` (C++20 Uniform Erasure)
explanation: Before C++20, removing elements from a vector required the awkward "Erase-Remove Idiom": `vec.erase(std::remove(vec.begin(), vec.end(), val), vec.end());`.
C++20 introduced unified free functions `std::erase(container, value)` and `std::erase_if(container, predicate)`.
Works uniformly across `std::vector`, `std::deque`, `std::list`, `std::string`, and associative containers.
keyRules: Use std::erase(vec, 42); to delete all instances of 42.
Use std::erase_if(vec, [](int x){ return x < 0; }); to delete matching elements.

codeSnippet.title: C++20 std::erase_if Clean Removal
codeSnippet.description: Eliminating the legacy erase-remove idiom with C++20 free functions

topics.pitfall: Calling `std::remove` without `vec.erase` leaves the vector at its original size with leftover garbage at the end.

quickCheck.question: What C++20 feature replaces the legacy Erase-Remove idiom (`vec.erase(std::remove(...), ...);`)?
quickCheck.explanation: C++20 added `std::erase` and `std::erase_if` free functions for uniform, intuitive element removal.

topics.title: Day 17 Capstone: High-Throughput Sliding Packet Window
explanation: Synthesizing Day 17 concepts into a Sliding Window packet buffer using `std::deque`.
Demonstrating fixed-capacity ring buffer mechanics, $O(1)$ front and back insertions, and cache-conscious stream management.
Standard architecture for network flow control and audio processing pipelines.
keyRules: Maintain window size by popping front when size exceeds threshold.
std::deque provides constant-time push_back and pop_front.

codeSnippet.title: Sliding Window Packet Stream Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Bounded FIFO window using std::deque

topics.pitfall: Using `std::vector` for a sliding window forces $O(N)$ element shifts on every `erase(begin())` call, destroying throughput.

quickCheck.question: Why is `std::deque` optimal for a sliding window buffer compared to `std::vector`?
options: `std::deque` supports $O(1)$ pop_front() without shifting existing elements
quickCheck.explanation: deque removes from the front in O(1) time, while vector requires shifting all N elements leftward.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 17 Capstone: Moving Average Calculator using std::deque
instructions: Implement a class `MovingAverage` with window size `N`.
Implement `double next(int val)` that inserts `val`, evicts if window exceeds `N`, and returns the current window average.
Test with a stream of 5 integers and print the moving averages.
hints: Maintain `m_runningSum` to achieve O(1) average calculation instead of looping.
Subtract `m_vals.front()` before popping.

keyTakeaways: `std::vector` is the default container due to contiguous memory and CPU cache locality.
`std::deque` provides $O(1)$ insertion at both front and back.
`std::list` provides iterator stability at the cost of heap fragmentation and cache misses.
C++20 `std::erase` and `std::erase_if` provide clean, unified element removal.

days.title: Associative & Hash Containers: Tree vs Hash Tables
days.subtitle: std::map / std::set (Red-Black Trees) vs std::unordered_map / unordered_set (Hash Tables)
days.overview: Compare ordered balanced binary trees with unordered hash tables in the STL. Learn algorithmic trade-offs (O(log N) vs O(1)), custom hash functions with std::hash, bucket load factors, and heterogeneous lookups.

topics.title: Ordered Containers (`std::map`, `std::set`): Red-Black Trees
explanation: `std::map<K, V>` and `std::set<K>` are implemented as Self-Balancing Binary Search Trees (specifically Red-Black Trees).
Guarantees strict $O(\log N)$ worst-case time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion.
Elements are ALWAYS maintained in strictly sorted order according to `operator<` or a custom comparator. In-order traversal visits keys in ascending order.
keyRules: Requires Key type to implement operator< (strict weak ordering).
Search, insert, and delete are strictly O(log N).
Elements are sorted; supports lower_bound() and upper_bound() range queries.

codeSnippet.title: std::map Sorted Ordering and Range Bounds
codeSnippet.description: Logarithmic search and ordered in-order iteration

topics.pitfall: Using bracket operator `map[key]` for search: if the key does not exist, `map[key]` default-constructs and inserts a new element into the map! Use `.find()` or `.contains()` instead.

quickCheck.question: What underlying data structure is used by `std::map` and `std::set` in the C++ standard library?
quickCheck.explanation: The C++ standard mandates logarithmic ordered guarantees, implemented via Red-Black Trees.

topics.title: Unordered Containers (`std::unordered_map`, `std::unordered_set`): Hash Tables
explanation: `std::unordered_map<K, V>` and `std::unordered_set<K>` are implemented as Hash Tables with separate chaining buckets.
Provides Average $O(1)$ constant time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion.
Elements are NOT sorted. Order depends on the hash function and bucket layout.
keyRules: Average time complexity: O(1). Worst case: O(N) during extreme hash collisions.
Requires Key type to support std::hash<K> and operator==.
Much faster than std::map for lookups when sorting is not required.

codeSnippet.title: std::unordered_map O(1) Fast Lookup
codeSnippet.description: Hash-based key-value lookups in constant time

topics.pitfall: Assuming `unordered_map` is always faster than `map`; for small collections (< 50 items), calculating hashes and allocating buckets can be slower than a simple flat array or tree.

quickCheck.question: What is the average time complexity of finding a key in `std::unordered_map`?
quickCheck.explanation: Hash tables achieve average O(1) lookup time via direct hash bucket indexing.

topics.title: Custom Hash Functions & `std::hash` Specialization
explanation: Primitive types and `std::string` have built-in `std::hash` implementations.
To use custom structs as keys in `std::unordered_map`, you MUST provide: (1) An equality comparison `operator==`; (2) A hash functor or `std::hash` template specialization.
Combine hash values using the boost hash_combine bit-mixing formula to minimize collisions.
keyRules: Formula: seed ^= hash(val) + 0x9e3779b9 + (seed << 6) + (seed >> 2);
operator== is mandatory for resolving hash bucket collisions.

codeSnippet.title: Specializing std::hash for Custom Structs
codeSnippet.description: Enabling custom types as unordered_map keys

topics.pitfall: Defining a hash function that returns the same constant integer for all objects degrades `unordered_map` performance to $O(N)$ linear search.

quickCheck.question: What two operations must a custom type support to be used as a key in `std::unordered_map`?
options: A hash function (std::hash<T>) and equality operator (operator==)
A copy constructor and destructor only
quickCheck.explanation: The hash table needs `std::hash` to pick a bucket, and `operator==` to check for equality inside that bucket.

topics.title: Bucket Layout, Load Factor & `rehash()`
explanation: `std::unordered_map` organizes elements into a dynamic array of "Buckets".
Load Factor = `size() / bucket_count()`. The default `max_load_factor()` is 1.0.

When the load factor exceeds 1.0, the container automatically performs a "Rehash": it allocates a larger array of buckets and re-hashes every existing element. Call `.reserve(N)` to avoid rehashing overhead in advance.
keyRules: Load factor > 1.0 triggers rehashing and re-indexing.
reserve(N) pre-allocates enough buckets to hold N elements without rehashing.

codeSnippet.title: Inspecting Buckets and Load Factors
codeSnippet.description: Monitoring hash table internals and rehash triggers

topics.pitfall: Frequent rehashing in real-time loops causes latency spikes; always call `map.reserve(expectedSize)` upfront.

quickCheck.question: What is the "Load Factor" of a hash table?
options: The ratio of elements to the number of allocated buckets (size / bucket_count)
The size of the keys in bytes
quickCheck.explanation: Load factor measures how full the hash table is by dividing element count by total buckets.

topics.title: Heterogeneous Lookup in Associative Containers (C++14 / C++20)
explanation: Historically, looking up a string literal in `std::map<std::string, int>` using `map.find("key")` constructed an expensive temporary `std::string` object on the heap!
C++14 added Heterogeneous Lookup for `std::map` using `std::less<>`.
C++20 expanded Heterogeneous Lookup to `std::unordered_map`: passing `std::string_view` searches the map directly without constructing a temporary `std::string`!
keyRules: std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>> enables transparent lookup.
Eliminates temporary string allocations during lookups.

codeSnippet.title: Zero-Allocation Heterogeneous Lookup
codeSnippet.description: Querying string maps with string_view without temporary allocations

topics.pitfall: Omitting `std::less<>` comparator falls back to `std::less<Key>`, which forces construction of a temporary `std::string` on every lookup.

quickCheck.question: What problem does Heterogeneous Lookup solve in C++ associative containers?
options: It eliminates creating temporary key objects (like std::string) during lookup with string_view or const char*
It allows storing multiple data types in the same map
quickCheck.explanation: Heterogeneous lookup allows searching using compatible types (like `std::string_view`) without allocating temporary key objects.

topics.title: `contains()` & `try_emplace()` in Modern C++
explanation: C++20 added `.contains(key)`: returns `bool`, replacing verbose `if (map.find(k) != map.end())`.
C++17 added `.try_emplace(key, args...)`: inserts only if the key does NOT already exist, constructing the value in-place without moving or copying if the key already exists.
Much safer and more efficient than `insert()` or `operator[]`.
keyRules: Use map.contains(key) for clean presence checks.
Use map.try_emplace(key, args) to avoid unnecessary value constructions.

codeSnippet.title: Modern map.contains() and try_emplace()
codeSnippet.description: Cleaner presence checks and efficient in-place insertion

topics.pitfall: Using `map[key] == value` to check if a key exists; this silently inserts a default element if the key is absent.

quickCheck.question: What method was added in C++20 to check if a key exists in a map without iterator boilerplate?
quickCheck.explanation: C++20 standardized `.contains(key)` across all associative and unordered associative containers.

topics.title: Multi-Containers: `std::multimap` & `std::multiset`
explanation: `std::multimap` and `std::multiset` permit duplicate keys.
Because keys are not unique, `operator[]` is NOT supported.
To retrieve all elements matching a duplicate key, use `.equal_range(key)` which returns a pair of iterators `[begin, end)` spanning all matching entries.
keyRules: Duplicate keys permitted.
Use auto [first, last] = mmap.equal_range(key) to iterate over duplicate matches.

codeSnippet.title: equal_range on std::multimap
codeSnippet.description: Handling duplicate keys in multi-containers

topics.pitfall: Calling `multimap.find(key)` only returns an iterator to the FIRST matching element, ignoring all subsequent duplicates.

quickCheck.question: What method retrieves all elements matching a key in a `std::multimap`?
quickCheck.explanation: equal_range(key) returns a std::pair of iterators covering all elements with the matching key.

topics.title: Day 18 Capstone: In-Memory Symbol Table with Fast Lookups
explanation: Synthesizing Day 18 concepts into a compiler Symbol Table using `std::unordered_map`.
Demonstrating custom structs, `try_emplace`, `contains`, and scope-level symbol resolution.
Forms the foundational core of compilers, interpreters, and database query planning engines.
keyRules: Fast O(1) identifier resolution.
Clean presence checking with .contains().

codeSnippet.title: Compiler Symbol Table Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Fast identifier lookup engine using modern unordered_map

topics.pitfall: Using `operator[]` on a const symbol table fails compilation; always use `.find()`.

quickCheck.question: Why is `std::unordered_map` preferred over `std::map` for compiler symbol tables?
options: Average O(1) lookup speed provides maximum compiler throughput for thousands of identifiers
Because symbol names cannot be sorted
quickCheck.explanation: Symbol tables perform massive volumes of lookups where average O(1) hash table speed is paramount.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 18 Capstone: Word Frequency Counter using std::unordered_map
instructions: Create a class `WordCounter` that accepts strings and tallies their frequencies.
Implement `void record(const std::string& word)` and `int getFrequency(const std::string& word) const`.
Ensure `getFrequency` does NOT insert default values for missing words.
hints: In `getFrequency`, use `m_counts.find(word)` instead of `m_counts[word]`.

keyTakeaways: `std::map` uses Red-Black Trees with guaranteed $O(\log N)$ sorted order.
`std::unordered_map` uses Hash Tables with average $O(1)$ constant lookup.
Never use `map[key]` for read-only inspection; use `.find()` or C++20 `.contains()`.
Heterogeneous lookup eliminates temporary key allocations when querying with `std::string_view`.

days.title: STL Algorithms (`<algorithm>`), Iterators & Lambdas
days.subtitle: The 5 iterator categories, std::sort, std::transform, std::accumulate & lambda predicates
days.overview: Master the algorithm engine of C++. Learn the 5 iterator categories, why raw for-loops are an anti-pattern in modern C++, standard algorithms (<algorithm>, <numeric>), custom lambda predicates, and execution policies for parallel sorting.

topics.title: The 5 Standard Iterator Categories
explanation: Iterators act as the glue connecting STL containers with STL algorithms.
1. Input Iterator: Read-once, single pass forward (e.g. `std::istream_iterator`).
2. Output Iterator: Write-once, single pass forward (e.g. `std::ostream_iterator`).
3. Forward Iterator: Multi-pass read/write forward (e.g. `std::forward_list`).
4. Bidirectional Iterator: Forward and backward traversal (`++`, `--`) (e.g. `std::list`, `std::map`, `std::set`).
5. Random Access Iterator: $O(1)$ pointer math, bracket indexing (`+`, `-`, `[]`, `<`) (e.g. `std::vector`, `std::array`, `std::deque`, raw pointers).
keyRules: std::sort requires Random Access Iterators (cannot sort std::list directly; use list.sort()).
Half-open ranges [first, last) encompass elements from first up to (excluding) last.

codeSnippet.title: Iterator Category Requirements
codeSnippet.description: Why std::sort requires Random Access Iterators

topics.pitfall: Passing non-random-access iterators (like `std::list::begin()`) to `std::sort` generates pages of template compilation errors; use container member sort instead.

quickCheck.question: What iterator category is required by `std::sort`?
quickCheck.explanation: std::sort uses Introsort (QuickSort + HeapSort), requiring O(1) random access jumps between elements.

topics.title: `std::sort` & Custom Lambda Comparators
explanation: `std::sort` is implemented as Introsort (a hybrid of QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort) with guaranteed $O(N \log N)$ worst-case time complexity.
By default, it sorts in ascending order using `operator<`.
You can supply custom comparator lambdas: `[](const auto& a, const auto& b) { return a.score > b.score; }` for descending or multi-field sorting.
keyRules: Comparators must implement Strict Weak Ordering (if a < b is true, b < a must be false; a < a must be false).
Using <= in a comparator violates strict weak ordering and can cause memory corruption or infinite loops.

codeSnippet.title: Custom Sorting with Lambdas
codeSnippet.description: Sorting custom objects by multiple criteria using std::sort

topics.pitfall: Writing `return a <= b;` instead of `return a < b;` in a comparator triggers undefined behavior in `std::sort` because `a < a` must strictly evaluate to false.

quickCheck.question: Why must comparator functions in `std::sort` use `<` (strict weak ordering) instead of `<=`?
options: Because `a < a` must evaluate to false; returning true for equal elements causes buffer out-of-bounds in QuickSort
quickCheck.explanation: Strict weak ordering mandates irreflexivity (x < x is always false); violating this causes QuickSort partitioning to overrun array bounds.

topics.title: Transformation Pipelines: `std::transform`
explanation: `std::transform` applies a transformation function to each element in a range and writes the result to an output iterator.
Can transform in-place (`vec.begin()` as destination) or write to an entirely different container using `std::back_inserter`.
Also supports binary transformation taking two input ranges and combining them.
keyRules: std::back_inserter(dest) calls push_back() automatically, resizing dest as needed.
Transforming in-place is highly cache-efficient.

codeSnippet.title: std::transform with std::back_inserter
codeSnippet.description: Functional mapping of ranges to new containers

topics.pitfall: Passing an empty destination vector without `std::back_inserter` causes out-of-bounds memory writes because `std::transform` does not allocate space on its own.

quickCheck.question: What iterator adapter allows `std::transform` to write into an empty vector by calling `push_back()` automatically?
quickCheck.explanation: `std::back_inserter` returns an output iterator whose operator= calls `push_back()` on the container.

topics.title: Reduction & Numeric Operations: `std::accumulate` & `std::reduce`
explanation: Found in header `<numeric>`.
`std::accumulate(begin, end, initVal, op)` folds a sequence into a single scalar value (e.g. summing elements, computing products, string concatenation).
C++17 introduced `std::reduce`: Unlike `accumulate` which is strictly sequential left-to-right, `reduce` is associative and can execute out-of-order in parallel across CPU cores!
keyRules: std::accumulate requires #include <numeric>.
Always match initVal type to desired output type: 0.0 for double, 0 for int, 0ULL for uint64_t.

codeSnippet.title: Fold Reductions with std::accumulate
codeSnippet.description: Summing and aggregating containers with custom operations

topics.pitfall: Passing an integer literal `0` as the initial value when summing floating-point numbers: `std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` truncates all intermediate results to `int`! Pass `0.0` instead.

quickCheck.question: What header file must be included to use `std::accumulate` and `std::reduce`?
quickCheck.explanation: <numeric> contains mathematical and reduction algorithms including accumulate, reduce, and iota.

topics.title: Searching Algorithms: `find_if`, `all_of`, `any_of`, `none_of`
explanation: Replace manual for-loops with expressive standard boolean search algorithms.
`std::find_if`: Returns iterator to first element matching predicate (or `end()` if none).
`std::all_of`: Returns `true` if ALL elements satisfy predicate.
`std::any_of`: Returns `true` if AT LEAST ONE element satisfies predicate.
`std::none_of`: Returns `true` if NO elements satisfy predicate.
keyRules: Short-circuiting: any_of stops scanning as soon as the first true is encountered.
Clean functional declarations eliminate nested loop bugs.

codeSnippet.title: Predicate Search Algorithms
codeSnippet.description: Declarative queries across collections

topics.pitfall: Calling `std::find_if` on empty containers returns `end()`; forgetting to check `it != vec.end()` before dereferencing causes crashes.

quickCheck.question: What does `std::any_of` return if an empty container is passed?
quickCheck.explanation: If a container is empty, there are no elements that satisfy the condition, so `any_of` returns `false`.

topics.title: Binary Search: `std::lower_bound`, `std::upper_bound` & `binary_search`
explanation: To search in $O(\log N)$ time across contiguous vectors, the container MUST be sorted in advance.
`std::binary_search`: Returns `bool` (true if element exists).
`std::lower_bound`: Returns iterator to the first element that is NOT LESS than value (>= value).
`std::upper_bound`: Returns iterator to the first element strictly GREATER than value (> value).
keyRules: The range must be sorted in advance; calling binary search on an unsorted range is undefined behavior.
lower_bound and upper_bound identify exact insertion ranges in O(log N).

codeSnippet.title: Logarithmic Binary Search Ranges
codeSnippet.description: lower_bound and upper_bound range queries on sorted vectors

topics.pitfall: Calling `std::lower_bound` on an unsorted vector produces invalid results or infinite loops.

quickCheck.question: What does `std::lower_bound(begin, end, val)` return on a sorted range?
options: An iterator to the first element that is greater than or equal to val (>= val)
An iterator to the element strictly less than val
quickCheck.explanation: `lower_bound` finds the first element not less than `val` (i.e. `>= val`).

topics.title: Parallel Algorithms with Execution Policies (C++17)
explanation: C++17 introduced multi-core Parallel Algorithms in `<execution>`.
Pass an Execution Policy as the first argument to over 60 standard algorithms:
1. `std::execution::seq`: Sequential single-threaded execution.
2. `std::execution::par`: Multi-threaded parallel execution across available CPU cores.
3. `std::execution::par_unseq`: Parallel and SIMD vectorized execution.
keyRules: Include <execution>. Requires linking with Intel TBB or GCC libgomp on Linux (-ltbb).
Predicates and lambdas must be thread-safe with no shared mutable state.

codeSnippet.title: C++17 Multi-Core Parallel Sorting
codeSnippet.description: Sorting 10,000,000 elements across all CPU threads

topics.pitfall: Using parallel execution policies on small collections introduces thread pool dispatch overhead that is slower than single-threaded execution.

quickCheck.question: What execution policy in C++17 enables parallel multi-threaded sorting?
quickCheck.explanation: `std::execution::par` directs the algorithm to execute in parallel across available CPU threads.

topics.title: Day 19 Capstone: High-Speed Analytical Telemetry Pipeline
explanation: Synthesizing Day 19 algorithms into an industrial telemetry data analytics pipeline.
Demonstrating `std::sort`, `std::transform`, `std::accumulate`, `std::copy_if`, and lambda predicates.
Zero raw loops; clean, expressive, composable data transformations.
keyRules: Express complex business logic via composable STL algorithm pipelines.
Avoid raw loops for standard filtering, mapping, and reducing tasks.

codeSnippet.title: Telemetry Analytics Pipeline Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Composing algorithms for filtering and statistical analysis

topics.pitfall: Re-inventing sorting and searching with hand-written nested loops introduces edge-case index bugs.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary architectural philosophy regarding raw loops in modern C++?
options: Replace raw loops with named, well-tested STL algorithms (e.g. std::transform, std::accumulate)
Always use while loops instead of for loops
Loops must run on the GPU
quickCheck.explanation: Replacing raw loops with STL algorithms improves readability, eliminates off-by-one errors, and enables parallel optimization.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 19 Capstone: In-Place Range Normalization Pipeline
instructions: Given a `std::vector<double>` of sensor readings, find the maximum value using `std::max_element`.
Use `std::transform` to normalize all elements in-place to the range `[0.0, 1.0]` by dividing by the maximum value.
Print the normalized vector.
hints: Use `*std::max_element(readings.begin(), readings.end())` to find the maximum.
Pass `readings.begin()` as both source and destination to `std::transform` for in-place mutation.

keyTakeaways: `std::sort` requires Random Access Iterators and Strict Weak Ordering.
Use `std::transform` with `std::back_inserter` for functional mapping.
`std::accumulate` (in `<numeric>`) folds ranges into aggregated scalar metrics.
Binary search functions (`lower_bound`/`upper_bound`) provide fast $O(\log N)$ range lookups.

days.title: Modern C++20: Concepts, Ranges & Modules
days.subtitle: Type constraints with concept & requires, composable std::views pipelines, and C++20 Modules
days.overview: Explore the biggest modern evolution of C++: C++20. Master Concepts to replace SFINAE with readable compile-time constraints, composable lazy evaluation pipelines with Ranges (std::views), and C++20 Modules eliminating legacy header includes.

topics.title: C++20 Concepts: Readable Compile-Time Type Constraints
explanation: Historically, template errors produced hundreds of lines of impenetrable compiler diagnostics when a type lacked a required method.
C++20 Concepts define named compile-time requirements on template parameters: `template <std::integral T> void process(T val);`.
If a caller passes an incompatible type (e.g. `double` to an `integral` concept), the compiler emits a single clean 1-line error: "constraints not satisfied: type is not integral".
keyRules: Use standard concepts from <concepts>: std::integral, std::floating_point, std::copyable.
Significantly improves compiler error readability and code documentation.

codeSnippet.title: Constraining Templates with C++20 Concepts
codeSnippet.description: Enforcing type constraints using standard concepts

topics.pitfall: Writing unconstrained templates (`template <typename T>`) allows completely invalid types into functions, producing confusing error messages deep in internal code.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of C++20 Concepts?
options: Clear compile-time error messages and explicit template requirements
They convert C++ code to Python
They allocate memory in the cloud
quickCheck.explanation: Concepts explicitly validate template arguments at compile time, turning pages of compiler errors into a single readable message.

topics.title: Defining Custom Concepts with `concept` and `requires`
explanation: You can define your own domain-specific concepts using the `concept` keyword and `requires` expressions.
A requires expression tests syntactic validity: does the type have a `.serialize()` method? Does `a + b` return a type convertible to `int`?
Syntax: `template <typename T> concept Serializable = requires(T a) { a.serialize(); };`.
keyRules: template <typename T> concept Name = requires(T x) { ... };
Can enforce method existence, nested types, and return type constraints.

codeSnippet.title: Custom Concept Definition
codeSnippet.description: Creating custom concept to enforce serialization interface

topics.pitfall: Expecting `requires` expressions to execute at runtime; requires expressions are strictly unevaluated compile-time syntax tests.

quickCheck.question: What keyword defines a compile-time concept in C++20?
quickCheck.explanation: C++20 introduced the `concept` keyword for defining named template type requirements.

topics.title: Abbreviated Function Templates with `auto` Parameters
explanation: C++20 allows using concepts directly with `auto` in function parameter lists.
Instead of writing `template <std::integral T> void f(T x)`, you can write simply: `void f(std::integral auto x)`.
Provides ultra-clean, terse syntax while retaining full compile-time template safety.
keyRules: void f(auto x); is an unconstrained template.
void f(std::integral auto x); is a constrained template.

codeSnippet.title: Abbreviated Function Templates (C++20)
codeSnippet.description: Constrained auto parameters in function signatures

topics.pitfall: Assuming `void f(auto x)` is a regular non-template function; it is actually a template that will be instantiated separately for each argument type.

quickCheck.question: What is `void print(std::integral auto x)` in C++20?
options: An abbreviated function template constrained to integral types
quickCheck.explanation: Using `auto` with a concept in a parameter list creates an abbreviated function template.

topics.title: C++20 Ranges & Composable Views (`std::views`)
explanation: Historically, STL algorithms required passing two iterators (`vec.begin(), vec.end()`) and could not be piped together.
C++20 Ranges allow passing the container directly: `std::ranges::sort(vec);`.
Even more powerful are `std::views`: lightweight, lazy-evaluated transformations piped together using the Unix pipe operator `|` (`vec | std::views::filter(...) | std::views::transform(...)`).
keyRules: Views are lazy: no computation happens until you iterate over the result.
Zero heap allocations: views are non-owning slices and adaptors.

codeSnippet.title: C++20 Ranges and Pipe Operator Views
codeSnippet.description: Composable lazy data pipelines using std::views and pipe |

topics.pitfall: Storing a view that references a temporary container: `auto v = getVector() | std::views::filter(...);` leaves `v` holding dangling references after `getVector()` temporary is destroyed.

quickCheck.question: When do operations inside a `std::views` pipeline execute?
options: Lazily on-demand as elements are iterated over
Immediately when the pipe expression is evaluated
quickCheck.explanation: Ranges views are lazy; calculations occur on-the-fly as iterators advance through the sequence.

topics.title: C++20 Modules: Replacing Legacy `#include`
explanation: For 40 years, C++ relied on textual `#include` preprocessor copying, leading to hours of redundant header parsing in large codebases.
C++20 Modules introduce compiled module interfaces (`import std;` or `import MyModule;`).
Modules are parsed ONCE into a binary AST format. They eliminate macro leakage, enforce boundary encapsulation, and speed up project compilation times by up to 10x.
keyRules: export module ModuleName; declares a module.
export void func(); marks a function visible to importers.
import ModuleName; loads precompiled module interface without macro pollution.

codeSnippet.title: C++20 Module Definition & Import Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Defining and importing compiled modules

topics.pitfall: Macros defined inside a module do NOT leak into importing files; if you rely on macro injection from headers, modules will intentionally isolate them.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary advantage of C++20 Modules over legacy `#include`?
options: Modules are compiled once into binary interfaces, drastically accelerating compile times and isolating macros
Modules eliminate the need for a compiler
Modules run in web browsers natively
quickCheck.explanation: Modules eliminate textual preprocessor copying, boosting compilation speed and preventing macro leaks.

topics.title: C++20 Coroutines: Stackless Asynchronous Generators
explanation: C++20 added native language support for Stackless Coroutines: functions that can suspend execution and resume later while preserving their local state.
Three new keywords: `co_await` (suspends until an awaitable completes), `co_yield` (suspends and emits a generator value), `co_return` (completes execution).
Extensively used for lazy sequence generators, asynchronous I/O event loops, and non-blocking network servers.
keyRules: Any function containing co_yield, co_await, or co_return is a coroutine.
Coroutines allocate a small coroutine frame on the heap to store local state across suspensions.

codeSnippet.title: Coroutine Generator Concept (C++20)
codeSnippet.description: Generating infinite sequences on-demand via co_yield

topics.pitfall: Passing references to local temporary objects into a coroutine: when the coroutine suspends and resumes later, the temporary is gone, resulting in dangling references.

quickCheck.question: Which C++20 keyword suspends a coroutine and emits a value to the caller?
quickCheck.explanation: `co_yield` pauses the coroutine and returns a generated element to the consumer.

topics.title: `std::format` & `std::print` (C++20 / C++23 Modern Formatting)
explanation: C++ historically had two formatting options: safe but slow/verbose iostreams (`std::cout << ...`), or fast but type-unsafe and vulnerability-prone C `printf`.
C++20 introduced `std::format` (based on the popular `{fmt}` library): Python-like curly brace formatting (`"{}"`) with full compile-time format string validation and extreme speed.
C++23 introduced `std::print` and `std::println`, allowing direct formatted printing to stdout without intermediate string allocations.
keyRules: std::format("{} has {} points", name, score);
Full compile-time validation: mismatched argument counts or types fail compilation.

codeSnippet.title: Modern std::format Syntax
codeSnippet.description: Typesafe Python-like string interpolation in C++20

topics.pitfall: Using `printf` with mismatched specifiers (e.g. `%d` with `int64_t`) causes stack corruption; `std::format` prevents this at compile time.

quickCheck.question: What is the advantage of `std::format` over `printf`?
options: It is completely typesafe and validates format strings at compile time
quickCheck.explanation: `std::format` combines the speed of printf with complete C++ type safety and compile-time format string checking.

topics.title: Day 20 Capstone: Ranges-Based Data Transformation Engine
explanation: Synthesizing Day 20 Concepts and Ranges into a clean stream processing engine.
Demonstrating custom Concepts, constrained auto parameters, and piped lazy `std::views`.
Showcases the apex of modern expressive, zero-cost C++20 software engineering.
keyRules: Enforce data constraints with concepts.
Pipe stream transformations lazily using std::views.

codeSnippet.title: Modern C++20 Stream Processing Pipeline
codeSnippet.description: Composing concepts and ranges for financial transaction filtering

topics.pitfall: Materializing lazy ranges prematurely using loops when you only need to pass them to standard algorithms.

quickCheck.question: What does the pipe operator `|` accomplish when used with `std::views` in C++20?
options: It composes lazy range transformations into a single readable processing pipeline
It performs a bitwise OR on all integers
It pipes output to the Linux shell
quickCheck.explanation: The pipe operator `|` composes range adaptors into functional, lazy data transformation pipelines.

practiceChallenge.title: Day 20 Capstone: Constrained Generic Math Library with Concepts
instructions: Define a custom concept `Numeric` that accepts any type satisfying `std::integral` or `std::floating_point`.
Implement a function `Numeric auto clampValue(Numeric auto val, Numeric auto minVal, Numeric auto maxVal)` that clamps `val` between `minVal` and `maxVal`.
Test it with both integer and floating-point inputs.
hints: Use `std::integral<T> || std::floating_point<T>` in the concept definition.
Constrain the function with `template <Numeric T>`.

keyTakeaways: C++20 Concepts turn cryptic template errors into clear, single-line compile diagnostics.
`std::views` pipelines provide lazy, allocation-free data manipulation via the `|` pipe operator.
Modules eliminate textual `#include` overhead, vastly accelerating compile times.
C++20 coroutines enable stackless asynchronous generators and cooperative multitasking.

days.title: Week 3 Capstone: Generic Thread-Safe LRU Cache & Exam
days.subtitle: Combining templates, list, unordered_map, mutex locking & Module 3 qualifying exam
days.overview: Synthesize all of Week 3 into the classic systems architecture component: a Generic Thread-Safe LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache. Combine templates, std::list, std::unordered_map, RAII mutex locks, and pass the Week 3 Qualifying Exam.

topics.title: LRU Cache Algorithmic Architecture
explanation: An LRU Cache requires two core guarantees:
1. $O(1)$ fast lookup of cached values by key.
2. $O(1)$ eviction of the least recently accessed item when capacity is exceeded.
To achieve both, we pair a `std::unordered_map` (for $O(1)$ key lookup) with a `std::list` (for $O(1)$ node splicing and order maintenance).
keyRules: std::unordered_map stores Key -> list::iterator.
std::list stores std::pair<Key, Value> in most-recent to least-recent order.

codeSnippet.title: LRU Cache Dual Data Structure Layout
codeSnippet.description: Coupling hash map with doubly linked list for O(1) performance
codeSnippet.code:
/*
  [std::unordered_map: Key -> ListIterator]
         |                  |
         v                  v
  [std::list:  (Key1, Val1) <-> (Key2, Val2) <-> (Key3, Val3) ]
               ^                                  ^
          Most Recent                         Least Recent (Eviction candidate!)
*/

topics.pitfall: Storing raw values in the list without the key makes it impossible to delete the key from the hash map when evicting from the back of the list.

quickCheck.question: Why does an LRU Cache store both Key and Value inside the doubly linked list nodes?
options: So that when the oldest node is evicted from the list, its key can be erased from the hash map in O(1)
quickCheck.explanation: When evicting the tail of the list, the cache must look up that node's key to remove it from the hash table.

topics.title: The O(1) Splice Operation in LRU Caching
explanation: When a cached item is accessed, it must move to the front of the list to become the most recently used.
In an array, moving an item to the front takes $O(N)$ shifts.
In `std::list`, the member function `m_list.splice(m_list.begin(), m_list, it)` unlinks and relinks the node in $O(1)$ time WITHOUT reallocating or copying!
keyRules: m_list.splice(dest, m_list, srcIt) is O(1) pointer relinking.
Iterator stability guarantees m_map iterators remain completely valid.

codeSnippet.title: O(1) Node Splicing on Access
codeSnippet.description: Relinking nodes to front without element copying

topics.pitfall: Erasing and re-inserting nodes instead of splicing allocates and deallocates heap nodes on every single cache read.

quickCheck.question: What method on `std::list` moves an existing node to a new position in $O(1)$ time without reallocation?
quickCheck.explanation: `splice()` unhooks and re-inserts nodes into another position in O(1) time without allocating or copying.

topics.title: Thread Safety with `std::mutex` & `std::lock_guard`
explanation: Caches in production servers are accessed concurrently by multiple worker threads.
Concurrent reads and writes to `std::unordered_map` or `std::list` without synchronization trigger race conditions, memory corruption, and crashes.
We protect all cache operations using a private `mutable std::mutex m_mutex;` and lock it via `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m_mutex);` in every public method.
keyRules: Mark the mutex mutable so const methods (like get() or size()) can lock it.
Use std::lock_guard for exception-safe scoped locking.

codeSnippet.title: Thread-Safe Scoped Locking Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Protecting concurrent cache access with mutable mutex

topics.pitfall: Forgetting `mutable` on `m_mutex` prevents calling `get()` or inspection methods on const cache references.

quickCheck.question: Why should a mutex in a class be declared with the `mutable` specifier?
options: To allow it to be locked and unlocked inside const member functions
quickCheck.explanation: `mutable` allows a member variable to be modified inside `const` methods, which is necessary because locking modifies the mutex state.

topics.title: Implementing the Complete `LRUCache<Key, Value>` Class
explanation: Bringing all components together into the production generic class template:
- Template parameters: `typename Key`, `typename Value`.
- `std::optional<Value> get(const Key& key)`: Looks up key, splices node to front, returns value.
- `void put(const Key& key, const Value& val)`: Inserts or updates; evicts LRU tail if capacity is exceeded.
- Full thread safety via `mutable std::mutex`.
keyRules: Return std::optional<Value> from get() to handle missing keys cleanly.
Eviction pops list.back() and erases corresponding entry from m_map.

codeSnippet.title: Production Generic Thread-Safe LRU Cache Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Complete O(1) thread-safe LRU Cache implementation in C++

topics.pitfall: Returning a raw reference `Value&` from `get()` in a multithreaded cache: another thread could evict the item, leaving the caller holding a dangling reference.

quickCheck.question: Why should `get()` return `std::optional<Value>` instead of a raw reference `Value&` in a multithreaded cache?
options: Because another thread could evict the item, making a reference dangling; returning by value (optional) is thread-safe
Because references are illegal in C++
To speed up CPU clock speed
quickCheck.explanation: Returning by value via `std::optional` guarantees the caller owns a safe copy that will not be invalidated if another thread evicts the item.

topics.title: `std::optional<T>`: Expressing Nullable Return Values
explanation: Before C++17, functions that might fail to return a value used output parameters with boolean return codes, or magic sentinel values like `-1` or `nullptr`.
`std::optional<T>` represents an object that may or may not contain a valid value.
Provides `.has_value()`, `operator bool()`, dereference `*opt`, and `.value_or(fallback)` for expressive, safe access.
keyRules: Zero heap allocations: std::optional stores T inline on the stack with a boolean flag.
opt.value_or(defaultVal) returns the contained value or fallback.

codeSnippet.title: std::optional Return Pattern
codeSnippet.description: Safe nullable returns without pointers or sentinels

topics.pitfall: Calling `*opt` or `opt.value()` when `opt.has_value() == false`: `*opt` is undefined behavior, while `opt.value()` throws `std::bad_optional_access`.

quickCheck.question: Does `std::optional<int>` allocate heap memory?
options: No, it stores the integer inline with a boolean presence flag on the stack
quickCheck.explanation: std::optional stores its value inline on the stack with zero dynamic heap allocation overhead.

topics.title: `std::variant<Ts...>`: Typesafe Tagged Unions
explanation: C-style unions (`union { int i; float f; }`) are type-unsafe: accessing the wrong member causes memory corruption.
C++17 `std::variant<Ts...>` is a typesafe tagged union. It knows which type is currently active and calls proper constructors and destructors.
Use `std::holds_alternative<T>(var)` to check active type, and `std::visit(visitor, var)` for pattern matching across types.
keyRules: Typesafe tagged union with zero dynamic heap allocation.
std::visit enables functional pattern matching over variants.

codeSnippet.title: std::variant and std::visit Pattern Matching
codeSnippet.description: Typesafe union handling integers, strings, and floats

topics.pitfall: Calling `std::get<T>(v)` when `v` holds a different type throws `std::bad_variant_access`.

quickCheck.question: What C++17 feature provides a typesafe tagged union with automatic destructor management?
quickCheck.explanation: `std::variant` is a typesafe union that manages object lifecycles and provides pattern matching via `std::visit`.

topics.title: Week 3 Synthesis & Generic Architecture Review
explanation: Consolidating all Week 3 milestones:
1. Templates & CTAD: Blueprints, compile-time instantiation, and class template argument deduction.

5. Algorithms & Lambdas: Composable data pipelines with `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>`.
6. Modern C++20: Concepts for explicit type constraints and Ranges for piped lazy evaluation.
keyRules: Prefer compile-time constraints and algorithms over runtime manual loops.
Use standard vocabulary types: std::optional, std::variant, std::string_view.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary architectural advantage of generic programming in C++?
options: Zero-cost abstractions: maximum reusability with zero runtime penalty compared to hand-written code
quickCheck.explanation: Templates generate optimized, inlined machine code tailored to exact types with zero runtime abstraction penalty.

instructions: Implement an `LRUCache` class with capacity 2.

questions.question: Why does C++17 `if constexpr` succeed where a traditional `if` statement fails when compiling code for different types?
options: The compiler evaluates the condition at compile time and completely discards the untaken branch without instantiating it
It converts all variables to strings

questions.question: What is the algorithmic time complexity of searching in `std::map` versus `std::unordered_map`?
options: std::map is O(log N) (Red-Black Tree); std::unordered_map is average O(1) (Hash Table)
std::map is O(1); std::unordered_map is O(log N)

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of C++20 Concepts over legacy SFINAE / std::enable_if?
options: Readable, explicit compile-time type constraints with clean single-line error messages
They eliminate the need for templates
They make functions execute in the kernel
questions.explanation: Concepts replace complex SFINAE boilerplate with explicit type requirements and concise error messages.

questions.question: What occurs when you access a non-existent key using bracket indexing `map[key]` on `std::map` or `std::unordered_map`?

days.title: Threads, Lifecycle & std::jthread (C++20)
days.subtitle: OS thread creation, RAII join wrappers, cooperative cancellation tokens & thread affinity
days.overview: Explore thread execution models in modern C++. Understand OS kernel threads, joining vs detaching hazards, C++20 std::jthread with auto-joining and stop tokens, thread-local storage, and passing references across execution contexts.

topics.title: The OS Thread Model and std::thread Internals
explanation: A `std::thread` is a handle to an OS kernel execution context (such as a POSIX pthread on Linux or a Win32 thread on Windows).
When constructed, the OS allocates a separate execution stack (typically 2MB to 8MB) and schedules the instruction pointer independently across available CPU cores.
C++ threads execute concurrently with the calling thread. The C++ runtime abstracts platform differences, but you must respect OS hardware limits.
keyRules: Each thread allocates its own execution call stack.
Spawning thousands of threads wastes gigabytes of memory and introduces heavy OS context-switching overhead.

codeSnippet.title: Spawning a Native Thread
codeSnippet.description: Creating an independent execution thread

topics.pitfall: Constructing a thread and letting it go out of scope without calling join() or detach() causes std::terminate() and an immediate program crash.

quickCheck.question: What happens if a std::thread object is destroyed while still joinable?
options: It automatically joins in the destructor
The thread is forcibly killed by the OS
std::terminate is called, crashing the program
It becomes a background daemon thread
quickCheck.explanation: In C++11/14/17, std::~thread() checks if joinable(). If true, it invokes std::terminate() immediately to prevent undefined behavior.

topics.title: Join vs Detach: Thread Lifecycle Hazards
explanation: `join()` blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes execution and releases OS resources.
`detach()` disassociates the thread handle from the underlying OS thread, allowing the thread to run independently in the background ("daemon thread").
Detached threads are dangerous: if `main()` exits, the entire process terminates immediately, abruptly killing any active detached threads without running destructors.
