questions.question: Why does C++20 std::jthread eliminate the fatal crash hazard inherent in std::thread?
options: It runs on the GPU instead of CPU
Its destructor automatically requests cancellation and calls join(), preventing std::terminate
It disables all exceptions in the application
It replaces threads with coroutines automatically
questions.explanation: std::jthread incorporates RAII into thread lifetime: if joinable upon destruction, it signals its stop_token and invokes join(), preventing the std::terminate call that std::~thread triggers.

questions.question: When synchronizing access to a shared resource between multiple reader threads and infrequent writer threads, which primitive delivers the highest concurrent read throughput?
options: std::shared_mutex with std::shared_lock for readers and std::unique_lock for writers
A busy-wait while loop with sleep_for
questions.explanation: std::shared_mutex permits unlimited simultaneous readers holding std::shared_lock, while giving exclusive access to writers holding std::unique_lock.

questions.question: What is False Sharing in multi-threaded C++ applications?
options: Multiple threads concurrently writing to separate variables that reside on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, causing constant cache invalidation
An invalid file descriptor in POSIX
questions.explanation: False sharing occurs when independent variables accessed by different threads map to the same CPU cache line (usually 64 bytes), resulting in severe performance degradation as cores invalidate each others caches.

questions.question: Why is AddressSanitizer (ASan) dramatically superior to manual debugging for memory defects?
options: It automatically fixes your code syntax
It instruments memory operations to catch buffer overflows, use-after-free, and leaks with low (~2x) CPU overhead and precise stack traces
It converts C++ code into Rust automatically
It only runs at compile time
questions.explanation: AddressSanitizer uses compiler instrumentation and shadow memory to detect buffer overruns, use-after-free, and leaks at runtime with detailed diagnostics and minimal runtime overhead.

questions.question: In a production Worker Thread Pool, why must worker threads release the queue lock BEFORE invoking task()?
options: The C++ language forbids executing functions inside lock scopes
Releasing the lock allows other worker threads to simultaneously pop work from the queue while the task is executing
Tasks can only be called from static member functions
The operating system will terminate any thread that executes a task while holding a lock
questions.explanation: If a worker thread kept the queue locked while running task(), no other worker could access the queue, serializing all task execution and defeating the purpose of a multi-threaded pool.

days.title: Asymptotic Analysis & Mathematical Big-O Foundations
days.subtitle: Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta, space vs time complexity, recursion trees & Master Theorem
days.overview: Transition from naive code execution to rigorous asymptotic reasoning. Master Big-O upper bounds, Omega lower bounds, Theta tight bounds, amortized runtime, auxiliary space analysis, and recurrence relations.

topics.title: The Language of Growth: Why Constant Factors Disappear
explanation: Asymptotic analysis evaluates how an algorithm runtime or memory scales as input size $N$ approaches infinity ($N \to \infty$).
We ignore machine-specific constants (CPU clock speed, compiler flags) because as $N$ grows from 1,000 to 1,000,000, the growth rate dominates the constant multipliers.
An $O(N)$ algorithm will always beat an $O(N^2)$ algorithm for sufficiently large $N$, even if the $O(N)$ algorithm has a constant factor of 100.
keyRules: Drop low-order terms: $3N^2 + 50N + 1000 \implies O(N^2)$.
Drop constant coefficients: $1000N \implies O(N)$.

codeSnippet.title: Growth Rates Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Comparing linear growth vs quadratic growth as N increases
codeSnippet.code:
# Comparing step counts between O(N) and O(N^2)
def compare_growth(n: int):
    linear_steps = n
    quadratic_steps = n * n
    ratio = quadratic_steps / linear_steps
    print(f"N = {n:,} -> Linear: {linear_steps:,} ops | Quad: {quadratic_steps:,} ops | Ratio: {ratio:.0f}x")

for n in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    compare_growth(n)

topics.pitfall: Assuming an O(N) algorithm is always faster than O(N^2) for tiny inputs (e.g., N=3): constant factors do matter for tiny N, but algorithms are designed for scaling.

quickCheck.question: What is the asymptotic Big-O classification of f(N) = 7N^3 + 150N^2 + 9999N + 42?
quickCheck.explanation: In asymptotic analysis, we drop non-dominant lower terms and multiplicative constants, leaving the highest-order term O(N^3).

topics.title: Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ)
explanation: - $O(g(N))$: Upper bound (asymptotic worst-case growth). $f(N) \le c \cdot g(N)$ for large $N$.
- $\Omega(g(N))$: Lower bound (asymptotic best-case growth). $f(N) \ge c \cdot g(N)$ for large $N$.
- $\Theta(g(N))$: Tight bound. $f(N)$ is bounded both above and below by $g(N)$.
In software engineering interviews, people colloquially say "Big-O", but they usually seek the tightest bound $\Theta(N)$.
keyRules: Big-O is an upper bound: saying linear search is O(N^3) is mathematically true, but not informative. Always provide the tightest upper bound.
Theta represents both upper and lower bounds simultaneously.

codeSnippet.title: Best, Worst, and Average Cases
codeSnippet.description: Linear search demonstrating distinct case complexities
codeSnippet.code:
def linear_search(arr: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    # Best Case: target at arr[0] -> Omega(1)
    # Worst Case: target at end or absent -> O(N)
    # Average Case: target at N/2 -> Theta(N)
    for idx, val in enumerate(arr):
        if val == target:
            return idx
    return -1

nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print("Best Case index:", linear_search(nums, 10))  # 1 operation
print("Worst Case index:", linear_search(nums, 99)) # 5 operations

topics.pitfall: Confusing "Worst Case" with "Big-O": Big-O is an upper bound for any function, while worst-case is the input scenario that requires the most steps.

quickCheck.question: What is the best-case time complexity of linear search on an array of size N?
quickCheck.explanation: If the target element is at index 0, linear search completes in exactly 1 operation, which is Omega(1).

topics.title: Space Complexity: Auxiliary Space vs Input Space
explanation: Total Space Complexity = Input Space + Auxiliary (Working) Space.
Input Space is the memory required to hold the inputs themselves.
Auxiliary Space is the temporary working memory allocated by the algorithm to solve the problem (call stack frames, hash sets, temporary arrays).
When interviewers ask for space complexity, they almost universally refer to Auxiliary Space.
keyRules: In-place algorithms have $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
Recursive call stacks consume $O(D)$ auxiliary space where $D$ is the maximum recursion depth.

codeSnippet.title: In-Place vs Out-of-Place Space Consumption
codeSnippet.description: Comparing O(1) auxiliary space vs O(N) auxiliary space
codeSnippet.code:
# Out-of-Place: O(N) auxiliary space
def reverse_copy(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [arr[i] for i in range(len(arr) - 1, -1, -1)]

# In-Place: O(1) auxiliary space
def reverse_in_place(arr: list[int]) -> None:
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        arr[left], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1

data = [1, 2, 3, 4]
reverse_in_place(data)
print("In-place reversed:", data)

topics.pitfall: Forgetting the implicit recursion stack when measuring space: recursive Fibonacci has depth N, so it consumes O(N) auxiliary stack memory even without explicit lists.

quickCheck.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of an algorithm that modifies its input array in-place using two integer pointers?
quickCheck.explanation: Two scalar integer pointers consume a constant number of bytes regardless of input size N, making auxiliary space O(1).

topics.title: Common Complexity Classes Ranked
explanation: From fastest to slowest:
1. $O(1)$: Constant time (hash map lookup, array index).
2. $O(\log N)$: Logarithmic time (binary search, balanced BST search).
3. $O(N)$: Linear time (array traversal, counting).
4. $O(N \log N)$: Linearithmic time (Merge sort, Heap sort, Tim sort).
5. $O(N^2)$: Quadratic time (nested loops, bubble sort).
6. $O(2^N)$: Exponential time (recursive power set, naive Fibonacci).
7. $O(N!)$: Factorial time (permutations, Traveling Salesperson brute force).
keyRules: If $N = 10^5$, an $O(N^2)$ algorithm does $10^{10}$ ops and will TIME OUT (> 1 second). You MUST aim for $O(N \log N)$ or $O(N)$.
If $N = 10^8$, only $O(N)$ or $O(\log N)$ can pass.

codeSnippet.title: Operations Estimate by Complexity Class
codeSnippet.description: Calculating ops for N = 10,000 across complexity classes
codeSnippet.code:
import math

N = 10_000
print(f"O(1):       1 operation")
print(f"O(log N):   {math.log2(N):.1f} operations")
print(f"O(N):       {N:,} operations")
print(f"O(N log N): {int(N * math.log2(N)):,} operations")
print(f"O(N^2):     {N**2:,} operations (Dangerous for N > 10,000!)")

topics.pitfall: Assuming O(N log N) is close to O(N^2): for N=1,000,000, N log N is ~20 million ops (instant), whereas N^2 is 1 trillion ops (hours of computation!).

quickCheck.question: If an interview problem has input constraint N <= 100,000 and a 1.0 second execution limit, which complexity is acceptable?
quickCheck.explanation: 100,000 ops * log2(100,000) is approx 1.7 * 10^6 ops, executing in ~10ms. O(N^2) would be 10^10 ops, exceeding the ~10^8 ops per second CPU threshold.

topics.title: Amortized Complexity: The Accounting Method
explanation: Amortized analysis evaluates the average performance of each operation over a worst-case sequence of operations.
Example: Dynamic array append (`push_back`). Most appends take $O(1)$.
Occasionally, when the array is full, it allocates double capacity and copies all $N$ elements, taking $O(N)$.
However, doubling happens only after $N$ cheap operations. Distributing that $O(N)$ copy cost over $N$ appends yields an AMORTIZED runtime of $O(1)$ per append.
keyRules: Amortized O(1) means any sequence of K operations takes O(K) total time.
Dynamic array resizing with geometric doubling (factor 2 or 1.5) guarantees amortized O(1).

codeSnippet.title: Simulating Dynamic Array Doubling Cost
codeSnippet.description: Tracking total copy costs over N appends
codeSnippet.code:
def simulate_dynamic_array(n: int):
    capacity = 1
    total_copies = 0
    
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if i > capacity:
            total_copies += (i - 1) # copy existing elements
            capacity *= 2
            
    print(f"Total elements appended: {n:,}")
    print(f"Total element copies during resizing: {total_copies:,}")
    print(f"Average copy cost per append: {total_copies / n:.2f} (Bounded by O(1)!)")

simulate_dynamic_array(100_000)

topics.pitfall: Increasing array capacity by a fixed constant (e.g. +10 elements each resize) results in O(N^2) total copy time, degrading amortized append to O(N)!

quickCheck.question: What is the amortized time complexity of appending an element to a dynamically resizing array that doubles capacity when full?
quickCheck.explanation: Because capacity grows geometrically (doubling), the expensive O(N) copy is amortized over N preceding operations, making each append amortized O(1).

topics.title: Recursion Trees and Call Stack Frame Space
explanation: To analyze recursive time complexity, draw the Recursion Tree.
Total Time = (Number of tree nodes) $\times$ (Work done per node).
Total Auxiliary Space = Maximum depth of the recursion tree $\times$ (Memory per stack frame).
Binary branching without memoization (like naive Fibonacci) creates $2^N$ nodes, leading to disastrous $O(2^N)$ time complexity.
keyRules: Recursion depth equals the longest root-to-leaf path in the recursion tree.
Stack Overflow occurs when recursion depth exceeds the OS stack limit (usually ~1,000 to 10,000 frames).

codeSnippet.title: Recursion Tree Depth and Calls
codeSnippet.description: Tracking total call count in naive divide and conquer

topics.pitfall: Assuming recursion space is proportional to total calls: space is proportional only to the MAX CURRENT DEPTH of the active call stack at any one instant.

quickCheck.question: For a recursive function with depth D that makes 2 branch calls at each step, what is the maximum auxiliary stack space?
quickCheck.explanation: The call stack only holds the currently active ancestor frames along the path from root to leaf, which is O(D) memory.

topics.title: The Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer Recurrences
explanation: The Master Theorem provides instant asymptotic bounds for recurrences of the form:
$T(N) = a \cdot T(N/b) + O(N^d)$ where $a \ge 1, b > 1$.
- Case 1: If $d < \log_b a$, then $T(N) = O(N^{\log_b a})$ (leaf-heavy, e.g. Strassen matrix multiplication).
- Case 2: If $d = \log_b a$, then $T(N) = O(N^d \log N)$ (balanced, e.g. Merge Sort: $a=2, b=2, d=1 \implies O(N \log N)$).
- Case 3: If $d > \log_b a$, then $T(N) = O(N^d)$ (root-heavy, work at root dominates).
keyRules: Binary search: $T(N) = 1 \cdot T(N/2) + O(1) \implies a=1, b=2, d=0 \implies \log_2 1 = 0 = d \implies O(\log N)$.
Merge sort: $T(N) = 2 \cdot T(N/2) + O(N) \implies a=2, b=2, d=1 \implies \log_2 2 = 1 = d \implies O(N \log N)$.

codeSnippet.title: Master Theorem Recurrence Solver
codeSnippet.description: Automated evaluation of Master Theorem cases

topics.pitfall: Applying the Master Theorem when b is not a constant division (e.g. $T(N) = T(N-1) + O(1)$ is linear decrement, NOT divide-and-conquer).

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of a recurrence T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N) by the Master Theorem?
quickCheck.explanation: Here a=2, b=2, d=1. Since log_2(2) = 1 == d, this falls into Case 2, giving O(N^1 * log N) = O(N log N).

topics.title: Algorithmic Problem-Solving Framework
explanation: Mastering DSA requires a repeatable step-by-step mental discipline:
1. Clarify constraints: What is $N$? Are numbers negative? Duplicates allowed?
2. Test edge cases: $N=0$, $N=1$, all identical elements, sorted, reverse sorted.
3. Formulate brute force: Always start with the simplest working solution and state its complexity.
4. Identify bottlenecks & patterns: Look for repeated lookups (Hash Map), sorted order (Binary Search / Two Pointers), or overlapping subproblems (DP).
5. Write clean code and dry-run with a small example before running.
keyRules: Never write code before clarifying input constraints and asymptotic targets.
State time and space complexity explicitly before writing the first line of code.
