keyRules: Used by C++ std::unordered_map and Java HashMap (converts to Red-Black Tree when chain length > 8).
Average lookup is O(1); worst-case is O(N) if all keys hash to a single bucket.

codeSnippet.title: Separate Chaining Hash Map Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Bucket array of linked key-value lists

topics.pitfall: Adversarial Hash Flooding Attacks: malicious attackers generate thousands of keys that hash to the exact same bucket, degrading server lookups from O(1) to O(N) and causing denial-of-service.

quickCheck.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of a hash table lookup when all N keys collide into the same bucket?
quickCheck.explanation: If all keys collide into a single bucket, the table degenerates into a singly linked list of size N, taking O(N) time to search.

topics.title: Collision Resolution: Open Addressing (Linear & Quadratic Probing)
explanation: Open Addressing stores all entries directly in the table array without secondary linked list nodes.
When a collision occurs at bucket $H$:
- **Linear Probing**: Check consecutive slots $(H + 1) \% M, (H + 2) \% M, \dots$ until an empty slot is found.
- **Quadratic Probing**: Check $(H + 1^2) \% M, (H + 2^2) \% M, \dots$ to reduce clustering.
Open addressing offers superior cache locality (contiguous memory), but requires tombstone markers for deletions.
keyRules: Requires load factor alpha < 0.7 (performance drops precipitously as table fills).
Deleted slots must be marked with a "Tombstone" (DELETED) so probe sequences do not abort prematurely.

codeSnippet.title: Linear Probing Hash Table
codeSnippet.description: Contiguous collision probing with tombstone deletions
codeSnippet.code:
class LinearProbingMap:
    DELETED = object() # Sentinel tombstone
    
    def __init__(self, capacity: int = 16):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.keys = [None] * capacity
        self.vals = [None] * capacity
        
    def put(self, key, val) -> None:
        idx = hash(key) % self.capacity
        while self.keys[idx] is not None and self.keys[idx] is not self.DELETED:
            if self.keys[idx] == key:
                self.vals[idx] = val # update
                return
            idx = (idx + 1) % self.capacity
            
        self.keys[idx] = key
        self.vals[idx] = val

lpm = LinearProbingMap()
lpm.put("alpha", 100)
lpm.put("beta", 200)

topics.pitfall: Setting a deleted slot to `None` in open addressing: this breaks the probe chain, causing lookups for elements inserted after that slot to incorrectly return "Not Found"!

quickCheck.question: Why are tombstone markers necessary when deleting keys in an open-addressing hash table?
options: To allow subsequent lookups to continue probing past the deleted slot instead of stopping at None
quickCheck.explanation: Linear probing terminates upon finding an empty (None) slot. A tombstone indicates that a key was deleted and subsequent probes must continue searching.

topics.title: Load Factor (α) and Dynamic Rehashing
explanation: Load Factor: $\alpha = \frac{N}{\text{Capacity}}$ (ratio of stored keys to total buckets).
As $\alpha$ increases, collisions skyrocket and lookup time degrades toward $O(N)$.
When $\alpha$ exceeds a threshold (typically $\alpha \ge 0.75$ for chaining, $\alpha \ge 0.5$ for open addressing):
1. Allocate a new bucket array with DOUBLE the capacity ($2 \times M$).
2. Rehash: Recompute bucket indices for all existing elements and insert them into the new table.
Amortized cost: Doubling ensures rehashing cost is amortized $O(1)$ per insertion.
keyRules: Standard rehashing threshold is alpha >= 0.75.
Rehashing is O(N) when triggered, but amortized O(1).

codeSnippet.title: Dynamic Rehashing Simulation
codeSnippet.description: Automatic capacity doubling when load factor threshold is breached

topics.pitfall: Copying old bucket indices into the new table directly: capacity changed from M to 2M, so bucket index `hash % new_capacity` is completely different and MUST be recomputed for every key!

quickCheck.question: What is the typical load factor threshold for doubling the size of a chaining hash table?
quickCheck.explanation: A load factor of 0.75 strikes the optimal engineering balance between memory utilization and low collision probability.

topics.title: Two Sum (The Classic Hash Map Benchmark)
explanation: Problem: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`.
Brute force checks all pairs in $O(N^2)$ time.
Hash Map Solution in a Single Pass:
- For each element `x`, its required complement is `comp = target - x`.
- If `comp` is already in our hash map, we found the pair! Return `[seen[comp], current_index]`.
- Otherwise, store `seen[x] = current_index`.
Runs in $O(N)$ time with $O(N)$ space.
keyRules: Store complement lookup: target - num.
Check map before inserting current element to prevent pairing an element with itself.

codeSnippet.title: Two Sum in O(N) Time
codeSnippet.description: Single-pass hash map complement matching

topics.pitfall: Pre-populating the entire hash map before checking: if `nums = [3, 2, 4]` and target is 6, checking 3 finds index 0 (itself!), returning `[0, 0]` incorrectly.

quickCheck.question: Why does single-pass Two Sum check the map BEFORE inserting the current number?
options: To avoid pairing an element with itself when target = 2 * num
Because dictionary keys must be unique
quickCheck.explanation: Checking before inserting ensures that the complement found in the map is a previously seen distinct element, never the current element itself.

topics.title: Group Anagrams: Canonical Key Hashing
explanation: Problem: Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together in any order.
Anagram invariant: Two strings are anagrams if and only if they possess identical character counts.
Two ways to construct a canonical hash map key:
1. **Sorted String Key**: `tuple(sorted(s))` -> $O(N \times K \log K)$ time.
2. **Character Count Tuple Key**: A 26-element tuple of counts `tuple(counts)` -> $O(N \times K)$ time (optimal!).
Group all matching words into a hash map list.
keyRules: Tuples are immutable and hashable in Python, making them valid dictionary keys.
Character count tuple achieves optimal O(N * K) runtime where K is max word length.

codeSnippet.title: Group Anagrams via Frequency Key
codeSnippet.description: Grouping anagrams with 26-element tuple hashing in O(N * K)

topics.pitfall: Using a mutable `list` as a Python dictionary key: lists are unhashable and raise `TypeError: unhashable type: list`. Always convert to `tuple(count)`.

quickCheck.question: Why must the 26-element count array be converted to a tuple before being used as a dictionary key in Python?
options: Tuples are immutable and therefore hashable; lists are mutable and unhashable
quickCheck.explanation: Python requires dictionary keys to be immutable so their hash codes never change; lists are mutable and cannot be hashed.

topics.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence: O(N) Hash Set Search
explanation: Problem: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence (e.g. `[100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]` -> 4 for `[1, 2, 3, 4]`). Must run in $O(N)$ time.
Sorting takes $O(N \log N)$, violating the constraint.
Hash Set Solution:
1. Insert all numbers into a hash set for $O(1)$ lookups.
2. Iterate through numbers in the set. Check if `(num - 1)` is in the set.
3. If `(num - 1)` is NOT in the set, this `num` is the START of a streak!
4. Count streak length: `while (num + length) in set: length += 1`.
Because each sequence is explored ONLY from its starting element, each number is visited at most twice, guaranteeing $O(N)$ total time!
keyRules: Only expand streaks when num - 1 is NOT in set (identifies sequence root).
Runs in O(N) time with O(N) auxiliary space.

codeSnippet.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence in O(N)
codeSnippet.description: Hash set streak discovery starting only at sequence roots
codeSnippet.code:
def longest_consecutive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    num_set = set(nums)
    max_streak = 0
    
    for x in num_set:
        # Check if x is the start of a consecutive sequence
        if x - 1 not in num_set:
            curr_num = x
            curr_streak = 1
            
            while curr_num + 1 in num_set:
                curr_num += 1
                curr_streak += 1
                
            max_streak = max(max_streak, curr_streak)
            
    return max_streak

print("Longest consecutive streak:", longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2])) # 4 ([1, 2, 3, 4])

topics.pitfall: Starting a while loop expansion for EVERY number without checking `x - 1 not in num_set`: this degrades performance to $O(N^2)$ on sequences like `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.

quickCheck.question: Why is the check `if x - 1 not in num_set` critical to guaranteeing O(N) time in Longest Consecutive Sequence?
options: It ensures the while-loop is entered only at the true beginning of a sequence, avoiding redundant scanning of sub-streaks
quickCheck.explanation: Without this check, elements in the middle of a streak would initiate redundant O(N) scans, degrading total runtime to quadratic O(N^2).

topics.title: Design HashSet & HashMap from Scratch (Without Built-ins)
explanation: Interview benchmark: Implement MyHashMap from scratch without using any built-in hash map or dictionary libraries.
Combine all principles learned today:
- Pre-allocate a prime-sized bucket array (e.g. 1009 or 2069).
- Implement bucket chaining with singly or doubly linked nodes.
- Implement `put(key, val)`, `get(key)`, and `remove(key)` in $O(1)$ average time.
- Handle collisions, updates, and key removals cleanly.
keyRules: Use a prime number capacity (e.g. 1009) to minimize collisions with simple modulo indexing.
Implement clean node traversal for updates and deletions.

codeSnippet.title: Complete Hand-Built MyHashMap
codeSnippet.description: Custom hash map with separate chaining from scratch

topics.pitfall: Allocating an array of 1,000,000 integers directly to mimic a hash map: wastes megabytes of RAM and fails if keys can be negative or strings.

quickCheck.question: Why is a prime number (like 1009) preferred as the capacity for a basic hash table using modulo indexing?
options: Prime modulo reduces clustering when keys share common divisors or patterns
quickCheck.explanation: Using a prime modulus ensures that key patterns sharing factors with table capacity do not all hash to the same subset of buckets.

days.title: Module 2 Capstone: Production LRU Cache Design
days.subtitle: Doubly linked list + hash map hybrid, O(1) eviction mechanics & Module 2 Qualifying Exam
days.overview: Synthesize linear pointer structures, doubly linked list mutations, and hash tables into the premier systems interview design challenge: the LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache. Build an uncompromising O(1) cache engine, followed by the Week 2 Qualifying Exam.

topics.title: The LRU Cache Challenge: Why Pure Arrays or Hash Maps Fail
explanation: An LRU (Least Recently Used) Cache holds a fixed capacity $C$.
Operations:
- `get(key)`: Retrieve value and mark key as Most Recently Used in $O(1)$.
- `put(key, value)`: Insert/update key and mark as Most Recently Used in $O(1)$. If full, evict the Least Recently Used key in $O(1)$.
Why single data structures fail:
- A Hash Map gives $O(1)$ lookup, but CANNOT track element access ordering in $O(1)$.
- An Array/List tracks ordering, but moving an element from middle to head costs $O(N)$ shifting.
- The Hybrid Solution: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List!
keyRules: Both get and put MUST execute in strict O(1) time.
Doubly linked list allows O(1) node removal given a node pointer.

codeSnippet.title: LRU Cache Architectural Blueprint
codeSnippet.description: Hybrid Doubly Linked List + Hash Map structure
codeSnippet.code:
# Blueprint Concept:
# Hash Map: key -> Node pointer (O(1) search)
# Doubly Linked List: Sentinel Head <-> Most Recent <-> ... <-> Least Recent <-> Sentinel Tail
# Moving a node to front:
# 1. Unlink node from current position (O(1))
# 2. Re-insert right after Sentinel Head (O(1))

topics.pitfall: Attempting to use a singly linked list for LRU Cache: deleting a node requires finding its predecessor, which takes O(N) search.

quickCheck.question: Why is a Doubly Linked List required instead of a Singly Linked List for O(1) LRU Cache eviction?
options: Doubly linked lists use less memory
A doubly linked node can unlink itself in O(1) using its prev pointer, without traversing from the head
Singly linked lists cannot store values
quickCheck.explanation: To delete a node in O(1) time, you need immediate access to its predecessor (node.prev.next = node.next), which only a doubly linked list provides.

topics.title: Doubly Linked Node & Sentinel Design for LRU
explanation: Each node stores `key`, `val`, `prev`, and `next`.

Why store `key` inside the node? When the cache is full, we must evict the least recently used node (`tail.prev`). To remove it from the Hash Map in $O(1)$, we must know its key (`del map[node.key]`)!
Maintain permanent dummy `head` (Most Recently Used side) and dummy `tail` (Least Recently Used side).
Sentinels eliminate all null checks during node insertions and removals.
keyRules: Node must store both key and value.
Sentinel head and tail ensure non-null pointer invariants.

codeSnippet.title: LRU Node and Doubly Linked Primitives
codeSnippet.description: Sentinel head/tail with O(1) add and remove primitives

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to store `key` in the linked node: you can pop the node from the list, but you cannot delete its entry from the hash map without an O(N) scan.

quickCheck.question: Why must the LRUNode store the `key` as well as the `val`?
options: So when the LRU tail node is evicted, its corresponding entry in the hash map can be deleted in O(1)
quickCheck.explanation: Evicting the LRU element gives us a node reference (tail.prev); to remove it from map, we need map.pop(node.key).

topics.title: The Full LRU Cache Implementation
explanation: Assemble the complete LRU Cache:
1. `get(key)`:
- If key not in map: return -1.
- Node exists: move node to head (remove from current spot, add to head).
- Return `node.val`.
2. `put(key, value)`:
- If key exists: update value and move to head.
- If key is new: create node, add to head, insert in map.
- If `len(map) > capacity`: remove `tail.prev` from list and delete from map.
keyRules: Every get and put moves accessed node to head.
Capacity overflow removes tail.prev.

codeSnippet.title: Complete Production LRU Cache Class
codeSnippet.description: Self-contained O(1) get and put LRU Cache
codeSnippet.code:
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.map = {} # key -> LRUNode
        self.head = LRUNode()
        self.tail = LRUNode()
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head
        
    def _remove(self, node: LRUNode):
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev
        
    def _add_to_head(self, node: LRUNode):
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node
        
    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.map: return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_to_head(node) # mark most recently used
        return node.val
        
    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.map:
            node = self.map[key]
            node.val = value
            self._remove(node)
            self._add_to_head(node)
        else:
            if len(self.map) >= self.capacity:
                # Evict least recently used (tail.prev)
                lru = self.tail.prev
                self._remove(lru)
                del self.map[lru.key]
            new_node = LRUNode(key, value)
            self._add_to_head(new_node)
            self.map[key] = new_node

cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 10)
cache.put(2, 20)
print("Get 1:", cache.get(1)) # 10 (1 is now MRU)
cache.put(3, 30)             # Evicts key 2!
print("Get 2:", cache.get(2)) # -1 (evicted!)
print("Get 3:", cache.get(3)) # 30

topics.pitfall: Evicting `tail` instead of `tail.prev`: `tail` is the dummy sentinel node! Evicting it destroys list invariants and crashes with AttributeError.

quickCheck.question: What node in the doubly linked list represents the Least Recently Used item to be evicted?
quickCheck.explanation: head is MRU sentinel, head.next is most recently used, tail is LRU sentinel, and tail.prev is the least recently used element.

topics.title: LFU (Least Frequently Used) Cache Architecture
explanation: While LRU evicts based on access recency, LFU evicts based on access frequency (with recency as tie-breaker).
Architecture:
- `key_to_node`: maps `key -> (val, freq, node)`.
- `freq_to_dll`: maps `freq -> DoublyLinkedList of nodes`.
- `min_freq`: tracks the minimum frequency currently present in the cache.
When an item is accessed: increment its `freq`, move it to `freq + 1` list. If its old list becomes empty and `freq == min_freq`, increment `min_freq`.
Achieves $O(1)$ get and put for frequency-based caching!
keyRules: Maintain min_freq scalar to find eviction bucket in O(1).
Tie-breaker within the same frequency is LRU.

codeSnippet.title: LFU Frequency Architecture Concept
codeSnippet.description: Frequency buckets with Doubly Linked Lists in O(1)
codeSnippet.code:
# LFU Architectural Model
# min_freq = 1
# freq_to_dll[1]: Node(B) <-> Node(C)
# freq_to_dll[2]: Node(A)
# Eviction: Pop from tail of freq_to_dll[min_freq]

topics.pitfall: Searching for the minimum frequency with a linear scan: would degrade eviction to O(N). Maintaining `min_freq` scalar guarantees O(1).

quickCheck.question: How does LFU Cache determine which node to evict when multiple keys share the same lowest frequency?
options: By using LRU (least recently used) among the tied keys
quickCheck.explanation: LFU specifies that if there is a tie in minimum access frequency, the least recently used key among them is evicted.

topics.title: Memory Overhead and Cache Line Prefetching in Linear Data Structures
explanation: Theoretical Big-O analysis ignores hardware cache lines, but real systems engineering requires mechanical sympathy:
- Dynamic Arrays (`std::vector`, Python `list`): elements contiguous in RAM. Fetching 1 element loads 64 bytes into L1 cache, prefetching adjacent elements.
- Linked Lists: each node requires separate heap allocation (`malloc`). Nodes are scattered across non-contiguous addresses. Traversing causes a cache miss on almost EVERY node!
In benchmarks, scanning an array is up to 50x faster than traversing a linked list of identical size due to CPU cache prefetchers.
keyRules: Favor arrays over linked lists unless O(1) splicing or pointer persistence is strictly necessary.
Pointer hopping degrades memory bandwidth.

codeSnippet.title: Memory Footprint Comparison
codeSnippet.description: Byte overhead of linked list node vs contiguous array
codeSnippet.code:
import sys

val = 42
# Contiguous list: 4-8 bytes per pointer reference in array
arr = [val] * 1000

# Linked node: object overhead + val reference + next reference = ~56 bytes per node
print(f"Array of 1,000 refs size: {sys.getsizeof(arr)} bytes")
print("Contiguous array is vastly lighter and cache-friendly!")

topics.pitfall: Using linked lists for everything because "insertions are O(1)": finding WHERE to insert requires an O(N) cache-miss traversal, making it slower in practice than array shifts.

quickCheck.question: Why is linear search through a dynamic array significantly faster in practice than traversing a linked list of identical size?
options: Arrays reside in contiguous memory, allowing CPU hardware prefetchers to stream cache lines into L1 cache without cache misses
Linked lists use Python code only
quickCheck.explanation: Spatial locality allows CPU cache controllers to preload contiguous 64-byte blocks, while linked lists suffer from pointer-chasing cache misses across scattered heap memory.

topics.title: Concurrency Hazards in Linear Structures (Thread Safety)
explanation: Standard data structures (Python lists, `std::vector`, `std::unordered_map`) are NOT thread-safe.
Concurrent mutations cause corrupted pointers:
- Two threads pushing to a stack simultaneously can overwrite each other's elements or leak nodes.
- Concurrent resizing of a hash table can trap linked chains in an infinite loop.
Production solutions:
- Mutex locking (`std::mutex`, `threading.Lock`).
- Lock-free atomic structures (Treiber Stack, Michael-Scott Queue).
keyRules: Never share mutable linked lists or hash maps across threads without synchronization.
Lock contention becomes the throughput bottleneck under high concurrency.

codeSnippet.title: Thread-Safe Synchronized Stack
codeSnippet.description: Mutex protected thread-safe LIFO stack

topics.pitfall: Assuming Python GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) makes all operations thread-safe: multi-step operations like `if not stack.empty(): stack.pop()` still suffer from race conditions without explicit locks.

quickCheck.question: What danger exists when multiple threads write to an unsynchronized hash table?
options: Memory corruption, lost writes, or infinite loops during bucket rehashing
quickCheck.explanation: Concurrent unsynchronized mutations cause race conditions that corrupt bucket pointers and can create circular pointer loops.

topics.title: Linear Structures Diagnostic Matrix
explanation: Use this mental checklist when selecting linear data structures in technical interviews:
- Need $O(1)$ random indexing? -> Dynamic Array (`vector`).
- Need frequent insertions/deletions at known positions without shifting? -> Linked List.
- Need LIFO parsing, undo history, or Next Greater Element? -> Monotonic Stack.
- Need FIFO processing, level-order BFS, or sliding window extrema? -> Monotonic Queue / Deque.
- Need $O(1)$ key-value search and existence testing? -> Hash Map / Hash Set.
- Need $O(1)$ cache eviction combining lookup and access recency? -> LRU Cache (Hash Map + Doubly Linked List).
keyRules: Match the access pattern to the data structure invariant.
Always specify time and space bounds before coding.

topics.pitfall: Using a linear structure where a tree or heap is needed (e.g. maintaining sorted order dynamically: inserting into array is O(N), balanced BST is O(log N)).

quickCheck.question: Which data structure combination provides O(1) get and O(1) put for an LRU Cache?
quickCheck.explanation: A Hash Map provides O(1) key-to-node lookup, and a Doubly Linked List enables O(1) node detachment and front insertion.

quiz.title: Module 2 Qualifying Exam: Linear Structures, Stacks, Queues & Hash Maps
quiz.description: Verify your mastery of linked lists, Floyd cycle detection, monotonic stacks/queues, and LRU Cache architecture.

questions.question: In Floyd's Cycle Detection algorithm, after slow and fast pointers meet inside a loop, how is the cycle entrance located?
options: By reversing the entire linked list
By resetting one pointer to head while leaving the other at the meeting point, then advancing both 1 step at a time until they collide
By doubling the speed of both pointers
By computing the hash code of all nodes
questions.explanation: Mathematical analysis proves that the distance from head to entrance equals the distance from the meeting point around the loop to the entrance. Advancing both at 1 step per iteration guarantees they meet at the entrance.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Sliding Window Maximum problem using a Monotonic Deque on an array of size N?
questions.explanation: Each element enters the deque at most once and leaves the deque at most once, bounding total operations across the entire algorithm to 2N = O(N).

questions.question: Why are tombstone markers (DELETED sentinels) mandatory when removing elements from an open-addressing hash table?
options: To ensure subsequent searches continue probing past the deleted slot instead of stopping prematurely at None
questions.explanation: In open addressing, a search probe sequence stops when it reaches an empty slot. If a deleted element were replaced with None, any element inserted after it in the probe chain would become unreachable.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of the pop() operation in a Queue implemented using two Stacks?
questions.explanation: Although a transfer from stack_in to stack_out costs O(N), it happens only when stack_out is empty. Each element is moved at most once across its lifetime, giving an amortized time of O(1).

questions.question: In a production LRU Cache, why must each node in the Doubly Linked List store the key as well as the value?
options: To print the key to console
So that when the least recently used node is evicted from the tail, its entry can be removed from the Hash Map in O(1) time
questions.explanation: When capacity is exceeded, the LRU node (tail.prev) is evicted from the doubly linked list. Without knowing node.key, removing that node from the hash map would require an O(N) search.

days.title: Binary Trees & Depth-First Traversals (DFS)
days.subtitle: Tree properties, recursion vs explicit stacks, Inorder, Preorder, Postorder & Morris traversal
days.overview: Transition from linear sequences to hierarchical branching trees. Master binary tree node mechanics, depth vs height, and the three canonical DFS traversals: Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder—both recursively and iteratively with an explicit stack.

topics.title: Tree Terminology & Mathematical Properties
explanation: A Tree is a non-linear hierarchical structure where each node has at most one parent and zero or more children.
A Binary Tree is a tree where each node has AT MOST 2 children (left and right).
Mathematical Invariants:
- A binary tree with $N$ nodes has exactly $N - 1$ edges.
- Maximum nodes at depth $d$ is $2^d$ (root is depth 0).
- Maximum nodes in a binary tree of height $h$ is $2^{h+1} - 1$.
- Minimum height of a binary tree with $N$ nodes is $\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor$.
keyRules: Leaf node: node with 0 children (left is None and right is None).
Height of node: number of edges on longest path down to a leaf.
Depth of node: number of edges from root down to that node.

codeSnippet.title: TreeNode Definition in Python
codeSnippet.description: Standard binary tree node class
codeSnippet.code:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

# Construct simple tree:
#       1
#      / \
#     2   3
root = TreeNode(1)
root.left = TreeNode(2)
root.right = TreeNode(3)
print(f"Root: {root.val}, Left: {root.left.val}, Right: {root.right.val}")

topics.pitfall: Confusing 0-indexed vs 1-indexed tree height: some definitions define height of single-node tree as 0 (edges), others as 1 (nodes). Clarify in interviews.

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a full binary tree of height h (where height of root is 0)?
quickCheck.explanation: Summing 2^0 + 2^1 + ... + 2^h yields 2^(h + 1) - 1 maximum nodes.

topics.title: Preorder Traversal: Root → Left → Right
explanation: Preorder processes the CURRENT node FIRST, then visits left subtree, then visits right subtree.
Uses:
- Creating a clone/copy of the tree.
- Serializing the tree into a flat string representation.
- Prefix expression evaluation.
Time: $O(N)$ visiting each node once. Space: $O(H)$ for call stack where $H$ is tree height.
keyRules: Order: Node -> Left -> Right.
In balanced trees: space is O(log N). In degenerate skewed trees: space is O(N).

codeSnippet.title: Preorder Traversal (Recursive & Iterative)
codeSnippet.description: Root-Left-Right traversal using stack
codeSnippet.code:
def preorder_recursive(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    res = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        res.append(node.val) # Root
        dfs(node.left)       # Left
        dfs(node.right)      # Right
    dfs(root)
    return res

def preorder_iterative(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    if not root: return []
    res, stack = [], [root]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        res.append(node.val)
        # Push right FIRST so left is popped first (LIFO)!
        if node.right: stack.append(node.right)
        if node.left: stack.append(node.left)
    return res

# Tree: 1 -> left: 2, right: 3
print("Preorder:", preorder_iterative(root)) # [1, 2, 3]

topics.pitfall: Pushing left child onto stack before right child in iterative preorder: because stacks are LIFO, pushing left first causes right to pop first, producing Root-Right-Left order!

quickCheck.question: Why do we push the right child before the left child onto the stack in iterative preorder traversal?
options: Because stacks are LIFO, pushing right first ensures left is on top and processed next
quickCheck.explanation: The stack pops the most recently pushed item first; pushing right then left places the left child on top of the stack.

topics.title: Inorder Traversal: Left → Root → Right
explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree, processes the CURRENT node, then visits the right subtree.
CRITICAL PROPERTY: In a Binary Search Tree (BST), Inorder traversal yields node values in STRICTLY ASCENDING SORTED ORDER!
Iterative approach: push all left children onto stack until hitting None. Pop node, process it, and move to `node.right`.
keyRules: Order: Left -> Node -> Right.
Inorder on a BST always produces non-decreasing sorted order.

codeSnippet.title: Inorder Traversal (Recursive & Iterative)
codeSnippet.description: Left-Root-Right traversal
codeSnippet.code:
def inorder_recursive(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    res = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        dfs(node.left)       # Left
        res.append(node.val) # Root
        dfs(node.right)      # Right
    dfs(root)
    return res

def inorder_iterative(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    res, stack = [], []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        # Traverse to leftmost child
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        res.append(curr.val) # Process Root
        curr = curr.right    # Visit Right
    return res

# BST: 2 -> left: 1, right: 3
bst = TreeNode(2, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3))
print("Inorder BST:", inorder_iterative(bst)) # [1, 2, 3] (Sorted!)

topics.pitfall: Resetting `curr = root` inside the loop: curr must advance to `curr.right` after processing the popped node.

quickCheck.question: What special property does an Inorder traversal possess when executed on a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
options: It outputs all node values in strictly sorted ascending order
quickCheck.explanation: Because a BST places smaller values in left subtrees and larger values in right subtrees, Left-Root-Right traversal naturally sorts the values.

topics.title: Postorder Traversal: Left → Right → Root
explanation: Postorder visits left subtree, visits right subtree, and processes CURRENT node LAST.
Uses:
- Deleting a tree safely from leaves up to root (freeing child nodes before parent node).
- Bottom-Up computations where parent needs results from BOTH children (tree height, maximum path sum).
- Postfix expression trees.
keyRules: Order: Left -> Right -> Node.
Children are guaranteed to be fully evaluated before parent node is processed.

codeSnippet.title: Postorder Traversal Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Left-Right-Root bottom-up processing

topics.pitfall: Attempting to calculate a bottom-up metric (like subtree sizes or tree height) in preorder: parent does not yet know child metrics! Use postorder.

quickCheck.question: Which traversal is ideal for bottom-up algorithms where a parent node requires answers from both children before computing its own value?
quickCheck.explanation: Postorder processes left and right subtrees completely before evaluating the root, enabling bottom-up aggregation.

topics.title: Morris Traversal: O(1) Auxiliary Space Tree Traversal
explanation: Standard recursive and stack-based traversals consume $O(H)$ auxiliary memory for stack frames.
Can we traverse a binary tree in $O(N)$ time with STRICTLY $O(1)$ auxiliary space without recursion or stacks?
Yes! Morris Traversal uses **Threaded Binary Trees**:
- For current node `curr`: if `curr.left` exists, find its Inorder Predecessor (rightmost node in left subtree).
- If predecessor's `right` is None: establish temporary thread `pred.right = curr` and move `curr = curr.left`.
- If predecessor's `right` is `curr`: thread already exists! Remove thread `pred.right = None`, process `curr`, and move `curr = curr.right`.
keyRules: Temporarily modifies tree leaf pointers, then restores them to original state before finishing.
Strictly O(1) auxiliary space.

codeSnippet.title: Morris Inorder Traversal in O(1) Space
codeSnippet.description: Threaded binary tree traversal without stack or recursion

topics.pitfall: Terminating Morris Traversal early upon finding a target: if you break out early without clearing active threads, the tree is left corrupted with cyclic pointer loops!

quickCheck.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of Morris Traversal?
quickCheck.explanation: Morris Traversal utilizes empty right-child pointers of predecessor nodes to track the return path, requiring zero stack or recursive memory.

topics.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
explanation: Problem: Find the maximum depth (height in nodes) of a binary tree.
Recursive formulation (Divide and Conquer):
Base case: if `root is None`, depth is 0.
Recursive step: $\text{max\_depth} = 1 + \max(\text{depth}(\text{root.left}), \text{depth}(\text{root.right}))$.
Time: $O(N)$ visiting every node. Space: $O(H)$ for call stack.
keyRules: Depth of empty tree is 0.
Depth of single root node is 1.

codeSnippet.title: Maximum Depth Calculation
codeSnippet.description: Postorder divide and conquer depth calculation
codeSnippet.code:
def max_depth(root: TreeNode) -> int:
    if not root: return 0
    left_h = max_depth(root.left)
    right_h = max_depth(root.right)
    return 1 + max(left_h, right_h)

# 1 -> left: 2, right: 3 -> left: 4
tree = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2), TreeNode(3, TreeNode(4)))
print("Max Depth:", max_depth(tree)) # 3

topics.pitfall: Confusing maximum depth with minimum depth: minimum depth must find the closest LEAF node (if one child is None, you cannot simply take min(0, right)).

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum recursion call stack depth for max_depth on a completely skewed linked-list-like binary tree of N nodes?
quickCheck.explanation: In a degenerate tree where every node has only one child, the tree height is N, consuming N call stack frames.

topics.title: Diameter of Binary Tree (Longest Node-to-Node Path)
explanation: Problem: Find the length of the longest path between ANY two nodes in a tree (path does not necessarily pass through root).
Length is the number of edges along the path.
At every node `curr`, the longest path with `curr` as its turning peak is:
$\text{path\_edges} = \text{left\_height} + \text{right\_height}$.
While calculating tree height bottom-up, maintain a global maximum diameter.
keyRules: Height helper returns max height down one branch (1 + max(left, right)).
Diameter updates with left + right at each node.

codeSnippet.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
codeSnippet.description: Postorder height return with global diameter update
codeSnippet.code:
def diameter_of_binary_tree(root: TreeNode) -> int:
    max_diameter = 0
    
    def get_height(node: TreeNode) -> int:
        nonlocal max_diameter
        if not node: return 0
        
        left_h = get_height(node.left)
        right_h = get_height(node.right)
        
        # Longest path turning at this node
        max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left_h + right_h)
        
        # Return height of this subtree to parent
        return 1 + max(left_h, right_h)
        
    get_height(root)
    return max_diameter

# 1 -> left: 2 (has children 4, 5), right: 3
d_tree = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(4), TreeNode(5)), TreeNode(3))
print("Tree Diameter:", diameter_of_binary_tree(d_tree)) # 3 (path 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 or 4 -> 2 -> 5)

topics.pitfall: Returning `left_h + right_h` to parent: a parent can only extend a path down ONE of its branches, so the helper function must return `1 + max(left, right)`.

quickCheck.question: Why does the helper function in diameter_of_binary_tree return `1 + max(left_h, right_h)` instead of `left_h + right_h`?
options: Because a path extending up to a parent can only continue down one child branch, not both
quickCheck.explanation: A path cannot branch in two directions at the child node and also continue upward into the parent.

topics.title: Balanced Binary Tree Validation in O(N) Time
explanation: A binary tree is Height-Balanced if the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than 1.
Naive approach calculates height for every node: $O(N^2)$ time.
Optimal Postorder Bottom-Up approach in $O(N)$:
- Helper function returns tree height if balanced, or `-1` if unbalanced.
- If left or right subtree returns `-1`, or `abs(left_h - right_h) > 1`, immediately return `-1` to prune execution.
Tree is balanced if `check_height(root) != -1`.
keyRules: Return -1 as error sentinel for early exit.
Runs in single pass O(N) time.

codeSnippet.title: Height-Balanced Binary Tree Validation
codeSnippet.description: O(N) bottom-up height verification with early pruning

topics.pitfall: Recalculating height from top down with `abs(height(node.left) - height(node.right)) > 1`: recalculating height at each level results in an O(N^2) algorithm.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of the optimal bottom-up Balanced Binary Tree check?
quickCheck.explanation: Each node is visited once during the postorder traversal, propagating heights upward in O(N) linear time.

days.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) & Level-Order Tree Problems
days.subtitle: Level-order traversal, Zigzag traversal, Right Side View & lowest common ancestor
days.overview: Traverse trees horizontally level-by-level using Breadth-First Search (BFS). Master queue-based level freezing, alternating Zigzag traversal, visible node projections (Right Side View), and Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) algorithms.

topics.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (BFS Queue)
explanation: Problem: Return the level order traversal of a binary tree's values as a list of lists (e.g. `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`).
Use a FIFO Queue (`collections.deque`):
1. Push `root` to queue.
2. While queue is not empty:
a. `level_size = len(queue)` (snapshot node count at current depth).
b. Pop `level_size` nodes, collect their values, and enqueue non-null children.
c. Append level values to result array.
Runs in $O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ space.
keyRules: Freeze level_size at start of each outer loop iteration.
Queue holds at most N/2 nodes at the widest tree level.

codeSnippet.title: Level Order Traversal
codeSnippet.description: Standard BFS queue pattern for 2D level matrix
codeSnippet.code:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root: TreeNode) -> list[list[int]]:
    if not root: return []
    res = []
    q = deque([root])
    
    while q:
        level_size = len(q)
        current_level = []
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = q.popleft()
            current_level.append(node.val)
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        res.append(current_level)
        
    return res

# Tree: 3 -> left: 9, right: 20 (children: 15, 7)
t = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print("Level Order:", level_order(t)) # [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]

topics.pitfall: Omitting the `if not root: return []` check: enqueuing `None` yields `[[None]]` instead of an empty list `[]`.

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum space occupied by the queue during level order traversal of a balanced binary tree with N nodes?
quickCheck.explanation: In a complete binary tree, the last leaf level contains approximately N/2 nodes, so the queue consumes O(N) memory at its peak.

topics.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
explanation: Problem: Return level order traversal in zigzag order (level 0 left-to-right, level 1 right-to-left, level 2 left-to-right, etc.).
Implementation Options:
1. Store current level values in a `deque`: if even level, append to right; if odd level, append to left (`appendleft`).
2. Standard BFS + reverse odd-indexed levels: `if level % 2 == 1: current_level.reverse()`.
Both run in $O(N)$ time with $O(N)$ space.
keyRules: Toggle a boolean flag `left_to_right = not left_to_right` at each level.
Deque appendleft avoids O(K) reverse cost.

codeSnippet.title: Zigzag Level Order Traversal
codeSnippet.description: Alternating left-to-right and right-to-left traversal

topics.pitfall: Reversing how children are enqueued into the BFS queue: queue children MUST ALWAYS be enqueued in left-to-right order to maintain level parentage; only the collected values are alternated!

quickCheck.question: In Zigzag traversal, how should children be enqueued into the primary BFS queue?
options: Alternate left-right and right-left each level
Always left child first, then right child
quickCheck.explanation: The traversal queue must maintain consistent spatial ordering of nodes for the next level; only value insertion into current_level alternates.

topics.title: Binary Tree Right Side View (Projection Photography)
explanation: Problem: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return values of nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.
BFS Approach: In level-order traversal, the RIGHTMOST node at each level is simply the LAST node processed in that level (`current_level[-1]`).
DFS Approach: Traverse `Root -> Right -> Left`. If `current_depth == len(res)`, this is the first time reaching this depth, so record `node.val`!
Both achieve $O(N)$ time.
keyRules: BFS: pick the last node of each level.
DFS: visit right before left and record first node seen at each depth.

codeSnippet.title: Right Side View via BFS
codeSnippet.description: Extracting rightmost node at every level
codeSnippet.code:
from collections import deque

def right_side_view(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    if not root: return []
    res = []
    q = deque([root])
    
    while q:
        level_size = len(q)
        for i in range(level_size):
            node = q.popleft()
            if i == level_size - 1: # last element in level!
                res.append(node.val)
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
            
    return res

# 1 -> left: 2 (has right: 5), right: 3 (has right: 4)
tree_proj = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, None, TreeNode(5)), TreeNode(3, None, TreeNode(4)))
print("Right Side View:", right_side_view(tree_proj)) # [1, 3, 4]

topics.pitfall: Assuming you only need to traverse down `node.right`: if the right subtree is shorter than the left subtree, lower nodes in the left subtree become visible from the right side!

quickCheck.question: Why does simply following `curr = curr.right` fail for Right Side View?
options: If the left subtree is deeper than the right subtree, nodes in the left subtree will be visible from the right side at lower depths
quickCheck.explanation: A left subtree with depth 5 alongside a right subtree with depth 2 exposes levels 3, 4, and 5 to the right side view.

topics.title: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in a Binary Tree
explanation: The Lowest Common Ancestor of two nodes $P$ and $Q$ is the deepest node that has both $P$ and $Q$ as descendants (a node can be a descendant of itself).
Postorder Recursive Algorithm:
1. If `root is None` or `root == p` or `root == q`: return `root`.
2. Recurse into left and right subtrees: `left = lca(root.left, p, q); right = lca(root.right, p, q);`.
3. If both `left` and `right` are non-null: $P$ is in one subtree and $Q$ is in the other! Therefore, `root` IS the LCA!
4. Otherwise, return the non-null child (`left or right`).
keyRules: If both left and right return non-null, root is the LCA.
Runs in O(N) time with O(H) call stack space.

codeSnippet.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree
codeSnippet.description: Postorder LCA discovery in O(N)
codeSnippet.code:
def lowest_common_ancestor(root: TreeNode, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode) -> TreeNode:
    if not root or root == p or root == q:
        return root
        
    left = lowest_common_ancestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = lowest_common_ancestor(root.right, p, q)
    
    if left and right:
        return root # Both found in opposite subtrees
        
    return left if left else right

n4 = TreeNode(4); n5 = TreeNode(5)
n2 = TreeNode(2, n4, n5)
n3 = TreeNode(3)
root_lca = TreeNode(1, n2, n3)

ancestor = lowest_common_ancestor(root_lca, n4, n5)
print("LCA of 4 and 5:", ancestor.val) # 2

topics.pitfall: Assuming the tree is a Binary Search Tree: in an arbitrary Binary Tree, you cannot use value comparisons (< or >) to branch; you MUST use postorder search.

quickCheck.question: What does it signify when both `left` and `right` recursive calls return non-null in lowest_common_ancestor?
options: One target node is in the left subtree and the other is in the right subtree, making current root the LCA
quickCheck.explanation: If both subtrees contain one of the target nodes, the current node is the lowest node where their paths diverge.

topics.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node (Level-Linked Tree)
explanation: Problem: Populate each node's `next` pointer to point to its next right node on the same level (like a linked list per level).
Level Order with Queue costs $O(N)$ memory.
O(1) Space Trick using previously established `next` pointers:
- Use the parent level as a linked list to connect the child level!
- `curr.left.next = curr.right`.
- If `curr.next` exists: `curr.right.next = curr.next.left` (connecting across different subtrees!).
- Advance `curr = curr.next` along the level, then drop down to next level.
keyRules: Parent level acts as the iterator for stitching the child level.
Achieves O(1) auxiliary space without queues or recursion.

codeSnippet.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in O(1) Space
codeSnippet.description: Parent-guided child stitching for complete binary tree
codeSnippet.code:
class NodeNext:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
        self.next = next

def connect_next_pointers(root: NodeNext) -> NodeNext:
    if not root: return root
    leftmost = root
    
    while leftmost.left: # While next level exists
        curr = leftmost
        while curr:
            # 1. Connect children of same parent
            curr.left.next = curr.right
            # 2. Connect across adjacent parent subtrees
            if curr.next:
                curr.right.next = curr.next.left
            curr = curr.next
        leftmost = leftmost.left
        
    return root

topics.pitfall: Connecting `curr.right.next = curr.next.left` without checking if `curr.next` exists: crashes on rightmost parent of each level.

quickCheck.question: How does connect_next_pointers achieve O(1) auxiliary space?
options: By utilizing the already-connected next pointers of the current level to traverse horizontally without a queue
quickCheck.explanation: The current level is already a singly linked list via next pointers, so it functions as a queue with zero memory overhead.

topics.title: Path Sum I, II & III: Backtracking and Prefix Sums on Trees
explanation: - **Path Sum I**: Does any root-to-leaf path equal target? Divide and conquer: `has_path_sum(root.left, target - root.val) or has_path_sum(root.right, target - root.val)`.
- **Path Sum II**: Return all root-to-leaf paths. Backtracking: append `node.val` to path, recurse, pop from path.

- **Path Sum III**: Path does NOT need to start at root or end at leaf (must go downwards). Prefix Sum + Hash Map on Tree in $O(N)$! Store running prefix sums in hash map during DFS, and remove on backtrack.
keyRules: Root-to-leaf checks must verify is_leaf: `not node.left and not node.right`.
Path Sum III: backtrack prefix counts `prefix_counts[curr_sum] -= 1` upon returning from subtree.

codeSnippet.title: Path Sum III via Prefix Sum Hash Map
codeSnippet.description: O(N) downwards path counting using backtracking prefix map
codeSnippet.code:
from collections import defaultdict

def path_sum_iii(root: TreeNode, target_sum: int) -> int:
    prefix_counts = defaultdict(int)
    prefix_counts[0] = 1
    total_paths = 0
    
    def dfs(node: TreeNode, curr_sum: int):
        nonlocal total_paths
        if not node: return
        
        curr_sum += node.val
        total_paths += prefix_counts[curr_sum - target_sum]
        
        prefix_counts[curr_sum] += 1
        dfs(node.left, curr_sum)
        dfs(node.right, curr_sum)
        prefix_counts[curr_sum] -= 1 # Backtrack!
        
    dfs(root, 0)
    return total_paths

# Tree: 10 -> left: 5 (has child 3), target = 8
p_tree = TreeNode(10, TreeNode(5, TreeNode(3)))
print("Paths with sum 8:", path_sum_iii(p_tree, 8)) # 1 (5 + 3)

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to backtrack `prefix_counts[curr_sum] -= 1`: counts from one branch would leak into parallel sibling branches, yielding inflated counts.

quickCheck.question: Why must `prefix_counts[curr_sum] -= 1` be executed upon returning from a subtree in Path Sum III?
options: To ensure prefix sums from the left branch are not visible when searching the right sibling branch
Because hash maps cannot store duplicate keys
quickCheck.explanation: Paths must only travel downwards; failing to remove the current node prefix sum would allow illegal zig-zag paths across sibling branches.

topics.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (LeetCode Hard)
explanation: Problem: Find the maximum path sum between ANY two nodes in a binary tree (can turn at any node; each node visited at most once).
Node values can be NEGATIVE!
At each node `curr` during postorder DFS:
1. Calculate max branch gain from left child: `left_gain = max(0, dfs(curr.left))` (discard negative branches with `max(0, ...)`).
2. Calculate max branch gain from right child: `right_gain = max(0, dfs(curr.right))`.
3. Turning path through current node: `curr.val + left_gain + right_gain`. Update `global_max`.
4. Return single branch gain to parent: `curr.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)`.
keyRules: Use max(0, gain) to ignore subtrees that reduce the total sum.
Return to parent includes at most ONE child branch.

codeSnippet.title: Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree
codeSnippet.description: Postorder branch gain and peak path tracking in O(N)
codeSnippet.code:
def max_path_sum(root: TreeNode) -> int:
    max_sum = float('-inf')
    
    def gain_from_subtree(node: TreeNode) -> int:
        nonlocal max_sum
        if not node: return 0
        
        # Discard subtrees that yield negative gains
        left_gain = max(0, gain_from_subtree(node.left))
        right_gain = max(0, gain_from_subtree(node.right))
        
        # Max path turning at current node
        current_path_sum = node.val + left_gain + right_gain
        max_sum = max(max_sum, current_path_sum)
        
        # Return maximum contribution to parent (only 1 branch allowed!)
        return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)
        
    gain_from_subtree(root)
    return max_sum

# Tree: -10 -> left: 9, right: 20 (children: 15, 7)
hard_tree = TreeNode(-10, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print("Max Path Sum:", max_path_sum(hard_tree)) # 42 (15 + 20 + 7)

topics.pitfall: Initializing `max_sum = 0`: if all nodes in the tree are negative (e.g. `[-3]`), the answer is -3, but initializing to 0 returns 0 incorrectly.

quickCheck.question: Why does max_path_sum wrap child gains in `max(0, ...)`?
options: Because if a child subtree has a negative net sum, we can simply omit that branch from the path
quickCheck.explanation: If extending the path down a child subtree produces a negative sum, including it would only decrease the total, so we choose not to extend into it (gain 0).

topics.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (Codec Architecture)
explanation: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree into a string and deserialize that string back into the original tree structure.
Serialization (Preorder with Sentinels):
- Traverse `Root -> Left -> Right`.
- If node is None, append sentinel `"#"`.
Deserialization:
- Split string by comma into an iterator/queue.
- Recursively pop next value: if `"#"`, return `None`. Else create `TreeNode(val)` and recurse for left and right!
keyRules: Sentinels for None eliminate all structural ambiguity.
Preorder traversal guarantees root is always the first token.

codeSnippet.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
codeSnippet.description: Preorder serialization with sentinel null tokens
codeSnippet.code:
class Codec:
    def serialize(self, root: TreeNode) -> str:
        vals = []
        def dfs(node):
            if not node:
                vals.append("#")
                return
            vals.append(str(node.val))
            dfs(node.left)
            dfs(node.right)
        dfs(root)
        return ",".join(vals)
        
    def deserialize(self, data: str) -> TreeNode:
        tokens = iter(data.split(","))
        def build():
            val = next(tokens)
            if val == "#": return None
            node = TreeNode(int(val))
            node.left = build()
            node.right = build()
            return node
        return build()

codec = Codec()
serialized = codec.serialize(hard_tree)
print("Serialized Tree:", serialized)
deserialized = codec.deserialize(serialized)
print("Deserialized Root Value:", deserialized.val) # -10

topics.pitfall: Attempting to serialize without None sentinels: without sentinels, an Inorder traversal sequence is also required to reconstruct the tree; with sentinels, Preorder alone suffices.

quickCheck.question: Why does Preorder serialization with null sentinels ("#") unambiguously reconstruct the tree without needing Inorder data?
options: Null sentinels explicitly record where subtrees terminate, removing all structural ambiguity
It works on full trees only
quickCheck.explanation: In standard traversals, two different tree structures can yield identical preorder outputs. Marking null leaf ends ensures a 1-to-1 unique mapping.

days.title: Binary Search Trees (BST): Invariants, Search & Mutations
days.subtitle: BST property, logarithmic search, node insertion, node deletion with successor & range validation
days.overview: Master the Binary Search Tree (BST) invariant: all left descendant keys < node key < all right descendant keys. Explore O(H) logarithmic search and insertion, three-case node deletion with in-order successors, BST range validation, and Kth smallest element.

topics.title: The BST Invariant & O(H) Search
explanation: A Binary Search Tree (BST) enforces the ordering invariant for EVERY node $X$:
- All keys in $X$'s left subtree are STRICTLY LESS than $X.val$.
- All keys in $X$'s right subtree are STRICTLY GREATER than $X.val$.
Searching in a BST:
- If `target == curr.val`: found!
- If `target < curr.val`: branch left (`curr = curr.left`).
- If `target > curr.val`: branch right (`curr = curr.right`).
Time: $O(H)$ where $H$ is height ($O(\log N)$ balanced, $O(N)$ skewed).
keyRules: The invariant applies to ALL nodes in the subtrees, not just immediate children!
Average search is O(log N).

codeSnippet.title: Iterative BST Search
codeSnippet.description: Logarithmic search branching left or right

topics.pitfall: Believing BST search is ALWAYS O(log N): if elements are inserted in sorted order `1, 2, 3, 4`, the tree becomes a skewed linked list with height N, degrading search to O(N). Balanced trees (AVL/Red-Black) fix this.

quickCheck.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for a key in an un-balanced Binary Search Tree with N nodes?
quickCheck.explanation: If keys were inserted in ascending order, the BST degenerates into a single long chain (height N), making search O(N).

topics.title: Validate Binary Search Tree (Range Constraint Propagation)
explanation: Problem: Determine if a given binary tree is a valid BST.
Common Mistake: Checking only immediate children (`node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val`). This fails if a right grandchild is smaller than the grandparent!
Correct Approach: Propagate valid numerical range `(min_val, max_val)` down the tree:
- Root must satisfy $(-\infty, +\infty)$.
- When branching left: update range to `(min_val, curr.val)`.
- When branching right: update range to `(curr.val, max_val)`.
Alternatively: Inorder traversal must be STRICTLY MONOTONICALLY INCREASING.
keyRules: Every node must satisfy min_val < node.val < max_val.
Duplicate values violate strict BST invariant (< and >).

codeSnippet.title: Validate BST via Range Constraints
codeSnippet.description: Propagating lower and upper bounds during DFS

topics.pitfall: Checking only `if node.left and node.left.val >= node.val`: this passes trees where a right descendant violates grandparent bounds.

quickCheck.question: Why does checking `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val` locally fail to validate a BST?
options: It fails to detect violations where a deep descendant violates an ancestor constraint higher up the tree
quickCheck.explanation: A node deep in the right subtree might be smaller than the root; local checks only examine immediate children, missing global violations.

topics.title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
explanation: Insertion in a BST is deterministic: the new key has a unique leaf slot that maintains the invariant.
Algorithm:
- Start at `root`.
- If `val < curr.val`: if `curr.left` is None, attach `curr.left = TreeNode(val)`. Else `curr = curr.left`.
- If `val > curr.val`: if `curr.right` is None, attach `curr.right = TreeNode(val)`. Else `curr = curr.right`.
Runs in $O(H)$ time and $O(1)$ space iterative.
keyRules: Iterative insertion uses O(1) auxiliary memory.
New keys are always inserted as new leaf nodes.

codeSnippet.title: Iterative BST Insertion
codeSnippet.description: O(H) search and leaf attachment

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to handle `root is None`: must return `TreeNode(val)` as the new root when inserting into an empty tree.

quickCheck.question: Where are new keys placed during standard BST insertion?
options: As a new leaf node at the position where the search terminated
quickCheck.explanation: Following the BST search path to a null pointer identifies the exact leaf location where the new key belongs.

topics.title: Delete Node in a BST (The Three Deletion Cases)
explanation: Deleting a key from a BST requires handling three distinct topological cases:
- **Case 1 (Leaf Node)**: 0 children. Simply remove the node (`return None`).
- **Case 2 (One Child)**: 1 child. Replace the node with its non-null child (`return node.left or node.right`).
- **Case 3 (Two Children)**: Find the Inorder Successor (the smallest node in the right subtree: leftmost child of `node.right`).
Copy the successor's value into the current node, then recursively delete the successor from the right subtree!
keyRules: Inorder successor is the minimum node of the right subtree: leftmost descendant.
Case 3 reduces to deleting a node with at most one child.

codeSnippet.title: Delete Node in BST
codeSnippet.description: Three-case deletion using inorder successor replacement
codeSnippet.code:
def delete_node_bst(root: TreeNode, key: int) -> TreeNode:
    if not root: return None
    
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = delete_node_bst(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = delete_node_bst(root.right, key)
    else:
        # Node to delete found!
        if not root.left: return root.right # Case 1 & 2
        if not root.right: return root.left # Case 2
        
        # Case 3: Two children -> find inorder successor (min in right subtree)
        successor = root.right
        while successor.left:
            successor = successor.left
            
        root.val = successor.val # replace value
        # Delete successor from right subtree
        root.right = delete_node_bst(root.right, successor.val)
        
    return root

# Delete 2 from bst_root (has children 1 and 3)
new_tree = delete_node_bst(bst_root, 2)
print("After deleting 2, root.left val:", new_tree.left.val) # 3 (successor replaced!)

topics.pitfall: Hard-deleting a node with two children by re-attaching its entire left subtree under the successor: this increases tree height unnecessarily and unbalances the tree.

quickCheck.question: What is the Inorder Successor of a node with two children in a BST?
options: The minimum (leftmost) node in its right subtree
The maximum node in its left subtree
quickCheck.explanation: The inorder successor is the smallest value greater than the target node, found by going right once, then left as far as possible.

topics.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
explanation: Problem: Given a BST, find the $K$-th smallest element ($1$-indexed).
Because Inorder Traversal visits nodes in strictly ascending sorted order, the $K$-th node visited during Inorder traversal IS the $K$-th smallest element!
Iterative approach with explicit stack:
- Drive left onto stack.
- Pop node, decrement $K$. When $K == 0$, return `node.val` immediately.
- Move to `node.right`.
Time: $O(H + K)$ early exit without traversing the entire tree!
keyRules: Early exit when K == 0 avoids full tree traversal.
Runs in O(H + K) time and O(H) space.

codeSnippet.title: Kth Smallest Element via Inorder Stack
codeSnippet.description: Early-exit iterative inorder traversal
codeSnippet.code:
def kth_smallest(root: TreeNode, k: int) -> int:
    stack = []
    curr = root
    
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
            
        curr = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return curr.val # Kth smallest found!
            
        curr = curr.right
        
    return -1

# BST: 3 -> left: 1 (has right: 2), right: 4
b3 = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1, None, TreeNode(2)), TreeNode(4))
print("1st smallest:", kth_smallest(b3, 1)) # 1
print("2nd smallest:", kth_smallest(b3, 2)) # 2

topics.pitfall: Dumping all node values into an array with full traversal and then indexing `arr[k-1]`: wastes O(N) space and time when K=1.

quickCheck.question: What is the best-case time complexity to find the 1st smallest element in a BST of N nodes using iterative inorder stack?
options: O(H) where H is tree height
quickCheck.explanation: The 1st smallest element is the leftmost node in the tree; navigating down the left spine takes O(H) steps, stopping immediately.

topics.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST (Exploiting Order)
explanation: In a general Binary Tree, LCA takes $O(N)$ because you must search both subtrees.
In a Binary Search Tree, we can exploit the BST ordering invariant to find the LCA in $O(H)$ time and $O(1)$ space!
- If both `p.val` and `q.val` are strictly less than `root.val`: LCA MUST be in the left subtree (`root = root.left`).
- If both `p.val` and `q.val` are strictly greater than `root.val`: LCA MUST be in the right subtree (`root = root.right`).
- Otherwise: `root` is the split point where $P$ and $Q$ diverge (or root equals $P$ or $Q$). Therefore, `root` IS the LCA!
keyRules: Split point is the LCA: p.val <= root.val <= q.val (or vice versa).
O(H) time and strictly O(1) space iterative.

codeSnippet.title: LCA in Binary Search Tree
codeSnippet.description: O(H) time and O(1) space split-point discovery

topics.pitfall: Recursing into both subtrees: unnecessary in a BST! You only branch in ONE direction at each step.

quickCheck.question: What identifies the Lowest Common Ancestor of p and q in a BST?
options: The first node whose value falls between p.val and q.val (the split point)
quickCheck.explanation: The moment p and q lie on opposite sides of a node (one < curr.val and one > curr.val), that node is their unique lowest common ancestor.

topics.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree (Height-Balanced)
explanation: Problem: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order, convert it to a height-balanced BST.
Divide and Conquer:
To ensure the tree is perfectly balanced, the MIDDLE element of the array must be chosen as the `root`!
- `mid = (left + right) // 2`.
- `root = TreeNode(nums[mid])`.
- `root.left = build(left, mid - 1)`.
- `root.right = build(mid + 1, right)`.
Time: $O(N)$ visiting each element once. Tree height is guaranteed $\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor$.
keyRules: Middle element is chosen as root to split elements equally (N/2 left, N/2 right).
Pass indices (left, right) rather than slicing arrays to save O(N) copy memory.

codeSnippet.title: Sorted Array to Balanced BST
codeSnippet.description: Recursive midpoint partitioning in O(N)
codeSnippet.code:
def sorted_array_to_bst(nums: list[int]) -> TreeNode:
    def build(left: int, right: int) -> TreeNode:
        if left > right: return None
        mid = left + (right - left) // 2
        node = TreeNode(nums[mid])
        node.left = build(left, mid - 1)
        node.right = build(mid + 1, right)
        return node
        
    return build(0, len(nums) - 1)

balanced_tree = sorted_array_to_bst([-10, -3, 0, 5, 9])
print("Root of balanced BST:", balanced_tree.val) # 0

topics.pitfall: Slicing the array `build(nums[:mid])`: slicing creates new array copies at every recursive call, increasing total time to O(N log N) and space to O(N log N). Pass indices instead.

quickCheck.question: Why does choosing the midpoint of a sorted array as the root guarantee a balanced BST?
options: It guarantees that the number of elements in the left subtree and right subtree differ by at most 1
Because the array length is even
quickCheck.explanation: Selecting the middle element divides the remaining elements into two equal halves of size N/2, ensuring equal tree heights.

topics.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
explanation: Given preorder and inorder traversals, reconstruct the unique binary tree.
Key Insights:
1. `preorder[0]` is ALWAYS the root of the tree!
2. Find the root's index in `inorder`: elements to the left belong to the LEFT subtree; elements to the right belong to the RIGHT subtree!
3. Precompute `inorder` value-to-index mapping in a Hash Map for $O(1)$ index lookups.
Total Time: $O(N)$ with $O(N)$ space.
keyRules: Use a hash map for inorder indices to eliminate O(N) searches.
Track boundaries with left and right indices.

codeSnippet.title: Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder
codeSnippet.description: Hash-map accelerated tree reconstruction in O(N)
codeSnippet.code:
def build_tree(preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> TreeNode:
    in_map = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}
    pre_idx = 0
    
    def helper(in_left: int, in_right: int) -> TreeNode:
        nonlocal pre_idx
        if in_left > in_right: return None
        
        root_val = preorder[pre_idx]
        pre_idx += 1
        root = TreeNode(root_val)
        
        mid = in_map[root_val]
        # Must build left subtree first because preorder is Root -> Left -> Right!
        root.left = helper(in_left, mid - 1)
        root.right = helper(mid + 1, in_right)
        return root
        
    return helper(0, len(inorder) - 1)

rebuilt = build_tree([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
print("Rebuilt tree root:", rebuilt.val) # 3

topics.pitfall: Calling `root.right` before `root.left`: `pre_idx` advances in preorder sequence (Root, Left, Right), so `root.left` MUST be built first.

quickCheck.question: Why must `root.left` be constructed before `root.right` when reconstructing from preorder traversal?
options: Because preorder traversal visits the left subtree immediately after the root, so pre_idx points to left subtree elements next
quickCheck.explanation: The preorder sequence places all nodes of the left subtree before any nodes of the right subtree.

days.title: Balanced BSTs: AVL Trees & Red-Black Tree Mechanics
days.subtitle: Tree balance factors, Left/Right rotations, double rotations LL/RR/LR/RL & Red-Black tree invariants
days.overview: Eliminate the O(N) worst-case degeneracy of unbalanced BSTs. Master self-balancing binary search trees: AVL Tree Balance Factors, Single Rotations (Left/Right), Double Rotations (LR/RL), and the five architectural invariants of Red-Black Trees powering production standard libraries.

topics.title: The Degeneracy Problem & Self-Balancing Rationale
explanation: An un-balanced BST degrades to $O(N)$ when keys are inserted in sequential order.
A Self-Balancing BST automatically performs local transformations during insertion and deletion to keep tree height bounded by $O(\log N)$.
Two industry standards:
- **AVL Trees**: Strictly balanced (balance factor $\in \{-1, 0, +1\}$). Faster lookups; slower insertions/deletions due to frequent rotations.
- **Red-Black Trees**: More relaxed balance (height $\le 2 \log_2(N + 1)$). Fewer rotations on insertion/deletion; powers `std::map`, `std::set`, and Linux kernel VM maps.
keyRules: Guarantees worst-case O(log N) for search, insert, and delete.
Local restructuring is achieved via Tree Rotations.

codeSnippet.title: Height Comparison: Unbalanced vs Balanced
codeSnippet.description: Demonstrating tree height explosion without rebalancing
codeSnippet.code:
import math

N = 1_000_000
unbalanced_height = N
balanced_height = math.ceil(math.log2(N))
print(f"For N = 1,000,000 nodes:")
print(f"Unbalanced BST Height: {unbalanced_height:,} steps (Fatal!)")
print(f"Balanced BST Height:   {balanced_height} steps (Instantaneous!)")

topics.pitfall: Assuming tree rotations change the in-order traversal: rotations are specifically designed to preserve the exact BST in-order sorted invariant while altering tree height.

quickCheck.question: What is the primary guarantee of a self-balancing binary search tree?
options: Tree height is strictly bounded by O(log N), preventing degenerate O(N) operations
quickCheck.explanation: Self-balancing trees maintain logarithmic height bounds through rotations, ensuring search, insert, and delete remain O(log N) in the worst case.

topics.title: Tree Rotations: Left Rotation & Right Rotation
explanation: A Tree Rotation is an $O(1)$ local pointer manipulation that changes tree height while preserving the Inorder traversal invariant.
- **Right Rotation** on node $Y$ (with left child $X$):
$X$ becomes the new parent. $Y$ becomes $X$'s right child. $X$'s former right child $T_2$ becomes $Y$'s left child.
- **Left Rotation** on node $X$ (with right child $Y$):
$Y$ becomes the new parent. $X$ becomes $Y$'s left child. $Y$'s former left child $T_2$ becomes $X$'s right child.
keyRules: Rotations take strictly O(1) time and require only 3 pointer updates.
Inorder sequence (A < X < B < Y < C) is identical before and after rotation.

codeSnippet.title: Right and Left Rotation Implementations
codeSnippet.description: O(1) pointer rotations preserving BST invariant
codeSnippet.code:
class AVLNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None
        self.height = 1

def right_rotate(y: AVLNode) -> AVLNode:
    x = y.left
    T2 = x.right
    # Perform rotation
    x.right = y
    y.left = T2
    # Update heights
    y.height = 1 + max(get_h(y.left), get_h(y.right))
    x.height = 1 + max(get_h(x.left), get_h(x.right))
    return x # new root

def left_rotate(x: AVLNode) -> AVLNode:
    y = x.right
    T2 = y.left
    # Perform rotation
    y.left = x
    x.right = T2
    # Update heights
    x.height = 1 + max(get_h(x.left), get_h(x.right))
    y.height = 1 + max(get_h(y.left), get_h(y.right))
    return y # new root

def get_h(node) -> int: return node.height if node else 0

topics.pitfall: Updating node heights in wrong order: y becomes a child of x after right rotation, so y's height MUST be recalculated before x's height.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of a tree rotation operation?
quickCheck.explanation: Rotations alter a constant number of pointer references (parent and child links), executing in strictly O(1) time.

topics.title: AVL Tree: Balance Factor & The 4 Rotation Cases
explanation: In an AVL tree, every node defines $\text{Balance Factor} = \text{height}(\text{left}) - \text{height}(\text{right})$.
Invariant: Balance Factor MUST be $\in \{-1, 0, +1\}$.
When an insertion causes $|BF| > 1$, four rotation cases restore balance:
1. **Left-Left (LL)**: $BF > 1$ and `key < node.left.val` -> Single Right Rotate(`node`).
2. **Right-Right (RR)**: $BF < -1$ and `key > node.right.val` -> Single Left Rotate(`node`).
3. **Left-Right (LR)**: $BF > 1$ and `key > node.left.val` -> Left Rotate(`node.left`), then Right Rotate(`node`).
4. **Right-Left (RL)**: $BF < -1$ and `key < node.right.val` -> Right Rotate(`node.right`), then Left Rotate(`node`).
keyRules: Outer imbalances (LL / RR) require 1 single rotation.
Inner dogleg imbalances (LR / RL) require 2 double rotations.

codeSnippet.title: AVL Tree Rebalance Dispatcher
codeSnippet.description: Selecting from the 4 rotation cases based on balance factor

topics.pitfall: Performing a single rotation for an inner dogleg (LR): single rotation on an LR imbalance leaves the tree unbalanced! Must left-rotate child first to transform into LL, then right-rotate parent.

quickCheck.question: What sequence of rotations resolves a Left-Right (LR) imbalance in an AVL tree?
options: Left Rotate the left child, then Right Rotate the node
quickCheck.explanation: An LR dogleg is straightened into an LL line by left-rotating the left child, followed by a right rotation on the unbalanced parent.

topics.title: Complete AVL Tree Insertion Implementation
explanation: Assemble the full recursive AVL insertion algorithm:
1. Perform standard BST recursive insertion.
2. Update height of current ancestor node: `1 + max(left_h, right_h)`.
3. Compute balance factor `get_balance(node)`.
4. If unbalanced, apply the appropriate rotation and return the new subtree root.
Guarantees height is strictly bounded by $1.44 \log_2 N$.
keyRules: Rebalancing unwinds along the recursion call stack from leaf to root.
At most ONE rotation (or double rotation) is needed per insertion.

codeSnippet.title: Complete AVL Tree Insertion
codeSnippet.description: Self-balancing AVL insertion with automatic rotations

topics.pitfall: Forgetting to return the rotated root up the recursion stack: if you do `right_rotate(root)` without reassigning `root = right_rotate(root)`, parent pointers remain attached to the old unrotated root.

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum number of rotations required to rebalance an AVL tree after an insertion?
quickCheck.explanation: A single rotation or double rotation at the lowest unbalanced ancestor completely restores the AVL invariant for the entire tree.

topics.title: Red-Black Tree: The Five Architectural Invariants
explanation: A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing BST where each node stores a color bit (`RED` or `BLACK`).
The 5 Invariants:
1. Every node is either RED or BLACK.
2. The root is ALWAYS BLACK.
3. Every leaf (NIL null pointer) is considered BLACK.
4. If a node is RED, both its children MUST BE BLACK (No two consecutive RED nodes!).
5. Every path from a node to any of its descendant NIL leaves contains the EXACT SAME NUMBER of black nodes ("Black-Height").
keyRules: Invariant 4 & 5 mathematically guarantee that the longest path (alternating red-black) is at most twice the length of the shortest path (all black).
Maximum height is strictly bounded by 2 * log2(N + 1).

codeSnippet.title: Red-Black Node Definition & Colors
codeSnippet.description: Core color constants and structural invariants
codeSnippet.code:
RED = True
BLACK = False

class RBNode:
    def __init__(self, val, color=RED):
        self.val = val
        self.color = color # newly inserted nodes are always RED!
        self.left = None
        self.right = None
        self.parent = None

# Why are new nodes inserted as RED?
# Because adding a RED node does NOT violate Invariant 5 (Black-Height)!
# It may only violate Invariant 4 (no red-red), which is easily fixed by recoloring or rotations.

topics.pitfall: Inserting new nodes as BLACK: inserting a black node immediately violates Invariant 5 (Black-Height) on that branch, which is much harder to fix than a red-red collision.

quickCheck.question: Why are newly inserted nodes in a Red-Black Tree colored RED by default?
options: Because red is faster to process
To preserve the Black-Height invariant (Invariant 5) along all leaf paths
quickCheck.explanation: Inserting a red node preserves the black-height invariant for all paths, limiting potential violations to the local red-child constraint (Invariant 4).

topics.title: Red-Black Tree Insertion: Recoloring vs Rotations
explanation: When a RED node is inserted under a RED parent, an Invariant 4 violation occurs.
The resolution depends on the color of the **UNCLE** node (sibling of the parent):
- **Case 1 (Uncle is RED)**: Simple Recoloring! Recolor Parent and Uncle to BLACK; recolor Grandparent to RED. Propagate check up to Grandparent.
- **Case 2 (Uncle is BLACK - Dogleg)**: Rotate child into a straight line.
- **Case 3 (Uncle is BLACK - Straight Line)**: Rotate Grandparent, swap colors of Parent and Grandparent. Done in $O(1)$ rotations!
keyRules: Red uncle = recoloring only (no rotations).
Black uncle = rotations required (at most 2 rotations per insertion).

codeSnippet.title: Red-Black Tree Insertion Logic Model
codeSnippet.description: Uncle color diagnostic for recoloring vs rotation

topics.pitfall: Assuming Red-Black Trees require many rotations: insertion requires at most 2 rotations; deletion requires at most 3 rotations.

quickCheck.question: In a Red-Black Tree, what action is taken when both parent and uncle are RED?
options: Recolor parent and uncle to BLACK, recolor grandparent to RED, and continue checking upward
quickCheck.explanation: When the uncle is red, a simple recoloring pushes the red property up to the grandparent without requiring any geometric tree rotations.

topics.title: AVL vs Red-Black Trees: Industrial Engineering Trade-Offs
explanation: When should you choose AVL vs Red-Black in production?

- **AVL Trees**: More strictly balanced (height $\approx 1.0 \log_2 N$). Lookups are faster because tree height is strictly minimal. Choose AVL when the workload is **READ-HEAVY** (e.g. database query indices, dictionary lookups).

- **Red-Black Trees**: Slightly more relaxed balance (height $\le 1.44 \log_2 N$). Insertions and deletions require fewer rotations (at most 2 or 3). Choose Red-Black when the workload has **FREQUENT WRITES/MUTATIONS** (e.g. Linux scheduler CFS, Java `TreeMap`, C++ `std::map`).
keyRules: Read-Heavy -> AVL Trees.
Write-Heavy or Balanced -> Red-Black Trees.
Both guarantee O(log N) worst-case time.

codeSnippet.title: Industrial Data Structure Selection Matrix
codeSnippet.description: Workload-driven balanced tree selector

topics.pitfall: Using an in-memory balanced tree for disk databases: disk blocks are 4KB; binary trees make too many pointer hops. Use B-Trees or B+ Trees for disk I/O.

quickCheck.question: Why do the C++ STL (std::map) and Java Collections (TreeMap) use Red-Black Trees instead of AVL Trees?
