options: Red-Black trees require fewer rotations on insertions and deletions, making general-purpose modifications faster
Red-Black trees do not require pointers
quickCheck.explanation: General-purpose libraries expect frequent insertions and deletions; Red-Black trees bound rotations to at most 3 per modification, reducing write overhead.

topics.title: B-Trees and 2-3-4 Trees: Scaling Beyond Memory Cache Lines
explanation: Red-Black trees are isomorphic to **2-3-4 Trees** (each black node grouped with its red children forms a 2-node, 3-node, or 4-node).
When data exceeds RAM and resides on SSD/Hard Drive, binary pointer chasing causes crippling disk I/O latency.
A **B-Tree** generalizes 2-3-4 trees to thousands of keys per node (e.g., $M = 1024$), matching the OS disk page size (4KB to 64KB).
A B-Tree of height 3 can index billions of database records with only 3 disk reads!
keyRules: B-Trees optimize for block storage and cache lines.
Multi-way branching keeps tree height extremely flat (typically 3-4 levels).

codeSnippet.title: B-Tree Fanout Demonstration
codeSnippet.description: Calculating records indexed by high-fanout B-Tree
codeSnippet.code:
def btree_capacity(order: int, height: int) -> int:
    # Each node has up to 'order' children
    return (order ** height)

fanout = 512 # 512 keys per 4KB disk page
print(f"B-Tree Height 1: {btree_capacity(fanout, 1):,} records")
print(f"B-Tree Height 2: {btree_capacity(fanout, 2):,} records")
print(f"B-Tree Height 3: {btree_capacity(fanout, 3):,} records (134 Million!)")
print(f"B-Tree Height 4: {btree_capacity(fanout, 4):,} records (68 Billion records in just 4 disk hops!)")

topics.pitfall: Using binary search trees for relational databases: reading single binary nodes from disk incurs millions of disk seeks.

quickCheck.question: Why are B-Trees preferred over Binary Search Trees for database storage engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB)?
options: High-fanout multi-way nodes match OS disk page sizes, keeping tree height flat and minimizing expensive disk I/O reads
quickCheck.explanation: With a fanout of hundreds or thousands of keys per node, B-trees can index billions of rows with only 3 or 4 disk page fetches.

days.title: Heaps & Priority Queues
days.subtitle: Binary heap array representation, Bubble-Up, Sift-Down, O(N) linear heapify & Top-K elements
days.overview: Harness the Priority Queue abstraction. Build binary Min and Max Heaps packed in contiguous arrays with zero pointer overhead, prove why Floyd's Heapify builds a heap in O(N) linear time, solve Top-K Frequent Elements, and build the Dual-Heap Median Stream engine.

topics.title: The Binary Heap & Contiguous Array Layout
explanation: A Binary Heap is a Complete Binary Tree (every level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right).
Because it is complete, it requires ZERO pointers! It is stored directly in a flat 0-indexed contiguous array:
- Root is at index `0`.
- For node at index `i`:
- Left Child: `2 * i + 1`.
- Right Child: `2 * i + 2`.
Max-Heap Invariant: `parent.val >= child.val` for all nodes.
keyRules: Parent index = (i - 1) // 2.
Children indices = 2*i + 1 and 2*i + 2.
Zero pointer overhead and maximum CPU cache locality.

codeSnippet.title: Heap Index Arithmetic
codeSnippet.description: Parent and child pointer-free array index math
codeSnippet.code:
def get_parent(i: int) -> int: return (i - 1) // 2
def get_left(i: int) -> int: return 2 * i + 1
def get_right(i: int) -> int: return 2 * i + 2

heap_array = [100, 19, 36, 17, 3, 25, 1, 2, 7]
print("Root:", heap_array[0])
print("Left child of root:", heap_array[get_left(0)])   # 19
print("Right child of root:", heap_array[get_right(0)]) # 36
print("Parent of index 4 (val 3):", heap_array[get_parent(4)]) # 19

topics.pitfall: Accessing child indices without verifying bounds `2 * i + 1 < len(heap)`: triggers out-of-range errors on leaf nodes.

quickCheck.question: What is the formula for the left child index of node `i` in a 0-indexed binary heap array?
quickCheck.explanation: In 0-indexed arrays, the left child is at index 2*i + 1 and the right child is at index 2*i + 2.

topics.title: Bubble-Up (Sift-Up) on Insertion: O(log N)
explanation: To insert an element into a heap:
1. Append the new value to the END of the array (preserving the Complete Tree property).
2. Bubble-Up (Sift-Up): Compare the new element with its parent `(i - 1) // 2`.
3. In a Max-Heap, if `child > parent`: swap them! Repeat until the invariant holds or the element reaches the root.
Because the tree height is strictly $\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor$, insertion takes at most $O(\log N)$ swaps.
keyRules: Appends at end, bubbles up to root.
Time complexity is O(log N).

codeSnippet.title: Bubble-Up Heap Insertion
codeSnippet.description: Pushing to end and bubbling up in O(log N)

topics.pitfall: Checking `while idx >= 0`: when idx is 0, parent is `(0 - 1) // 2 = -1`, which wraps around to the back of the Python list! Must be `while idx > 0`.

quickCheck.question: What is the maximum number of swaps performed during a heap push operation on N elements?
quickCheck.explanation: The element travels up from a leaf along a single branch to the root, bounded by tree height log2(N).

topics.title: Sift-Down on Extraction: O(log N)
explanation: To extract the root (maximum element):
1. Save `root_val = heap[0]`.
2. Move the LAST element of the array to index `0`, and pop the last slot (`O(1)`).
3. Sift-Down: Compare the new root with its children (`2i + 1` and `2i + 2`).
4. Swap with the LARGER of the two children (in Max-Heap). Repeat until invariant holds or a leaf is reached.
Guarantees $O(\log N)$ extraction time.
keyRules: Always swap with the LARGER child in a Max-Heap (or SMALLER child in a Min-Heap).
Moving last element to root maintains complete tree shape.

codeSnippet.title: Sift-Down Heap Pop
codeSnippet.description: Extracting root and restoring invariant via sift-down
codeSnippet.code:
def pop_max(self) -> int:
    if not self.heap: raise IndexError("pop from empty heap")
    if len(self.heap) == 1: return self.heap.pop()
    
    root_val = self.heap[0]
    self.heap[0] = self.heap.pop() # move last to root
    self._sift_down(0)
    return root_val

def _sift_down(self, idx: int):
    n = len(self.heap)
    while True:
        largest = idx
        left = 2 * idx + 1
        right = 2 * idx + 2
        
        if left < n and self.heap[left] > self.heap[largest]:
            largest = left
        if right < n and self.heap[right] > self.heap[largest]:
            largest = right
            
        if largest == idx: break
        self.heap[idx], self.heap[largest] = self.heap[largest], self.heap[idx]
        idx = largest

MaxHeap.pop_max = pop_max
MaxHeap._sift_down = _sift_down

print("Extracted max:", h.pop_max()) # 30
print("New root:", h.heap[0])         # 20

topics.pitfall: Swapping with whichever child is valid instead of the larger child: if left is 25 and right is 30, swapping with 25 violates the heap property with the right child!

quickCheck.question: Why must we swap with the larger of the two children during Sift-Down in a Max-Heap?
options: Because the new parent must be greater than BOTH children; choosing the largest child guarantees this
quickCheck.explanation: If you swapped with the smaller child, the larger child would still be greater than the new parent, violating the Max-Heap invariant.

topics.title: Floyd's Heapify: Why Building a Heap is O(N) Linear Time
explanation: Naive insertion of $N$ elements into an empty heap takes $N \times O(\log N) = O(N \log N)$.
Floyd's Heapify transforms an arbitrary array of $N$ elements into a valid heap in strictly $O(N)$ linear time!
Algorithm: Start at the last non-leaf parent index `(N // 2) - 1` and call `sift_down` backwards to index 0.
Mathematical Proof: Most nodes are near the leaves and do almost 0 swaps; only the few nodes near the root do $O(\log N)$ swaps. The sum $\sum_{h=0}^{\infty} \frac{h}{2^h} = 2$, proving exact $O(N)$!
keyRules: Start sift_down from (N // 2) - 1 down to 0.
Heapify is O(N) time (NOT O(N log N)).

codeSnippet.title: Floyds Linear O(N) Heapify
codeSnippet.description: Building a heap in place in linear time
codeSnippet.code:
def heapify(arr: list[int]) -> None:
    n = len(arr)
    # Start at last non-leaf parent and sift down backwards
    for i in range((n // 2) - 1, -1, -1):
        idx = i
        while True:
            largest = idx
            left = 2 * idx + 1
            right = 2 * idx + 2
            if left < n and arr[left] > arr[largest]: largest = left
            if right < n and arr[right] > arr[largest]: largest = right
            if largest == idx: break
            arr[idx], arr[largest] = arr[largest], arr[idx]
            idx = largest

raw_data = [4, 10, 3, 5, 1]
heapify(raw_data)
print("Linear Heapified Array:", raw_data) # [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]

topics.pitfall: Calling sift_up from index 0 to N: sift_up takes O(N log N) total time! Linear O(N) is achieved ONLY by bottom-up sift_down.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of size N using Floyds Heapify?
quickCheck.explanation: Because the vast majority of nodes reside at or near leaf levels where sift-down depth is small (0 or 1), the geometric sum converges to O(N).

topics.title: Heap Sort: In-Place Comparison Sort
explanation: Heap Sort achieves $O(N \log N)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
1. Build a Max-Heap from the array in $O(N)$ using Heapify.
2. For $i$ from $N - 1$ down to 1:
a. Swap `arr[0]` (current max) with `arr[i]` (placing max in its permanent sorted position at end).
b. Call `sift_down(0)` on the reduced heap of size $i$.
Result: In-place sorted array with zero buffer allocations!
keyRules: Time: O(N log N) best, worst, average.
Auxiliary Space: strictly O(1) in-place.
Unstable sorting algorithm.

codeSnippet.title: Heap Sort Implementation
codeSnippet.description: In-place O(N log N) sorting with Max-Heap
codeSnippet.code:
def heap_sort(arr: list[int]) -> None:
    n = len(arr)
    # 1. Build max heap in O(N)
    for i in range((n // 2) - 1, -1, -1):
        _sift_down_range(arr, n, i)
        
    # 2. Extract max to back of array
    for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        arr[0], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[0] # swap max to sorted position
        _sift_down_range(arr, i, 0)     # re-heapify remaining elements

def _sift_down_range(arr, limit, idx):
    while True:
        largest = idx
        left = 2 * idx + 1
        right = 2 * idx + 2
        if left < limit and arr[left] > arr[largest]: largest = left
        if right < limit and arr[right] > arr[largest]: largest = right
        if largest == idx: break
        arr[idx], arr[largest] = arr[largest], arr[idx]
        idx = largest

nums = [12, 11, 13, 5, 6, 7]
heap_sort(nums)
print("Heap Sorted:", nums) # [5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13]

topics.pitfall: Believing Heap Sort is faster than Quick Sort in practice: while both are O(N log N), Heap Sort has poor cache locality (jumping across array indices 2i+1 and 2i+2), making it 2x-3x slower than QuickSort in real hardware benchmarks.

quickCheck.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of Heap Sort?
quickCheck.explanation: Heap Sort rearranges elements directly within the existing input array, requiring strictly O(1) auxiliary memory.

topics.title: Top K Frequent Elements (Min-Heap of Size K)
explanation: Problem: Given an integer array `nums` and integer $k$, return the $k$ most frequent elements.
Sorting frequencies takes $O(N \log N)$.
Min-Heap Optimization of Size $K$:
1. Count frequencies using a hash map: `counts = Counter(nums)`.
2. Iterate through frequency pairs `(count, num)`. Push to a Min-Heap of size $K$.
3. When heap size exceeds $K$: pop the minimum element (`heappop`).
At the end, the heap contains the $K$ elements with the HIGHEST frequencies!
Time: $O(N \log K)$ (much faster than $O(N \log N)$ when $K \ll N$).
keyRules: Use a MIN-HEAP to maintain the TOP-K elements (smallest of the top-K is popped).
Space is O(N + K).

codeSnippet.title: Top K Frequent Elements via Min-Heap
codeSnippet.description: Bounded heap of size K in O(N log K) time
codeSnippet.code:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    # Min-heap storing tuples: (frequency, num)
    heap = []
    
    for num, freq in counts.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (freq, num))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap) # evict element with smallest frequency
            
    return [num for freq, num in heap]

print("Top 2 frequent in [1,1,1,2,2,3]:", top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2)) # [2, 1]

topics.pitfall: Using a max-heap of all N elements: pushing all N elements takes O(N log N) time; keeping a bounded MIN-heap of size K takes strictly O(N log K).

quickCheck.question: Why do we use a MIN-heap (instead of a max-heap) to find the top K largest elements?
options: The min-heap root stores the smallest of the top-K candidates, allowing instant O(1) eviction of the lowest contender when capacity is breached
quickCheck.explanation: A bounded min-heap keeps the smallest element at the root, making it trivial to discard the least viable contender whenever size exceeds K.

topics.title: Find Median from Data Stream (Dual-Heap Architecture)
explanation: Problem: Design a data structure that supports adding numbers from a continuous stream and finding the current median in $O(1)$ time.
The Dual-Heap Balancing Architecture:
- `small`: A **Max-Heap** storing the lower half of numbers (simulated with negated values in Python).
- `large`: A **Min-Heap** storing the upper half of numbers.
Invariants:
1. Every element in `small` $\le$ every element in `large`.
2. Size invariant: `len(small) == len(large)` OR `len(small) == len(large) + 1`.
Median is either `small[0]` (odd count) or `(small[0] + large[0]) / 2.0` (even count) in instantaneous $O(1)$!
keyRules: small is Max-Heap; large is Min-Heap.
Insertion takes O(log N); finding median is O(1).

codeSnippet.title: Dual-Heap Median Finder
codeSnippet.description: Max-heap and min-heap maintaining dynamic stream median

topics.pitfall: Re-sorting the array on each insertion: `arr.sort()` on every `addNum` costs $O(N \log N)$ per addition ($O(N^2)$ overall), timing out completely.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity to retrieve the median using the Dual-Heap MedianFinder?
quickCheck.explanation: The roots of the small max-heap and large min-heap are immediately accessible at index 0, enabling O(1) constant-time median retrieval.

topics.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays (K-Way Heap Merge)
explanation: Given $K$ sorted arrays with total $N$ elements, merge them into a single sorted array in $O(N \log K)$ time.
Algorithm:
1. Insert the first element of each of the $K$ arrays into a Min-Heap: `(val, array_idx, element_idx)`.
2. Pop the minimum element from the heap and append to `result`.
3. If that array has more elements, push its next element `(arr[next_idx], array_idx, next_idx)` into the heap.
4. Repeat until heap is empty.
Runs in $O(N \log K)$ time and $O(K)$ auxiliary space.
keyRules: Heap size never exceeds K.
Tracks array index and element index alongside value.

codeSnippet.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays via Min-Heap
codeSnippet.description: K-way merge in O(N log K) time and O(K) space
codeSnippet.code:
import heapq

def merge_k_sorted_arrays(arrays: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    heap = [] # (value, array_index, element_index)
    
    # 1. Initialize heap with first element of each non-empty array
    for i, arr in enumerate(arrays):
        if arr:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (arr[0], i, 0))
            
    res = []
    # 2. Extract min and push next element from that array
    while heap:
        val, arr_i, el_i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        res.append(val)
        if el_i + 1 < len(arrays[arr_i]):
            next_val = arrays[arr_i][el_i + 1]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (next_val, arr_i, el_i + 1))
            
    return res

lists = [[1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], [3, 6, 9]]
print("Merged K Arrays:", merge_k_sorted_arrays(lists)) # [1..9]

topics.pitfall: Concatenating all arrays and running full `sort()`: takes O(N log N) and fails to exploit the pre-sorted property of the K individual arrays.

quickCheck.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of K-way heap merge?
quickCheck.explanation: The min-heap holds at most one element from each of the K arrays at any given time, requiring O(K) auxiliary space.

days.title: Tries (Prefix Trees) & Prefix Automata
days.subtitle: TrieNode architecture, insert, search, startsWith, wildcards & prefix search engines
days.overview: Explore the Prefix Tree (Trie) data structure designed for ultra-fast string retrieval and autocomplete dictionaries. Master TrieNode branching, O(L) word insertion and prefix matching, wildcard pattern matching with dots, and memory compaction.

topics.title: The Prefix Tree Architecture: Eliminating Redundant Prefixes
explanation: A Trie (pronounced "try", from reTRIEval) is a multi-way tree structure where each node represents a common prefix character.
All descendants of a node share the prefix associated with that node.
Each node contains:
- `children`: Hash map or fixed array of 26 child references.
- `is_end_of_word`: Boolean flag indicating if a word terminates at this node.
Key Advantage: Searching for a word of length $L$ takes $O(L)$ time, COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT of how many millions of words ($N$) are stored in the dictionary!
keyRules: Search time is O(L) where L is string length, not dictionary size N.
Common prefixes (e.g. "car", "cart", "carpet") share the same root path nodes.

codeSnippet.title: TrieNode Class Definition
codeSnippet.description: Core building block of prefix trees

topics.pitfall: Storing the full word or character inside the node: the character is represented by the EDGE (key in the `children` dictionary), not stored inside the child node itself.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity to search for a word of length L in a Trie containing 10,000,000 words?
quickCheck.explanation: Trie lookup follows exactly L character links from root to leaf, executing in O(L) time regardless of how many millions of words exist in the Trie.

topics.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree): Insert, Search & StartsWith
explanation: Implement the canonical Trie API:
- `insert(word)`: For each char in word, if not in `curr.children`, create new `TrieNode`. Move `curr = curr.children[char]`. At end, set `curr.is_end_of_word = True`.
- `search(word)`: Follow char links. If any char is missing, return `False`. At end, return `curr.is_end_of_word`.
- `startsWith(prefix)`: Follow char links. If prefix exists, return `True` (does NOT require `is_end_of_word` to be true!).
keyRules: search() requires is_end_of_word == True.
startsWith() only requires that the path exists.

codeSnippet.title: Complete Trie Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Insert, Search and StartsWith methods in O(L)

topics.pitfall: Returning True in `search("app")` when only "apple" was inserted: "app" is only a prefix, not a full word. `is_end_of_word` prevents this false positive.

quickCheck.question: What is the difference between search(word) and startsWith(prefix)?
options: search only works on capital letters
search requires is_end_of_word to be True at the terminal node, while startsWith only requires that the path exists
quickCheck.explanation: search confirms that a full word was inserted; startsWith confirms that at least one word in the Trie begins with that prefix.

topics.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (Wildcard Matching)
explanation: Problem: Support `addWord(word)` and `search(word)` where `word` can contain the dot character `.` which matches ANY letter.
If character is a letter: follow the single child link `curr.children[char]`.
If character is `.`: RECURSE across ALL active children in `curr.children.values()`! If ANY recursive branch returns True, return True.
DFS Backtracking over Trie branches for wildcard resolution.
keyRules: Dot wildcard branches into all existing children.
Runs in O(M) for exact words; worst case O(26^L) for all-dot words ("...").

codeSnippet.title: Wildcard Word Dictionary with Dots
codeSnippet.description: Trie search with DFS branching on "." wildcard

topics.pitfall: Checking 26 letters naively in a loop when `c == "."`: only iterate over `node.children.values()` to avoid testing non-existent branches.

quickCheck.question: What happens when a "." wildcard is encountered during WordDictionary search?
options: DFS branches into all existing children of the current Trie node
quickCheck.explanation: The dot can match any character, so the algorithm explores every child branch currently branching from that node.

topics.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array (Bitwise Trie)
explanation: Problem: Given an integer array `nums`, return the maximum result of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]`.
Brute force checks all pairs in $O(N^2)$ time.
Bitwise Binary Trie in $O(N \times 31) = O(N)$ time:
1. Insert 31-bit binary representation of each number into a binary Trie (children are `0` and `1`).
2. For each number, greedily traverse the Trie to maximize XOR: at bit $B$, if the current bit is $b$, we PREFER to take the OPPOSITE bit $1 - b$ (since $b \oplus (1-b) = 1$).
3. If opposite branch exists, take it and set bit $B$ to 1 in result; else take matching branch.
keyRules: Binary Trie has fixed alphabet {0, 1}.
Greedy choice: always pick opposite bit to maximize leading 1-bits.

codeSnippet.title: Maximum XOR via Binary Trie
codeSnippet.description: Greedy bitwise opposite-branch traversal in O(32N)

topics.pitfall: Scanning from bit 0 up to 30: greedy bit selection MUST proceed from most significant bit (bit 30) down to 0, because a 1 in a higher place value outweighs all lower bits combined!

quickCheck.question: Why does the Bitwise Trie for Maximum XOR prioritize the opposite bit (1 - bit) at each step?
options: Because XOR of opposite bits (0 ^ 1 or 1 ^ 0) produces a 1 bit, maximizing the resulting number
quickCheck.explanation: The XOR operation produces 1 when bits differ; choosing the opposite bit at high bit positions maximizes the numeric result.

topics.title: Word Search II: Backtracking on 2D Board with Trie (LeetCode Hard)
explanation: Problem: Given an $M \times N$ board of characters and a list of words, find all words on the board (adjacent letters, no reusing cells).
Naive DFS per word searches board $K$ times: $O(K \times M \times N \times 4^L)$ -> Time Limit Exceeded.
Trie Optimization: Build a Trie of ALL words once.
Run ONE single DFS from each board cell matching against the Trie:
- If current board prefix is not in Trie: prune immediately (stops millions of dead search paths!).
- When a Trie node has `word`: record word into output, and set `node.word = None` to prevent duplicate answers.
keyRules: Store word string directly at terminal Trie node to avoid reconstructing strings during DFS.
Prune child nodes after words are matched to accelerate subsequent searches.

codeSnippet.title: Word Search II with Trie and Board Backtracking
codeSnippet.description: Trie-guided DFS pruning on 2D character matrix

topics.pitfall: Using a visited set `(r, c)` instead of mutating board `board[r][c] = "#"` in place: hash set operations add massive overhead in tight 2D DFS loops.

quickCheck.question: Why is a Trie vastly superior to standard Word Search for multiple words?
options: Tries use less memory than arrays
The Trie allows the board DFS to search for ALL words simultaneously, pruning invalid prefixes in O(1) before recursing further
quickCheck.explanation: Instead of re-searching the board for each of the K words, a single board traversal explores valid prefixes for all K words simultaneously.

topics.title: Memory Footprint Optimization in Tries: Radix Trees (Compressed Tries)
explanation: A standard Trie has high memory consumption because every single character allocates a `TrieNode`.
If a word like `"internationalization"` has no branching children, allocating 20 separate nodes is wasteful.
**Radix Tree (Patricia Trie)**: Compresses non-branching chains into a single edge containing the entire substring (e.g. edge `"internation"`).
Used in Linux IP routing tables and Git commit hash indexing, reducing node count by up to 80%.
keyRules: Radix trees merge nodes with a single child into single multi-character edges.
Drastically reduces pointer memory overhead.

codeSnippet.title: Radix Tree Edge Compression Concept
codeSnippet.description: Compressed prefix nodes for memory reduction
codeSnippet.code:
# Standard Trie for "test", "team":
# root -> 't' -> 'e' -> ('s' -> 't', 'a' -> 'm')

# Compressed Radix Tree:
# root -> "te" -> ("st", "am")
# Saves 2 intermediate node allocations!

topics.pitfall: Implementing a Radix Tree when strings share only single characters: compression is beneficial only when long non-branching common substrings exist.

quickCheck.question: What optimization does a Radix Tree (Compressed Trie) perform compared to a standard Trie?
options: It compresses single-child node chains into single edges containing multi-character substrings
quickCheck.explanation: Radix trees eliminate redundant single-child intermediate nodes by merging non-branching paths into multi-character edge labels.

topics.title: Trie Autocomplete and Suggestion Engines
explanation: How do search bars (Google, Amazon) display autocomplete suggestions as you type?
1. Navigate down the Trie matching the user's typed `prefix`.
2. Once at the prefix terminal node, perform a DFS to collect all leaf words in that subtree.
3. Production optimization: Store the Top-5 most frequent words directly at each TrieNode! This eliminates the subtree DFS entirely, delivering $O(L)$ instant autocomplete suggestions!
keyRules: Store precomputed top suggestions directly on nodes for instant O(L) response.
Update suggestion lists during word insertion.

codeSnippet.title: Instant Autocomplete Suggestion Trie
codeSnippet.description: Caching top suggestions on prefix nodes in O(L)

topics.pitfall: Running an unbounded DFS on every keystroke: on large dictionaries, finding all words under a common prefix like "a" visits millions of nodes, lagging the UI.

quickCheck.question: How do production search engines achieve sub-millisecond autocomplete suggestions using Tries?
options: By querying a remote SQL database
By precomputing and caching the top-K highest-ranked words directly at each prefix Trie node during indexing
By running binary search on all words
quickCheck.explanation: Caching the top suggestions directly inside each node allows queries to read the answer in O(1) immediately upon reaching the prefix node.

topics.title: Hierarchical Structures Diagnostic Guide
explanation: How to choose between Trees, BSTs, Heaps, and Tries:
- Need hierarchical parent-child relationships and subtree expressions? -> Binary Tree (DFS/BFS).
- Need dynamic ordered collection with $O(\log N)$ search, insert, min/max, predecessor/successor? -> Balanced BST (AVL/Red-Black).
- Need continuous access to the extreme element (min or max) with $O(1)$ peek and $O(\log N)$ updates? -> Binary Heap (Priority Queue).
- Need prefix matching, string dictionary search, autocomplete, or bitwise XOR? -> Trie (Prefix Tree).
keyRules: Heaps do NOT support fast arbitrary search: searching a heap is O(N). Use a BST if you need to search for arbitrary keys.
Tries are specialized for strings and bitwise integers.

codeSnippet.title: Hierarchical Selector Guide
codeSnippet.description: Automated requirement-to-structure selector

topics.pitfall: Attempting to use a Heap when you need to search for arbitrary elements: heaps only organize the root min or max; finding an arbitrary key in a heap requires an O(N) scan.

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity to search for an arbitrary element in a standard Binary Min-Heap of size N?
quickCheck.explanation: Heaps only guarantee ordering between parents and children (not left vs right siblings), so searching for an arbitrary key requires checking all N elements in O(N) time.

topics.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU / Union-Find) Foundations
explanation: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) maintains a collection of disjoint sets partitioned across elements $0$ to $N - 1$.
Two core operations:
- `find(x)`: Returns the canonical representative (root) of the set containing $x$.
- `union(x, y)`: Merges the set containing $x$ with the set containing $y$.
DSU is represented as an inverted tree where each node points to its parent: `parent[i] = i` initially.
Without optimizations, trees can degenerate to chains of height $N$, making operations $O(N)$.
keyRules: parent array initializes to parent[i] = i.
find(x) traverses parent pointers to root.

codeSnippet.title: Naive DSU Implementation
codeSnippet.description: Parent-pointer tree representation

topics.pitfall: Using naive DSU without optimizations: chaining makes `find()` run in O(N) time, failing graph connectivity algorithms.

quickCheck.question: What does the find(x) operation return in Disjoint Set Union?
options: The canonical representative (root) of the set containing x
The number of elements in the set
quickCheck.explanation: find(x) traverses upward through parent pointers until it reaches the root node that uniquely represents that connected component.

topics.title: DSU Optimization: Path Compression & Union by Rank
explanation: Two optimizations compress DSU from $O(N)$ to nearly $O(1)$ amortized time:
1. **Path Compression**: During `find(x)`, make every node along the path point DIRECTLY to the root: `parent[x] = find(parent[x])`. Flattens tree to height 1!
2. **Union by Rank (or Size)**: Always attach the shorter tree under the root of the taller tree to minimize height growth.
Together, operations run in $O(\alpha(N))$ time, where $\alpha$ is the Inverse Ackermann Function ($\alpha(N) < 5$ for all practical universe inputs, effectively $O(1)$!).
keyRules: Path compression: parent[x] = find(parent[x]).
Union by rank attaches smaller tree under larger tree root.
Amortized runtime is O(alpha(N)) ~ O(1).

codeSnippet.title: Optimal DSU with Path Compression and Rank
codeSnippet.description: Inverse Ackermann near-constant time DSU
codeSnippet.code:
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n
        self.count = n # connected components count
        
    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        if self.parent[x] != x:
            # Path compression: points directly to root!
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])
        return self.parent[x]
        
    def union(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        root_x = self.find(x)
        root_y = self.find(y)
        if root_x == root_y:
            return False # Already in same set!
            
        # Union by rank
        if self.rank[root_x] < self.rank[root_y]:
            self.parent[root_x] = root_y
        elif self.rank[root_x] > self.rank[root_y]:
            self.parent[root_y] = root_x
        else:
            self.parent[root_y] = root_x
            self.rank[root_x] += 1
            
        self.count -= 1
        return True

dsu = DSU(5)
dsu.union(0, 1)
dsu.union(1, 2)
print("Are 0 and 2 connected?", dsu.find(0) == dsu.find(2)) # True
print("Are 0 and 3 connected?", dsu.find(0) == dsu.find(3)) # False
print("Connected components:", dsu.count)                 # 3

topics.pitfall: Omitting path compression: union by rank alone gives O(log N). Path compression alone gives O(log N). ONLY BOTH TOGETHER achieve O(alpha(N)) ~ O(1).

quickCheck.question: What is the time complexity of DSU operations when combining both Path Compression and Union by Rank?
quickCheck.explanation: The combination of path compression and union by rank guarantees that any sequence of M operations takes O(M * alpha(N)) time, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function (<= 4 in practice).

topics.title: Redundant Connection: Cycle Detection with DSU
explanation: Problem: Given an undirected graph starting as a tree with $N$ nodes plus ONE additional edge that creates a cycle, find and return that redundant edge.
DSU Cycle Detection Algorithm:
1. Initialize DSU with $N + 1$ elements.
2. For each edge `(u, v)`:
- If `find(u) == find(v)`: both nodes are ALREADY connected in the same component! Adding this edge creates a cycle. Return `[u, v]` immediately!
- Else: `union(u, v)` to connect them.
Runs in $O(N \times \alpha(N)) \approx O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ space.
keyRules: An edge between two nodes already sharing the same root creates a cycle.
O(N) single-pass cycle detection.

codeSnippet.title: Redundant Connection Cycle Detection
codeSnippet.description: DSU edge inspection finding cycle-creating edge in O(N)

topics.pitfall: Using DFS/BFS for every edge: running DFS to check connectivity for each edge takes O(N^2), whereas DSU achieves near-instant O(N).

quickCheck.question: How does DSU determine that an edge (u, v) creates a cycle?
options: If find(u) == find(v) before union is called
If u and v are odd
quickCheck.explanation: If find(u) == find(v), a path already exists between u and v; adding another direct edge between them forms a cycle.

topics.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
explanation: Problem: Given $N$ nodes labeled $0$ to $N-1$ and a list of undirected edges, find the total number of connected components.
DSU Solution:
- Initialize `dsu = DSU(n)`. Component count starts at $N$.
- For each edge `(u, v)`: call `dsu.union(u, v)`. If union succeeds (merging two previously separate components), decrement component count by 1.
- Final answer is `dsu.count`!
Runs in $O(N + E \cdot \alpha(N))$ time.
keyRules: Every successful union decreases connected components by 1.
Final component count is n - successful_unions.

codeSnippet.description: Tracking component count decrement on union

topics.pitfall: Counting unique values in `dsu.parent` array: parent pointers are not fully flattened until `find()` is called on every element! Use `dsu.count` or call `len(set(dsu.find(i) for i in range(n)))`.

quickCheck.question: Why is `len(set(dsu.parent))` an unreliable way to count connected components?
options: Because some nodes may still point to intermediate ancestors rather than the ultimate root if find() was not called on them
quickCheck.explanation: Path compression flattens paths only when find() is invoked; inspecting dsu.parent directly includes uncompressed intermediate parent references.

Algorithmic Pipeline:

2. Map each email to its owner name.
3. For each account, union all its emails together with its first email in a DSU.
4. Group emails by their canonical DSU root: `groups[dsu.find(email_id)].append(email)`.
5. Sort emails and format output `[name, sorted_emails...]`.
keyRules: Map emails to integer IDs for fast DSU manipulation.
Union all emails belonging to the same account.

They have the same number of emails
They were created on the same day

topics.title: Memory & Cache Layout of Pointer Trees vs Binary Heaps
explanation: Compare hardware performance between Tree structures:
- **Binary Search Trees & Tries**: Node-based pointer structures. Each node requires independent heap allocation. Visiting nodes forces pointer dereferencing, causing frequent CPU L1/L2 cache misses.
- **Binary Heaps**: Contiguous array layout. Elements are stored packed in RAM. Visiting child indices `2i + 1` takes advantage of CPU prefetch buffers.
Whenever priority operations are needed, prefer array heaps over tree-based priority queues.
keyRules: Array heaps have zero pointer overhead and superior cache locality.
Trie nodes can be flattened into array tables for production engines.

codeSnippet.title: Cache Locality Demonstration
codeSnippet.description: Array sequential memory vs heap pointer hops
codeSnippet.code:
# Memory Layout Comparison:

quickCheck.explanation: Contiguous array storage allows modern CPUs to fetch 64-byte cache lines that hold multiple adjacent heap elements simultaneously.

questions.question: Why does Floyd's Heapify algorithm construct a binary heap from an unsorted array in O(N) linear time instead of O(N log N)?
options: Because the vast majority of nodes are at or near the leaf levels where sift-down height is 0 or 1, and the mathematical summation converges to O(N)
Because it runs on multiple CPU cores simultaneously
Because heaps do not require sorting
questions.explanation: In a complete binary tree, half the nodes are leaves (height 0), a quarter have height 1, an eighth have height 2, etc. The sum sum(h / 2^h) converges to a constant, making total work O(N).

questions.question: What invariant is required for Inorder traversal to output values in strictly ascending sorted order?
options: The tree must be a complete binary tree
The tree must be a valid Binary Search Tree (BST)
The tree must be an AVL tree
The tree must be a Max-Heap
questions.explanation: In a Binary Search Tree, all left subtree values are smaller and all right subtree values are larger; Left-Root-Right traversal naturally sorts the values.

questions.question: In an AVL Tree, what sequence of rotations is required to rebalance a Left-Right (LR) dogleg imbalance?
options: A single Right Rotation on the parent
Left Rotate the left child, then Right Rotate the unbalanced parent node
A single Left Rotation on the parent
questions.explanation: Left-rotating the left child straightens the dogleg into a Left-Left line, which is then balanced by right-rotating the parent node.

questions.question: How does the Dual-Heap MedianFinder maintain the median of a streaming data source in O(1) retrieval time?
options: By sorting the array on every insertion
By balancing a Max-Heap for the lower half of values and a Min-Heap for the upper half, so the median is always at the heap roots
By storing values in a circular deque
questions.explanation: Dividing elements into a lower-half max-heap and an upper-half min-heap places the median elements directly at index 0 of the heaps for instant O(1) access.

questions.question: What combined optimizations allow Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) to achieve O(alpha(N)) ~ O(1) amortized time per operation?
options: Path Compression (pointing nodes directly to root during find) and Union by Rank (attaching shorter tree under taller tree)
questions.explanation: Combining path compression (flattening paths during find) with union by rank (minimizing tree height growth) bounds operations to the inverse Ackermann function O(alpha(N)).
